Under his influence, I stopped trying to turn up the volume, accepted being an introvert and held him in mind whenever anyone equated quietness with dullness. Fast-forward 35 years – to a time when influencers squeal and preen, flogging every last grain of themselves to the attention economy – and the Roses guitarist seems a few degrees cooler for existing on his own terms, leaving something to the imagination, and treating Jonathan Ross with chilly disdain. Perhaps we could all stand to be a little more Squire?

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.title: Vance front and center in Republican midterms push – is this a dry run for a White House bid?
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.author: Robert Tait
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.text:
Vice-president’s visibility has risen as Trump’s popularity wanes, but path to inherit Maga throne is more complicated than it may seem

A day after JD Vance suggested Donald Trump would endorse him if he runs for president, the vice-president shifted awkwardly in the Oval Office as his boss was asked about the remark.

“He’s a very talented person, and he’s a very good person,” Trump said of the man standing behind him, with a forced smile this week. “But we’ve literally – I don’t think we’ve ever talked about,” the president claimed, leaving the assertion unconfirmed.

As the campaign for the congressional midterms has intensified, the vice-president’s visibility has risen. If Trump and Vance truly have yet to discuss his presidential prospects, they are firmly in the minority in Washington.

While many aspects of this political era remain extraordinary, the core question hanging over Vance is one that has been asked for decades: is the vice-presidency a platform, or a poisoned chalice, for those who dare to dream of higher office?

Having spent only two years as a US senator before Trump tapped him in 2024 as his running mate, Vance has hit the campaign trail in recent weeks like a seasoned veteran – making stump speeches on behalf of Republican candidates as the party struggles to retain its grip on the US Senate and House of Representatives amid Trump’s plunging approval ratings.

He has held rallies in states such as Iowa, Florida, Texas, Alaska, Georgia, Michigan and his native Ohio in a criss-crossing odyssey that compares to that of Trump, who has told voters to behave as though he were on the ballot.

With secretary of state Marco Rubio – widely seen as his main rival for the next Republican nomination – focused on fighting the fires sparked by Trump’s global agenda, analysts believe Vance’s campaigning roadshow is intended as a dry run for a 2028 presidential bid. Each stop enables him to build contacts and goodwill, which he can call on in the likely event of him seeking the nomination in less than two years’ time.

Matthew Dallek, a political historian at George Washington University, said Vance was trying to “build up chits” aimed at making Trump’s Make America Great Again (Maga) movement “remember that he was a good soldier”.

“He is trying to do what a lot of smart vice-presidents have done throughout history, and that’s to earn some credit out there with state and and congressional candidates,” said Rick Wilson, a former Republican strategist who now runs the anti-Trump Lincoln Project, “so that when he kicks up a campaign machine in two years, people owe him something”.

Time and again over the past two years Vance has slipped into “explainer-in-chief” mode, providing a more palatable narrative in the wake of Trump’s more extreme statements, impulses or policy decisions. Critics have branded the practice as “sane-washing”, whereby the verbally dextrous vice-president tries to use his facile language skills to normalize otherwise outlandish utterances or actions.

In recent months, Vance – after publishing a book on his conversion to Catholicism – has rationalized a meme posted by Trump on his Truth Social platform that seemed to depict him as Jesus Christ. He also tried to deny, or at least reinterpret, Trump’s words when he told journalists that he did not think about Americans’ financial situation in conducting the war with Iran.

And just last weekend, he defended the president against charges of corruption in a CBS town hall event, when told that many voters were concerned that Trump was making money from cryptocurrency. “You can make all kinds of criticisms of our policies and decisions, but I’ve not once seen evidence that Donald Trump has enriched himself,” Vance replied. (Trump’s personal fortune has surged from $2.3bn in 2024 to $6.5bn this year, according to Forbes.)

His slavishly supportive comments have naturally been welcomed by Trump, but they also highlight the problems Vance may face in trying to become the president’s heir as head of the Maga movement. While unstinting loyalty is the coin of the realm in the Trump-dominated Republicans, the president’s vice-like grip on the party presents a fundamental challenge to anyone hoping to step out from his shadow and assert an independent persona aimed at wooing the base.

The fate of Trump’s first vice-president, Mike Pence – who had to be evacuated to an underground shelter in the US Capitol on 6 January 2021, as pro-Trump rioters called for his execution following his refusal to overturn the 2020 presidential election result – serves as a salutary warning of the high price that autonomy may exact.

“Vance has two choices,” argued Kurt Bardella, a former Republican congressional staffer who left the party in 2017. “Either ride Trump all the way to the island of irrelevancy, or break with him and incur his wrath.”

“Neither are great options,” he added. “The political reality is that anyone who is tethered to Trump will face an electoral backlash. Trump will continue to erode democratic norms as his grip on power wanes.

“That will force people like Vance into untenable positions that they have proven unable to navigate. They’ll have to either double down on the crazy or break up with him and alienate the primary base he needs to win the nomination.”

Even if Vance were to attempt a clean break after securing the Republican nomination, the historical portents at not encouraging.

Al Gore attempted to put clear blue water between himself and Bill Clinton after becoming the Democrat nominee in 2000. “I stand here as my own man,” he told the party’s convention, in a bid to avoid an electoral backlash over the then president’s impeachment over his affair with Monica Lewinsky, a White House intern.

In the event, Gore lost the election to George W Bush – losing his own state of Tennessee, where he had been a US senator – despite excluding Clinton from the campaign trail.

“The Gore example is useful because it’s someone who tried to distance himself, didn’t do so very successfully – and he was doing so from a pretty popular president,” said Dallek of George Washington University. “When you’re vice-president, you can only get so much distance from the president, and if you try to distance yourself, you’re going to antagonize the people who supported the president, and create the impression that you’re not just disloyal, but two-faced.”

Vance, therefore, has limited options in how to pitch himself for the presidency.

“Even JD Vance doesn’t fully have a theory of the case yet of why he should be president,” said Wilson. “He is going to sort of play this out and say, ‘I’m going to see what the terrain looks like in mid-2027, then calibrate my message, my campaign and my personality to what I think will win.’

“But is not really something that works in the age of authenticity that we supposedly live in now. It’s harder for somebody to fake being anything anymore than it ever has been in politics.”

Underpinning such a wait-and-see approach is Vance’s reputation as a “shape-shifter”, capable of jettisoning previously held principles. Years before becoming a Trump supporter, he declared himself a “never Trumper”. He labelled Trump “cultural heroin” and voiced fears he could be “America’s Hitler” before forming an alliance with him after first presidency ended in 2021.

Vance’s self-anointed role as Trump’s “explainer-in-chief” positions him to sell himself as “all the things you love about Donald Trump without the craziness and the chaos”, Bardella suggested.

But Vance’s vitriolic personal attacks on Democratic candidates in the midterms, such as the Kansas Senate candidate, Adam Hamilton, and James Talarico, who is in a cliffhanger race with the Trump-endorsed Republican Ken Paxton for the Texas Senate race, could prefigure another weapon a Vance presidential campaign might use : demonizing opponents.

“One of the previews that we’ve had is that he is going to define the Democratic party as this radical leftwing communistic anti-American threat to the future of the country,” said Dallek.

Vance will need to sell himself to two audiences, according to Joe Walsh, a former Republican congressman who is now a Democrat: Trump’s Maga support base, and the broader electorate after winning the nomination.

“He cannot sell himself to the second audience if he doesn’t make the sale with the first audience, and that means sticking to Trump and going full Maga.”

But so well-honed has Vance’s rightwing identity become, argued Walsh, that expressing views that would appeal to Trump supporters would require little simulation.

“I don’t know what he actually believes, but he’s taken on a lot of these Maga beliefs,” he said. “JD Vance is more pro-Putin than people realize – more pro-Russia, more anti-Ukraine. JD Vance is very skeptical of Israel. Vance really does have a lot of the Maga beliefs.”

What may stymie his presidential aspirations, some observers believe, is not ideology but personality.

After being repeatedly mocked for his awkward persona on the campaign trail during the 2024 presidential election, Vance remains a grating presence on the stump, with attempts at humor often falling flat.

The trait appeared to be on display last week in the town of Tyler in Texas when a male supporter shouted: “I love you.”

“I love you too, sir. In a totally platonic way, to be clear. I’m the vice-president, not James Talarico,” he said, referring to the Democratic Senate candidate, whose sexuality Vance and other Republicans have repeatedly questioned, without evidence or obvious cause.

Tara Setmayer, a former Republican communications director on Capitol Hill, said Vance’s inability to project authenticity threatened his presumed frontrunner status. “JD Vance comes across as so manufactured. There’s nothing authentic about him, and people see right through it,” she said. “You can see that coming across when he goes out there and tells these jokes or tries to be funny and it lands like a lead balloon, because he’s not inherently secure with himself.

“As much as JD Vance thinks he is the Maga heir apparent, he’s not. There’s a lot of consternation about him. He’s not completely won the Maga base by any means.”

Wilson agrees that Vance was seen as an unsatisfactory substitute by many diehard Trump supporters, and said his ascension to the Republican nomination was not assured. “JD Vance is not Donald Trump, and he will never be,” he said. “The modern voter out there in the world is not interested in Diet Trump. They want the full experience.

“Vance is more facile than Trump. He can change his personality to adjust to the room. Trump, for all of his evils and corruption and craziness, is the genuine article. He didn’t change everything he believed overnight to achieve something political. He’s always been the asshole that he is. Vance is the asshole that you want him to be.”

The biggest encumbrance of all, argued Dallek, might be the tendency of the vice-presidency to become a poisoned chalice. Almost four decades have passed since the last serving vice-president won election as president.

“The vice-presidency historically was seen as a terrible job – very little power, and not that much of a stepping stone,” he said. “It’s tough to begin with for a vice-president to win essentially a third term, and there’s a reason why it’s only happened once in modern times [with George HW Bush in 1988].

“It’s not the best springboard for the presidency at any time, and especially when Americans hate the establishment, think Washington is corrupt, and distrust people in positions of power.

“JD Vance is still very much subject to the laws of vice-presidential politics – and in that, I think he is similar to a lot of his predecessors.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Surging turnout, with Democrats voting more: key takeaways from early voting data
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Shrai Popat and Lucy Campbell
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
With just 11 days until the US midterm elections, Democrats need a net gain of four seats to reclaim Congress

With just 11 days until the US midterm elections, early voting data is rolling in nationwide. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to reclaim the majority in each chamber of Congress. Here is where the numbers stand as of Friday:

As of Friday afternoon, more than 23 million Americans had already voted in person or by mail. Among the key battleground states, Michigan and Ohio have each passed 900,000 ballots cast, while Georgia has recorded almost 1.5m early votes, North Carolina more than 1.2m, Florida almost 2.2m and Texas more than 2.8m, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab, as of 23 October.

While midterms typically favor the party out of power, turnout this year is being driven in part by widespread public frustration over crucial issues including Donald Trump’s handling of the economy, the cost-of-living crisis and his deeply unpopular war on Iran. The backlash – reflected in the president’s record-low approval ratings – have left Republicans fighting hard to defend seats in places where Trump won by wide margins just two years ago.

Early voting is soaring compared with the last midterms in many of the battleground states, which will decide control of the Senate.

In Georgia, early votes already represent more than 40% of the total turnout from the 2022 midterms. Texas is at 35% and North Carolina 33%, while Florida is at 27%. Michigan and Ohio are recording similarly high paces.

Registered Democrats account for 45% of early ballots cast, compared with 30% from Republicans (tracking returned ballots, not candidate selection). The party gap is particularly pronounced in North Carolina, Kansas and Iowa – all states that traditionally favor Republicans.

While Republicans have historically preferred to vote on election day, strategists worry this widened margin signals a “red undertow” – GOP voters staying home due to frustration over high gas prices, the conflict in Iran and sweeping tariffs.

At the same time, Democrats have been energized, with Trump’s growing unpopularity and voter frustration over affordability, which they believe has given them opportunities to flip seats they haven’t won in decades.

More than 57m mail-in ballots have been requested or sent nationally – greater than the 52m requested in 2022 – according to NBC News, using data from TargetSmart. The University of Florida’s Election Lab has the figure for mail-in ballots requested at more than 59m.

Despite executive orders from the Trump administration attempting to restrict mail-in voting, which the supreme court struck down in September, voters continue to utilize the process at pre-pandemic rates.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: ‘Bolso shows all signs of fascism’: the journalist who predicted Brazil’s future – and paid the ultimate price
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Jonathan Watts
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Dom Phillips warned that Jair Bolsonaro would make life more dangerous for reporters and the Amazon rainforest, and that his sons were even more extreme

“Bolso shows all signs of fascism, as do his supporters,” the murdered British journalist Dom Phillips told me before his death. “His sons are all more extreme if anything.”

These words were written in 2018 by the Guardian contributor shortly before the election of the far-right former army captain Jair Bolsonaro as president of Brazil – a prospect that Dom viewed with dread.

As he predicted back then, this would lead to more mortalities, more destruction of the Amazon rainforest and more danger for journalists. His own life and death were to prove the prescience of this foresight.

Dom was killed four years ago alongside the Brazilian indigenous expert Bruno Pereira, but his views feel alarmingly relevant once more as Brazil braces for a presidential runoff this Sunday in which a member of the far-right Bolsonaro clan is once more a favourite to win – despite all the dangers that poses to the environment and those who seek to protect it.

Polls suggest Flávio Bolsonaro – the son of Jair Bolsonaro – is narrowly ahead of the Workers party incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Although the difference between them is within the margin of error and Lula appears to have gained momentum, the possibility of another Bolsonaro administration is likely to fill any friends of Dom and Bruno with alarm.

Dom was no diehard political leftist. In an earlier election, he shocked me by expressing support for the centre-right challenger Aécio Neves because he felt the then Workers party administration had become too entangled in corruption. But while Dom eschewed ideology, he had clear ideas about the importance of sound, considerate government in the interests of people and the planet.

He saw the Bolsonaro family as a menace to both. Looking back through our exchanges of WhatsApp messages, I am struck by the prescience of his observations.

Some may be inclined to normalise Flávio as just another candidate, or to assume that all politicians are as bad as each other. That was certainly not how Dom saw things – and he came to pay the ultimate price for his efforts to address those concerns.

“I don’t think I have ever been so negative about Brazil’s future. Spent a week in Manaus, everyone seemed to be voting for Bolsonaro,” he wrote ahead of the first-round vote in 2018. “ If he wins, what would it be like living here? It’s like a ‘carte blanche’ to attack anyone his mob disagrees with.”

Two weeks later, he observed the creeping hostility towards the media at a Bolsonaro press conference, which he said was packed with rightwing supporters who loudly booed a journalist that they considered unfriendly.

This followed a physical attack on the organiser of an anti-Bolsonaro women’s group. “Chilling times here,” he wrote on 12 October of that year.

“This is a very dark and worrying period and it is only going to get worse. My sense if [sic] that it is also going to become more dangerous for journalists.”

He detailed the changes he was already seeing – the proliferation of lies, a hardening of discourse online and a rising sense that violence was acceptable. He predicted more people would die as a result of Bolsonaro’s policies, and the wider environment would also pay a heavy price.

Over the following years, Dom’s reports for the Guardian confirmed his worst fears. Bolsonaro’s mismanaged response to the Covid crisis contributed to more than 704,000 deaths – the second highest toll in the world after the US.

His four years in power saw the highest level of Amazon deforestation of any presidential terms. Orwellian misinformation campaignsincluded efforts to blame environmental groups for forest fires and to boast – contrary to all the evidence – that his government was saving the Amazon.

In August 2019, Dom told me these claims were “staggering even by Bolsonaro standards, especially given Flávio Bolsonaro’s bill to get rid of legal reserves”, the latter a reference to a proposal by the then president’s son – and now presidential candidate – to remove one of the greatest protections for the rainforest.

Dom also came under social media attack after he politely asked the president about Amazon deforestation at a press conference. Bolsonaro snapped back, “the Amazon is Brazil’s, not yours, OK?” – a reply that was instantly spread across networks to suggest the nationalist had bested the foreigner.

Dom felt he had been set up. “The smile doesn’t last for long,” he observed. “Wonder how much of the Amazon will be gone by the end of Bolsonaro’s first term?”

That answer to that question would be 45,000 sq km (17,400 sq miles) over Bolsonaro’s 2019-2022 period in office, roughly equivalent to the loss of more than a million trees a day, and 59.5% higher than the previous four years.

Dom never got to report on that. He too was cut down, murdered alongside Bruno on 5 May 2022 close to the Javari Valley indigenous territory while he was researching a book titled How to Save the Amazon.

The man who confessed to their killing was a fisher named Amarildo da Costa de Oliveira, who is now on trial. He apparently resented Bruno’s efforts to prevent him invading the indigenous territory, incursions that were illegal but encouraged by the president’s weakening of protections, rhetoric against environmental groups and tacit acceptance of lawlessness. As Dom had foreseen, Bolsonaro had made life more dangerous for journalists and the forest.

Jair Bolsonaro lost office later that year and was then convicted for attempting a military coup to overturn the election results. Dom had also anticipated this: “He is a criminal and I sincerely hope one day I see him being arrested by those federal police guys in the balaclavas in black,” he wrote in 2021.

I am sure Dom would have been cheered by last week’s government announcement of record low deforestation in the Amazon and the neighbouring Cerrado savanna thanks to strong enforcement during Lula’s current four-year term.

Such gains look precarious now that one of Bolsonaro’s “more extreme” sons is frontrunner in the presidential runoff and has promised, if he wins, to free his father and give him any job of his choice in the government.

Is there time for Lula to turn this around? How much worse could a second Bolsonaro family administration be? How much life – people, trees and other species – will die if they return to power?

https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/ng-.title: My mother donated her body to science. I really wasn’t prepared for what came next
https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/ng-.author: Meaghan O'Connell
https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/ng-.text:
The process included a gala featuring medical students doing aerial yoga and singing Taylor Swift to donors’ families. In some way, it was absolutely perfect

When my mother, Erin O’Connell, was diagnosed with a rare and aggressive cancer in late 2022, one of her first thoughts was: “What will I do if I can’t work?”

At the time, she was 62 years old and working as a physical therapist in Portland, Oregon, where she had recently moved to live closer to me and my family. Reluctantly, she filed for short-term disability from her job and paused her training to become a volunteer search and rescue EMT.

My mom was 40 when she started physical therapy school. I was already a teenager. Despite her newfound stress, I remember how deeply it affected me to watch her fall in love with her work. The year she took anatomy lab she told my sister and me – and anyone who would listen – that dissecting a real human body was the coolest thing she had ever gotten to do, and when she died, she wanted to donate her body to science, too.

I spent so much of my childhood wanting nothing more than my mother’s hard-earned approval, and here she was, utterly devoted to a dead body. On some level, I was jealous of that cadaver.

Now here I was, 25 years later, with my mom’s illness progressing, printing out the paperwork from the nearest med school: “Enrollment Form To Bequeath a Body On Behalf of an Individual”. And all I could think was how jealous I would be of the students who would dissect my mother – who would get to do what I never could, crack her open and peek inside.

This paperwork, though, was its own form of clarity. My mom was going to die, too young and against her will, but we had a plan – an easy, free, meaningful one at that.

Of course, the reality ended up being more complicated and more absurd than I imagined.

After her death, my mom’s body was transported to Oregon Health & Science University (OHSU), just across the river from where we had both lived in Portland.

I worried that, in my grief, I might drive to campus to find out where she was. Would I be tempted to wander the halls, looking for her? Better not to dwell on it, I decided. Instead, I imagined she had been shipped elsewhere, used for something vaguely embarrassing like rectal science or dentistry.

Every year, roughly 25,000 Americans sign up to donate their bodies to science after death. But demand far outstrips supply. According to Tamara Ostervoss, director of OHSU’s body donation program, “it remains an unpopular choice,” partly because so few people even know it’s an option. In Oregon, she told me, only about 1% of people choose to donate their bodies.

For my mom, the registration process was simple: a two-page consent form, signed in front of two witnesses. My mom agreed that her family would not profit from the donation or any discoveries that resulted from it, and that we would have no say in how her body was used. She chose to have her remains cremated and mailed back to us. Eighteen months later, they arrived in a red, white and blue US Postal Service box marked “HUMAN REMAINS”, with an illustration of an urn on the side.

By the time I spoke to Ostervoss, the remains were safely in my closet – and I had a darkly funny story about my awkward visit to the post office to prove it.

Still, talking to the woman who had overseen my mom’s donation was emotionally fraught. As Ostervoss likes to say, your life dictates how you go on to teach others. Thanks to the progression of her cancer, my mom was missing so many internal organs by the end that I joked she would have given some poor anatomy student a pretty limited education.

It’s a credit to Ostervoss’s professional, respectful demeanor that she didn’t laugh so much as smile warmly, with pity in her eyes.

I didn’t tell her that, when my mom was still alive, I had asked her how she would feel if she ended up sold to one of those Bodies exhibits from China. Would my kids recognize her without her skin on?

You can decide what happens to your body after you die, if you’re willing to plan ahead. But that doesn’t necessarily mean that, once you’re no longer there to insist, your family will follow through with your plans.

If your loved ones are firmly opposed to body donation, they can simply call a funeral home instead. Which is why, if you’re considering donating your body to science, it’s a conversation worth having while you’re still alive.

Most families, though, fall somewhere in the squeamish-but-accepting middle. “We’ve had families where they might not choose it for themselves, but they really want to honor and support their loved ones’ wishes,” Ostervoss said. “So they’re more along the lines of, “I don’t want to hear anything about it, I don’t want to know about it. I just want to support my mom.”

For me, the mild unease of never knowing exactly what happened to my mom’s corpse at the university was peanuts compared with the prospect of being upsold a coffin by a funeral director while I waded through grief. According to the National Funeral Directors Association, the average cost of burial in our home state of Oregon is $7,895 and the average cost of cremation is $5,812 – numbers that don’t even include a funeral or memorial service.

With body donation, you can always do a memorial later, but in the meantime there are no grief-stricken decisions about embalming or viewings. No deciding what goes on the gravestone, no grave. What does happen is a brief phone screening (in our case, by a hospice nurse), followed by a brief, in-person physical assessment. Then, voilà, off my mom went to fulfill her destiny as, in the language of the body program, someone’s first patient.

The reality is that about 25% of registered donors don’t meet the eligibility requirements at the time of death, per Ostervoss’ estimate. “It’s like medical school,” she said, “Not everyone gets in.”

A common disqualifier is high or low body weight, and privately my sister and I feared my mom had lost too much to be accepted. When she was, I found myself literally jumping up in the air to cheer. “She passed her final test!” I wrote to her sibling group chat, triumphantly. “PTL!” her sister wrote back. Praise the Lord!

Was it odd to feel jubilant on the same day I watched my mother take her final breath? Absolutely, but it was also a gift. It really did feel like her version of a med school acceptance, I told Ostervoss.

Those 150 bodies who do “get in” are able to go on to teach approximately 5,000 learners across the state of Oregon, encompassing not just the first-year medical students you might think of, but surgical residents and practicing doctors, dentists and other healthcare workers.

For students, the benefits of learning about human anatomy and practicing procedures on the real thing, with no risk of hurting them, are intuitive and obvious – the difference between a flight simulator and piloting an airplane. Think of all the variation in vasculature and body size. In reality, no surgeon would see the same internal organs twice. It’s the kind of thing that can’t be replicated, not even with advanced 3D models with haptic feedback.

The emotional side of the student experience is another story. Facing your cadaver for the first time as a new med student has always been a rite of passage, but as western life expectancy increases and our end-of-life rituals become more and more sanitized, anatomy lab is more and more often students’ first encounter with a dead person.

Historically, med school programs have dealt with this by cultivating what the writer Mary Roach calls “a sort of sink or swim mentality about dealing with death”, a kind of future doctor hazing ritual that encouraged future providers to desensitize themselves.

Roach talked to the director of the medical anatomy program at Vanderbilt University, Art Dalley, who says that, “There was a time not all that long ago when students were taught to be insensitive, as a coping mechanism.” In the past, she writes: “Humor – at the cadaver’s expense – was tolerated, condoned, even.”

Not so in our current era. Instead, I received an invitation to a gala in the mail.

At OHSU, the anatomy class culminates in what Ostervoss calls, “the body ceremony”, a 25-year tradition where students plan a memorial to honor the donors and families who have made their education possible.

The service was created to honor the donors, but it’s also important emotionally for the students who are encouraged to have conversations with the families at the reception afterward.

After a year of almost willful dissociation on my part, it was a bizarre experience to be welcomed in. The invite explained that the service would include a slideshow of the 100 or so donors who had given their bodies that year. Students would show their gratitude through performances and reflections they had programmed themselves.

It sounded bizarre but earnest, like a talent show for death. I was thrilled.

Once we were in the auditorium, my eyes darted over to the section of nervous future doctors in new blazers and kitten heels. There was a kind of aura of promise about them, and I felt almost maternally proud. It was clear that families and students had a wild interest in each other and my heart raced as I scanned the rows, looking, as I imagine they did, for some glint of recognition.

I leaned over to whisper to my sister, a note of hope in my voice. “Do you think they’ll recognize us?”

“But maybe our height?” (My mother, like us, was around 5ft tall with shoes on.)

In accordance with HIPAA laws, no one would tell us who dissected whom. It was clear what a bizarre human exchange we had been party to, despite never having met. It had to be acknowledged, ritualized. Otherwise, it made no sense.

Not that a collective death talent show made a whole lot of sense either. As the students took the stage to share their talents – someone played Taylor Swift’s Bigger Than The Whole Sky, a member of the school of dentistry’s class of 2028 sang Sweet Creature by Harry Styles – I wanted to feel something like closure, but all I could muster was affectionate bemusement.

When two svelte near-adults took the stage in spandex (their leggings a respectful shade of black) and did what I can only assume was aerial yoga accompanied by Debussy, I had to avoid eye contact with my sister to avoid laughing. Still, as they balanced on each other’s shoulders and knees in midair, I had the urge to text my mom, to tell her how weird it was. I wished I believed she could see it. I know she would have thought it was cool.

When a chaplain got to the podium. “We know that your loved one’s participation in this program has probably complicated your grief, and prolonged it.” She talked about how when someone dies, there is a human need for closure, and we families probably hadn’t quite gotten it yet. They wanted to acknowledge the sacrifice we had made.

Truthfully, I hadn’t thought of it as a sacrifice at the time, more like a “get out of jail free” card, but I was beginning to understand. The chaplain’s words reminded me of the recurring dreams I had had after the two polite, somber men had taken my mom’s body away in a sprinter van. In real life, my sister and I had watched her take her last breath. When it happened it was so obvious, on an almost existential level, that to check her pulse would have been absurd. We didn’t need a nurse to come out. We declared her dead ourselves.

In sleep, though, my subconscious had its say. In recurring dreams, my mom would show up, back from the morgue and on her doorstep again, a little worse for the wear. She would push past us to get inside, clearly miffed we had sent her away prematurely.

After enough of these dreams, I came to understand why we bury our dead. Sure, no one wants the finality of loss but maybe the brain has a hard time moving on without it. It wasn’t until the chaplain alluded to this that that I realized that the lack of closure was exactly what I wanted. I didn’t want to move on. The ambiguity, the mystery even, meant the story of my mother wasn’t over yet.

Near the end of the ceremony, families were invited up to speak. When it was my turn, I gripped the podium, shaky-voiced but not crying. I remember knowing for certain what my mom would want me to say.

I told the students about my mom’s own experience in anatomy lab, all those years ago. The way our dining room had been overtaken by her schoolwork – the table strewn with flash cards and textbooks, colored-pencil anatomical drawings papering the walls. Those years we would find candy corn and York peppermint patty wrappers in the couch cushions – Mom’s study snack of choice.

She was more scatterbrained and short-tempered than ever, but I loved watching her find something she loved, something that was only hers. She learned a kind of devotion, then, an awe that would stay with her even in the darkest days of her illness.

A few weeks ago, after getting up the nerve to ask Ostervoss, I signed a HIPAA form and a media release to find out how my mom’s body came to be of use after she died. Five days later, a media relations specialist from the university forwarded me the answer in the body of an email. It read:

During her time with us, Erin played a crucial role in teaching spine anatomy, associated surgical techniques, and stereotactic and functional neurosurgery skills at OHSU. Through these educational experiences, neurosurgery and neurology trainees gained greater foundational knowledge that will inform their patient care throughout their careers.

After supporting these learners, she went on to teach in several orthopedic residency training courses.

In total, 121 learners directly benefited from your mother’s gift. Her legacy will live on through countless patients cared for by the healthcare professionals she helped educate.

Reading it, I felt the thrill of new information, of something happening in the world of my mother.

Then came the pang of loss, knowing that the one person who would truly appreciate this information was necessarily not available to receive it.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Attention LaMelo Ball: only losers boast about avoiding diaper duty | Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The basketball star seems proud to leave the job to his partner. That’s so last century

Nobody can accuse the basketball star LaMelo Ball of being bad at his job. That said, the Minnesota Timberwolves point guard doesn’t seem to be a huge fan of dribbling.

Ball has a nine-month-old son, LaOne, with his partner Ana Montana (real name: Analicia Chaves) and is apparently uninterested in dealing with all the body fluids that come with a baby.

“You’re a dad now,” the sportscaster Ernie Johnson Jr said to Ball during an ESPN interview on Wednesday. “Are you a diaper changer?”

“Nah, my girl do all that,” Ball replied. “We got a good gameplan going on. So I know what I gotta do, bring to the table, she know what she gotta do, bring to the table.”

Johnson, to his credit, seemed disappointed by this answer. “Oh man, you don’t know what you’re missing, I’m telling you that.”

“I did it before, you feel me? I’ve definitely did it before, [but] it’s just not my job,” Ball clarified. “You know what I’m saying? It’s not my job.”

Well, actually, excuse me while I mumsplain here, but it very much is your job. A baby doesn’t care that you signed a five-year contract extension worth up to $260m in 2023. Parenting is a 24/7 commitment no matter how much money you make.

Ball and Montana (and, presumably, a team of hired help) are obviously free to share domestic duties however suits them. Nobody expects a professional athlete to be as hands-on as a parent with a more flexible schedule.

But going on TV and boasting about how you don’t change diapers? That’s an extremely outdated look. A 1982 study based on fathers in Britain found 43% of fathers had never changed a nappy (as diapers are called in the UK). By 2000, that figure had dropped to 3%. Meanwhile, the average time US dads spend caring for their offspring daily has quadrupled over the past 50 years and about 85% of dads say parenthood is one of the most important aspects of their identity. Being a hands-off dad is now very last century.

Still, even though modern fathers are doing a lot more, they’re still held to different standards than mothers. Imagine if a female athlete said changing diapers wasn’t her job: the rightwing pitchforks would be instantly out for her.

It doesn’t matter how accomplished a woman is in her career; there’s still an expectation that her identity as a mother comes first. Particularly under the Trump administration, which is trying to foster a whole new generation of tradwives.

Ball is only 25, so I’ll give him some grace. But I hope the backlash to his comments makes him realize that only complete losers boast about not changing diapers. A case in point: Donald Trump.

“I would never ask to change [Barron],” the president told the New York Post in 2006. “Melania probably wouldn’t let me. I’d just do it wrong.” Asked whether he’d ever changed the diapers of his four other children, he said he probably had, but couldn’t remember.

There’s a phrase frequently applied to men who pretend they’re incapable of doing basic domestic chores in order to wriggle out of them: weaponized (or strategic) incompetence. In Trump’s case, however, it may not actually be weaponized incompetence. It may just be incompetence.

Which leads me to present a modest proposal. In the future, we should apply the Diaper Test™ to any man in the running for a high-powered job. If he can’t clean up his own child’s mess, he’s sure to make a mess of the job.

Two days after a New York district attorney reopened the alleged Cornell University gang-rape case, the Polymarket gambling app allowed people to bet on the results of the investigation. According to Defector, Polymarket initially said nothing about why they were letting people bet on a traumatic sexual assault case, before issuing a PR statement full of corporate gobbledegook. “Markets bring objective, data-driven insight into how a matter like this is moving through the legal system, on a topic that deserves far more transparency and honest attention,” the statement read. Monetizing sexual assault is feminism now, apparently! Polymarket then reconsidered this position. After about three weeks of being up, the bet has been removed from the platform.

Adam Gabbatt examines why the president keeps “offering unsolicited, and increasingly unhinged, assessments of men’s bodies”.

In 2021, a near-total ban on abortion took effect in Poland. Now the lower house of parliament has approved two bills that would remove some criminal penalties for people who help women access abortion care and would allow a termination if there was a foetal abnormality. While that sounds like a small step in the right direction, the draft laws are likely to be vetoed by the conservative president, Karol Nawrocki. Women are now protesting on the streets in more than 20 Polish cities demanding access to legal abortions.

It’s not just Poland that seems determined to be at odds with the rest of Europe on abortion. The hereditary prince of Liechtenstein, who will never need an abortion himself, has used his veto for the first time to kill off a bill that would have eased the country’s draconian laws.

Israeli attacks killed yet another child in Gaza this week as the territory faces a new risk of famine.

Democrat Amy Acton is running against Republican Vivek Ramaswamy to be governor of Ohio. It’s a tight race and Ramaswamy clearly thinks he can’t win on merit because he’s stooped to putting out a revolting attack ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother, Donna Arthur, whose former husband has been accused of sexually abusing Acton when she was a child. In the ad, Arthur accuses Acton of lying “her entire life”. There’s been bipartisan backlash to the ad, but JD Vance has mounted a vigorous defense, saying he’s “disgusted” by fellow Republicans who have criticized it. On Thursday, Trump also endorsed the ad, calling it “very powerful”.

Remember when the Nordic phenomenon of slow TV was being touted as the antidote to the frenetic nature of modern life? Well it’s back! A 24-hour Finnish TV show that follows the progress of a dog and her six newborn puppies has become a massive hit. The show has an accompanying 24-hour webcam, Pentulive (Puppy Live), which is very soothing. I recommend tuning in whenever you feel like the world’s gone barking mad.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Israeli soldiers raze neighbourhood in Hebron, driving families from homes
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Julian Borger in Jerusalem
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
PM Benjamin Netanyahu vows ‘to destroy this place’ in retaliation for militant attack on army checkpoint

Israeli troops have levelled a neighbourhood in Hebron, driving out hundreds of families in collective punishment for a militant attack on an army checkpoint outside the West Bank city, local Palestinian authorities said.

The Hebron municipality estimated that 35 hectares (86 acres) had been destroyed or marked for destruction and about 1,500 people had been evicted from their homes by Saturday afternoon in the district of Ein Deir Baha. The whole city of 250,000 people was sealed off by checkpoints on every point of entry.

Videos sent by a Hebron resident showed a substantial area of devastation with every house over several blocks flattened in an urban area. One video showed soldiers marking Palestinian houses with a sprayed black cross, another showed a bulldozer tearing down a stone wall on a hillside and another showed a large residential building festooned with Israeli flags.

People said the building was the home of a prominent Hebron family that had been commandeered as a temporary military headquarters.

The large-scale demolitions follow an attack on Friday on an Israeli military checkpoint outside Hebron by two gunmen. After a 20-minute gunfight, two Israeli soldiers were killed, three injured and the two gunmen were also killed.

Israeli elections will take place in four days and the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and the extreme-right finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, travelled to the site of the attack to promise an immediate and ferocious response.

Netanyahu said Israel would “act to destroy this place”. Smotrich who is standing for election in a smaller coalition party, had himself filmed wearing body armour in front of a Palestinian building being demolished. He said he had ordered “the immediate demolition of a wide row of illegal Arab structures adjacent to the attack site”.

Smotrich also called for “a comprehensive military campaign … exactly like in Gaza and Lebanon”. Ein Deir Baha, the focus of the demolitions, was alleged to be the home district of the two gunmen.

A spokesperson for the Hebron municipality said that about 300 families had been evicted. Some had taken refuge in the homes of friends and relatives, while the municipality said it had opened community halls and children’s play areas to shelter others.

A Palestinian news agency, Wafa, reported Israeli plans to displace a further 2,500 people. “We are being collectively punished for something we neither did nor supported,” a Hebron civil rights activist, Issa Amro, said. “Our suffering is being turned into political material for Israel’s elections, while innocent families pay the price.”

Amro said his sister’s family was one of the hundreds driven out of their homes.

“We are talking about hundreds of families who left their homes because of this, and they are not at all connected to what happened yesterday [Friday],” Amro said in a telephone interview. “It’s a very big area and we don’t know what’s going on, whether it is only election propaganda or if it’s a serious plan from decisions on what to do after the election.”

The Israeli army was approached for comment on the operations and on videos showing extensive devastation.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Aston Villa and Jackson end Manchester City’s perfect run with stunning win
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Will Unwin at Villa Park
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Manchester City have added a loss in the Premier League to the one to the Premier League, as their perfect on-pitch record vanished at Aston Villa. The two most in-form strikers in England did battle and it was Nicolas Jackson’s double that meant his side come out on top against Erling Haaland.

City are certainly infallible, losing for the fourth time in a row here, and it was a reminder that life will not always be as simple as their first seven games. Mistakes cost them as Marc Guéhi and Gianluigi Donnarumma played their part in Jackson’s goals, which will give him greater pleasure as they ended Enzo Maresca’s perfect start.

Aston Villa started at lightning pace while City cowered. City were so ponderous in the opening stages they gave away a corner after being penalised for taking too long over a goal-kick. After two mistakes last weekend against Ipswich gave away goals, Guéhi would have hoped for a more reassured performance, but he was once again punished for the opener, miscontrolling a Rúben Dias pass to allow Jackson in, with the striker rifling home in the sixth minute.

City did not look like a side who had won every Premier League game thus far. The hosts, on the other hand, had forgotten their mid-table tag and were more reflective of the team sitting second in the Champions League standings with three wins out of three.

The inflatable fruit enthusiasts got to witness an improving situation on the pitch as City enjoyed plenty of possession in and around the Villa area, but Iliman Ndiaye, who had a penalty claim waved away, and Rayan Cherki, were thwarted by Zion Suzuki’s reactions. Villa defended with commitment and discipline to limit the space available with great success.

While City constantly threatened and Ndiaye struck the post, there was always a nagging doubt that Villa could cause problems on the counterattack. Jackson against the unfortunate Guéhi was starting to look like a mismatch, as the defender was unable to cope with the speed and physicality of the striker. Guéhi was booked for pulling down Jackson on the edge of the area to leave him in a precarious position on every level, forcing him to be replaced at the break.

The entertainment and exhilaration of the first half was always going to be difficult to sustain, but there was no backing down from either side. City’s endeavour was rewarded in the 53rd minute when Ndiaye got the better of Ian Maatsen and found Haaland finally able to connect with a cross, heading home from close distance for his 13th of the season. It is hard to keep that man quiet.

There was a sense City could take control of the match and went close through Josko Gvardiol and Doku, but once again lapsed. Villa did not need an invitation to burst into life and were unable to contain them as the ball moved quickly from back to front, with Jackson sending the ball out to Ibrahim Mbaye before getting on the end of the cross for his second. Donnarumma should have done better, letting the shot slip under him.

The academy trio Phil Foden, Rico Lewis and Ryan McAidoo were sent on to change things for the visitors and they provided energy, but when chasing the game there was a loss of focus. Passes and crosses were misdirected and needless bookings were collected. If City could point to perfection before this, the label was rapidly fading as the seconds ticked by.

Jackson went off with eight minutes left to a standing ovation. Haaland had a very late chance to level, but Maatsen cleared off the line, to ensure Jackson and Villa claimed the glory.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: ‘It feels like a fairy tale’: American Paula Moltzan wins first World Cup race by 0.01sec
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Bryan Armen Graham
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
American Paula Moltzan became the oldest woman to claim her first Alpine skiing World Cup victory on Saturday, edging Albania’s Lara Colturi by just one-hundredth of a second in a thrilling season-opening giant slalom at Sölden, Austria.

Moltzan, who was fifth after the opening run, produced a superb second descent to finish with a combined time of 2min 14.82sec, narrowly denying Colturi, who finished in 2min 14.83sec. Germany’s Emma Aicher completed the podium, 0.52sec behind the Minnesota native.

“It feels like a fairy tale right now,” Moltzan said afterward. “Pretty unreal and I think it will take a minute to settle in.”

The victory marked a long-sought breakthrough for Moltzan, who debuted on Alpine skiing’s top flight in 2012 and was dropped from the US ski team a decade ago. The 32-year-old, who won bronze in the team combined event at the 2026 Milano Cortina Olympics, had finished second or third in 10 previous World Cup races in 13 seasons without ever reaching the top step of the podium.

Starting the second run in fifth place, the American clocked 1min 7.86sec to move four places up the standings and set a target that none of the remaining contenders could beat.

Colturi, who had been sixth after the opening run, came agonizingly close to denying Moltzan her moment, finishing just 0.01sec adrift.

Aicher also made a significant move, climbing from ninth after the first run to third, while Sweden’s Sara Hector slipped from second to fourth, 0.63sec off the winning pace.

Moltzan’s American teammate Mikaela Shiffrin, seeking a record-extending 111th World Cup victory, had led after the opening run but struggled in increasingly foggy conditions, sliding wide on one turn, and fell to seventh overall, 0.83sec behind the winner.

Shiffrin, who equalled the women’s record with her sixth overall World Cup title in March, has described the new campaign as an “exploration season” in which she plans to race less frequently in her signature slalom discipline to concentrate on giant slalom and super-G. The 31-year-old has not won a giant slalom race since December 2023, despite holding the women’s record with 22 career victories in the discipline.

For Moltzan, the result represented an immediate reward for a bold late-career equipment change. In May, she ended an 18-year association with French manufacturer Rossignol to join Van Deer–Red Bull Sports, becoming the first woman to race for the Austrian brand, which had previously supplied only male skiers.

“It does really feel real, but we’ve put in a lot of hard work this summer developing this ski and it feels like this is kind of a pinnacle that it’s paying off and we did all the right things,” she said.

The result also gave the United States two skiers inside the top seven, with AJ Hurt finishing 13th, Elisabeth Bocock 14th and Nina O’Brien tied for 16th.

Moltzan has also been making headlines away from the slopes. In an interview with the Athletic published on Friday, she discussed her campaign to expand fertility treatment coverage for US Olympic athletes, a cause she has promoted by racing with a floral uterus design on her helmet.

The Minnesotan has argued that female athletes should not have to choose between pursuing their sporting ambitions and starting families, and is pushing for greater fertility benefits through the US Olympic and Paralympic Committee.

For now, Moltzan has every reason to savor the biggest victory of her career, achieved on the Rettenbach glacier in the traditional opening race of the World Cup season. “I can’t imagine a better start,” she said. “I’m really, really, really excited and I can’t wait to see everybody who’s here cheering us on.”

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Rising US star Fred Richard wins first world gymnastics title with floor gold
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Guardian sport and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
American Frederick Richard won the floor exercise title at the world gymnastics championships in Rotterdam on Saturday, finishing ahead of Britain’s Jake Jarman and Israel’s Artem Dolgopyat.

With US gymnastics great Simone Biles looking on as a spectator in the Netherlands, the 22-year-old Richard secured his first world title, edging out Jarman by just 0.033 points after scoring 14.633. Jarman, the defending world champion, was among a field that included the last two Olympic gold medallists.

“I hope this is a lesson to everybody that you don’t have to wait to get the win to say you will be a champion,” Richard said afterward. “You don’t have to know when it’s going to happen or how it’s going to happen, but believing it every second of every day does pay off. I’m proof of that now.”

Richard became the first American man to win a world title on floor exercise since Paul Hamm shared gold in 2003. He is also the first American man since Danell Leyva to win medals across team, all-around and individual apparatus events at the Olympics and world championships.

Richard, who won bronze in the all-around event at the 2023 world championships in Antwerp, also helped the United States win team bronze at the Paris 2024 Olympic Games.

Elsewhere on Saturday, Brazil’s Rebeca Andrade claimed her third world title on vault, with Americans Claire Pease and Skye Blakely taking silver and bronze respectively. It was a first individual world championship medal for the 17-year-old Pease, while Blakely added to the all-around gold she won on Friday.

The championships conclude on Sunday with the remaining apparatus finals, including the women’s balance beam and floor exercise and the men’s vault, parallel bars and horizontal bar.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Australia crush England in women’s Rugby League World Cup statement win
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Jack Snape
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
The Jillaroos sent a reminder to English rugby league that it is losing touch with the best in the world with a 78-0 hammering in Perth. The 15-tries-to-none victory confirmed the gulf in athleticism and skill between the two hemispheres and reminded fans the rugby league universe now orbits the Pacific.

The one-sided result showed last year’s 90-4 embarrassment in Las Vegas was no outlier and England’s women’s team must urgently refocus in time for next week’s showdown with Samoa if they are to reach the semi-finals.

England had not beaten the Jillaroos in four previous meetings and they made it hard for themselves with a dismal opening five minutes. They were offside from the kick-off, putting them on the back foot immediately.

The Australia full-back, Tamika Upton, slipped through the England line on her first carry. Seconds later, backrower Tiana Penitani-Gray – shifted into the starting lineup – drew two tacklers and passed to winger Jaime Chapman, who walked over.

It got worse with England’s debutant half-back, Jenna Foubister, put the ensuing kick-off out on the full. Jillaroos’ five-eighth, Jocelyn Kelleher, who made her own bow for Australia last week, launched it on the last tackle with precision, arcing it over the England winger Anna Davies. Chapman read the trajectory and leapt into the sky, coming down with the ball over the line for a sparkling try.

Chapman’s afternoon had started perfectly, but a knock-on handed England the ball inside 20m. Davies appeared to sneak around the Australia defence early in the set for a try, but the video referee spotted her knee sliding on to the sideline before the ball was grounded. It was as close as England would come and from there the match was played almost exclusively up the other end.

Upton was having it all her own way. Another two linebreaks, including another on a kick return and she had accumulated more than 100 metres before the 20-minute mark. In one remarkable effort, Upton appeared to be held by the England full-back, Fran Goldthorp, but she shrugged her off and put Kelleher over for Australia’s third try. Julia Robinson, shifted into the centres from the wing, crossed for the fourth.

Robinson was forced off when the shoulder of Shaylee Bent collected her in a tackle and she walked off clutching her arm. That injury – suspected to be a broken wrist – triggered another debut and on came the Roosters’ NRLW premiership winner Sariah Paki, a two-time Olympian in rugby sevens.

The difference in strength and athleticism between the sides was stark and after Olivia Kernick almost barged over the ball went left to emphasise that skill also favoured the hosts. Half-back Tarryn Aiken engaged the line, freezing the cover defence with a straight decoy run from Paki, and Kelleher powered over the line.

The contest was already over, but the Jillaroos captain, Isabelle Kelly, showed no mercy in crossing to make it 30. Winger Abbi Church, brought into the starting side, finished a flowing attack and it was 36-0, more points than minutes at half-time.

Aiken, Kernick and replacement Quincy Dodd crossed early in the second half to post the half-century as the Jillaroos cut through the defence seemingly at will. With twice the possession, three times the run metres and 13 line breaks to none and still 20 minutes on the clock, this was a contest between colonial frenemies that was long over.

Fortunately, the best team of the world were in the mood for entertaining. One chip and chase from Kelleher was regathered then handed off to Upton who put over Church. It was the best moment of the match and proof even a shellacking like this can draw a smile.

Forward Makenzie Weale scored a try on debut after coming off the bench, sprinkling the stacked scoreboard with an ounce of storyline. Penitani-Gray, Kelly and Bent added late four pointers to bring the final score to 78-0, giving the England fans in Perth after their men had earlier defeated France 82-0.

Australia play Wales next Sunday in Sydney, another almost automatic victory for the hosts. The going will get tougher in the semi-finals. A likely clash looms against Fiji, who pushed the Kiwi Ferns in the opening round and easily accounted for Papua New Guinea 40-4 in Port Moresby earlier on Saturday.

England face a challenge in their third match against Samoa, who thrashed Wales 76-0 on Friday. After this defeat they will need a win on Friday to make their way into the semi-finals, where they will probably meet New Zealand. But given the Samoans held the Jillaroos to 40 points last week, the underwhelming England might want to have their bags packed.

https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/o.title: ‘Cuts mean jobs’: Skydance staff brace for shake-up after $110bn megamerger
https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/o.author: Mark Sweney
https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/o.text:
Battle far from over after Paramount and Warner Bros deal creates new global entertainment powerhouse

“It feels like the calm before the storm,” says an executive at Skydance, the newly minted media empire formed from the megamerger of Paramount and Warner Bros Discovery (WBD). “David has got what he wanted, but now there is a price to pay.”

Earlier this month, David Ellison, Skydance’s chief executive, sealed the $110bn (£82bn) deal, creating a global powerhouse spanning two Hollywood studios each more than a century old, the TV networks HBO, MTV and Discovery, and news outlets CBS and CNN.

Having seen off a rival bid from Netflix and faced significant political and industry opposition, in a process Ellison told employees was at times “downright ugly”, the battle is far from over for Hollywood’s newest magnate.

With an aggressive target of reducing an eyewatering debt load of more than $80bn in just three years, it is what is going to be cut, sold and restructured that will be uppermost in the minds of Skydance’s more than 53,000 employees.

Ellison, 43, who studied film and acted in the 2006 film Flyboys before moving into producing, is targeting $6bn in savings within three years. Executives and financial backers are steering away from the need for swingeing job losses, but a memo from management earlier this month warned that there would be “difficult decisions that affect our workforce”.

“It is business as usual but, to be honest, everyone is worried about what happens next,” says another Skydance executive. “Cuts inevitably mean jobs.”

There are also concerns about the political direction of the new entity, given Ellison’s closeness to Donald Trump – a longtime friend of his father, Larry, who co-founded the software company Oracle. David Ellison has pushed back at such framing, stating: “We do not want to politicise the company.”

Nevertheless, fears in the news division have been stoked by events at Paramount before the merger. It came under fire for cancelling the long-running Late Show with Stephen Colbert after its host said it had paid a “big fat bribe” for settling a $16m lawsuit with Trump.

Days later, US regulators agreed the $8.4bn merger of Paramount with Ellison’s Skydance Media, with Trump ally Kenneth Weinstein’s appointment as ombudsman at CBS News to root out “complaints of bias” as one of the conditions to get regulatory approval.

Christiane Amanpour, CNN’s international anchor, criticised the “ideological realignment of CBS” and warned that changes and cuts could lead to the potential “destruction” of flagship news show 60 Minutes. This week, she announced she was leaving CNN after 43 years, although her exit is not thought to be tied to the new ownership.

CNN staff were relieved at Skydance’s decision shortly after closing the deal to keep Mark Thompson, the former New York Times boss and BBC director general, as chair and chief executive.

Many had feared that the network, which alongside MS Now and Politico had faced a now-lifted White House media ban in apparent retaliation for critical coverage of Trump, might face a sweeping overhaul that could have seen the divisive Bari Weiss, the editor in chief of CBS News, installed at the top.

While Thompson has said that Skydance supports CNN’s independence, fresh concerns over rightwing influence emerged this week when it was reported that Elon Musk, a Trump ally and supporter of far-right causes through his X platform, has invested $1bn for a stake in the media conglomerate.

“The preservation of editorial independence is a growing concern among media consumers,” said Mike Proulx, an analyst at Forrester. “Private wealth is getting a greater foothold on public information channels.”

In terms of creative television output, star performers such as HBO will be left to keep churning out the all-important hits the business needs.

Ellison immediately extended the soon-to-expire contract of Casey Bloys, promoting the HBO boss to also oversee streaming services Paramount+ and HBO Max, to ensure the golden goose keeps making must-watch dramas such as The White Lotus, Game of Thrones, The Pitt, Succession and The Sopranos.

However, there are longer-term questions over some of the group’s cable and TV channels – such as MTV, Nickelodeon, the UK’s Channel 5 and Network 10 in Australia – which are in decline but still account for 70% of profits, according to CreditSights.

“In a world where the majority of consumers can access content through a smart TV, it should be a natural consideration to sell physical broadcast assets,” said Brian Wieser, chief executive of consultancy Madison and Wall.

“At a Skydance level they have made the choice to go all in on streaming. But the problem you have is maybe you don’t get offered enough to sell it, and, given the cashflow we know they make, they might be better served to hold on.”

Newly filed accounts for Channel 5 show the broadcaster paid a £215m dividend to Paramount last year. In the UK, the culture secretary only cleared the takeover after Ellison made commitments including pledging to keep Channel 5 operating as a free-to-air, public service broadcaster until at least the end of 2034. However, according to sources, these agreements do not preclude any potential sale of Channel 5 in the future.

Last month, Paramount moved its £300m TV advertising sales business from Sky’s sales team to Channel 4. That came after WBD extended its deal for Sky to handle its £90m-£100m ad sales business from January, covering TNT Sports, Discovery, Animal Planet and streaming service HBO Max. However, multiple media sources believe now the Skydance deal is done the business will eventually also move to Channel 4.

The megamerger also paves the way for BT to exit its joint venture with WBD – TNT Sports – which would finally end the telecoms company’s costly foray into pay-TV sport after almost 15 years.

Last year, Paramount outbid WBD for the rights to Champions League football, the flagship rights owned by TNT Sports. That blow prompted BT to write off the entire value of its stake in the joint venture.

However, with Ellison intending to merge Paramount+ with HBO Max, the rights will effectively be retained, and viewers will not have to sign up to yet another streaming or pay-TV service to watch all top-flight football.

Skydance says it will spend an estimated $30bn a year on content across all divisions, and as part of the takeover Ellison promised to release at least 30 major films a year until 2031.

This promises to be a boon for the UK production industry, especially for WBD’s studio at Leavesden, which is home to all of its DC superhero franchises and the forthcoming Harry Potter TV series destined for HBO Max this Christmas.

However, Warner is enduring one of its worst box office showings for years, the most recent flop being Tom Cruise’s Digger, prompting Ellison to put Paramount’s leadership in charge of both studios.

Analysts point out that Ellison is unlikely to maintain that level of moviemaking beyond the five-year pledge, as it goes against the grain of a Hollywood trend towards fewer films and lessons from past takeovers.

Since Disney’s acquisition of Rupert Murdoch’s entertainment assets in 2019, which included the then 20th Century Fox and Fox Searchlight studios, the number of film releases has broadly halved.

“After the 2031 deal ends there will be fewer films, obviously,” says Tom Harrington, a media analyst at Enders. “It has never happened before when there has been a takeover that more have ended up being made.”

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: Met says it shared allegations about Meghan’s father with her but not other forces
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Harry Taylor
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Scotland Yard says it shared letter about Thomas Markle Sr allegations in 2019 but did not pass claims to other agencies

The Metropolitan police have confirmed they gave a letter to the Duchess of Sussex in 2019 concerning “alleged offending” involving her father, after accusations arose on Friday about Thomas Markle Sr having child sexual abuse images.

Scotland Yard said it had received a letter in January 2019 making a number of allegations about offending outside Britain.

The police force said it had passed the information on to the Duke and Duchess of Sussex’s office, but it did not pass it on to “other law enforcement agencies”.

The Sun newspaper published claims that Meghan’s half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, claimed he had found a stash of images belonging to their father at his former home in the Philippines.

On Friday, Meghan said she had been made aware of these allegations by the Met, and that she was “deeply distressed” by them.

The duchess, who is estranged from her father said in a statement she had broken off contact to protect her children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five. He has never met them.

Meghan’s father has denied the allegations and told the Daily Mail the accusations were “sick lies”.

The Met said it was considering whether to refer itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) to review its actions.

In a statement, a Metropolitan police spokesperson said: “Following a thorough review of Met police systems and records, we have confirmed that in January 2019, we received a letter containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom. It was sent to the MPS (Metropolitan Police Service) Protection Command to raise concerns in relation to the security of the Duchess of Sussex.

“The letter was reviewed and a decision was made that it should be passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness. The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies.

“The MPS is reviewing the handling of this matter in 2019 and considering whether a referral to the IOPC is necessary to review our approach.”

In a statement on Friday, issued through her spokesperson, the duchess said: “I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed.

“In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan police and Royalty and Specialist Protection [Rasp]. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.

“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them. I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.

“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.”

She later said she had misremembered the year the Met had contacted her, and confirmed it had been 2019, not 2018 as she said on Friday.

A spokesperson for the Duchess of Sussex said: “In recalling events from more than seven years ago, without the benefit of a diary entry or contemporaneous record, it is understandable that she may have been mistaken by a few months.

“If the MPS holds a time-stamped record confirming that the letter was reviewed in 2019, that should be treated as the accurate reference point for when it was received and shared with the duchess.

“I think it is reasonable to recognise that she is doing her best to recall the precise timing of events that were not diarised at the time, and that any discrepancy of a few months is an understandable consequence of that passage of time.”

Sources said that although Meghan was made aware of the allegations in 2019, she had been unable to speak publicly to avoid jeopardising any future investigation and because speaking out could have resulted in legal action against her.

The Sun reported that Markle Jr told detectives in the Philippines he had discovered “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sexual abuse images on computers and mobile phones stored in four large boxes at the home in Cebu where Markle Sr was living until he returned to the US in May after having a stroke.

Markle Jr, 60, said he had also contacted the FBI in the US, the Sun reported.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: The World Series of the have-nots is here. But baseball’s money problem isn’t going away | Tom Dart
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Tom Dart
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
Baseball’s two best regular-season teams are also among its lowest spenders. But their unlikely World Series comes with a warning about the sport’s future

The best pitcher in baseball led the best team to victory over the second-best team? Weird.

A World Series that makes the logical feel novel began on Friday as the Milwaukee Brewers beat the Tampa Bay Rays 3-2 in Game 1. Of course the Brewers, with their MLB-topping 103 regular-season victories, should be facing the 98-win Rays on the grandest stage. But of course, since these are two of the smallest and lowest-budget franchises in the sport, they shouldn’t.

That this best-of-seven title decider is at once a shocking cold shower and a comforting warm bath is largely explained by the absence of the two-time defending champions, the Los Angeles Dodgers, who were swept 4-0 by the Brewers in the National League Championship Series.

In the US, all World Series games will air on Fox and Fox Deportes, with streaming available through Fox One. In the UK, the series will be carried by TNT Sports. In Australia, fans can watch on ESPN, with streaming available through Disney+ and Kayo Sports.

That was a philosophical battle with a drop-mic ending: the revenge of the nerds. Analytics over affluence, a triumph for the teams who scrimp and strategize rather than simply lobbing money at the best free agents each offseason.

The Dodgers have parlayed financial dominance into winning the National League West division in 13 of the past 14 years. At the start of this season there was every reason to expect they would win their third World Series in succession. But instead of spending this title fight lamenting the Dodgers’ dominance and fretting that money has made baseball dull and dynastic, we have the first match-up in 46 years – and second since 1920 – between two teams that have never won a World Series.

A country where the world’s richest person has reportedly made political donations in excess of $442m in this election cycle is culturally conditioned to believe that wealth wins. Yet baseball is, after all, still a sport where the won-lost standings and the salary tracker are not fully interchangeable.

Here are successful teams, boasting talents as luminous as Rays third baseman Junior Caminero and Brewers catcher William Contreras, with payrolls less than half the size of the most lavish spenders. Milwaukee’s annual outlay ($146m according to Spotrac) ranks 19th in the 30-team league with Tampa Bay ($96m) in 28th position. And the Rays reached this point by beating the Cleveland Guardians, who have MLB’s smallest payroll, in the American League Championship Series.

Only the Dodgers, Brewers, Atlanta Braves and New York Yankees have more regular-season wins in the 2020s than the Rays, who are in their third World Series. Tampa Bay, founded as an expansion franchise in 1998, reached the final in 2008 (where they lost to the Philadelphia Phillies) and in the Covid-wracked 2020 season, losing to the Dodgers at the makeshift site of Globe Life Field in Texas.

The Brewers’ only other World Series appearance was a loss to the St Louis Cardinals in 1982. Though there are suspicions that national television audiences will be meager for a series between small-market teams lacking superstars, the games in Milwaukee are some of the hottest tickets in World Series history. On one resale site the asking price for standing-room only tickets to Saturday’s Game 2 in Milwaukee was north of $3,000.

The first clash held moderate value for the neutral spectator. It was a night with a fast start, a false finish and some messy, unmemorable baseball in the middle. Where ordinary pitchers throw fastballs, Jacob Misiorowski, MLB’s strikeout leader in the regular season, hurls fireballs. Pitching on 11 days’ rest, the 24-year-old started his night with the quickest pitch ever recorded in a World Series, a 103.5mph screamer to leadoff hitter Yandy Díaz.

Misiorowski surrendered one run in five innings’ of work. “Not perfect, but good enough to get a win,” he said. Milwaukee led 3-1 after the seventh but Tampa Bay mounted a late rally, scoring a run in the ninth to induce a tense, if gauche, finish. The visitors loaded the bases but catcher Liam Hicks appeared to hit into a game-ending double play. The Brewers celebrated but the fireworks and high-fives were premature.

The Rays challenged the decision, which was overturned on review. This confirmed that shortstop Cooper Pratt had taken his foot off second base too early as he threw to first, and also that Milwaukee fans can boo almost as loudly as they cheer.

Still, there was more than enough air left in the lungs of the fans at American Family Field to reboot the celebrations after the teams returned to the field and closer Trevor Megill struck out outfielder Jonny DeLuca for the win, for real. “It’s a big credit to Trev for locking back in right there and making some huge pitches after. You know, you kind of have that emotional dump and then you have to get back on it.” Brewers slugger Christian Yelich told Fox Sports. It was perhaps early evidence that in a series that is likely to be decided by fine margins, Milwaukee’s formidable bullpen might ultimately make the difference.

Pat Murphy, the Brewers manager and Bruce Springsteen superfan who was FaceTimed by The Boss in midweek, declared Contreras the “player of the game” after he drove in a run and threw out two attempted base-stealers, neutralizing a key strategy for Kevin Cash’s aggressive Rays.
