Manchester city council has strongly denied claims of a “sweetheart deal” with Abu Dhabi after researchers at the University of Sheffield concluded it had “sold the family silver too cheaply” by giving the land to Abu Dhabi at a cheaper rate than comparable developments.

In 2017, three years after the first Abu Dhabi deal and the year Burnham became Greater Manchester mayor, council leaders made another huge bet. They paid £42m for a hollowed out retail park next to the £1bn Manchester Life development, described at the time as the biggest ever land purchase in Manchester city centre.

Its price was at least six times higher per acre than the adjacent land sold for £5m to Sheikh Mansour – and it would later be identified as the permanent future home of Burnham’s No 10 North.

This former retail park was also a partnership with Abu Dhabi. Again, the terms were shielded from scrutiny as members of the public were excluded from council hearings – but inside the town hall, the fallout was significant.

A senior council property officer, Dominic Hayes, resigned abruptly in March 2018 over concerns about the deals the council was doing with Mansour’s group. He listed a series of complaints in an email to the council chief executive, Joanne Roney, who the previous year had succeeded the all-powerful Howard Bernstein when he retired after 29 years in charge.

In a tense meeting days after the resignation, a senior council figure, Eddie Smith, is said to have told colleagues that Hayes had thrown them “under a bus” and that the leadership was furious. According to contemporaneous notes by a colleague, seen by the Guardian, Smith said Hayes had made “not acceptable [and] possibly dangerous” criticisms of a Manchester City board member who was a key figure in the Manchester Life deal.

Smith is then said to have commented: “You don’t criticise the council’s relationship with the football club in this organisation and hope to survive.” Smith, who left the council in 2020, denies making the comment.

Yet Hayes’ concerns were serious enough to warrant an internal investigation into governance at the council. It found that anxieties about the council’s deal-making were not limited to just one officer.

A second senior employee told auditors they were concerned that the council had “overpaid” for the rundown retail park, according to an official record of the meeting. That officer raised concerns that the Abu Dhabi-led project was “driving the master planning for a site they didn’t own”.

When Burnham became prime minister in July, the site was tipped as the permanent home for No 10 North. As scrutiny of the Abu Dhabi link grew in October, these plans were quietly shelved.

Council sources noticed a change of approach under Leese’s successor, Bev Craig, when she became council leader in December 2021.

Craig ordered a review of the Manchester Life deal to make sure it was “all legal, all above board”, she told BBC Radio Manchester this month, adding: “The answer was yes.”

One of the reviews commissioned by Craig, who succeeded Burnham this year as Greater Manchester mayor, was published in July. It found that while the deals with developers such as Abu Dhabi had delivered “significant benefits”, there were “weaknesses in documentation, monitoring and assurance”, particularly around the profit-sharing nature of these deals.

Prof Jonathan Silver, a University of Sheffield researcher who has analysed the Manchester Life deal, said the growing buy-up of land and property by Emiratis raised “major concerns about the fragility of the ‘Manchester model’ and its reliance on attracting flows of international finance, whatever the cost”.

Silver said there were “urgent questions” about what would happen to the hundreds of homes in the Manchester Life developments if Sheikh Mansour was forced or decided to sell Manchester City in light of the cheating scandal.

Leese remains confident the Abu Dhabi deals were a huge success for the city. Asked whether he would have handled the partnership any differently given the concerns raised by academics and others, he said: “No. Nothing that I can think of. It is a phenomenally good deal for Manchester.”

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: I gave my ex our house and half my savings, but now I feel resentful | Ask Annalisa Barbieri
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Annalisa Barbieri
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
Your feelings are understandable. Exploring and accepting them may help you move on

I was with my ex-partner for more than 20 years. We were mostly happy and I expected us to be together for life. For well over half the relationship, I was the sole breadwinner and, at my ex’s request, managed our finances. We were reasonably well off, with savings and without a mortgage. We even had a holiday home, albeit a static caravan.

I retired early, and the problems we had in our relationship grew. We had both loved travel, but I was repeatedly told we couldn’t afford it, which I knew was nonsense. I went back to work in a demanding new field, but my ex showed no interest. I spent more time away from home and began therapy (my suggestion of couples’ therapy was rejected). After a year of therapy, I said I was leaving.

My ex said we couldn’t afford to split up. So, I gave them the house and more than half the savings, and moved to the caravan. In the last six years I have bought a new house, have a wonderful new partner and have travelled. I am successful in my work and doing things I dreamed about for years.

But I can’t let go of my resentment of my ex. The many material things I brought to the relationship and left behind. The fact that my ex is living in a house worth twice my own. That I turned myself inside out to provide for someone but never got any credit.

These things are petty. I look for a book that I paid for, and realise my ex took it, and I can’t stop thinking about it. I want to let it go, but how?

You didn’t say whose name the assets were in – joint names, their name or only yours. You didn’t mention children either. This would substantially change things. I am working on the assumption that you voluntarily gave all this to them with no legal guidance to do so and no children were involved. If so, then I don’t think how you feel is at all unreasonable and I am astounded.

I went to UKCP-registered psychotherapist Hazel Hyslop who also wanted to “acknowledge your courage and resourcefulness. You have shown that you can make difficult decisions and create a different life for yourself.”

But it’s understandable, Hyslop said, “that you feel confused by your resentment. From the outside, it appears you’ve moved on. Yet emotionally, part of you may still be living with the unfairness of what happened. Accept and acknowledge your feelings and give yourself permission to feel them. You might find that makes it easier to move forward.”

It’s not petty to be annoyed that a book, or anything else, is with your ex. Because it’s not just about the book, is it?

Hyslop said: “The book may represent everything you feel you contributed and left behind. Your money, possessions, labour, care and responsibility. Your resentful feelings may be saying: ‘What I gave mattered. I mattered. Why was this never recognised?’ These feelings are not petty. They may be signals that an important part of your experience still needs to be acknowledged.”

Resentment alerts us that a line has been breached. It’s an important emotion, often aligned with anger. Maybe you could put your energies into naming the line that’s been crossed and how it makes you feel. If you can tune into it I really think a lot may lighten.

You could also try writing it all down; that may make you furious, but it can really help (you don’t need to do anything with the letter). I don’t think you realise just how resourceful you are. But isn’t it exhausting having to be that person? I hope your new partner can lighten some of this for you going forward and look after you.

Every week, Annalisa Barbieri addresses a personal problem sent in by a reader. If you would like advice from Annalisa, please send your problem to ask.annalisa@theguardian.com. Annalisa regrets she cannot enter into personal correspondence. Submissions are subject to our terms and conditions. The latest series of Annalisa’s podcast is available here.

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.title: Zadie Smith tells Dua Lipa inequality has made culture clashes feel ‘existential’
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.author: Ella Creamer
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.text:
Novelist says demise of Britain’s ‘incredible’ welfare system and housing struggles have led to deeper divisions

The novelist Zadie Smith has said that inequality has made culture clashes feel “existential”, adding that it has become “natural to look to your left and think ‘who the fuck are you?’”

In an interview with Dua Lipa as part of the Southbank Centre’s London literature festival, Smith argued that the demise of Britain’s “incredible, historic” welfare system has led to greater divisions.

The pair discussed Smith’s debut novel, White Teeth, which was published in 2000 and primarily set in the last three decades of the 20th century.

Asked by Lipa about how attitudes towards multiculturalism have changed since the 80s and 90s, and the current “dividing line” on immigration in UK politics, Smith pointed to increased inequality and unemployment.

“When you’re living in basically decent housing, when you hurt yourself you know you can go to hospital and be treated just like the rich kid down the road – then the differences [with others] become interesting, sometimes annoying, but not existential,” said the novelist.

“Now, they’re existential. When you can’t get a job, when there’s no housing, when your schools are falling apart, when the hospitals are falling apart – now it feels existential.”

White Teeth traces the stories of three families – the Joneses, the Iqbals and the Chalfens – and is set in Kilburn and Willesden in north-west London, where Smith grew up. The writer praised her state education, saying it has stood her “in incredibly good stead” throughout her life. “I can talk to anyone. The posh kids up the hill? Not so much.

“Now, when you look at my neighbourhood, the same schools, the same situations – everything is harder, everybody is poorer, everybody is struggling more,” she continued. “It becomes very, very natural to look to your left and think ‘who the fuck are you?’ That is an economic and structural question.”

Smith encouraged developing “a nostalgia for the left”. While “you don’t want the LGBTQ+ politics of the 80s, you don’t want the racial prejudice” depicted in White Teeth, “do you want the healthcare and the schools and the education? I think you do. So it’s about looking back and seeing what was of value – and what was [of] value to me was a social democracy that basically functioned, and might function again if people cared about it, wanted it, believed it could happen again.”

On the writing process for White Teeth – which she began when she was 21 and was published when she was 24 – Smith said that she finished the acclaimed novel in the aftermath of being broken up with and moving back in with her mum.

“Everybody else was out clubbing, I was like, ‘I’m fucking stuck in this room, finishing a novel,’” she said. But Valentine’s Day was approaching, and “all my girlfriends were like ‘we gotta go out, go on the pull’.” She ended up finishing it on 14 February and then “literally ran straight out to the club” – so the ending of the novel is “a chaos”, she said, adding that this is “why young people shouldn’t write novels”.

Since White Teeth, Smith has written five novels – The Autograph Man, On Beauty, NW, Swing Time and The Fraud – along with short stories and nonfiction. Her most recent book was the essay collection Dead and Alive.

Lipa and Smith also discussed facing criticism for their works, with Lipa saying that “learning to live with reviews – bad reviews, good reviews” was “one of the hardest things for me to learn to deal with”. Smith said that literary criticism is “absolutely essential” because it “helps develop taste”.

“I’m very interested in criticism,” added Smith. “Even if it’s a bad review of me, if it’s well written, if it’s intelligent … I quite love ‘takedowns’.”

London literature festival runs until 1 November, with speakers selected by Lipa including Patti Smith, Malorie Blackman and Hisham Matar. Lipa runs a book club, Service95, through which she interviews authors on a monthly basis.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/ng-int.title: Ten days that could shake the world: democratic norms at stake in four pivotal elections
https://www.theguardian.com/world/ng-int.author: Julian Borger senior international correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/world/ng-int.text:
Brazil, Israel, Serbia and the US are holding elections within the space of 10 days. Will the authoritarian right cement its global gains, or can pro-democracy forces make a comeback?

Four elections on four continents within 10 days could profoundly reshape global politics, propelling the world further along its current authoritarian trajectory or marking a limited comeback for democratic norms.

In all four contests, basic democratic norms are at stake at a time when autocracy is advancing worldwide at an alarming rate. According to the Sweden-based V-Dem Institute, which uses multivariable assessment tools, the democratic freedoms enjoyed by the average global citizen are down to levels last seen in 1978 – long before the fall of the Berlin Wall and the collapse of communism in Europe.

The cluster of four pivotal elections could either halt that trend or reinforce it. In each contest, pro-democracy parties are in close races with current or aspiring autocrats. The outcomes in each case are likely to have spillover effects in their regions and beyond.

On Sunday, Brazil will hold runoff presidential elections with a candidate from the far right in the lead. If he wins, Flávio Bolsonaro is threatening to “change the constitution”, pardon his father for plotting a coup, and ease environmental restrictions, a critical issue for the Amazon rainforest.

On the same day, the semi-autocracy run by Aleksandar Vučić in Serbia for the past 12 years will face its stiffest challenge in the form of an unconventional student-led protest movement, fielding a slate of little-known academics and technocrats running on the simple slogan “Serbia or Mafia?”.

On Tuesday, it will be the turn of Benjamin Netanyahu to face his challengers at the polls. Israel’s leader for 19 of the past 30 years has overseen a prolonged period of democratic backsliding and spiralling human rights abuses. He is wanted by the international criminal court for war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, and risk heightened legal jeopardy from an ongoing corruption trial at home if he loses. His far-right coalition is currently trailing an opposition block.

On 3 November, at the tail end of this potentially historic 10 days, Donald Trump’s imperial-style presidency is facing a rebuke from US voters in midterm elections, with at least one chamber of Congress, and possibly two, likely to fall to the Democrats. They will then however face an uphill task in seeking to rein in Trump’s excesses which have seen the US plummet down the V-Dem Institute’s Liberal Democracy Index.

By the time the US counts its votes on Tuesday, the world could look a markedly different place. Not only are the four looming contests bunched together, they are also interwoven. Trump’s Maga movement has given overt political support to Netanyahu, Vučić, and Bolsonaro. Israeli-built Pegasus spyware has been found in the phones of student and pro-democracy activists in Serbia. Bolsonaro is strongly pro-Israel and is promising to follow the US lead and move the Brazilian embassy to Jerusalem. The US has provided much of the ordnance for Netanyahu’s wars. Serbia is committed to spending $2bn on Israeli defence systems and in September, the two countries opened a joint plant making surveillance and attack factory.

Victory for the authoritarian right in one country will bolster counterparts in others, and conversely win for pro-democratic campaigners in each contest will give hope and encouragement to their allies around the world.

The four elections may be closely interlinked, but the struggle between authoritarianism and democracy takes on very different forms in each country. The odds are different in each case, as are the stakes, but they are all close races.

Brazil has enjoyed a democratic resurgence since Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva took office on the first day of 2023, defeating an attempt by his far right populist predecessor to overturn the October election result. According to V-Dem’s measures, it now has better democratic credentials than the UK, and far better than the US.

The loser in those elections four years ago, Jair Bolsonaro, an ex-soldier who served under Brazil’s 21-year military dictatorship and still admires it, was sentenced to 27 years in jail for trying to stage a coup to hold on to power. Now his son, Flávio, is seeking to follow in his footsteps, and goes into the second round of the election on Sunday with a small but significant lead over Lula.

The younger Bolsonaro has not only pledged to free his father, but also to punish members of the judiciary involved in his prosecution. If he wins, he will have a supportive rightwing majority in Congress to work with and has vowed to change the constitution and “re-democratise the country”. The term harks back to the transition from military rule in 1985, and for the Brazilian left, it has a chilling Orwellian ring coming from the mouth of an avowed admirer of prominent members of the junta.

Bolsonaro has campaign on hard-line law and order policies addressing the chronic issue of high crime. He argues for lowering the age of criminal responsibility to below 18, sending more teenagers to jail, and calling for judicial reforms, which his critics suggest he intends to mount an attack on the independence of the courts.

Over his 12 years as president, Aleksandar Vučić has steadily corroded the pillars of Serbia’s democracy. He and his allies have taken over almost all the country’s broadcast channels, with the result that he is the overwhelming presence on the nation’s television screens over the course of the current election campaign. The future of the last two independent news channels is now in doubt, as they were bought during the campaign by a Portuguese investor with links to the ousted Hungarian regime of Viktor Orbán.

The ruling Serbian Progressive party (SNS) has turned ministries and other state institutions into political tools to the extent that, in the words of Raša Nedeljkov, the programme director of the Center for Research, Transparency and Accountability, “the line between the state and the parties is almost deleted”.

Until now, the opposition parties seeking to curb Vučić have been weak and divided, but Serbian politics was transformed two years ago by the collapse of a concrete canopy on a crowd of people at a railway station in Novi Sad, killing 16 people. The tragedy crystallised a deep reservoir of disillusion across the country, and produced a student-led mass movement which has survived state intimidation since then, and is now fielding a full list of candidates against the SNS.

The candidates, like the students who nominated them, disagree among themselves on key political issues but they demonstrate a purist adherence to direct democracy. Decisions are taken by large plenum meetings, and no one has been allowed to emerge as an identifiable leader.

To win on Sunday, the students will have to break the mould of Serbian politics, and in particular, Vučić’s hold on his loyal base in the countryside. If they come close, there is a risk of unrest and violence. The SNS has a record of paying bands of thugs to disrupt opposition rallies, and those gangs may appear at polling sites if Vučić feels threatened. The students too have vowed to take to the streets to defend the victory they expect on Sunday.

Israeli democracy has always been partial. Palestinians in the occupied territories do not have the vote or many other rights, while Israeli settlers next door to them are treated as full citizens and provide vital backing for Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition government. That government however will be fighting for its survival in Tuesday’s parliamentary elections.

Palestinians with Israeli citizenship are about a fifth of the population but are consistently under-represented in the Knesset. They turn out to vote in smaller numbers than Israeli Jews, with many viewing participation as pointless in a system which systematically excludes them. The main opposition bloc challenging Netanyahu is ruling out a coalition with Arab parties, even if it means the difference between a clearcut victory and an uncertain deadlock, once Knesset seats have been assigned.

Netanyahu has been Israel’s leader on and off for most of the past three decades, but in the nearly four years of his current term, in coalition with extreme settler-backed parties, he has mounted an offensive on Israeli democratic norms, seeking to limit the independence of the judiciary in the name of “reform”, putting pressure on the independent press, and politicising the police, army and internal security service, Shin Bet.

The opposition bloc, led by former general Gadi Eisenkot, shares much of Netanyahu’s outlook when it comes to Palestine, largely supporting the war in Gaza and refusing to countenance a two-state solution. But it is determined to expunge the corruption of his government and its autocratic excesses. It is expected to win more seats than the government coalition in Tuesday’s election, but fall short of a clear majority. For that they may have to forge an understanding with Israel’s long ignored Palestinian minority.

No western country in modern times has “undemocratised” itself as rapidly as the US in less than two years of Donald Trump’s second term in office. With a Congress dominated by loyal Republicans and a mostly acquiescent supreme court, he has forged an imperial presidency, frequently governing by executive order decrees, and turning state institutions into political tools – including organs of internal security, such as the justice department and the FBI – which have been weaponised against political opponents, independent prosecutors and journalists.

Administration policy, domestic and foreign, has been used to generate self-enrichment opportunities for Trump’s family and friends.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has been vastly expanded with lightly trained but heavily armed recruits, and deployed across the country, trampling the civil rights of anyone, predominantly Latinos, suspected of being an illegal immigrant.

With the president’s approval ratings at record lows, the Democrats have a good chance of winning a majority in the House of Representatives and the slimmer possibility of winning the Senate too.

Even if they gain control of both chambers, however, there are limits on how far they can go to rein the authoritarian excesses of the Trump presidency. He can be expected to use his veto freely, and Democrats will not have the votes required to overturn it, or to defeat a Republican filibuster in the Senate.

In theory, Congress has the power of the purse and could try to make funding for government departments and agencies conditional on reforms. A Democratic majority would also use its control over committees to open several investigations into corruption and other wrongdoing, issuing subpoenas to government officials.

On both counts, though, the Trump administration could simply choose to ignore Congress and refuse to cooperate. The most immediate outcome of a Democratic win is therefore likely to be prolonged constitutional crisis before there is any recovery in democratic norms.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: Cocaine-linked crimes on the rise in Britain as consumption surges
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Michael Goodier and Robyn Vinter
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Exclusive: Wastewater analysis in England suggests people took roughly 2.5bn lines of drug in one year

Ageing users and record deaths – the data behind Britain’s £9.8bn-a-year cocaine habit

British police are recording a growing number of crimes linked to cocaine, including assaults, domestic abuse and dangerous driving, as figures show consumption has surged across England.

A Guardian investigation has found police forces across Britain recorded a 10% rise in crime rates associated with the class A drug since 2019, while the Home Office estimates cocaine usage at sites across England has risen by 26% since 2021.

Cocaine is a powerful and addictive stimulant that causes euphoria, overconfidence, restlessness and paranoia. Experts have warned its use can cause already fraught situations to escalate, potentially leading to violent incidents.

The rise in consumption in recent years can be partly explained by historically low costs, while purity levels have remained high. Analysis of wastewater suggests people in England consumed 123,000kg of cocaine in 2024-25. That’s equivalent to roughly 2.5bn lines of cocaine, at an estimated street value of almost £10bn.

Police recorded at least 29,922 crimes mentioning the word cocaine in 2025 – equivalent to 63.4 for every 100,000 people. That was up from 57.7 cases for every 100,000 in 2019. Figures up to May this year suggest that number could increase again in 2026 to about 64 cases in every 100,000 people – a rise of more than 10% over seven years.

Martin Gallagher, an author and organised crime expert who served as a police officer in Scotland for 28 years, said cocaine use had become normalised: “It went from being the drug of the social elite to being something taken off the cistern of a toilet in a local pub.”

A majority of cocaine-associated crimes last year were drug offences – but 18% were violent crimes, including stalking and harassment and one murder case. Just under 4% of crime reports mentioning the word cocaine were sexual offences, including 344 rapes.

Separate figures highlight cocaine’s role in domestic abuse cases. Nearly six in 10 police drug tests carried out on people arrested on suspicion of domestic abuse were positive for cocaine between July 2025 and June this year.

The data, drawn from the Home Office’s drug test on arrest programme, is not representative, as some tests were only taken after police already suspected drug use. However, the results tally with a 2023 pilot study that found 59% of domestic abuse suspects tested positive for cocaine or opiates.

Harry Sumnall, a professor in substance use at Liverpool John Moores University, said: “Scientific reviews have found no strong evidence that cocaine directly induces violent behaviour, but domestic violence is often rooted in power, and both perpetrators and survivors describe cocaine intoxication escalating loss of control and jealousy, leading to violent incidents, and making existing abuse more frequent and more severe.”

He cautioned that a mention of cocaine in a crime record did not prove the drug had caused the offence.

Separate DVLA data obtained by road safety charity IAM RoadSmart found that drug-driving offences overtook drink-driving offences for the first time last year. There were 30,707 drug offences added to driving licences (up by 28% since 2022), and 29,769 drink-driving offences (down by 17%) in 2025.

Government figures suggest that cocaine and cannabis are the most common illegal drugs involved in road fatalities. Figures obtained by the RAC suggest that drug-drivers are far more likely to reoffend than drink-drivers – meaning a smaller subset of repeat drug-drivers could be behind the rise.

Paul Court, a deputy chief constable who is deputy lead for drugs for the National Police Chiefs’ Council, warned that demand for illegal drugs sustained a “highly profitable criminal market built upon violence, exploitation and intimidation”, and that police enforcement alone was not enough to solve the problem.

An independent report last year by the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs found that the UK lacked a coordinated drug prevention strategy with dedicated funding – despite international evidence showing drug prevention programmes work.

Court added: “We have to reduce demand, prevent people being drawn into drug use in the first place, reduce harm and ensure those whose offending or vulnerability is linked to drug dependency have opportunities to access treatment and support.”

The Guardian contacted all 45 police forces in the UK under the Freedom of Information Act requesting figures for crimes mentioning the word cocaine. Of these, 39 responded with data. Not every force had records for each year or a breakdown of the types of crime associated with the drug. London’s Metropolitan police were not able to provide any data.

Data was taken from keyword searches of police summary notes, so do not necessarily mean that cocaine formed part of the offence. The figures may include some crimes tangential to the drug – for example, if a witness stated someone was known to use cocaine. Other crimes, where the drug was misspelled or mentioned in a different part of the notes, may be missing.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/ng-i.title: How cocaine conquered the UK: in pubs, festivals and workplaces the drug has become an everyday habit
https://www.theguardian.com/society/ng-i.author: Guardian Staff
https://www.theguardian.com/society/ng-i.text:
Previously considered a middle-class drug, price drops have made cocaine more widely available, and created a new set of problems

Ageing users and record deaths – the data behind Britain’s £9.8bn-a-year cocaine habit

Lisa* is watching Scissor Sisters at a festival in the Lake District, a can of cider in hand, dancing along to the music on a sunny afternoon.

The 30-year-old has a few days off from her job as a veterinary nurse in Gateshead, where she lives with her fiance. She loves going to festivals, especially as “I love meeting new people,” she says.

She is confident and makes friends at the festival very easily. The reason for that? “I’m on a bit of coke,” she says.

It is a crime largely hidden in plain sight – and one many people would barely consider a crime. However, it could land her a maximum sentence of seven years in prison, though for a first offence it is more likely to be a police caution. But she’s unlikely to be caught, especially at a festival, where over the course of the weekend numerous people admit to the Guardian to taking cocaine – or trying to get hold of it – and are seen openly taking it.

By many estimates, use of the class A drug is soaring. Wastewater analysis suggests people in England consumed 123,000kg of cocaine in 2024-25, a rise of 26% since 2021. That’s equivalent to roughly 2.5bn lines of cocaine, at an estimated street value of almost £10bn.

Cocaine is a powerful and addictive stimulant that causes euphoria, overconfidence, restlessness and paranoia. A Guardian investigation has found a 10% rise in recorded crimes where the drug was mentioned since 2019.

Research from wastewater samples in 2022 carried out by Imperial College London and released earlier this year found that cocaine use spiked during major sporting and music events, heatwaves and bank holidays.

Its reputation as a middle-class drug still stands, though it has become more available across different demographics, as prices have dropped year-on-year and reached “historically low levels” last year. That wider use brings wider problems.

Cocaine was thought to have been a major factor in the 2021 widespread disorder at Wembley stadium during the Euro 2020 final, when thousands of ticketless fans breached safety barriers to get access to the ground. Lady Casey’s independent review later that year found that “excessive consumption of alcohol and cocaine” were fuels of a “febrile atmosphere”.

More than half of fans who responded to a survey in the aftermath of the incident said they had seen open drug use at Wembley stadium or on the way from the station.

“People were taking cocaine in front of us [and] my sons cried for most of the game,” one person quoted in the report said. A safety official was quoted as saying: “Drug usage was noticeable. It took four or five stewards to try and hold someone down – more than the number it usually takes when fans are drunk.”

Cocaine was a factor in the 2024 summer riots when some of the perpetrators of violence were found to be in possession of it or have taken it before the riots erupted. Two rioters also later pleaded guilty to selling it. Open cocaine use was also seen at the Unite the Kingdom rally, a far-right anti-immigration protest in London last year.

But cocaine was – and still is – a party drug, popular at nightclubs, student house parties, middle-class dinner parties and now in the pub.

At a West Ham pub in east London, a pub manager explains she cleans cocaine residue off surfaces in the toilets most mornings. It is a pub for people who live and work in the area and for West Ham fans who are regulars on match days.

“It seems to be so blended with the concept of a night or even a day out for a lot of people ... It has been very normalised [and it’s] just a thing that you can quite blatantly and overtly do.”

She says the ubiquity of cocaine has become “significantly worse” over the past five years.

While other drugs are more obvious – they have a strong smell or leave their users visibly intoxicated or even incapacitated – cocaine can be harder to spot, which is a problem for publicans.

There can be telltale signs though, she says, such as when a punter appears to be getting agitated, leaves the pub and then comes back some time later, going straight to the toilets. “I’ve had real idiots, and they’ve been very blatant, and it’s been easy to kick them out.”

The manager believes people often take cocaine in an effort to “sober up” so they can continue drinking, “which obviously does not actually work but a lot of people believe it does”.

“Now you’ve got the impaired judgment from alcohol but you’ve also got the alertness from cocaine. That for me is a really big problem because that’s when you get potentially very volatile behaviour. That’s probably the point that I would call the most dangerous, both in terms of people behaving erratically, but also because they don’t realise how drunk they are. They are – at that point – a danger to themselves in terms of me having to call an ambulance or something.”

Cocaine use becomes particularly obvious when punters get into fights. “I had a 60-something-year-old man beat up a 70-something-year-old man in the toilet, knock his teeth out, because he said that the other guy had allegedly called him a cunt,” she says. “Now I understand that there are egos involved and that people can be volatile – and there’s all kinds of silly petty rivalries going back decades amongst some of the customers – but you’re not telling me that’s a normal reaction.”

She says she has spent years working in hospitality, managing different venues, and she thinks the problems that come from cocaine use can be seen in both cheap chains and expensive country gastropubs.

“But technically none of us can talk about it because none of us can admit that drug-taking takes place on our premises,” she says. “Everyone’s scared of losing their licence.”

What wastewater analysis cannot reveal is whether more people are taking cocaine, or more is being taken by those who are habitual users, or both.

For some people, cocaine is simply a part of life, something taken every day, even while at work.

The first time Will* took cocaine was at about the age of 15. “I remember it being stimulating, like I felt kind of chatty. I felt a lot of my social anxiety-based inhibitions fade away and, in the space of that, I was really confident and felt kind of unstoppable, in a sense.”

Things quickly escalated to him dealing the drug. “I was a 16-year-old with like half a fucking kilo of cocaine in my bedroom.”

He began selling to friends and friends of friends, though he admits he was an “atypical” dealer. He was from a relatively wealthy family in Essex, surrounded by teenagers with a lot of disposable income.

“That would pay for my usage of it,” he says, earning as much as £7,000 in a weekend.

“But then over the last like 20 years, it has developed much more into a coping mechanism,” the 37-year-old says.

A carpenter in TV and film, he has used it to help with long hours, being the first on set and the last to leave. It is so common among his colleagues that he says parts of the industry “basically run themselves on cocaine”.

He has “successfully hidden it from professional relationships so easily” and says people he interacted with at work would have no idea he was taking coke in the workplace.

“It can really seem like a good idea but it ultimately isn’t. [It’s fine] until you realise that you’ve built the physical dependency and then you go a day without it and you’re like dragging yourself through mud.”

At one point he counted up and realised he had spent £35,000 in one year on cocaine. He says: “I was like, oh my god, that’s a lot of money.”

He has managed to cut down on his use substantially, from “spending thousands of pounds a week doing cocaine every single day to someone who’s spending maybe £120 to £180 a weekend”. But even still, he thinks he will probably never stop taking it.

“I’m trying to be in control of it as opposed to being fully sober, because I don’t really see myself as someone who is ever gonna be fully sober.”

*Lisa’s name has been changed. Will spoke to the Guardian on the condition of anonymity. His name has also been changed.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Brazilians vote in presidential election runoff pitting leftist Lula against far-right Bolsonaro
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Incumbent president lost in first round to senator and son of convicted ex-president

Brazilians are going to the polls on Sunday in a highly unpredictable runoff in which the leftist president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, is attempting an unprecedented comeback against the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who won the first-round vote.

Bolsonaro’s surprise victory despite not leading most polls made him the favourite three weeks ago, but since then Lula’s campaign has gained ground, and the two go into the contest virtually tied.

The gap between them was the narrowest ever recorded in a first round, at less than 2% of the vote, and the 81-year-old president has spent much of the runoff campaign focused on turnout – abstention reached a record high in the first round and disproportionately affects his voters – and on stoking fears over what a return to power by a member of the Bolsonaro family could mean.

A congressman for more than 20 years with few bills passed, the 45-year-old Bolsonaro is the eldest son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is under house arrest serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup to overturn his 2022 defeat to Lula.

The senator has promised that if elected he will pardon his father, and with an even more conservative congress taking office next year he has vowed to “change the constitution and re-democratise this country”, sending chills through those who fear he could follow in his father’s authoritarian footsteps.

“We’re facing two completely different projects for the country,” said voter Nuno Rau, 63, an architect and writer. “One points towards the end of social rights and the end of democracy itself; on the other side is someone who fought for income distribution and free public education. I may have criticisms of Lula, but there is no way to choose Bolsonaro,” he added.

Aparecida Moreira, a 62-year-old lawyer, will vote for Bolsonaro mainly because of the “iron fist” security policy he proposes, including building five “mega-prisons” inspired by those of El Salvador’s populist autocrat Nayib Bukele.

“I agree with Bolsonaro’s idea of chemical castration for rapists, because there is no crime worse than rape,” said Moreira, adding that voting for Lula would be the same as voting for the “dictator” Alexandre de Moraes, the justice who, despite not having been appointed by Lula, is widely associated with him by Bolsonaro supporters because he oversaw the former president’s conviction.

Both Flávio Bolsonaro and Lula drew large crowds to their final campaign rallies on Saturday in Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo and Belo Horizonte.

With each side of supporters virtually “crystallised”, the election will be decided by the small number of voters who identify with neither candidate.

Bolsonaro began the runoff campaign with a lead and the support of most other defeated candidates, but instead of growing, he stagnated in the polls while Lula gained support.

Many analysts saw this as the result of part of the population suddenly waking up to the “fear” of a Bolsonaro returning to power, as well as controversies including the fact that the senator is under investigation in two federal police inquiries over alleged corruption and money laundering.

Lula, by contrast, radically changed his digital strategy and benefited from student-led protests across the country, most of which did not even involve the president.

“In the first round, Lula’s campaign failed to connect with the population, but now it has been civil society movements that have driven his growth,” said the political scientist Helcimara de Souza Telles.

Whatever the result, the race is expected to be decided by a narrow margin in Latin America’s largest country, with an electorate of 159 million.

Many analysts believe that if Lula overturns his first-round defeat, Bolsonaro could follow his father’s example from four years ago and refuse to concede, and that Donald Trump, a longstanding ally of the Bolsonaro clan, could refuse to recognise the result.

“Trump wants to ‘colonise’ all of Latin America in pursuit of its own interests,” said Telles, adding that, with rightwing candidates having won all seven presidential elections held in Latin America since Trump began his second term, Brazil is one of the few countries in the region still offering any resistance to the US president.

“So a Bolsonaro victory would mean losing Brazil to a model of autocracy backed by the US,” she added.

https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2026/.title: Carving out a greener future: how the Swiss ski resort of Laax is meeting the climate crisis head on
https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2026/.author: Kevin Rushby
https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2026/.text:
Gondolas on demand, electric piste-grooming and chemical-free snow cannons – how Laax is ‘greenstyling’ its future

It’s the worst ski resort nightmare: hillsides of shaggy yellow grass streaked with slush under a leaden sky that’s coughing up sleet. Parts of Europe – places previously accustomed to crisp snow fields and pristine blue skies – are now facing this calamity, something meteorologists might describe as a British winter.

Not everywhere, of course. Only lower altitudes are seeing such disasters. Higher up, normal service continues. I’m in the Swiss resort of Laax, where most of the slopes are at about 2,000 metres, lofty enough to be snow-secure, for now. The halfpipe is busy with dudes in baggy trousers and headphones nonchalantly practising their double corks. On the traditional pistes there are four-year-olds who could probably ski before they could walk. And then – Switzerland has its wacky side – three young men in first-world-war greatcoats on antique wooden skis propel themselves with rough-hewn quarter-staves.

Is all this destined to disappear, perhaps in our children’s lifetimes? To put it in stark, white and black terms: are ski resorts in the same predicament as oil-dependent desert states, watching their one key source of wealth dwindle and disappear?

If so, Laax is not going down without a fight. This unusual Swiss resort, close to the Austrian border, is making a bold attempt to be carbon neutral by 2030, a goal that requires cutting out all oil use, making all energy generation sustainable, and reducing food waste to zero. Stung by climate crisis criticism levelled at the ski industry, this community is now far ahead of most. What I have come to see may turn out to be the future of winter sports.

Down in Laax, I meet Reto Gurtner, 71, CEO of the Flims Laax resort. His father built the first ski lifts back in 1962. “Although there had been summer visitors since the 19th century, Laax was a poor village back then,” says Gurtner.

In the 1970s, something significant changed. Gurtner went to study at UCLA and, under the California sun, discovered skateboarding. Even now the memory makes his eyes light up. “They were inventing new sports and I loved the style: no nationalism or militarism. Skateboards, mountain bikes, snowboards – if you did a good run, everyone applauded. It didn’t matter who you were. There was a freedom about it.”

He came home with a degree in economics, but more importantly perhaps, a snowboard and a mountain bike. “We went up on the glacier and built the first halfpipe with shovels.”

At first, there was a lot of resistance. Local ski outfitters refused to stock snowboards, while in summer, farmers were outraged at the sight of cyclists pelting down mountain tracks. “We made every cyclist wear a bib,” says Gurtner with a chuckle. “Then the farmers thought it was a race and were fine with that.”

Conversation with Gurtner is a wild ride. We cartwheel through Steve Jobs, the German poets and the Wu-Tang Clan, as he describes how his visionary approach evolved into something he calls “greenstyle”, an optimistic and well-designed future.

That vision is found in all the new buildings around the resort, nowhere more so than the ski lift in the neighbouring village of Flims, where I head with local guide Doris Rellstab. “The new gondola system does away with unoccupied ski gondolas going up and down the mountainside,” she says. A complex algorithm allows skiers to choose one of five destinations up the mountain, despatching individual gondolas, which balances energy efficiency with passenger demand. As we are lifted smoothly up over the fir trees, the quiet efficiency of this on-demand system becomes immediately apparent.

Rellstab tells me how things have changed in the half century since she began teaching winter sports. “Yesterday, I taught my first Arab group. They were a lot of fun.”

Our destination is Segnes, high above the treeline at 2,100 metres. Having left the gondola, we don snow shoes and head into a bowl-like snow-filled valley. A couple of miles ahead, the valley ends in a sheer rock face topped by a jagged range of peaks. “That’s the Tschingelhörner,” says Rellstab. “Can you see the line in the rock below the peaks? That was once a geological mystery.”

In 1848, the celebrated geologist Roderick Impey Murchison arrived here with a local expert, Arnold Escher von der Linth. Older rocks were overlaying younger, a puzzle for which there was no explanation. It took more than a century for scientists to solve the problem: the ancient African tectonic plate was riding up over the younger European one. The world was indeed upside down.

In summer, this area is covered in rare Alpine flowers and there’s a mountain hut to stay in. Next to us are the tracks of a snow hare. “Wildlife is doing well here,” says Rellstab. “The wolf and lynx have both returned.”

In fact, climate change appears to be assisting wolves in the Alps. The first Alpine pack was recorded in 1993, and by 2021 there were more than 250, with an annual growth rate of about 25%. Switzerland, once entirely wolf-free, now has about 40 packs. Rellstab shows me a website where sightings are monitored. There are conflicts with farmers and hunters, but the numbers keep growing, an indication that parts of the ecosystem are doing well out of retreating snowlines.

Perhaps more surprising is that lack of snow is not a big worry to the resort. As Gurtner points out: “Laax is not snow-dependent. A halfpipe or a snow freestyle playground doesn’t need a lot, and we make it with hydro power. And we’ve got mountain bikes and amazing hikes.”

Later that day, I am up on the mountain with my skis, wandering around on blue runs. Conditions are a bit icy and I’m playing safe, finding myself on a less frequented route that dips down into the valley. And then I come over a ridge and the snow on either side is gone – only the piste remains, a broad band of white curling down through green pasture dotted with lovely old barns. Cannon snow is more durable, surviving longer when the “real” stuff melts. Most Alpine ski stations are already reliant on it, but unlike many, Laax does not add any chemical or biological additives to the water in its cannons. With sustainable power sources and electric piste-grooming machinery now becoming available, cannon snow is not as environmentally destructive as it may appear.

At the foot of the hill, I reach the village of Falera, neighbour to Laax. There is one old chair lift, clanking and squeaking, and as I approach it comes to a halt. “Sorry,” says the attendant, “we are closed now.”

I wander into the village, all hand-hewn barns with neat log stacks. I can’t see any cars. If Laax is taking the technological solution, its neighbour appears to have chosen a less frenetic and more traditional route to net zero. After 20 minutes, a bus (electric, naturally) appears. As I ride back to Laax, I check the wildlife website that Rellstab recommended. And I get a shock. According to a CCTV report from a few hours earlier, a wolf had walked within a mile of me. Outside my hotel, I jump off the bus. Evening is falling. I wait for a line of silent cars to go by. With electric motors everywhere, the town is hushed. Climate change, I reflect, is nothing if not unpredictable. When the wolves howl, you will hear them.

The trip was provided by Flims Laax and rental equipment by Ecoski . Trains run from Zurich via Chur and the Rhine Gorge to Ilanz, where there’s a bus service to Laax. Inghams offers a seven-night trip to Laax from £1,618pp B&B, including flights

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Don’t call me ‘mumsy’ – the contempt behind that word makes me livid | Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
It means to be drab, homely or old-fashioned – ‘motherly’, essentially. Why can’t we have some respect for mothers, instead of deriding them?

A recent newspaper headline – “Sorry Radley! These dated handbag brands will make you look mumsy – here’s where stylish A-listers and Royals are shopping instead” – reminded me of a word I despise: “mumsy”.

My list of words that make me want to throw things is varied and long, but “mumsy” is near the top. The quality of being mumsy means to be drab, homely or old-fashioned, essentially “motherly”. Something about the casual misogynistic contempt it carries makes me livid. So livid I might even use “that voice”. You know. The scary mum voice that turns misbehaving children in supermarkets into stone.

“Mumsy” crops up in fashion coverage, which in autumn is unduly focused on the new school-run “style rules”. Articles about how to look chic at the school gate and short-form videos about “what the cool mums are wearing” add to this feeling that the last thing you, as a mother, would want to appear as is what you actually are: someone’s mum.

Of course, it’s understandable, and totally normal, to not want to be entirely defined by your reproductive status. Few of us want our entire identities to be “mother”. I still remember the shock I felt when a health professional first referred to me as “Mum” instead of by my name. It can feel as though you have ceased to be a person in society’s eyes. Add to that the fact your body’s changed because you’ve made and birthed a whole human being, and that you are now responsible for that other human being’s every want and need, drastically limiting the time you have to attend to personal style and grooming, and it can feel hard to know who you are now.

These conflicting feelings are never a reason to deride mothers in general, though, or to act like “I’m not a regular mom, I’m a cool mom”. There’s a reason Amy Poehler’s comic Mean Girls catchphrase has proved so legendary. There’s something inherently ridiculous about working to deny something that you so irrevocably are and will always be. The harsh reality that dawns on you as you transition from not-mother to mother is that you are for ever changed. You can try to dress it up all you want, but the fact is that you’re someone’s mum now.

New theories of matrescence tell us that this change is a lot more complicated than suddenly wearing really naff jeans, although you might be doing that too (or be simply too sleep-deprived to give a toss that you’re wearing really naff jeans. Or using the word “naff”, which is probably also mumsy). The concept of mumsy changes according to the era you are living in. In the 1990s, all the mums wore high-waisted Levi’s 501s, which we even came to call “mum jeans”. This came to be co-opted by fashion brands, albeit using the slightly less mumsy sounding “mom”. I wouldn’t have been caught dead in mum jeans. What am I wearing now, as I type this? That’s right, a pair of vintage 501s. It all comes back round eventually. The teenagers I pass on the school run every morning would never.

I look at how their baggy jeans are soaking up the puddles and pigeon piss all the way up to their knees and am not nostalgic. This must have been the sort of zen that my own mum felt; I feel confident in my personal style. That doesn’t mean that fear of mumsiness doesn’t try to stalk us all regardless. The anxiety around this question is palpable on forums such as Mumsnet: what shape of jeans should we be wearing now? Are coloured trainers fashionable?

I’m not going to pretend that I don’t care at all, but I would think less of someone who uses the word “mumsy” about other women. I will never forget, long before I had a child myself, one writer I know saying of another that her work was “a bit mumsy”. The writer in question wrote brilliantly and hilariously about parenthood, and also about a lot of other things. I found the way that “mumsy” was used to reduce and deride her intelligence and the quality of her work deeply unpalatable. I also recall an editor saying that she hated seeing the word “mum” in print. I suppose she preferred the more literary sounding “my mother”, which has its place but, let’s be honest, it’s not how most of us speak.

It made me realise that it isn’t just fashion, then, that is resistant to mumsiness but culture more generally, and that’s only going to change when mothers and the work they do are afforded the respect they deserve. As it stands, to become a mother is to not only be confronted with biological reality and structural sexism, but to somehow navigate this without dressing, writing or sounding too much like a mother. Perhaps, like the fashion writer Frankie Graddon, whose Substack’s strap line is: “I’ve had a baby, not a style crisis”, the solution is to simply be “Mum-ish”. Whatever. You can prise my 501s from my cold, dead hands.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: US seized American heir’s cellphone in violation of treaty agreement, lawyer says
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Timothy Pratt
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
James ‘Fergie’ Chambers, in prison in Spain, has applied for asylum as US seeks extradition over alleged Hamas support

US authorities seized wealthy activist James “Fergie” Chambers’s cellphone at some point after Spanish police arrested him in July without notifying him or his attorneys, the Guardian has learned.

Chambers, a US citizen and wealthy donor to leftwing and humanitarian projects, is imprisoned in Madrid. His case is the first known instance of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation tied to money Chambers has donated to support Palestinians, including the Sameer Project, in Gaza.

The extradition request also includes charges associated with a protest against Elbit Systems, an Israeli weapons manufacturer.

Chambers’s legal team discovered that the phone was no longer in the custody of the national court in Madrid and had been turned over to the FBI upon inquiring about it Tuesday, according to attorney Aitor Martínez.

This occurred despite the team having received written guarantees from the court that the phone “would remain under the court’s custody while the extradition request was resolved” – as both Spanish law and the extradition treaty between the two countries require, Martínez said.

“I’ve never seen anything like this in an extradition case,” he said. “Spanish judicial authorities can’t surrender control over the personal effects of a person sought in extradition just because a foreign government has asked for them … and now a judge has secretly turned over Fergie’s phone to the US.”

The defense has filed a petition with an appeals court seeking immediate return of the phone – as well as a detailed explanation of the phone’s chain of custody, who authorized what and when and whether or not the US had accessed the phone’s contents.

It is assumed the office of Félix Bolaños, the Spanish minister of justice, would have to get involved in bringing the phone back, Martínez said.

Chambers has asserted through his attorneys and partner, the actor and activist Stella Schnabel, that the extradition is politically motivated. He has applied for political asylum from prison. Under Spanish law, an asylum applicant cannot be extradited until the asylum process is completed.

He remains imprisoned after a judge denied a petition for provisional release earlier this month, asserting in part that his wealth made him a flight risk.

Chambers, a self-described communist and anti-imperialist, is heir of the Cox family, owners of Atlanta-based Cox Communications. As part of a settlement in which his family severed ties with him at the time, he sold stock back to his family worth about $250m in mid-2023. Since then, he has been funding an estimated 100 projects in 20 countries, according to Schnabel.

Chambers’s views and donations have been extensively profiled in US media, and his public comments on Israel and Gaza have brought controversy. A week after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel, he posted on X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’/There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for/No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong/It’s simply genocide/Like it has been.”

His legal team is now asserting that various Spanish and international laws governing both extradition and political asylum have been violated by US authorities seizing his the phone without legal due process.

The Spanish courts are handling the extradition case and could take months to decide whether to hand Chambers over to the US. Meanwhile, Martínez noted, a 1970 treaty between the two countries stipulates that the possessions of a person sought in extradition can only be released to the requesting country – in this case, the United States – if and when extradition has been granted.

As for the political asylum claim, “Chambers’s status as an asylum applicant means the court can’t ignore its obligations to protect him, or give information about him to the country alleged to be persecuting him,” Martínez said.

Schnabel told the Guardian she retrieved Chambers’s personal effects last month at the prison where he is detained, including keys and identification. It is unclear whether Spain had already surrendered his phone to the US by then; Martínez said that the judge assured him on 20 July that the phone was in the court’s custody.

“I’m not surprised,” said Schnabel, referring to the apparent suspension of due process driven by the FBI’s request.

“It’s exactly in line with this administration not following the rules of the legal system.”

https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.title: ‘I’m not someone who has sex to music. I like uncomfortable silence’: Katherine Ryan’s honest playlist
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.author: As told to Rich Pelley
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.text:
The comedian unashamedly loves the Spice Girls’ Wannabe and cries to Boyz II Men, but which novelty song changed her life?

The first song I fell in love with My mother would sing and dance and cook and clean in the kitchen, as many 80s moms did, to divas like Madonna and Paula Abdul. Material Girl made me think: “This is who I want to be.”

The first single I bought I bought three records at the same time – Jagged Little Pill by Alanis Morissette, a Sheryl Crow single and Waterfalls by TLC – from Sam the Record Man in Sarnia, Ontario, with money I’d saved up from doing chores around the house. My uncle was always trying to influence me with Canadian music, and he wasn’t wrong for doing so.

The song I do at karaoke Probably Son of a Preacher Man. Although I think karaoke is the best way to let many people know straight away that you are an attention-seeking alcoholic, so I do try to stay away from it.

The song I inexplicably know every lyric to Give me a wine, and somehow I know all the words to the entire score of Hamilton, even though I’ve only seen it twice. [Sings Satisfied] “I’m a girl in a world in which my only job is to marry rich. My father has no sons, so I’m the one who has to social climb for one. I’m the oldest and the wittiest and the gossip in New York City is insidious.”

The best song to play at a party Anything early-2000s hip-hop or R&B, like Gasolina by Daddy Yankee.

The song I can no longer listen to What I Am by Will.i.am with Sesame Street. It makes me cry because he’s giving positive affirmations to young kids about being strong and being the best version of yourself. I can’t even get through it because it makes me so sad. I start worrying that these kids need Sesame Street and Will.i.am to tell them that they’re special.

The song I secretly like, but tell everyone I hate If I like a song, I just like it. Every Spice Girls song – I have no shame. I don’t need to be a music snob. I would crank up Wannabe any time, anywhere.

The best song to have sex to I’m not someone who has sex to music. I like uncomfortable silence. But if I had to choose, Let Me Love You by Mario.

The song that changed my life The Chanukah Song and Ode to My Car by Adam Sandler. I would have been about 11 or 12, and it was the first time I thought: “Oh, wait a minute. These can be funny and make music. You can make trauma a little bit funny, or at least be trauma-adjacent. You can make darker subjects funny.” I listened to his album over and over.

The song that gets me up in the morning Currently, I’m So Happy by Ms Rachel because we have so many small children. It has a really great message. I really love what’s available for kids now.

The song that makes me cry Water Runs Dry by Boyz II Men. I wanted to use it in The Duchess. It’s meant to be about a romantic partner, but whenever I heard it I thought of my daughter growing up. It’s about two people not communicating properly any more and wanting to get back to where they started, and I thought about that relationship changing as she got older.

Katherine Ryan has partnered with meal-subscription service Gousto. See what-the-food.co.uk for more.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: Signs suggest Thomas Markle Sr may be ‘sex offender of the grossest kind’, says Philippine minister
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Oliver Holmes
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Exclusive: Forensic analysis of found images continues as Meghan’s father denies possessing child sexual abuse images

All signs point to Thomas Markle Sr being a “possible sex offender of the grossest kind” although a full forensic investigation will give a “definitive picture”, the Philippine interior minister has told the Guardian.

Authorities in the south-east Asian country are analysing digital images allegedly belonging to the estranged father of the Duchess of Sussex that were said to have been found at his former home in Cebu. Meghan’s half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, reported to authorities last week that he had apparently discovered a stash of child sexual abuse images.

“In these cases where family disputes are mixed up, we have to consider all the angles,” said Jonvic Remulla, the interior minister. “Right now all signs point to a possible sex offender of the grossest kind. We want to be sure before we release the findings. The forensics data will be complete in a week.”

Remulla said a statement would be released once the data had been analysed, without giving a specific date. “Please give us a week to determine the contents and to come up with a definitive picture,” he said. “We will release a statement then.”

Markle Sr has denied possessing child sexual abuse images, telling the Daily Mail the accusations were “sick lies”.

Philippine police are also investigating a laptop found at the home in Cebu where Markle Sr had been living until he returned to the US earlier this year.

In a statement given to Agence France-Presse, Remulla said the Philippine national police inspected Markle’s former home and found a “trove of child pornography materials as well as a laptop”.

“The PNP will coordinate with their counterparts to locate and take appropriate legal actions against Mr Markle if found that there is sufficient evidence to charge him,” he said.

Markle told the Mail the computers had not been in his possession since he left Mexico with his son in 2025 and moved to the Philippines “for a fresh start”.

He said: “I’m shocked, I’m hurt and I’m very upset that my son is making these accusations against me. I could never do what I’m being accused of. It’s the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.

“This is bullshit. It’s just a bunch of lies. It’s sick. I have no idea why Tom is trying to destroy me with these lies.”

Meghan has said she is “deeply distressed” over the allegations, which were first reported in the Sun. She said she had broken off contact with her father to protect her children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five. He has never met them.

On Saturday, the Metropolitan police confirmed they gave a letter to Meghan in 2019 concerning “alleged offending” involving her father, but said they did not pass it on to other law enforcement agencies. Scotland Yard is considering whether to refer itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) to review its actions.

In a statement, a Met spokesperson said: “Following a thorough review of Met police systems and records, we have confirmed that in January 2019 we received a letter containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom. It was sent to the MPS [Metropolitan Police Service] Protection Command to raise concerns in relation to the security of the Duchess of Sussex.

“The letter was reviewed and a decision was made that it should be passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness. The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies.

“The MPS is reviewing the handling of this matter in 2019 and considering whether a referral to the IOPC is necessary to review our approach.”

In a statement on Friday issued through her spokesperson, the duchess said: “I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed.

“In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.

“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them. I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.

“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.”

She later said she had misremembered the year in which the Met had contacted her, and confirmed it had been 2019, not 2018 as she said on Friday.

A spokesperson for the duchess said: “In recalling events from more than seven years ago, without the benefit of a diary entry or contemporaneous record, it is understandable that she may have been mistaken by a few months.

“If the MPS holds a time-stamped record confirming that the letter was reviewed in 2019, that should be treated as the accurate reference point for when it was received and shared with the duchess.”

Sources said that although Meghan was made aware of the allegations in 2019, she had been unable to speak publicly to avoid jeopardising any future investigation and because speaking out could have resulted in legal action against her.

The Sun reported that Markle Jr told detectives in the Philippines he had discovered “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sexual abuse images on computers and mobile phones stored in four large boxes at the home in Cebu. Markle Jr, 60, said he had also contacted the FBI in the US, the Sun reported.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘Talking to every single person matters’: ‘prairie populists’ canvass the rural US heartland to win in midterms
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Rachel Leingang in Arthur, Nebraska
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Democratic and independent candidates stump the US midwest and prairie states, hoping to win over Republican strongholds

In this final stretch of the US midterm elections, Democrats and independents could win back communities and towns across America’s rural heartlands through a combination of resurgent “prairie populism”, local despair over the impact of Donald Trump’s agenda and an old-fashioned tenet of shoe-leather politics: showing up everywhere.

When Dan Osborn rolled into one of the most rural counties in Nebraska earlier this month, he started walking into businesses in the tiny main drag of Arthur, ready to meet whomever he could in the town of about 100.

For an independent making a run for the US Senate in a red state, every vote matters – even the ones in solidly Republican areas that political candidates often overlook. Osborn is touring all 93 counties in the state before election day; he has about a dozen left.

He’s one of several high-profile candidates seeking to win over areas the left and center ceded to Republicans in the last decade-plus. They’re running on populist messages rooted in the agrarian culture of their states, harkening back to politicians who stood up to corporate interests in previous generations by tying together farmers and workers who felt abandoned by both political parties.

In Iowa, the Democratic US Senate candidate, Josh Turek, calls himself a “commonsense prairie populist”. Sam Forstag, a Democrat running for Congress in Montana, has emphasized economic populism in his campaign to flip a red district, saying he wants to fight for “people like the kid I was growing up, whose belly is full because of food stamps”.

One writer referred to the politics of Kansas pastor Adam Hamilton, a Democrat, as a “populism of decency”, comparing Hamilton to William Jennings Bryan, a late-1900s evangelical populist from neighboring Nebraska who was known as the “great commoner”.

“For me, populism is not doing things through a political lens, through party lens, but your political north star always being, what is best for the people?” Turek said. “So for me, it’s what is best for Iowa. What’s best for Iowans, particularly what’s best for the middle class? What’s best for the workers? What’s best for rural communities? What’s best for small family farms?”

The candidates often push back on attempts to label their politics, and instead emphasize their pragmatism and willingness to work with politicians of any political background. Hamilton’s campaign, for instance, said he looked up to Bob Dole, the late longtime Republican US senator from Kansas, and said Hamilton would work with anyone.

“It’s how Kansas got the Farm Bill that has supported farmers and low-income kids for decades – by working together, Democrats and Republicans, to deliver for our state,” Hamilton’s campaign said.

This election cycle adds in datacenters and artificial intelligence to the populist platform, drawing on anti-corporate and anti-elite sentiments and a desire in rural areas to maintain their land, and their lifestyles, away from big tech interference.

“I’ve never seen our party so quickly adapt to where the voters were on an issue, and really leaning into where the voters were, versus poll-testing it to death,” said Jane Kleeb, the chair of the Nebraska Democratic party. “I think that’s been a lesson now for candidates to say it’s OK to talk about these local issues that people are talking about.”

In the late half of the 19th century, the left-of-center populist movement in the US focused on small farmers. The chief enemy was the railroads, said Cory Haala, a history professor at South Dakota State University who wrote a book on midwestern progressive populism.

Railroads bought up land and charged exorbitant rates to farmers who needed to ship their goods to other parts of the country. These farmers, often working together with organized labor, pushed to regulate railroads and stand against out-of-state interests, he said.

Some of the hallmarks of the movement persist today: a state-run bank in North Dakota, as well as a state-run flour mill; political parties such as the Democratic-Farmer-Labor alliance in Minnesota. Throughout the 20th century, progressive populism ebbed and flowed, with another peak in the 1980s in response to the farm crisis, when poor economic conditions led to massive small farm failures.

Populists and farming-focused Democrats won for decades throughout the prairie and midwestern states, from Tom Harkin in Iowa and Byron Dorgan in North Dakota to Tom Daschle in South Dakota and Bob Kerry in Nebraska. By 2013, though, USA Today called them a “fading species”.

“The conversations that we’re seeing around anti-monopoly, around antitrust and around datacenters are providing new flashpoints for the kind of populist organizing that was successful in the 1980s, in the 1930s and earlier than that,” Haala said. “It is an oftentimes out-of-state, kind of faceless corporate endeavor.”

Heidi Heitkamp, a former US senator who was the last Democrat to win statewide in North Dakota, noted that her win wasn’t that long ago – she won in 2012, then lost her re-election in 2018. Her successor, Republican Kevin Cramer, recently told Out of State, a rural policy newsletter, that he was glad he wasn’t on the ballot this year.

Heitkamp told the Guardian that the Democratic party decided it was easier to grow its base in the suburbs than to maintain any kind of presence in rural America. Chuck Schumer, the Democratic leader in the US Senate, said as much in 2016: “For every blue-collar Democrat we lose in western Pennsylvania, we will pick up two, three moderate Republicans in the suburbs in Philadelphia.”

Now, candidates rooted to their states, speaking to the economic trouble their neighbors are facing with high gas prices, tariffs, rural hospital healthcare woes and datacenters, are trying again to win over these voters. Democrats and independent populists need to respond directly to these concerns to build back their reputations and ultimately expand their representation, Heitkamp said.

“Rural areas are heavily dependent on being able to get in the car and afford to drive,” she said. “And where people once upon a time believed that this administration would solve those challenges, they’ve lost faith.”

In Arthur, Osborn first talked to a handful of locals at the town’s market, then went next door to the Bunkhouse – a restaurant with walls lined with antlers, animal skins and Nebraska license plates.

He grabbed a burger with a couple of supporters who heard he’d be in town, then talked to other tables, first apologizing for the frequency of political ads, and then explaining who he was. “I’m not a Republican, I’m not a Democrat, I just wanna work for workers,” he said.

Wins – or even narrow losses – in these areas would signal to national Democrats and independents where to invest in 2028, and how to run campaigns that can win over skeptical voters in rural states.

If Osborn loses, “then it’s just business as usual”, he said. “And then it’s just an R winning because they’re an R. And they don’t come to Arthur, because they don’t need to. And I don’t want to think about that future.”

Kristy Ferguson, who lives in Arthur, wasn’t sure if she would vote before she left town to winter in Florida, but a friend from Florida texted her and said she needed to vote for Osborn before taking off. She voted that morning, heard Osborn was in town and went to find him. She knew of three left-leaning people in town, and called them to come meet him, too.

“I didn’t really know there was a chance” he could win, Ferguson, a 72-year-old independent, said. “I hope he can be in the Senate, so that’s a valuable vote.”

Ray, a 75-year-old Democrat from Arthur who met with Osborn at the Bunkhouse, said he liked the fact that Osborn wasn’t rich, that he was a Nebraska local and that he wanted to help people. He could remember when gas prices were 30 cents a gallon, he said; now they were “ridiculous”.

Does he think Osborn can win? “I hope he does, but who knows,” he said. “If people get fed up enough with these other clowns that are running.”

Osborn, a former union leader, brings together workers and farmers in his politics, like the prairie populists did to stand up to corporate interests. He’s running on an anti-corruption, anti-two party system, pro-working class platform. “When we talk about prairie populism, that’s the counter to populism – just enriching your buddies,” he told the voters.

He next went to Hyannis, a slightly bigger town about 30 minutes away through rolling hills and whipping wind, for another small meeting, this time in a bank conference room with skeptical questions from the few people who showed up. They asked him about his stance on abortion, social programs, immigration and Islam. On abortion: “I’m 100% pro-life in my own personal life. I would never advocate for that. But I’m also pro-choice.” On social programs, he wants to protect social security and keep it solvent. He supports reforming immigration policies and says Nebraska needs immigrants to fill jobs. And on Islam: “I think everybody has the freedom to worship however they want.”
