A Wall Street Journal headline had bleak news for the GOP, saying: “Republicans are facing the worst political environment in farm country in decades.”

All this dismay could go far to elect Democratic Senate candidates in rural states: Josh Turek in Iowa, Adam Hamilton in Kansas, Roy Cooper in North Carolina and James Talarico in Texas, not to mention the independent progressive Dan Osborn in Nebraska.

John Tsitrian, a South Dakota business executive who writes about rural America, didn’t mince words about who’s to blame.

“Farmers are hurting thanks to Trump’s apocalyptic screw-up,” he wrote. Perhaps the biggest screw-up, in Tsitrian’s view, has been the loss of global markets caused by Trump’s never-ending trade wars, which he said have caused long-lasting “structural damage” to US farmers.

Before Trump’s first term, the US and Brazil each provided about 40% of China’s soybean imports. But as a result of Trump’s repeated trade wars with China and China’s search for more reliable, less antagonistic trading partners, the US now provides just 23% of China’s soybeans, with Brazil providing over 60% and Argentina 10%. With China importing around $60bn worth of soybeans annually, that means a painful loss of $10bn a year in US soybean exports.

Trump has long been known to seek to shovel money, often lots of money, to people who are angry at him. Just look at his shameless plan to hand out $5,000 to every American adult.

Seeing how upset farmers are about sky-high diesel prices, Trump announced a new handout on Monday at a rally in Kansas – he promised $8bn in emergency aid to US farmers in what he called the Harvest Fuel Relief Program. It seemed like a desperate, last-ditch effort to rescue Kansas’s incumbent Republican senator, Roger Marshall. That came after Trump announced a previous $12bn bailout of farmers last December.

While acknowledging that farmers need emergency aid, South Dakota’s Tsitrian wrote, “Today’s tough farm economy, in regular need of federal cash infusions, is the result of a disaster that has a specific name attached to it: Donald Trump. Unlike most disasters, this one was utterly foreseeable.”

Across rural America, there is fast-increasing frustration, dismay and anger about economic conditions, Trump’s policies and GOP lawmakers whom farmers have long supported.

“This Republican-led Congress has not done their job,” said Hansen, the Farm Union president. “They have not helped our nation’s farmers in our time of need, and it is time for a change.”

Steven Greenhouse is a journalist and author, focusing on labor and the workplace, as well as economic and legal issues

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Harry Styles says his laptop has been dead for six years. Is he just showing off? | Emma Beddington
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Emma Beddington
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
He is either being insincere – knowing he could buy an entire Apple store if he wanted – or he is genuinely overwhelmed by tech. If it’s the latter, he has my sympathy

Clips of the “epic conversation” (rambling, blokey chat) Rolling Stone orchestrated between Harry Styles and Thom Yorke keep appearing online, and none more often than the one in which Styles declared his laptop has been dead for about six years. “I don’t know where the charger is,” Styles laughed, prompting a predictable rash of “his computer is NOT OK” jokes from 6 Music dads everywhere.

Is this charmingly relatable, or … not? One personal finance influencer declared it “a deeply unlikeable clip”, seeing it as the kind of tech-free flex you can get away with only if you are rich and famous. It’s true that the ability to protect your peace by withdrawing from the brain-liquefying churn of online life is a privilege inaccessible to most people, who need tech to function and earn a living. Opting out means delegating digital drudgery to other people: Christopher Nolan’s determination not to have email must be a massive pain for his entourage. I bet Ed Sheeran not having a smartphone is extremely inconvenient, too – someone else must always have to put the hotel into Google Maps, arrange the Deliveroo dinner and order the Uber.

This dead laptop business does feel slightly disingenuous – Styles could have an entire Apple store delivered if he fancies a tech upgrade. But I’m inclined to feel more tolerant. He says he uses his phone to write songs, and maybe there is an element of overwhelm at play? I’m always losing cables and procrastinating over tech issues. “I don’t understand why you’re waiting for it to die when you’ll really be in trouble,” my husband said crossly to me this morning as I fought to turn off my ancient phone, which had decided once again that typing was forbidden. But I’m filled with dread and confusion at the thought of replacing it (what model, how many GBs, must I engage with the Cloud?) and my life isn’t too busy or demanding; I can’t imagine what it’s like when you are a global icon on a world tour.

So, in case he is floundering not flexing – Harry, check your sock drawer. That’s where I found my charger last time I lost it.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Could Europe’s autumn of discontent threaten the survival of the EU? | Catherine De Vries
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Catherine De Vries
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Anger on the streets could increasingly turn against the EU itself if it can’t show why cooperation makes people’s lives better

Europe is living through an autumn of unusual discontent. What protesters from Paris to Milan to Madrid share is a deepening anxiety about the future and a growing anger at the gap between what they expect from their governments and what they feel governments are delivering, whether the issue is unaffordable housing, stagnant wages, the spiralling cost of living or failing schools.

The electoral consequences of the failure to get a grip on this public anger are already with us. Spain goes to the polls next month in a snap election called after parliament voted down key housing reforms. France begins the process of electing a new president in April, while Poland, Italy and a string of smaller states will vote before the end of 2027. The stakes could not be higher.

At the same time, national leaders face mounting pressures from abroad. Issues such as Ukraine, uncertainty over US security guarantees and economic competition with China demand more European cooperation, even as national politics makes this increasingly difficult. Governments face popular demands to deliver security and prosperity, just as their capacity to do so independently is shrinking. This leaves Europe with a difficult question: how can countries whose leaders are increasingly struggling at home find the common ground needed to act together abroad?

If the EU did not exist, Europeans would have every reason to invent it. Together, its members form a market of 450 million people and an economy of almost €19tn, the third largest after the US and China. No individual EU country comes close to that weight on its own. Germany, the largest, has 84 million people and an economy about a sixth the size of the US’s. Twenty of the 27 member states have fewer than 12 million inhabitants, less than half of Shanghai’s. In a world of tariffs and export controls, it is scale that secures a seat at the table.

But this rationale for cooperation does not make the EU’s survival inevitable. This political project has often been declared on the brink of collapse; the most recent crises include Brexit, the pandemic and energy shocks. Yet it has proved remarkably durable, responding with improvised solutions that previously seemed impossible.

The very traits that infuriate Eurosceptics – slow decision-making, endless negotiations and messy compromises – are, counterintuitively, sources of strength for Europe. The dispersion of power between governments, parliaments, courts and EU institutions makes the system hard to capture and compromises tend to stick.

The EU’s staying power lies in its capacity to adapt despite disagreements, while helping countries achieve what is termed “effective sovereignty”. Nominal sovereignty is the right to decide alone, even when deciding alone – as the UK has discovered to its cost since it left the club supposedly to regain its sovereignty – changes little. Effective sovereignty is the capacity to shape outcomes on energy, trade, migration or defence that no European state can control by itself. And the EU has itself adapted: its fully paid-up members remain the core but non-members such as Norway and Switzerland participate on defence, security, energy and economic policy. The EU has an interest in bringing Britain back into closer cooperation too, even if not exactly as it looked pre-Brexit.

But the EU’s resilience should not be taken for granted. Negotiations over the next seven-year budget, worth almost €2tn, show just how hard it is to achieve consensus. While everyone agrees on the need for greater European security and economic competitiveness, countries can’t agree on who should foot the bill. France, for example, is pushing for new EU-wide taxes, which others resist.

Even so, growing domestic political instability does not necessarily mean there will be paralysis in Brussels. Quite the opposite – it creates an impetus to act. With France’s presidential election approaching, Emmanuel Macron has urged fellow leaders to strike a budget deal by Christmas, warning that political room for manoeuvre would shrink in the new year if Marine Le Pen succeeds him.

Le Pen no longer talks about taking France out of the euro or a Brexit-style referendum. But her platform would undermine the union from within, turning the EU into a “Europe of Nations” and threatening cuts to France’s contribution to the EU budget.

Whether political change comes through elections, protests or new compromises in Brussels, public discontent cannot simply be negotiated away. This brings us back to the streets. French, Italian and Spanish citizens want functioning public services, affordable housing, economic and national security, and a sense that they have some control over their futures.

Younger Europeans, in particular, face growing uncertainty about their economic prospects, from finding affordable housing to securing stable employment. So far, this pessimism has not translated into widespread rejection of the EU. Recent polling suggests that young Europeans remain among the EU’s strongest supporters, with 90% favouring greater unity among member states and 78% wanting the EU to have more resources to act.

This gives Europe an opportunity, but also a responsibility, to turn that support into tangible improvements in their lives. That is the real test in the years ahead. Decisions about defence, industrial policy and social protection will involve difficult trade-offs, and not everyone will benefit equally. But if European cooperation becomes better at preserving institutions than at responding to citizens’ concerns, the discontent now spilling on to the streets could increasingly turn against the EU itself. The EU has repeatedly shown that it can survive political crises. Now it must ensure that the people living through them can do more than merely get by.

Catherine De Vries is professor of political science at IE University in Madrid. She is the co-author with Alexandros Kentikelenis of How Europe Survives

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Premier League: 10 talking points from the weekend’s action
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Guardian sport
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Bournemouth’s transfer nous puts United to shame, Araújo is winning admirers at Anfield and Suzuki adapts swiftly at Villa

The three Bournemouth goalscorers cost a combined £85m, joining from Vasco da Gama, Middlesbrough, and Porto. The Cherries are smart at investing, far more so than Manchester United, who have wasted a lot of money by failing to look outside the box for players like Rayan, Marcus Tavernier and Evanilson. United may not have the wealth they previously showed in the transfer market but Bournemouth are showing what can be done within a budget and, more importantly, will be able to make a profit on signings. United, however, only know losses as everyone’s price tag diminishes the moment they come through the Old Trafford door. Jason Wilcox and others can point to certain factors that are against them but there are quality signings to be made at the right price if you have the ability to find them. Will Unwin

Aston Villa were quite happy to sell Emiliano Martínez but many feared it would be difficult to find an upgrade on the World Cup-winning goalkeeper. They have seemingly done so in the form of the £30m signing Zion Suzuki, who was superb against Manchester City. Nicolas Jackson’s goals stole the headlines but Suzuki’s bounty of saves ensured that Villa were victorious, while also impressing with his distribution. ”He’s ambitious. I think it’s very important, his mentality,” Unai Emery said. “Of course, we need a keeper first to save us in the goal, but as well we need one keeper to try to help us in our buildup. And in buildup, he’s a really fantastic player because he can play short, he can understand where is the superiority to break the opponent’s press. He has qualities to do long ball, getting our players in attack. So, we are very, very impressed how he adapted so quick with us.” WU

Aside from the reaction to the half-time and full-time scores from Old Trafford, the biggest noise at Anfield was generated by Ronald Araújo showing no mercy in his challenges on Malick Yalcouyé and Charalampos Kostoulas. The on-loan Barcelona defender immediately endeared himself to the Kop with his commitment and quality, and was again in commanding form to help Andoni Iraola record his first Premier League home win as Liverpool head coach. “I think we all enjoyed watching Ronald fighting,” said Iraola. “He’s very good in the duels. Even the first goal, he wins two duels in a row and defensively he’s been really, really good. I’m happy for him because I’ve taken him out in the last two games because we needed more offensive things. But he has continued working with no issues and today we needed him more. He has given a very, very good 90 minutes.” Andy Hunter

João Pedro is unlikely to make a swift return after picking up an injury in training. The Chelsea striker missed the defeat to Tottenham and had a scan on Sunday. Xabi Alonso did not sound optimistic after the Spurs game. The expectation is João Pedro will miss this week’s games against Liverpool and Manchester United as a minimum, leaving Alonso with problems in attack. It was strange he did not start Danny Welbeck against Spurs. Chelsea had no focal point and there are questions over their depth. Emmanuel Emegha, another struggling with injury, is yet to play since joining from Strasbourg. It is fair to wonder if selling Nicolas Jackson to Villa was the right move. Chelsea have played two league games without João Pedro this season and have lost both without scoring a goal. Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers are not as effective without him. Jacob Steinberg

Barney Ronay: Glitch in Chelsea’s coding costs Alonso while resurgent Spurs are all systems go

Mikel Arteta says he has been compiling a dossier of evidence of other managers straying outside the technical area after the Arsenal manager was shown a yellow card during the 2-0 win over Everton. It was his second of the season and leaves the Spaniard at risk of suspension if he gets one more, although Arteta suggested he is by no means the worst offender. “There are managers who have the record in the league, 36 times in 10 minutes [they] leave the touchline – no yellows,” he said, naming no names. “I am clipping all of that so I now have a massive storage of images, so if somebody comes to me I can say: ‘I am not in the record yet.’ Somebody else has the record so let’s see. Then it’s 36 yellow cards in 10 minutes for the managers. I don’t know what we are going to do – let’s see.” Ed Aarons

Nico González cost Manchester City £50m when they signed him early in 2025, as part of that January spree as Pep Guardiola tried to arrest the first real slump of his Premier League career. Although he started nine league games that season and 17 last, González made very little impact at the Etihad. He probably wasn’t even the best Nico González in world football, given the Argentinian winger’s performances for Juventus and Atlético. But the Spanish Nico González clearly is a player of substance, his calm in midfield one of the few undoubted positives for Newcastle so far this season. Only Lewis Hall has made more tackles per game than him, he set up Sven Botman’s goal at Coventry, while he’s made more key passes per game than anybody other than Harvey Barnes. At £48m, he may end up representing extremely good value. Jonathan Wilson

To ask a question that might be a segment on the Football Cliches podcast, is there a more “swirling litter” venue in the Premier League than the Stadium of Light? At this point it should be obvious this was not a classic. In part that is down the conditions – long balls ran away from players on both sides with frequency, and crisp packets were the only thing to trouble the nets at either end. Managing the Europa League was always going to be a challenge for Sunderland and returning from a midweek trip to Poland to earn a point against a team who have had a week to prepare is a good result, even if the Black Cats finish the weekend at the foot of the table. Tom Bassam

In spectacular style, Oscar Bobb’s wait for a first Premier League goal for Fulham came to an end at Coventry. Bobb was signed in January, fitting the recruitment template that brought success and stability under Marco Silva, a manager adept at regenerating talent. Social media footage from the away end showed Fulham fans ask what Bobb, weaving and bobbing, was doing only for him to feint past two Coventry defenders and score. That broke the deadlock when Coventry appeared fully capable of claiming a point or better. It remains to be seen whether Álvaro Arbeloa possesses the some restorative powers as Silva. After two wins in succession, two clean sheets and a first win away from Craven Cottage since February, early-season panic has dissipated. For now. If survival is Fulham’s first objective, then successive wins over the promoted teams Hull and Coventry were minimum requirements. Though should Fulham aim much higher? Silva departed because his ambitions were not met. John Brewin

Brentford are still yet to win away from home in the league but are also unbeaten on their travels. The draws at Leeds, Bournemouth and Aston Villa can be considered decent results, but this goes in the missed opportunity pile. So far Hull have presented a stiffer challenge at MKM Stadium than predicted, but in terms of expectations for Brentford this fixture has more in common with playing Sunderland at home than it does with their previous draws on the road. Against Sunderland and at Hull, Keith Andrews’ side struggled when the onus was on the them to make the game. The Bees play like they would rather not have the ball. In this one, they had plenty of shots – 14 in total – but only Dango Ouattara and belatedly Jaidon Anthony truly troubled Konstantinos Tzolakis. Brentford need Igor Thiago firing again. TB

With Nottingham Forest the Premier League’s joint-lowest scorers, the pressure on Liam Delap is increasing. At Ipswich, where he was a rare bright spot with 12 goals in the relegation season of 2024-25, Delap was booed on every touch. The jeers got louder when each of his four attempts on goal missed their target. Only three of 18 Premier League shots in a Forest shirt have been on target. The raw materials that Chelsea moved for in summer 2025 remain present, the physical prowess and ability to find promising positions. The finishing touches are, at present, lacking, when Forest need someone to start scoring. Failing to take their chances at Portman Road left Forest in the relegation zone, endangering Oliver Glasner, when the ownership is trigger-happy with managers. Chris Wood, previously Forest’s talisman, came on in the 89th minute for Delap, but has been no super-sub so far, without a goal or assist from seven cameo league appearances. JB

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Wolff hails Antonelli’s US Grand Prix demolition as the Italian’s ‘best race yet’
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Giles Richards in Austin
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
The Mercedes team principal, Toto Wolff, has paid tribute to his driver Kimi Antonelli, who all but closed out his first Formula One world championship with a victory at the US Grand Prix that Wolff described as the Italian’s best race yet.

After the win at the Circuit of the Americas Wolff was also at pains to point out the considerable efforts made by a host of others in bringing the young Italian to having one hand on a record-breaking title.

After his victory in Austin, Antonelli needs to finish only ninth or better at the Mexican Grand Prix this weekend. He could finish outside the points as long as he is also in front of his teammate George Russell and Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton, the only two other drivers still mathematically in the running. If he seals it in Mexico City he will become F1’s youngest world champion at just 20 years old.

His victory at the Circuit of the Americas from pole position with a controlled, dominant run largely at the front of the field, was his ninth of the season and has moved him to within touching distance of the title, and Wolff heralded it as Antonelli’s best drive.

“On Kimi’s side obviously the main headline is that [it is] for me the best race that he’s delivered so far,” said Wolff. “Getting off the start with the inferior tyre and then controlling it at all times. Exceptional. I think he’s outperformed the car.”

When asked if it matched Antonelli’s superb drive from 19th to victory at the Italian Grand Prix, Wolff acknowledged that that too was special but insisted he felt the win in Austin was up there with that drive and Antonelli concurred.

“Monza was a super special one and one that I will remember forever,” Antonelli said. “But this one probably in terms of execution was better, because the way we built up and the way we built the performance throughout the weekend was very good.”

Wolff believed it was all the more impressive given how difficult Antonelli’s rookie season had been in 2025 when at times he struggled with the car and made mistakes that caused some to question whether Mercedes had been correct to promote him to the team so soon. Doubts he felt Antonelli had comprehensively silenced.

“There are many people that said last year after nine races without points, he shouldn’t be in a Mercedes. People in other teams that said he shouldn’t even be in Formula One,” said Wolff. “All of that now is extremely satisfying to see what he’s able to deliver, how he’s working with the team, with Bono [race engineer, Peter Bonnington] and yielding the results. But it wasn’t an easy road.

“It’s been 30 or more years that I’ve tried to understand racing drivers’ brains and I still don’t know what has happened over the winter. His ability to process and deliver something that’s outstanding which we didn’t see coming.”

Mercedes took Antonelli on as part of their driver development programme when the Italian was 12 years old and have supported him through karting and in the feeder series to F1 since then.

Wolff was the driving force behind bringing Antonelli into the team to take Lewis Hamilton’s seat when the British driver left for Ferrari. Wolff was insistent he felt the young Italian was ready to step up, however he maintained that Antonelli’s success should not be viewed as having come from nowhere but rather was the product of many years and the input of many people.

“I wasn’t the one responsible for it,” said Wolff. “It was teamwork. It was our junior team around [Mercedes’ driver development advisor] Gwen [Lagrue] that discovered him when he was 11.

“Credit to that group that have developed him over the many years. I read an interview [with Ferrari vice chairman] Piero Ferrari last week where he said: ‘What a talent, he reminds me of Niki Lauda’. And I’m thinking, people don’t get that this is the work of nine years.

“The development of nine years, the hardship over nine years, the integration of the team, the working with the engineers, millions in the development of his career, of his ability, of his character together with his parents. It’s just not that it landed like this.”

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Three roles and a goal: USMNT’s ‘super player’ Alex Freeman is breaking out for Villarreal
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Jeff Rueter
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
The Orlando City product scored his first goal in La Liga, playing three positions in a comeback win over Valencia

While most of La Liga’s oxygen was consumed by the first El Clásico since José Mourinho’s return to Real Madrid, another rivalry put Alex Freeman in spotlight position.

While not among the most storied derbies in Spain, Valencia v Villarreal has grown into a regional contest with considerable teeth since billionaire Fernando Roig bought Villarreal rather than following his brother, Paco, as the head of Valencia.

For Freeman, who came off the bench in last week’s Champions League loss to Liverpool, his first taste of the rivalry on Saturday came in a somewhat unfamiliar position – left-back. The 22-year-old largely looked the part away from his usual spot on the right, living up to Mauricio Pochettino’s recent praise of his reading of the game.

Freeman had opportunities to test his left foot, creating a pair of chances before Valencia opened the scoring from the penalty spot. It seemed Villarreal’s best chance at an equalizer would come through a set piece, but instead it came from the run of play – and Freeman was there to finish it.

The Orlando City product switched back to his usual station at right-back after a few 65th-minute substitutions, and was asked to provide width as a right midfielder subbed off. It quickly proved a wise adjustment. Villarreal worked down the left in the 69th minute, lopping a cross to Freeman just inside the area. Freeman prodded the ball through a thicket of Valencian bodies, finding the narrowest of windows between the goalkeeper and his last defender, to score his first goal in La Liga.

Freeman was later moved to a third station, moonlighting at right midfield as Iñigo Pérez brought on another defender. While not directly involved in the last-gasp winner, Freeman kept his run down the flank even as Villarreal worked up the left and center to keep the defense laterally stretched. Most Villarreal players collapsed to their knees as the final whistle blew. Not Freeman, who instead walked around and congratulated his teammates.

After the game, Pérez lauded Freeman as one of four “top-level” full-backs available to him who “are fundamental, vital to developing my vision of football.”

“We need them to be very versatile, and in this case, Alex is a super player,” Pérez added. “He can easily play center-back, full-back, left-back, further forward, wing-back; he’s even played on both flanks for his national team. Therefore, this versatility and dynamism, combined with his skill level, means that, for a coach, the confidence to field him in any position or ask him to do things that might surprise him makes me bolder, and, as you’ve seen, he’s able to play with astonishing composure.”

Named man of the match for his efforts, it’s easy to forget that Freeman hasn’t even spent a year in Europe. He only officially left Orlando on 29 January, and Villarreal look smart for signing him before his star-making turn at the World Cup, securing his future for an initial fee of $4m.

His next move may require an extra digit, though there are still elements to be refined. Valencia’s veteran forwards found it too easy to get better positioning to beat Freeman in the air to aerial distribution, planting firmer in their stances and reading angles a half-second quicker than the American. Some of that could come down to playing on the opposite flank from his usual spot, but it’s still an adjustment one can expect him to make with increased playing time. He has previously struggled to use his dribble to create extra space from his defender, although he did have a few valuable upfield scampers before Villarreal were reduced to 10 men in the 79th minute.

It was the latest strong shift for a player who Pochettino has long seen as having world-class potential.

“He is so humble, he has an amazing profile, he always listens,” Pochettino said after Freeman scored in the US’s World Cup win over Australia on 19 June. “You really enjoy being with him, coaching him, and [he] is an amazing player. For me, [he has potential] to be one of the best players at his position in the world.”

Freeman is already a rarity for US men playing abroad: a defender who can change games for a Champions League-level club. No player has become a brighter star since Pochettino arrived as US manager, and Freeman is only just getting started.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Fernandes gamble leaves Carrick to carry the can for United’s institutional failures | Will Unwin
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Will Unwin at Old Trafford
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Leaving out his captain was doomed to fail but so are the club under the current leadership and the fans at Old Trafford know that all too well

Dropping your captain, who has held the team together for most of the past five years, is a bold move from a man whose job is on the line. It was very much a make-or-break decision from Michael Carrick to leave out Bruno Fernandes against Bournemouth. It did not work and Carrick knew the consequences if it failed and will probably pay the price for it, but he should not be alone.

Carrick said the decision to drop the Portuguese playmaker was purely based on football reasons but criticising his manager after the desperate defeat to Como cannot have helped. Clearly Carrick disagreed with his captain’s comments on the lack of pressing in the Champions League fixture. It was somewhat telling that Lisandro Martínez kept his place despite pointing out the director of football, Jason Wilcox, was a hindrance to the club the previous week.

Fernandes has been a long way from his best this season, with three goals and one assist in the Premier League, all in one game against Ipswich. It would have been justifiable to give someone else an opportunity in the No 10 role, especially when the squad contains far too many of those. But then, no one at United is in form, so keeping an angry Fernandes in position may have made more sense. United have won almost half the Premier League fixtures Fernandes has started since he joined in 2020, and less than a third when he is absent.

Some question Fernandes’ attitude based on his complaints when things are not going right, but that is his way of showing he cares. He may not be a leader in the Bryan Robson or Roy Keane mould but is certainly the one who sets the example, shown by a banner in the Stretford End depicting the two former captains and Eric Cantona alongside the word “STANDARDS”. Those have dipped here. This is a mid-table team, made worse by a lack of desire.

Everything was pedestrian in thought and execution. One promising attack lost momentum and United decided the most sensible course of action was to pass the ball all the way back to Senne Lammens, resulting in deserved boos. It felt like a moment that indicated Carrick’s days were coming to an end.

Hypotheticals are pointless, as was Youri Tielemans, Fernandes’ replacement. The central midfielder has not impressed since joining from Aston Villa in the summer and the extra responsibility for an experienced player did not spur him on. He was ponderous in midfield, repeatedly losing the ball as he struggled to cope with the pace of the game against a Bournemouth team eager to press and hunt in pairs. The No 10 is supposed to be a creative influence in the final third but the Belgian was a lost boy against men.

A poorly defended first goal resulted in the inevitable cutting by the cameras to a sullen Fernandes sunk into his seat on the bench. It was a goal that summed up the mood at Old Trafford, Rayan was left in space to volley home at the back post after Ayden Heaven needlessly gave away a free-kick. He looked miserable and the majority inside the ground felt exactly the same.

United lack pace across the pitch so require someone in key areas to speed up play, but Tielemans is not capable of doing so. His main influence on the match was getting booked in the first half, which all but confirmed his exit at the break. It was telling that Carrick turned to Matheus Cunha to take over the duties behind the labouring Bryan Mbeumo in the desperate hope he could spark his team into life.

Carrick has been left with an unbalanced squad, lacking quality in key areas. It would be hard to suggest on Sunday’s viewing that United were the Champions League team and Bournemouth in the Europa League. The Cherries can boast a wealth of smart recruitment, acquiring the likes of Adrien Truffert and Rayan – two players who would walk into the United team – for half a Harry Maguire.

The shambles of the third goal was on Lammens and Maguire, the former for running out too fast and the latter for not knowing how to run fast. Evanilson nipped in and flashed in the definitive game-ender. It sent Fernandes back to the bench with the expression of a man who had sipped sour milk. The final insult came when Carrick sent on the academy graduate Shea Lacey and left his captain to brood.

It is not solely one bottle; the whole dairy has curdled. Carrick can take some of the blame; the Glazers, Sir Jim Ratcliffe, Wilcox and Omar Berrada should receive more. United are not fit for purpose and the supporters’ ire was largely aimed at the directors’ box, demanding the owners sell up and go home, with slightly less savoury language. The Old Trafford faithful know where the fault lies, offering more creativity than any of their team with a fine repertoire of chants against the hierarchy, most pointedly at Wilcox, whose signings left Carrick in trouble before the season started.

Carrick had his name chanted, the full-time boos not for him. The manager – for now – did a lap of honour, cheered by the fans who jeered the players. Another era is nearing an end and finding reasons to be optimistic would be a greater waste of time than playing up front for United. Change will almost certainly come but it will not be enough.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Anthropic files for listing on US stock market with valuation of more than $1.5tn
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Blake Montgomery
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Market debut of the company behind the chatbot Claude will be one of the largest in US history

Anthropic has publicly filed for a stock market listing, one of the largest debuts in history. The company’s float on the US market is likely to be a high-water mark in the multitrillion-dollar AI boom and a test of its financial viability.

Analysts and investors have valued the San Francisco-based company, founded in 2021, at more than $1.5tn. The company, which will will list under the symbol ANT, confidentially filed with US financial regulators for an initial public offering in June.

“We believe AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history,” the company’s investor prospectus reads. Anthropic researchers and executives have repeatedly warned of AI’s potential to cause human extinction.

A leader in the race to create powerful artificial intelligence models and a bellwether of the American AI boom, Anthropic offers the chatbot Claude as its flagship product, which has text generation features as well as advanced coding and cybersecurity capabilities. CEO Dario Amodei founded the company after quitting OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT.

Anthropic’s audited filings will offer the first public glimpse of its financial health, which have been the object of intense speculation in recent months as questions of a potential AI bubble swirl.

The company detailed rapidly rising revenue in the prospectus: $41m in 2023, $386m in 2024, $4.585bn in 2025 (an increase of more than 1,000%), then $16.286bn in the first six months of 2026 alone. The company disclosed that, as of the end of June, it had raised $141.1bn.

Despite the increasing revenue, Anthropic disclosed a net loss of $80bn for the first half of 2026.

As of 30 September, Anthropic said it had more than 14,000 enterprise customers – 11,900 of which had $100,000 or more of revenue, more than 1,900 that had $1m or more revenue and about 250 enterprise customers that had $10m or more revenue.

“The speed and depth of our enterprise customer adoption are powerful evidence of Claude’s position at the frontier of AI,” Anthropic executives wrote.

The filing contains some of the hyperbolic language characteristic of AI companies predicting the miraculous potential of their technology. Describing the potential of AI agents, semi-autonomous chatbots that can carry out tasks on behalf of users, Anthropic executives wrote: “The result is something without historical precedent: what we refer to as a country of geniuses in a datacenter, available to every organization and sector of the economy.”

However, investing in Anthropic and the development of a model that the company claims could revolutionize knowledge work across industries comes with a great deal of risk. Anthropic listed more than 90 pages of potential risks to its business. For one, a “substantial portion” of the company’s revenue comes from a limited number of customers and losing any of them could put a huge dent in their revenue. A quarter of Anthropic’s revenue comes from its top five customers, though no single customer represents more than 10% of their business.

The company also has incurred $6.2bn in debt as it built out its infrastructure and grew its business, which includes convertible notes issued to Amazon Web Services in 2023.

The misuse of AI and Claude in particular also poses a considerable risk to Anthropic’s business. When it comes to AI, there are four categories of potential risk, executives wrote: misuse by bad actors, loss of control, authoritarian abuse and economic disruption. Anthropic’s most capable models have “capabilities that could provide meaningful assistance to malicious actors seeking to develop chemical, biological, or other dangerous weapons”, the company’s executives wrote. The company deploys technical safeguards, “but such safeguards are incomplete, may be outdated in light of evolving threat models, have been and may in the future again be circumvented, or may fail to operate as intended.”

The company disclosed that in September 2025, staffers documented what they believe was the first large-scale cyberattack that didn’t rely on significant human intervention. Anthropic “detected and assessed with high confidence that a Chinese state-sponsored hacking group manipulated our Claude Code tool into attempting infiltration into roughly 30 global targets, including large technology companies, financial institutions, chemical manufacturing companies, and government agencies”.

Anthropic has been embroiled in a feud with the Trump administration over the use of the startup’s products in warfare, which culminated in the designation of the company as a supply chain risk, a first for an American company. This prevents any military agency from contracting with Anthropic. The company has challenged the blacklisting.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: High-level delegation visits Iran to try to avert flare-up with US and Israel
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey travel to Tehran as bellicose rhetoric heightens

High-level diplomatic delegations from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have travelled to Tehran in an attempt to prevent renewed fighting between Iran and the US and Israel as rhetoric sharpens on both sides.

Security officials and diplomats at Monday’s meeting were expected to discuss how Iran could persuade the Houthis in Yemen to end their crippling missile and drone attacks on infrastructure in Saudi Arabia. With fighting raging across Yemen, the Houthis claimed to have closed Riyadh airport and inflicted heavy damage on the Saudi economy.

The officials were also understood to be discussing Iran’s possible inclusion in a new security pact involving Islamic countries.

The Saudi defence minister, Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, and the head of Turkey’s intelligence service, Ibrahim Kalın, were to meet Iran’s top security officials and negotiators to push for a deal between Tehran and Washington.

The three countries signed a defence agreement in Mecca in August. Some in Iran feared the deal was constructed to challenge Tehran, but the signatory countries have insisted it is simply a mutual defence pact.

The balance between exploring a new long-term security architecture and demanding Iran start to compromise in the conflicts in which it is engaged will be critical. It is possible the two sides came to the meeting with different priorities.

The Iranian foreign ministry has often proposed a security pact for the region in which Iran, as opposed to the US, plays a role, and the US-Iran conflict has potentially reopened the debate among Gulf states about whether the heavy presence of US bases in their countries is a source of reassurance or insecurity. Oman is one Gulf state to have explored a regional security pact that includes Iran.

No Gulf state openly supported the US-Israeli attack on Iran either last year or this February, but some have covertly cooperated in the operations. Iran has sought to defend itself by attacking US bases and energy infrastructure in the Gulf states.

Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei, said the meeting could pave the way for broader regional cooperation on security based on shared interest.

“The events of the last two years, especially the past eight months, have shown that sustainable and reliable security in our region will only be possible by building trust and cooperation among the countries of the region,” he said.

Javad Zarif, a former foreign minister and long-term advocate of a regional security alliance called for “a comprehensive regional network based on non-aggression, mutual trust building, and shared prosperity”.

“Regional security is not imported, it must be created by the people of this very region together,” he said.

He published his message alongside an image of verses 103 and 159 from Surah Ali ‘Imran, the third chapter of the Qur’an. The verses emphasise being saved from a fiery pit by avoiding division, fostering unity, seeking forgiveness and consulting others.

The meeting takes place against a backdrop of continued Pentagon briefings about a major US military buildup in preparation for a possible assault after the midterm elections. Qatari mediators, it was confirmed, spent much of Sunday in Tehran seeking terms for Iran to reopen the strait of Hormuz.

Israeli media reports claimed the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has been trying to browbeat the military into provoking a war with Iran before the Israeli elections on Tuesday.

Donald Trump’s repeated call for Netanyahu to be re-elected only adds to the mood in the region that modern-day US and Israel have the potential to be a long-term source of insecurity in the region.

The idea of a security pact with Iran will be resisted in large parts of the Middle East after the damage Tehran has been prepared to inflict on the economies of the region, either directly or through the use of intermediaries such as the Houthis. Iranian hardliners also increasingly argue Iran’s security best lies in trying to assemble a nuclear bomb, ending the fatwa on the possession of a weapon of mass destruction.

A pact likely to take many months to negotiate may also not be a solution to Washington’s demand that Iran reopen the strait of Hormuz before US sanctions are lifted.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: Russell Brand had ‘insane sexual appetite’ and bad behaviour on ‘another level’, trial told
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Emine Sinmaz
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Brand, charged with rape and sexual assault, was ‘sleeping with people day and night’, former assistant alleges

Russell Brand had an “insane sexual appetite” and his bad behaviour was on “another level” to that of other celebrities, his former personal assistant has told a court.

Helen Berger told police she had seen Brand treat women badly and that she once had to stop his mother and girlfriend walking in on him having sex with someone in his dressing room.

She also alleged she witnessed the 51-year-old comedian receiving oral sex in a toilet cubicle and once found a celebrity leaving his bedroom in the morning.

Brand faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999. He denies all the charges.

Wearing a grey suit and white shirt, Brand sat still in the dock as statements from prosecution witnesses were read to Southwark crown court on Monday.

Berger worked for Brand from June 2006 to February 2007, when the TV personality was at the height of his fame. She said the job was one of the hardest she had had because Brand had “non-stop energy”, and she left because she was “sick of him” and burnt out.

“Though I’d worked with celebrities before and seen a lot of people normalising bad behaviour, this was on another level. I think everyone else normalising and dismissing Russell’s behaviour made me think, I guess, this is just the way it is,” Berger said in the May 2024 police statement.

Describing his behaviour, she added: “He was always in his underwear, he loved walking around in his underwear with no shirt on. I remember Sadie Frost came over to interview him. He did the whole interview in his underwear and no shirt and an open robe.”

At the time, Brand had filming commitments for Channel 4’s Big Brother as well as MTV and the BBC, a radio show, a national comedy tour, a weekly Guardian column, and was writing a book.

“In addition to his busy work, he had an insane sexual appetite and was sleeping with people day and night. He was very open about what his needs were,” Berger said in the statement, which was read out by the prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC.

“He never seemed happy after sex, more so depressed,” Berger alleged. “There were times when I was at his house and he would be on a deadline … and he would get antsy and joke with me: ‘May I go and have sex now?’”

She recalled Brand turning to the website Myspace to find random women to sleep with and how women, including an unnamed celebrity, would often be at his flat in Camden, north London, for sexual liaisons. “He was like a peacock, women always approached him,” she said.

When Brand was recording an MTV show, Berger alleged, he told her to ask women for their phone numbers, which she said made her feel uncomfortable.

She alleged that on other occasions she had to keep Brand’s mother and girlfriend away from his dressing room because he was having sex, and she overheard him receiving oral sex in a women’s toilet. Berger described overhearing Brand talking and recognising his trademark cowboy boots in the cubicle next door.

Berger recalled that when Brand was headlining the Edinburgh festival, he ended his show by asking that anyone with “a vagina and heartbeat” meet him at a pub afterwards. Many women showed up, Berger said, and she later found him having sex in the shower at the apartment he was renting.

“I never witnessed Russell doing anything against the law,” she said, before adding: “I did see Russell treat women poorly.”

She recalled how he was once “hitting on” a woman who revealed she had a boyfriend, before Brand “turned in a way” that startled his then PA. “He literally just switched off his charm and moved on to the next woman,” Berger said.

The court also heard a witness statement from the manager of a woman who said she was sexually assaulted by Brand when she worked at Channel 4 in 2009. The manager said she recalled the alleged victim telling her that Brand’s associates Jack Bayles and Gareth Roy had “told her she had to give Mr Brand a massage” or he would not continue with the day’s recording.

The manager recalled being told that Bayles and Roy “were both there the whole time and watched and laughed while Mr Brand sexually assaulted her right in front of them”.

The sister of a woman who alleges she was sexually assaulted and then orally raped by Brand at a Soho bar in 2004 told the court she was “upset and almost in shock” the next morning.

In 2023, the woman called her sister in tears and told the “full story” of what had happened, the court heard. “It sounded like she was struggling to catch her breath,” the witness recalled. “She said his [Brand’s] eyes had gone completely black and he was possessed or had been a completely different person.”

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.title: ‘A cultural moment’: smash hit doc You Can See Everything continues to dazzle America
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.author: Jesse Hassenger in New York
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.text:
Nathan Fielder’s three-hour Elizabeth Holmes film has become a pop culture phenomenon but at a sold-out Times Square screening, no one was quite sure what to think

In You Can See Everything, it’s Elizabeth Holmes’s partner who makes for 2026’s timeliest villain

Secrets, lies and a shock A-list cameo: how You Can See Everything became the film of the year

When I see a film a second time during its theatrical run, it’s typically to take someone else who hasn’t yet seen it, at least in part hoping to witness their reaction to a piece of art that excited or moved me in some way. Seeing Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder’s You Can See Everything a second time in New York City on a Saturday night was that impulse writ larger. This is a movie garnering a surprisingly sizable audience, and outsized audience reactions to go along with it; rewatching it in a full 300-seat auditorium offered the opportunity to re-experience that sense of discovery. Perhaps more to the point, almost everyone I knew had seen it already; all I could do was observe strangers.

This documentary, peering into (and helping to create) a hall of mirrors around the famed med-tech scammer Elizabeth Holmes, has become the box office story of the fall, actually rising 25% on its second weekend to gross another $19.5m – a rare feat even given its expanded screen count. With over $45m in North America, it’s already one of A24’s biggest movies ever; it could wind up in the company’s top three, and way up on the list of the highest-grossing nonfiction features. If You Can See Everything isn’t quite an Obsession-level cash cow, it’s probably even more surprising that a three-hour documentary whose existence was only announced about eight weeks ago is on track to make more money than high-profile new releases like Practical Magic 2, Verity and Street Fighter, among others. It’s also outgrossed co-director Oppenheim’s fellow A24 surprise hit Primetime, which has the benefit of genuine movie star Robert Pattinson.

A few of the viewers I spoke with following the 8pm showing of You Can See Everything at New York’s AMC Empire (typically one of the highest-grossing venues in the country for any number of new releases, where Everything is currently showing on three to five screens depending on the time of day) had also seen Primetime, aware of the connection between the two films. Just as many, however, were not high-frequency moviegoers, at least not by New York standards. Despite an obviously youthful demographic – perhaps owing to the high tolerance for hustle and/or bustle required to trek out to Times Square, I couldn’t find anyone over 30 – there were several viewers who hadn’t been to the movies in months. (The answer to the question of what movie they last saw in theaters ranged from the month-old Primetime to the obligatory summer mega-blockbuster The Odyssey to, yes, Obsession.) Hardly anyone claimed to be a documentary aficionado, either; no one cited a recent documentary they had seen in theaters, saying they were more likely to catch that sort of thing on streaming, if at all.

So what drew them to a big-screen experience featuring both an entertainer (Nathan Fielder) and a subject (Elizabeth Holmes) more closely associated with television? Most of the twentysomethings I spoke with had some combination of familiarity with Fielder’s more overtly comic work – one woman said this seemed “on brand” for him – and awareness of the notoriety of Holmes, the latter usually stemming from the non-documentary TV series The Dropout, which also figures into the film. Each seemed to provide a surprise hook for a big-screen feature – like a more thoughtful version of seeing a movie because it has Anne Hathaway or Spider-Man (not that there’s anything wrong with following either of those into the dark). To a cinema diehard, this seemed almost counterintuitive; were people really being enticed into theaters by faces they knew largely from couch-bound TV binges? Was this effectively serving as a three-hour crossover between The Dropout and The Rehearsal?

There was a sense that this unexpected team-up was part of the sell, with the WTF nature of that idea intact. The extra promise, though, seemed to be that You Can See Everything would offer something more surprising and less easily spoiled than a typical streaming event. The 23-year-old sitting next to me said that she got the impression from social media – specifically, clips on Instagram and TikTok – that this was “a cultural moment”, as she put it. Multiple viewers echoed that sentiment about seeing a handful of clips via social media, and hearing buzz indicating that the movie simply was “unlike anything else out [at the movies]” and had to be seen firsthand to be believed - or at least to be experienced with the proper amount of spoiler-free, audience-vibing surprise. Remarkably, though the movie had been out for over a week and already discoursed at least halfway to death online, none of these twentysomething viewers reported having any idea about the unexpected pivot the movie made at its halfway mark – especially impressive given that it involves another marquee name added to the mix.

During the movie itself, that mystery guest felt like she was winning fans in real time; she even got a round of spontaneous applause by describing Holmes’s partner, Billy Evans, as “batshit crazy”. But while early screenings had been described as meeting with rapturous audience engagement driven by the film’s surprises, this one felt more unpredictable in its alternating waves of laughter and murmuring discomfort. Early in the film, Holmes gets teary talking about the potential separation from her children as she prepares to leave for her prison sentence in a few weeks. Both times I’ve watched it with a full audience, Fielder’s reaction – “that must be hard” – drew one of the movie’s biggest laughs, seemingly for how flatly obligatory it sounds. Yet if this moment primed the audience for peals of cringe-comedy laughter or outright derision toward either Fielder’s affect or Holmes’s refusal to accept responsibility for her deception, that’s not exactly how the movie played out. The movie often cuts to Fielder lurking within proximity of the Holmes family during tense moments; though the mechanics of these de facto reaction shots are similar, sometimes they drew big laughs and sometimes what felt more like hushed suspense. It was as if viewers were deciding moment to moment whether they were watching dark comedy or something more menacing. Though the disparaging of Evans got an enthusiastically cathartic reaction, applause when the movie threw to its end credits was scattered and uncertain.

It’s not unprecedented for a movie to garner audibly mixed reactions. But something Oppenheim and Fielder seem to have cracked is allowing an audience to feel satisfied and impressed by those reactions, which would often serve as a death knell to a prospective blockbuster. When I asked people after the show for their immediate impressions of the film, one woman said it was “funnier than I expected”, while another was surprised by the sympathy she felt for Holmes at times despite feeling “on guard” about what to believe from her.

The most common reaction, however, was a kind of admiring confusion. They weren’t exactly sure what to think, a feeling that’s not traditionally music to a film executive’s ears. Because its initial release was in fewer than a thousand theaters, You Can See Everything hasn’t been subjected to the traditional and finicky CinemaScore polling that asks opening-night audiences for a grade, and seems to inexplicably augur disappointment with anything that’s not at least a B+. But PostTrak, another polling service, shows highly positive results. This could carry the movie past the $100m mark in North America, something only ever accomplished by one other documentary: Michael Moore’s hot-button Fahrenheit 9/11, which had the advantage of election-year currency and a film-maker coming off an Oscar win.

Is this phenom, in conjunction with the surprise smash of Obsession and the less shocking but still staggering success of The Odyssey, indicative of movie audiences willing to grapple with more than they’ve been given credit for in the past? Or, along with the film’s three-hour runtime, is it more of an example of how traditionally TV-based projects are afforded a leeway that narrative films rarely receive from general audiences? As with the movie itself, clear answers haven’t emerged, and probably won’t. At very least, though, it offers some clear respite from the applause-mongering of the IP-driven, fan-focused era. Those movies won’t be banished by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, but by the time the next Avengers rolls around, they might feel, however slightly, like a narrower slice of the cinematic experience.

https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.title: ‘My death was reported in Rolling Stone’: how the Zombies made Time of the Season
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.author: Interviews by Chris Broughton
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.text:
‘A year after we broke up, we heard that two bands had started touring the US as the Zombies. One group said they were the originals but with a new singer – because I’d been killed in a car crash’

Our first single, She’s Not There, was one of the first songs I wrote, when I was 18. It remained our only hit in the UK by the time we recorded our second album, Odessey and Oracle, in 1967 – this was only three years later but it felt like a lifetime. We’d recently signed to CBS and had been given £1,000, which even then was not a huge amount of money. We recorded pretty quickly in a few sessions spread over six months, producing ourselves for the first time.

Time of the Season was the last song I wrote for the album. I was sharing a flat with our bass player Chris White, and we were going to each other’s rooms and playing the different things we had. I said: “I think I’ve just written a song that could be a hit.”

The lyrics reflected the mood of the time. In 1967 there were pictures of war on TV, and people were seeing what a devastating thing it was and saying: “I’m not going to be part of this.” The “Who’s your daddy?” line was, in a way, going back to Gershwin’s Summertime, one of the first songs we performed together, but “Is he rich like me?” had kind of a double meaning: “rich” in the sense of understanding how to live.

We recorded at EMI Recording Studios, later known as Abbey Road. The Beatles were in before us making Sgt Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band – we had the benefit of some of the same recording engineers, in particular Geoff Emerick. He found this special way of marrying the bass and the tom-tom sound. I suggested the clap before the beat and a vocal sound after, which became the exhalation.

We soon used up our £1,000, but because of the tight timeframe we were working to, there was a spontaneity and freshness that was very valuable. It’s a method I try to preserve. It’s just much more fun.

I was learning Time of the Season while we recorded it. Standing where the vocal mic had been set up, I was looking at this big red recording light with a clock underneath it while I tried to get it right. The studio was very strict about sessions finishing on time, and there were these guys with long brown coats moving equipment about. On one occasion, we were standing around a piano working out harmonies and they wheeled it out in the middle of a take.

Rod always has an overview of his songs in his head – he can hear the drum track, what the bass should be playing and what the lead vocal should be doing. He’s extremely good at phrasing, so he was in the control room saying: “No, this phrase should be on the beat but the next phrase should be pushed …” Meanwhile, all the time I’m watching the big hand creeping towards five o’clock.

Things got a little bit heated. I was saying, “If you’re so bloody good, you come in here and sing it,” and he said, “You’re the bloody lead singer, you stand in there until you get it right!” The language was probably richer than that. It makes me smile now to think I was breaking off from saying the most terrible things to Rod to sing these angelic lines: “It’s the time of the season for loving …”

Rod likes to think I disliked Time of the Season, but I just thought there were more commercial songs on the album. Care of Cell 44, to me, sounded like the epitome of a hit single, but obviously I was wrong – it was released ahead of Odessey and Oracle and wasn’t successful. By the time the album came out in Terry Quirk’s misspelled sleeve, the band had split.

The following year, Al Kooper left the American band Blood, Sweat & Tears and became a staff producer at CBS. He’d just visited London where he bought about 80 albums that weren’t available in the US, and later said Odessey and Oracle was the one that really stood out. On his first day at CBS he went to see the label’s president, Clive Davis, and said: “Whatever it costs, we have to get this album.” And Davis said: “We already have it. We were going to pass on it – it’s not commercial.”

Al fought for it, and CBS released two singles that disappeared without trace. I think Time of the Season was only put out as a favour to Al, but one DJ in Boise, Idaho, would not stop playing it, and that was where our luck turned. It gradually picked up huge radio interest.

By then, it was well over a year since we’d broken up and we were all doing other things, but we soon heard that a couple of other bands had started touring the US as the Zombies – one included two members of ZZ Top. The manager of one of these bands claimed they were the original members with a new singer, because Colin Blunstone had been killed in a car crash. It turned out my death was reported in Rolling Stone.

The original Zombies didn’t play together again until 1997, when a box set was launched at the Jazz Cafe in London. I was singing with my solo band, but the other guys came up on stage and let it be known they wanted to play – we hadn’t planned it or rehearsed. We did She’s Not There and Time of the Season and it sounded really good. I thought: “You know what? There really was something special about that band.”

Can you say a song’s got legs? Time of the Season wasn’t a success in the UK charts, but people know it. It’s often used in films set in the 1960s but also appears in commercials, where it sounds really current. I’ve never quite worked out how it can be both of its time and timeless.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Lula miraculously beat the Brazilian far right and Donald Trump. But have no doubt: the region is still in peril | Jordana Timmerman
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Jordana Timerman
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
After the rejoicing, it will be vital to learn the lessons. The rightward shift is neither inevitable nor irreversible, but progressives cannot rest for a moment

The impossible happened. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won a fourth term in Sunday’s runoff election in Brazil, overturning Flávio Bolsonaro’s first-round lead in a historic comeback. No candidate has ever lost the first round and won the second, until now. Grassroots mobilisation, alongside social welfare policies, helped turn the contest into a referendum on Brazilian democracy, rallying voters against a candidate seeking to restore the legacy of his father, Jair Bolsonaro, imprisoned for plotting a coup after his 2022 defeat. Lula’s victory suggests that defending democracy can still be a powerful electoral argument against the ascendant right.

Having already consolidated most of the leftwing vote, Lula had limited room to attract supporters of other candidates after his first-round defeat. His best chance lay in mobilising abstainers and reconnecting with working-class voters. The Workers’ party intensified its grassroots and digital campaigns, using social media influencers and messaging networks to reach supporters. Nearly 3 million more Brazilians voted in the runoff, and Lula gained ground across the country, particularly in major cities and his north-eastern strongholds. He also appealed to voters’ immediate economic concerns, drawing on a record of reducing poverty and inequality, and increasing benefits under Bolsa Família, the landmark welfare programme he launched in 2003. Lula framed the election as a choice between protecting social gains and democratic institutions, or returning to the Bolsonaro family’s attacks on both, warning that his opponent would compromise Brazil’s sovereignty by aligning himself with Donald Trump.

The implications extend far beyond Brazil. Lula’s victory interrupts a regional trend: rightwing candidates have won seven presidential elections across Latin America in the past 18 months. Two decades ago, Lula was among the leaders of Latin America’s pink tide, a succession of leftwing governments that reshaped the region’s politics and sought greater autonomy from Washington. Today, he finds himself resisting a new regional wave moving in the opposite direction, without a comparable coalition of allies.

Lula’s victory is welcome, but we shouldn’t forget that Flávio Bolsonaro won more than 48% of valid votes, demonstrating the enduring strength of a movement with substantial representation in an increasingly rightwing congress. His proposals on security and the economy appealed to voters frustrated by high living costs, including working-class Brazilians who had traditionally supported Lula. This mirrors the success of authoritarian-leaning right candidates across the continent. Frustration with crime, economic insecurity and established political parties has propelled a new right promising tougher security policies and attacking progressive social agendas. From Nayib Bukele in El Salvador, to Javier Milei in Argentina, to the recent election of Abelardo de la Espriella in Colombia.

The emerging rightwing alliance is, in many ways, the mirror image of the pink tide, developing in close alignment with Trump and his ambitions to reassert US dominance over the hemisphere. The relationship is mutually reinforcing: rightwing leaders who gained ground through domestic discontent look to Washington to consolidate their power, while the US relies on those same governments and movements to advance its strategic interests. In his victory speech, Lula said the surge of street support in recent weeks “was a demonstration that this country refuses to be anyone’s back yard”. His declaration directly challenges the so-called Donroe doctrine, which asserts an expanded US role in policing the region.

Since returning to office, Trump has used endorsements, sanctions, tariffs and financial assistance to reward allies and put pressure on opponents. He backed rightwing candidates in Honduras and Colombia. He has turned a blind eye to Salvadoran president Bukele’s negotiations with criminal organisations (Bukele denies having made an informal pact with these organisations). And ahead of Argentina’s 2025 legislative elections, he offered Milei a $20bn financial lifeline while warning that US generosity depended on the electoral outcome.

Security provides a particularly powerful instrument for this alignment. The Trump administration has invoked the fight against “narcoterrorism” to expand its military role and apply pressure on governments to accept Washington’s priorities. Terrorist designations have helped justify the operation that captured Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela, threats of unilateral strikes against Mexican cartels and joint military operations in Ecuador. Washington has also discussed similar operations with Colombia. The designations do not themselves authorise military action, but they strengthen the administration’s justifications to intervene beyond US borders.

Brazil demonstrates how this strategy can also serve Washington’s allies outside government. The Bolsonaro family had itself sought Washington’s intervention against the Brazilian judiciary during Jair Bolsonaro’s prosecution. The Trump administration imposed tariffs on Brazil and sanctions against supreme court justice Alexandre de Moraes. Following lobbying from the Bolsonaros, Washington also designated Brazil’s two largest criminal organisations as foreign terrorist organisations, reinforcing Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign message that Lula was failing to confront organised crime.

The stakes extend beyond the Bolsonaro family’s political fortunes. Washington has pressed Lula for access to Brazil’s critical minerals as it seeks to reduce dependence on China. Lula has defended Brazil’s freedom to trade with other partners.

Brazil shows that Trump’s interventions can backfire. In 2025, Lula’s approval ratings rose after Washington threatened punitive tariffs over Jair Bolsonaro’s prosecution. The president turned the dispute into a defence of national sovereignty, making resistance to foreign interference a defining theme of his re-election campaign. The electoral effect of Trump’s involvement is difficult to isolate, but the backlash helped Lula mobilise support. Combined with grassroots organising, appeals to democracy and social welfare policies, it offers one possible response to the regional right’s advance.

Yet a defining feature of that resistance is that it has remained national. Brazil’s size gives it a capacity to resist Washington that none of its neighbours possess. Lula has also been pragmatic in keeping that resistance national, rather than attempting to forge a regional coalition against Trump’s hemispheric ambitions. He also faces a strengthened right at home. Flávio Bolsonaro has refused to concede, seeking to annul the election over a last-minute extension of voting hours that both campaigns had requested. Electoral authorities maintain that the extension did not affect the outcome.

The region’s rightward shift also obscures a fragmented political landscape. Across Latin America, deeply divided electorates have produced closely contested elections, complicating claims that either the left or the right has established a durable political hegemony. Brazil is a case in point: Lula’s victory interrupted the right’s advance, but nearly half of voters backed a candidate who embraced much of Trump’s agenda.

Lula’s victory shows that the rightward shift is neither inevitable nor irreversible. But the movement retains substantial electoral support, influence over the political agenda and a powerful ally in Washington. Brazil may have stopped the blue tide at its borders, but it has yet to emerge as a regional bulwark against it.

Jordana Timerman is a journalist based in Buenos Aires. She is the managing editor of The Ideas Letter and compiles the Latin America Daily Briefing

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: I used to think I had impeccable taste in music. My kids taught me to stop being a snob | Myke Bartlett
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Myke Bartlett
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Music may not define them in the way it defined many of my generation, but my children still know a good tune when they hear one

There was a moment, some years ago in a St Kilda summer, when our family was driving along a busy street, the car windows down, belting out Eric Carmen’s Make Me Lose Control. I had one of those out-of-body experiences parents sometimes get, where you get a clear view of your younger, cooler self looking on in a state of acute embarrassment and despair.

There is no better way to examine your own prejudices than attempting to raise children engaged in cultural things. Taking their lead has led me to strange territories, including ballet, medieval festivals and the Gruffalo stage show. But as we enter the hinterland of adolescence, music continues to be the most revealing and unpredictable of journeys.

Full disclosure – I am a recovering music snob. My introduction to journalism was being a “rock journalist” (imagine the thrill of that business card) for Cream magazine in the early noughties. Having misspent much of my youth behind the counter of record stores, I was one of those (mostly) young men who saw High Fidelity as a kind of secondhand memoir. Oh, how we judged you for your love of mainstream pap.

And yet. The wonderful thing about kids and music is they like what they like. No child is born with an innate sense of cool or cringe. And, being kids, they tend to like fun things. When ours were of an age to move on from Play School records, we let them roam free at local op-shops and choose CDs for their cheap boombox at home. For $1, we ended up with an eight-disc set of Best of the 80s. This proved to be life-changing.

I had no nostalgic love for 80s pop. When I was developing my own music taste, my idea of upbeat pop was Morrissey imagining his girlfriend in a coma. Good times! But suddenly our lives were soundtracked by Tears for Fears, A-ha and Bananarama. I knew it was serious when our eldest chose the Beach Boys’ Kokomo as the soundtrack to her final kindergarten presentation.

I am grateful for the new music and artists our kids have since discovered. Their ever-changing playlists (a source of much conflict on car journeys) have introduced me to diverse acts from Chappell Roan via Raye to sea shanties and modern folk. But the greatest gift has been the chance to realise how wrong I was about music I already knew.

It turns out Queen isn’t tacky and overblown but joyous and extraordinary. Belinda Carlisle didn’t perform disposable fluff but some of the most perfect pop songs ever written. Likewise, the Bangles. Cyndi Lauper? Genius. Cheap Trick? Actually quite good.

And who knew that Bowie’s richest period wasn’t the albums Hunky Dory to Low but the first three tracks of Let’s Dance? (With an honourable mention for his and Jagger’s drunken singalong version of Dancing in the Street.) Who knew? The kids knew.

What is interesting about this generation of kids is how omnivorous and eclectic they are when it comes to music. The streaming age means almost all of music history is available to everyone, all of the time.

New music no longer dominates the old. It’s no harder to hear Eddie Cochran’s Twenty Flight Rock than the Weeknd’s Blinding Lights.

The tastes of their parents no doubt play a part – there’s no getting away from how many 80s-themed parties and discos our kids have attended – but their musical world seems far wider than that of my parents, whose music library fitted neatly on to a single, narrow shelf.

The algorithm also plays its part, of course. Given our family shares a streaming library, I am long resigned to my recommended listens and favourites being corrupted by the children’s choices. But I try to remind myself they are not polluting the river so much as widening the banks.

Outside the house, I am conscious that other algorithms are influencing their listening habits in the same way radio and television once influenced mine. Our kids aren’t yet on social media, but their current playlists are informed by music heard at various sporting events (the Killers, MGMT and Summer of ’69 tend to be on high rotation).

I certainly wasn’t listening to music from 40 years earlier when I was 13. More nostalgically, I miss the musical subcultures that were so important and so rigidly defended when I was coming of age. The contained bubbles of popularity allowed by social media enclaves don’t seem quite the same.

Our kids have been able to build musical identities out of the very best pop, rock and, uh, however we’re classifying sea shanties without being pinned to the zeitgeist. Sometimes that involves Olivia Dean, sometimes Eric Carmen, sometimes a forgotten track from The Transformers: The Movie soundtrack.

Music may not define them in the way it defined many of my generation, but they still know a good tune when they hear one.

So, yes, listening to music through the ears of my kids has taught this old snob to listen without prejudice or embarrassment. Because it turns out that serious and important music doesn’t always last, but the fun stuff goes on for ever.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: The horse that ushered in Manchester United’s tragic arc | Jonathan Wilson
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Jonathan Wilson
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
There’s plenty of blame to go around at Old Trafford. Like all downfalls it started with a seemingly small, unconnected moment

And so here we are again, at that point as the nights draw in and Manchester United prepare to sack a manager. Autumn: season of mists, mellow fruitfulness and a crisis at Old Trafford. Sunday’s 3-0 home defeat to Bournemouth, coming on the back of last week’s 4-1 reverse against Como, made clear what many had feared from the moment Michael Carrick was given the job on a permanent basis: that he isn’t up to it.

But then, who could be? When you’ve burned through a long list of managers in 13 years, it’s perhaps worth considering whether the manager is really the problem. Could some blame perhaps go to the director of football, Jason Wilcox, or the chief executive, Omar Berrada, the people making the appointments? Or perhaps to Sir Jim Ratcliffe, the cost-cutting tax exile and minority shareholder with responsibility for sporting operations?
