Or to the Glazer family, who plunged the club into debt with a leveraged buyout in 2005 and have since made calamitous decision after calamitous decision, reducing the most successful club in English league history to a mid-table laughing stock with a roof that leaks symbolically?

It’s worth remembering where all this began. The United story has taken on the aspect of a classical tragedy and, like all good tragedies, it begins with a small, seemingly unconnected moment, amplified by pride, that ends up bringing the whole edifice crashing down.

In 1999, Mull of Kintyre, a horse owned by the Irish millionaire John Magnier, won the Gimcrack Stakes at York. Traditionally, the winning owner would give a speech at the Gimcrack Dinner, but Magnier was a shy man who hated public speaking so he asked his friend, the United manager Alex Ferguson, to give the speech on his behalf. The racing establishment, though, refused: it had to be the owner. To spite them, Magnier named Ferguson as the owner of another horse, Juniper. The following year, Juniper was narrowly beaten in the Gimcrack Stakes. Magnier, though, was determined. So the year after that, he made Ferguson the owner of Rock of Gibraltar, which had won its first three races. Rock of Gibraltar won the Gimcrack easily and Magnier, waving a metaphorical two fingers at the racing authorities, watched Ferguson give the speech.

Magnier was largely making mischief, but he was also happy to do a favor for a friend, to give Ferguson a better experience of racing, and he benefited from the association of the horse with such a famous name. In addition, Ferguson did not get on well with the United chairman, Martin Edwards, and had a sense that football clubs were becoming good investments. Accordingly Magnier and his associate JP McManus bought shares in United. (The full story is explored by the journalist David Walsh here).

It turned out, though, that Rock of Gibraltar was a much better horse than anybody had realized, winning seven Group One races in a row. The stud fees would be worth tens of millions of pounds. Ferguson believed the verbal deal was that he could choose 50% of the prize money won by Rock of Gibraltar (about £800,000) or 50% of the stud fees, which ended up being worth tens of millions. He went for the latter. Magnier’s recollection was rather different: 5% of the prize money or one stud nomination a year.

Ferguson sued and, with his name on the ownership documents, probably would have won had it gone to trial. But then rumors started to spread about some of Ferguson’s financial dealings at United. Paid actors at United’s annual general meeting raised awkward points, then Magnier and McManus sent a list of 99 questions to the United board, which mysteriously found their way into the Daily Mail. United were highly embarrassed. Fans began to demonstrate against Magnier and McManus at race meetings. A settlement was reached, with Ferguson paid £2.5m to drop the action. But the damage was done.

Magnier and McManus had decided to sell their shares in United, and another shareholder was ready and waiting: Malcolm Glazer. Ferguson backed Glazer, who launched his leveraged buyout. Magnier and McManus sold up in 2005 for £260m, a profit of a little under £100m. Had they waited for Ratcliffe, who bought a similar stake in 2024, they would have received roughly £1bn more than that. For Ferguson, a threat had been dealt with.

The problem was that Glazer and his family would prove some of the worst club owners in English history. For 20 years, United have been addled by debt and have made consistently terrible footballing decisions. Ferguson’s team was good enough, and his personality big enough, that United won five league titles and a Champions League after the takeover, but once his genius had gone, there was nothing left.

A mismatched squad built up over seven flawed managerial appointments and a multiplicity of conflicting approaches will not readily be sorted out. Carrick is the latest victim of a crisis 21 years in the making. For the want of a horse a club was lost.

This is an extract from Soccer Desk, a newsletter from the Guardian US. Subscribe for free here.

https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.title: ‘What’s the safest way to defrost chicken?’ We’re answering your food safety questions
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.author: Filter editors, Rachel Sherman and Caroline L Schauer
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.text:
We’re hosting a live Q&A on 26 October at noon ET (4pm GMT) on the Guardian US site with guest experts Rachel Sherman and Caroline L Schauer. Sign up or sign in to ask

The Drexel food lab tested the best air fryers (the Cosori, a hands-down winner), the best nonstick cookware (Our Place, trendy and top of the line) and much more

An Instagram user asks: Do we really have to put food in the fridge right away after eating?

double quotation markRachel: Storing food quickly is the safest answer, but it also depends on the situation and the food itself. If you are able to keep the food warm (say a soup over low heat) and it stays out of the temperature danger zone, you have a little more leeway. The scientific answer is that water activity plays a big role in food safety as well. Bacteria, yeast and pathogens can thrive in wet environments. That is why dryer foods like cookies, can usually stay on the counter for a few days, while foods with a higher water activity, like soups, need to be stored.

A reader asks in a callout question: Is non-stick cookware truly necessary? (My short answer: No; addiction to convenience often leads us to dismiss such queries.)

double quotation markCaroline L Schauer: Non-stick cookware is excellent for low-fat cooking of delicate, sticky foods at relatively low temperatures, but I would state that it is useful but not necessary. Well-seasoned pans can produce the same effects.

Catherine in Seattle asks in a callout question: What is your recommendation for an 8-inch non-toxic sauté pan that can handle high heat?

double quotation markRachel: Cast Iron is always a safe bet. It can handle high heat, comes in a variety of shapes and sizes, and is non-toxic. Another options is the Titanium Always Pan Pro from Our Place. They have an 8.5-inch pan that is safe up to 1000F.

Not only is it safe but it is also non-stick, passed our egg test, and gave a good sear on our proteins. If you want to read more about our testing an the pan, you can find our article on the seven best non-toxic cooking pans in the US here.

A reader from British Columbia asks in a callout question: I thawed a chicken, then plans changed. Is it really a problem to refreeze it?

double quotation markRachel Sherman: The answer to this question goes back to the temperature “danger zone” of of 40 to 140 degrees Fahrenheit. If you have taken your chicken from the freezer and defrosted overnight in the refrigerator, it is probably safe to refreeze it. However if there is a chance the chicken temperature has risen into the “danger zone” during your thawing process, I would not risk it. The USDA has guidelines on their website if you want to read more.

But between nonstop food recalls and warnings of Pfas “forever chemicals” in everything from pans to takeaways boxes, these days it can seem like it’s as much about what you keep out of your kitchen as how you cook. The quality of what you buy matters.

That’s what the Filter US is here for. We’re your guide to buying fewer, better and more sustainable things. Our reviews are independent and trustworthy, and our buying advice is informed by years of rigorous testing and expert knowledge.

Join us live in conversation with guest expert Rachel Sherman, associate director of the Drexel Food Lab, and Caroline L Schauer, department head and professor of materials science and engineering at Drexel University.

Drexel has reported on the best cheese storage containers and found instant coffee that’s so good it beat drip in a blind taste test. Through rigorous tests, they determined the Cosori to be the best, most consistent air fryer (and it’s Pfas-free!), while Our Place and Lodge came out on top in testing to find the best nonstick pan.

No question is too big or too small (as long as it’s about what happens in your kitchen). Sign up or sign in to ask.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: ‘Democracy always’: Lula vows no return to dictatorship in Brazil after election win
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Tom Phillips in São Paulo and Tiago Rogero in Brasília
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Leaders and governments worldwide congratulate Lula on dramatic comeback seen as an important signal to rest of Latin America

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the Brazilian president, has vowed that dictatorship and fascism will never return to Brazil after winning a historic fourth term in power by defeating his far-right opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro.

“This is God’s work – and it’s thanks to all of you,” Lula told tens of thousands of supporters who had gathered in central São Paulo in the early hours of Monday to celebrate his dramatic election comeback.

A few hours earlier Lula pulled off the most stunning political fightback in modern Brazilian history, bouncing back from a first-round defeat in early October to trounce Bolsonaro by more than 4m votes in the runoff.

“Today is a historic day,” Lula declared, before telling a sea of elated supporters: “Democracy always, dictatorship never again. Democracy always, fascism never again.”

Never, since the return of democracy after the 1964-85 military regime, had the first-round loser managed to win the second vote.

But Lula did precisely that on Sunday, prompting joyous scenes on the streets of São Paulo and cities all across Brazil, where he won 64.2m votes to Bolsonaro’s 59.8m – a 51.79% to 48.21% victory. That was at least 10m more votes than Lula secured in the first round.

“This is a huge victory for the Brazilian people who in the second round had the chance to think about what President Lula means for the environment, for the defence of our national health service and our education system and the Brazilian constitution. And the risks that the extreme right candidate entailed,” Lula’s health minister, Alexandre Padilha, told the Guardian shortly after the result was confirmed at the hotel where the president’s team was following the count in São Paulo.

“It’s a massive victory – not just for Brazil. It’s also an important signal to the rest of Latin America and to the world,” Padilha added.

Following in the footsteps of his father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who refused to concede after losing the 2022 election to Lula and was later convicted of plotting a coup, Flávio Bolsonaro rejected the result. Bolsonaro called Lula’s victory “sacanagem”, a Portuguese word which roughly translates as “bullshit”.

But political leaders and governments from across the spectrum were quick to recognise Lula’s victory.

“Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won,” tweeted Mexico’s leftwing president, Claudia Sheinbaum.

“The global progressive resurgence has just begun,” wrote Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez.

Rightwing South American leaders also recognised Lula’s victory, with Chile’s president, José Antonio Kast, calling Lula to offer congratulations and Peru’s president, Keiko Fujimori, saluting “the Brazilian people for this democratic day”.

The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said: “Democracy and multilateralism have won in Brazil.”

A spokesperson for China’s foreign ministry said: “China respects the choice of the Brazilian people.”

There was silence from Donald Trump, whose administration had been rooting for a Bolsonaro victory that would have seen the so-called pro-Trump “orange wave” continue its sweep across the region into Latin America’s largest democracy.

In the lead-up to Sunday’s vote, the US had been accused of seeking to influence the result through a campaign of economic and diplomatic pressure.

Erika Hilton, a transgender lawmaker who recently became the most voted woman in Brazil’s congress, said those efforts had failed. “We have defeated the interference of the US government, which thought it could turn our country into its backyard. Brazil and the Brazilians are too gigantic to be anybody’s backyard,” she said.

Lula’s victory will also have profound consequences for the environment and the Amazon rainforest in what is the world’s most biodiverse nation.

On the eve of the vote, the former environment minister Marina Silva had warned that, if elected, Bolsonaro would seek to finish the “perverse project” of rainforest destruction started by his father, whose 2019-2022 administration saw a surge in deforestation.

On Sunday night, Silva was in a buoyant mood, telling the Guardian: “My heart is happy and filled with gratitude to God and the Brazilian people.”

“The thing I most feared was that our Indigenous territories would be invaded again [under another Bolsonaro government]. Now, I am certain that they will be preserved and that there is no risk of illegal miners returning to destroy these populations,” Silva added.

For Flávio Bolsonaro, the future looks bleak. As the scale of Lula’s victory became clear on Sunday night, the mood at the Brasília mansion where Bolsonaro was watching the count soured, with what had initially seemed like a lively birthday party turning into something resembling to a wake. Like football supporters heading for the exits midway through the second half because their team is being thrashed, crestfallen guests began heading home.

One of them approached the dozens of journalists waiting for Bolsonaro’s speech to shout that it was the “north-east’s fault”, insulting the region where Lula has historically won most of his votes.

One photograph circulated by Lula supporters showed a dejected Bolsonaro in tears, although it was taken on the eve of the vote. Another image showed a red-faced Bolsonaro flanked by visibly mortified allies as they came to terms with their defeat. São Paulo’s pro-Bolsonaro governor, Tarcísio de Freitas, sits next to him covering his face with his hand.

On Paulista Avenue, where huge crowds had gathered to hear Lula speak, one reveller wore a costume of Flávio Bolsonaro behind bars. Some suspect the senator is likely to flee the country to the US once his term runs out in February and he loses parliamentary immunity. Bolsonaro is facing a series of federal police investigations over suspected misdeeds, including money laundering, although he maintains he is innocent.

Lula supporters delighted in the idea that the far-right politician may soon join his father, who is serving a 27-year sentence for his coup attempt, in jail.

“Oh, how awful! Poor little thing!” João Maluf, a 27-year-old psychologist, shouted sarcastically he held up his mobile phone to the crowd to show them a photograph of a visibly distraught Bolsonaro. “We want rid of these fucking Bolsonaros,” Maluf said.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Fifteen-year-old arrested in shooting near Florida university that injured 12
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Richard Luscombe in Miami
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
All but one of the victims sustained gunshot wounds as boy faces 11 charges of attempted second-degree murder

Officials in Florida have charged a 15-year-old boy with 11 counts of attempted murder following a mass shooting at a college homecoming party on Saturday.

Six adults and six minors were injured, all but one with gunshot wounds, in the gunfire near the Florida Agricultural + Mechanical University (Famu) campus in Tallahassee.

It was among five mass shootings over the weekend – cases in which at least four victims were wounded or killed, according to the Gun Violence Archive. The archive, a nonpartisan resource, has recorded 386 such cases in the US for the year so far.

On Monday, the Tallahassee police department posted on Facebook that detectives had arrested a suspect in the Famu shooting two days earlier. The agency identified the suspect as Anthony Rivers III, 15.

Police do not typically identify criminal suspects who are minors, though the severity of the charges facing Rivers made him an exception. He faces 11 charges of attempted second-degree murder and one of possession of a firearm by a delinquent after being arrested on Sunday, police said.

Tallahassee police chief Lawrence Revell said in a statement that the investigation into Saturday’s shooting was ongoing, and further arrests were possible.

“What should have been a weekend of celebration in our community instead became a night of fear and violence for the victims and their families,” Revell said.

“While this arrest marks a significant step forward, our work is far from over. We remain committed to holding those responsible accountable and getting answers for every family [affected] by this tragedy.”

The department earlier said three of the victims were seriously wounded, with one in critical condition in the hospital. Nine others had gunshot wounds, the agency said – and another person injured an ankle as they attempted to escape the gunfire.

The shooting took place just before 8pm on Saturday at an intersection near the university’s Bragg stadium, where a homecoming football game had just ended. Officers were on the scene quickly and carried some of those injured to safety through a mass of people, Revell said.

According to police, Rivers opened fire after an altercation between two groups of people who were known to each other. None of those struck was believed to have been an intended target, Revell said.

Revell on Sunday thanked members of the community who had come forward with cellphone video of the shooting and its aftermath, which he said was “vital to investigative efforts”.

Famu president Marva Johnson posted a video message on X on Sunday condemning the “senseless and despicable” violence of the night before.

“As a neighbor and community partner, we are providing our full assistance to the Tallahassee police department,” she said. “Our pride, our identity, and our future will not be defined by the challenges we face, but how we respond to them together.”

https://www.theguardian.com/global/ng-in.title: Self-destructive or helpful? How to harness envy for you benefit
https://www.theguardian.com/global/ng-in.author: Adrienne Matei
https://www.theguardian.com/global/ng-in.text:
In her new book, Envy, Stacy Kim explains how to understand the feeling, identify your deeper desires and use them to achieve your goals

In the 16th-century poem The Faerie Queene, envy is a ghoulish figure riding a ravenous wolf, sad to see the fortune of others and “wonderous glad” of their hardship. It’s not a flattering depiction; better to be thankful for what we have, rather than dwell on such a bitter and self-destructive feeling, right?

Maybe not. “I think that when we don’t examine our envy, that’s when it leads us astray,” says Dr Stacy Kim, social scientist, life coach and author of the new book Envy: Why Wanting What They Have is the Key to Getting What You Want. Kim wrote the book after seeing the way envy came up for her coaching clients and reflecting on the role it had in her own life. The book is informed by social science and philosophy research, as well as her personal and professional experiences.

To Kim, a lifelong envier who says sibling rivalry propelled her to fast-track a PhD in educational policy and leadership, envy tells you “there’s something important here,” Kim says. “Envy signals to us our goals,” as well as “what is within our reach”, as we tend to envy people similar to ourselves more so than, say, superstars.

But how to transform envy from sulky to superpower? Kim gave us some points to consider.

Envy is “simply wanting something that someone else has”, Kim says. “Everyone envies – it’s normal.”

Yet it comes in different forms. In 2009, Dutch researchers explored and formalized the concepts of “malicious” and “benign” envy. Malicious envy happens “when you are so focused on the person that has what you want” and you want to “take them down”, like the evil queen who hoped to kill Snow White, explains Kim. Benign envy, however, is more like admiration-meets-motivation: it helps you “focus on what it is that you want”, Kim says, rather than sabotage.

Jealousy, meanwhile, is a whole different ballpark. It usually involves three parties and the threat of losing a special status or relationship to another person.

Next comes what Kim calls “probably the most important part of the examination”: looking past the thing you covet to the “intangible desire” buried deep within. It’s often not so much the object you’re craving but “the feeling you think you’re going to get” when you acquire or achieve it, she says. Kim’s envy of people with bigger apartments, for instance, “is really not just about the apartment”, but rather a desire for a calm, uncluttered home.

Once you’ve named the deeper desire, you can look for alternative routes to fulfill it. For Kim, that might mean spending “more time decluttering”. If you have a goal that is out of reach, be creative; if you have a pang of envy watching a 20-year-old ballet dancer but you’re 42 and have never taken a class, you might be interested in being able to move more confidently in your own body. An adult beginner dance course could help with that. If you envy the young, you can access the feeling of a promising new life experience by getting out of your comfort zone and trying something novel and intimidating, like visiting a new country or pursuing further study.

When a pang of envy strikes, Kim’s mnemonic tool for processing it is an acronym: SIReN. Here’s what it stands for:

Similar target: “You remind yourself: ‘Hey, the reason why I’m feeling this envy is because what I want is within my reach,’” she says.

Relevant comparison: Identify which specific domain – something you care about or already participate in – is relevant to your desires

Negative emotion: How long does it last? How intense is the message it’s sending? This tells us how important the feeling is.

Humans are “social beings”, Kim says, and this means we often mirror what everyone else wants – French academic René Girard called this quality mimetic desire. As a result, it’s easy to fall into the trap of keeping up with the Joneses, says Kim.

With envious clients, Kim likes to use a technique from psychologist Robert Leahy that can help identify your priorities: imagine you are nothing, a perfect void. Then, one by one, add one thing back into your life. The things you reach for first signal what you value most. Note what they are – your body, your family, your work, your possessions, or something else – and the order they arise in.

In Kim’s experience, the exercise often emphasizes that “deep connections with people you care about”, being of service to others, and meaningful work are what people most need to be happy – not superficial wants like an expensive car or country club membership.

An individual you envy today might become a mentor, friend or role model tomorrow. If you know the person, Kim says, “ask some questions” about how they achieved their goals – “usually people will want to be helpful.”

If that feels unsafe or they’re a stranger, Kim advises “researching that person”. If it’s appropriate and you feel comfortable – for instance, they’re an artist with a feedback form on their website – you could send them a compliment or thank you note for the work they’ve done that has affected you without “asking anything in return”.

This might feel odd to you, and that’s understandable. In Korea, Kim says, the word 부럽다 (buleobda) essentially means “I envy you,” and is “an acceptable phrase to use” as an everyday conversation starter. But in the US, coping to envy might feel exposing and odd, even if honest vulnerability could spark a connection between you and another person. Try “I admire you” or “I’m really curious about how you did that,” instead.

Envy can come from focusing on people you perceive as being ahead of you. Kim suggests also checking, “Who’s behind me? Or who’s next to me?”

When a goal feels impossible, whether because of structural inequalities or just bad luck, you can “hook arms” with people in a similar situation, and look for ways to help each other make progress, she says. Alternatively, offering to collaborate with, share information with or be a mentor to people who may, in fact, admire and envy you can not only boost your self-esteem, but also build useful connections and earn you the respect of your peers. When those around you succeed, “you can own some of that success too,” says Kim. A zero-sum game mentality or scarcity mindset isn’t typically as satisfying or useful for overcoming challenges, she notes. Solidarity can be much better.

Becoming more aware of envy doesn’t mean the complicated feeling won’t affect you. It may always be unsettling to feel envious of another person, and even to realize you’re an object of envy to others; as Kim says from experience: “Just because you study envy doesn’t mean that it goes away.” And yet, to an extent, envy is normal and unavoidable. Recognizing why it shows up and how it can be harnessed for good can be a valuable skill.

Envy: Why Wanting What They Have is the Key to Getting What You Want by Stacy S Kim is out now via Balance

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Manhunt under way in Tennessee after convicted murderer escapes prison
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Maya Yang
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Officials say Jacob Morley, who is serving a life sentence for a 2022 murder, escaped from a facility in Tiptonville

Tennessee officials have mounted a manhunt after a convicted murderer’s escape from a state prison on Sunday evening.

The Tennessee department or correction (TDOC) on Monday announced that Jacob Morley, 28, escaped from the Northwest correctional complex in the community of Tiptonville. Local outlets reported that staff noticed Morley was unaccounted for at about 11.30pm on Sunday.

After staff conducted an emergency headcount, prison surveillance footage showed Morley breached the perimeter fence and escaped the prison in his TDOC uniform, the local news outlet WATE reported.

TDOC describes Morley as being 5ft 11in and 240lbs with green eyes and brown hair.

Morley was serving a sentence of life imprisonment for the 2022 murder of Cody Birchfield, a Tennessee man who was initially reported missing in February 2022.

Birchfield’s body was discovered buried beneath Morley’s home about a month later.

Morley was also convicted of aggravated burglary, evidence tampering, evading arrest and vandalism.

“Do not attempt to apprehend this fugitive,” TDOC said in a statement, adding that any information on Morley’s whereabouts should be reported to TDOC at (844) 832-3463.

Morley’s escape comes more than a year after manhunt was launched after the escape of 10 detainees from a New Orleans jail in what was one of the largest such breakouts in recent memory.

All 10 escapees – who got out of the jail through a hole in a wall behind a toilet – have since been recaptured.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Serbia’s Student List preparing for talks on forming government despite no clear leader
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Jon Henley and Ana Milosavljevic in Belgrade
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Non-hierarchical movement is seeking to ‘rebuild society’ in Balkan country after years of authoritarian rule

Serbia’s triumphant but untested Student List movement is preparing to start talks on forming a government capable of reversing 14 years of increasingly authoritarian nationalist rule, after a seismic weekend election win.

Supporters of the movement, which has no experience of government, took to the streets in the west Balkan country on Monday after the strongman former president, Aleksandar Vučić, was defeated in a historic landslide.

Vučić conceded defeat late on Sunday, bringing his domination of Serbian politics to an abrupt end and capping two years of anti-government protests triggered by the collapse of a canopy at the Novi Sad railway station that killed 16 people.

With 100% of ballot samples counted, projected results from the Centre for Free Elections and Democracy in Belgrade showed the Student List on 53% of the vote, giving it 141 MPs in the 250-seat parliament, while Vučić’s Serbian Progressive party (SNS) won 39%, giving it 103. The remaining seats went to national minority party lists.

As yet, there are few clues as to how the winning movement, built around collective decision-making, will actually govern. Its candidates included academics, actors and farmers as well as students, but it is deliberately leaderless with no hierarchy, so it is unclear who it will appoint as the prime minister and cabinet.

Prominent Student List figures include: ​Ilija Srdanović, a cardiologist who headed the candidate list; Dejan Šoškić, a former central bank governor; and Radomir Saičić, a chemistry professor at Belgrade ​University who spoke on behalf ‌of the List after its ​victory.

Much like Péter Magyar’s Tisza party, which ended Viktor Orbán’s 16 years of illiberal government in Hungary this spring, the List faces public institutions staffed with civil servants loyal to the outgoing regime, complicating the task of institutional overhaul.

“Everyone in the student movement, and every candidate on the list, has a complete and very clear understanding of the weight of the responsibility before us,” said Ana Mirković, a university educationist, psychologist and Student List candidate.

“We do not see the election result as gaining power and privileges, but as taking on a historic debt to our own people and to our own children.”

Mirković told the Guardian the movement’s first priority was “the social and psychological detoxification” of the country.

Vučić’s 14-year rule has been described as a “textbook regime” of autocracy, with his party extending control over the media, judiciary and other state institutions and elections marred by registration irregularities, media bias and voter bribes.

The students’ platform centres on a pledge to fight corruption and restore the rule of law, including creating an independent police unit accountable to prosecutors, not the interior ministry, and a purge of police officers linked to organised crime.

It also aims to ban appointments of party loyalists to state-owned companies and to promote financial accountability and public scrutiny – by new independent bodies – of all major state infrastructure contracts ⁠to curb the misuse of public funds.

Mirković said the new government would dismantle a “system of intimidation” that encouraged “fear and polarisation”, by “urgently opening up” the media, putting an end to pressure on public-sector workers and “stopping institutional violence”.

She added that the aim was to “rebuild society from the ground up: full disclosure of all contracts and financial flows; depoliticising and strengthening the judiciary; renewing the education and healthcare systems”, and that state capture should “never again” be possible.

The Student List deliberately kept divisive foreign policy issues, including relations with the EU and Russia, in the background. The Kremlin said on Monday it hoped the new leaders “understand that cooperation with Russia is in Serbia’s interests”.

Dušan Vučićević, an analyst, said that, from the outset, the movement “insisted as much as possible that Serbia must first and foremost address domestic political issues – the literal dismantling of every institution, from the national to the local level”.

The students’ win marks a profound political shift in Serbia and could potentially offer inspiration to other student movements that have cropped up across Europe in recent weeks demanding better education standards and prospects.

However, Vučićević said it was distinct from other protests. “This experiment in grassroots democracy ultimately secured more than 50% of the vote,” he told Agence France-Presse, but it was “unclear whether a similar model could work in other countries”.

Nikola Burazer, programme director at the Belgrade-based Centre for Contemporary Politics, said on Monday that the movement’s decision-making process also needed to “be sped up”, as its process for choosing candidates “actually took a long time – months”.

He added: “After people are done celebrating and thinking about what happened yesterday, we will focus a bit more on what’s coming up, and how the government will look. Twenty-four hours ago that all seemed like a fantasy.”

On Sunday, Vučić, who maintained close ties with Russia throughout his tenure, blamed his party’s defeat on “the direct support of various European countries and the US deep state, the one that is also against President Trump”.

International leaders, meanwhile, joined a chorus of welcome to the students on Monday. “This is clearly a new chapter in the history of the country and its people,” said the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

“We wish ⁠Serbia success, real development, and warm ⁠relations with the European community. ​We in Ukraine thank Serbia for respecting our people, our state, and our independence. And we always celebrate our shared achievements.”

The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, said Berlin would “actively support Serbia’s European path” after the victory, saying the students “with their demand for the rule of law, fighting corruption and fundamental freedoms, have reached the people”.

Serbia’s constitution requires the new parliament to convene within 30 days of the official election result, and sets a 90-day deadline after that for formation of the new government.

The country must also hold new presidential elections before 27 December, since Vučić stepped down to run for prime minister.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Mourinho’s plan comes together as Real Madrid relaunch with clásico statement | Sid Lowe
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Sid Lowe
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
It was just like old times as José Mourinho ended a night at the Camp Nou with a knee slide and three points

José Mourinho had already done the por qué?, the printout and the press conference no-show in under 100 days. Now he’s done a knee slide too, and in the perfect place: back where it all began and where it can all begin again. When Kylian Mbappé scored the first in the clásico on Sunday night, Real Madrid’s manager hardly moved, sitting in the shadow of the bench, but when the striker got the second to win it with time running out, that was different. Mourinho leapt into the light, throwing himself to the grass, the knees of a 63-year-old’s trousers muddy as a schoolboy’s, stuck his tongue out and pumped his fists.

He does so love it when a plan comes together. To the right of him, the bench was emptying, subs joining the players in sprinting towards the south-west corner. As they leapt about, dodging the bottles thrown towards them from the end, way, way up in the furthest corner and stuck inside a glass box like a bunch of David Blaines, the small group of Madrid fans who had come were going mad. In the main stand, a thousand phones were raised. And 600km west, back in Boadilla, Thibaut Courtois was watching his teammates from the sofa at home, presumably wrapped in a blanket and cradling a cup of Lemsip. On the morning of the biggest game there is, he awoke with flu, forced to miss out.

“We have the best goalkeeper in the world, but none of us cried because Thibaut couldn’t play,” Mourinho said. Plenty might have felt like it, more reason to be fearful. But the coach called Andriy Lunin, the sub goalkeeper so serious he bought a roll of astroturf and spent the pandemic diving round the living room of his flat, and told him this was his moment: “You train to play, not to sit on the bench, so go on.” As for the rest of them, the manager told them nothing changes: the plan remains in place. By the time they headed back to the dressing room, “Fucking get in!” echoing along the Camp Nou corridor, so it had proved.

Thirteen years later, Mourinho was back in Barcelona for a clásico and he had guided Madrid to a 2-1 win. It wasn’t supposed to be like this, or maybe it was. Barcelona, the team who had won nine in a row, banging in 4.3 goals per game, had been beaten by Madrid, the team who had lost twice already and, truth be told, were mostly just not very good. The night it could have been all over, the title race done when it’s not even in November, was instead the night it finally started. “If you leave here nine points behind, it’s very heavy psychologically; if it’s six, it’s more balanced; if it’s three, that’s different,” Mourinho said.

This was different, and so is the season now. Counting the clásicos all those years ago, Mourinho racked up his sixth consecutive meeting with Barcelona without defeat, and there had been no parked bus, nor many lumps kicked. They didn’t just desperately hang on, although there was a moment when Dean Huijsen saved a shot with his face. Nor had they just waited for a moment, resisting and then robbing it, even if João Cancelo did insist: “That’s Madrid; they don’t have many chances but they score them.” The final shot count said 18-10 to Barcelona, and possession was 62% Barcelona’s.

“The way we won is important: you can win luckily or by defending a lot. But we won with calmness and totally deservedly. We did it by being organised, concentrated and having the courage to come out from the back,” Mourinho said. And if that might have been pushing it a little – and, let’s face it, the analyses might be different had Lunin not made an astonishing save from Gerard Martín or Lamine Yamal’s second-half shot not faded just past the post – he had a point.

Barcelona were not at their best. They had been hurried and imprecise, Rodri telling his teammates to lower their “pulse rate” as they came out for the second half. Lamine Yamal somehow missed an extraordinary chance just before the break. And when they did tighten the screw in the second half, they couldn’t break the wall. Xavi Espart was forced off, yet another injury at the back, the failure to sign a centre-back in the spotlight again. Yet this was still a faster, more aggressive, tighter Madrid than anyone expected. Asked to define it, Lunin went for “discipline and attitude”. And if that is partly about occasion, the least you can ask for, it’s more than you sometimes get.

Besides, it was also more than that. More than Marc Cucurella getting under Lamine Yamal’s skin, although he certainly succeeded. They went for the space beyond Barcelona’s full-backs: superb in his first clásico, aged 19, Yan Diomandé – the left winger – got more touches than any Madrid player, and protected his full-back as well. But it was more than that, too. More than the wonderful winning goal, a flash of inspiration with Jude Bellingham going all Nureyev, the ball flitting between his feet and Gabriel Jesus’s legs, pirouetting to release Eduardo Camavinga. This was a team with an idea and a victory that vindicated their manager, some kind of resurrection.

Before the game, Rodri said that one of Madrid’s tricks is to convince you that they’re not that good, but insisted he wouldn’t fall into that trap. Still he felt that plan particularly. Pedri did too. Bellingham dealt with Rodri, Bernardo Silva with Pedri. Pressed and tired too, according to Hansi Flick, neither truly took control. The inclusion of Arda Guler and Silva – the surprise in the middle, starting his first league game in six weeks – underlined an intention for Madrid to keep the ball when the could. They actually had a midfield, which was new. From the back they tried to build, draw Barcelona in. And if a time came when they had to wait, to put bodies in before the ball, well, they would do that too. Six times Barcelona shots were blocked. At least twice more, shots were taken from their toes. At the other end, meanwhile, Madrid attacked with an intent and an incision that probably drew the clearer chances: the xG showed 1.19 v 1.94.

Alaves 1-1 Malaga, Rayo Vallecano 0-3 Elche, Racing Santander 2-1 Espanyol, Valencia 1-2 Villarreal, Atlético 1-0 Deportiva A Coruna, A Bilbao 4-0 Getafe, Celta Vigo 0-0 Real Betis, Real Sociedad 2-1 Levante, Barcelona 1-2 Real Madrid

Victory puts Madrid three points behind Barcelona and, Federico Valverde claimed, “will give us a kickstart”. It has taken 10 weeks but it’s game on. Hay liga, as they like to say. There is league. There is Madrid too. Something has shifted, starting in Rome, where 70 dreadful minutes gave way to 20 pretty good ones, another inexplicable comeback actually having something of an explanation too. The changes were impossible to ignore. Valverde and Aurélien Tchouaméni no longer the partnership in the middle, Valverde going to right-back instead. Guler playing. Diomandé playing. And, yes, Vinícius Júnior not playing. “I’m not stubborn; I can change,” Mourinho said. Madrid have won five in a row now; something was seen that night, a way ahead. They’ve won every game since Vinícius was suspended, facile and perhaps even cruel though that may be to say. And since Mourinho grew a beard, if you believe in that kind of thing.

Before the clásico, Mourinho had said it wasn’t fair to compare his team, a side in construction and a long way from the finished product, to Barcelona. He insisted that he was still getting to know his players; he hadn’t been there long, after all. After the clásico, he admitted: “We have improved, we can’t hide that.” The idea has shifted, almost like it was an epiphany: “I’ve learned something about the middle of the pitch; I have learned that a mixture is better, that it is better to have a combination of qualities than two players of similar characteristics.” In short, Tchouaméni and Valverde doesn’t work. There needs to be some football in there somewhere, and so a shift started. Sunday came as a kind of confirmation, a hope, an identity emerging.

“The best Madrid is born at the Camp Nou,” ran the headline in El País. “Madrid are here now,” AS’s cover said. “I won’t let them have their heads on the moon; if we win this and then don’t win at the Sardinero, it won’t mean much,” Mourinho said, but this was a start, not just an end in itself. At full-time, Mourinho headed on to the pitch and shook Lunin’s hand as all around players embraced. High in the north-east corner, Madrid’s fans stayed and sang. Back home, Courtois was watching. He had “a horrible night” on Saturday, they said, but now he was feeling a little better. They all were.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Doubles players sign open letter pleading with tennis chiefs to ‘protect’ format
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Tumaini Carayol
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
More than 150 doubles players on the men’s ATP tour have signed an open letter addressed to the ATP board and management imploring the men’s tennis governing bodies to reconsider controversial doubles reforms and “protect” the format in professional tennis.

The subject of potential reforms to the ATP has been a significant issue since players were informed in a meeting during Wimbledon that the ATP was conducting a review of its doubles regulations and potential changes could see doubles draws being halved at the ATP events in 2028. Under these proposals, ATP Masters 1000 events would host only 16 doubles teams and the main draws at ATP 500 and 250 events would accommodate only eight teams.

The proposals could also lead to the total prize money distributed to doubles players being halved from 20% to 10%, with the remaining money allocated towards singles players. The news provoked significant criticism from a large group of doubles players at Wimbledon, and they have spent subsequent months organising to resist the reforms. In addition to over 150 active players, the letter has been signed by more than 20 national federations and legends of the sport.

In the open letter, the players state: “The current plans would shift about $20m (£15m) in prize money from doubles to singles, while cutting a significant number of professional opportunities for doubles specialists. That shift would make it much harder for talented players to build and sustain a doubles career. A healthy professional sport cannot rely solely on a small group of top stars; it needs pathways for players to develop, compete and earn a living.”

Sem Verbeek, the 2025 Wimbledon mixed doubles champion and one of the players spearheading the campaign, told the Guardian that the doubles players feel the ATP’s potential reforms threaten the future of doubles and that the ATP has not sought to collaborate with doubles players to shape the future of the discipline.

“The A to B with these proposals is really threatening not only the history, but also the present and future of the whole discipline of professional men’s doubles,” he said.

“The livelihoods of a lot of players are at stake here, and not only that, I think also the dreams of any young player that wants to pursue a doubles career are really in big jeopardy.

“I think that one of the big reasons that we have so much support for this open letter is to really provide the ATP with a platform to get in touch with us and make this more of a collaboration rather than a one-sided review that they keep saying is ongoing. But any real data and real numbers and real requests that we have have not been answered so far. And I think that’s why a lot of active players are so frustrated with this because we have a lot of ideas.”

The ATP management views doubles as an unsustainable loss leader, and it intends to redistribute some of the money currently reserved for doubles to singles players, an initiative doubles players believe pits singles and doubles players against each other despite the fact that they are all members of the same association.

“The main message that we want to send is the ATP really has to ­balance short-term economic growth with the legacy that it has built,” Verbeek said. “We understand that the ATP and ­tennis as a whole is entertainment is a business but you also have a responsibility to all of your fans worldwide to protect and grow the legacy of both disciplines of your sport.

“It’s been clear so far I think for a lot of people, if you look at how inaccessible doubles is from a viewership standpoint, that the ATP has under-invested and under-marketed the discipline so far. So we really just want to invite the ATP to really meaning­ful collaborations and meaningful discussions on how we can grow this part of the sport without damaging the future of it and allowing people to have a celebratory career in doubles. And I think that’s part of the reason that so many legends have signed on.

“For some reason the generation of decision makers that are in the ATP right now feel like a doubles career is not a real tennis career. And that to us is ludicrous. It should be celebrated. It’s a discipline that has provided a lot of history and should provide a lot of future and it shouldn’t be looked at as, let’s say, a failed singles career or something like that.”

This month the ATP announced widespread reforms to the calendar, schedule and rule book. In a Q&A attributed to the ATP chief executive, Andrea Gaudenzi, on the ATP website, the men’s tennis governing body addressed its potential doubles reforms. “Doubles will continue to be a core part of the ATP Tour,” ­Gaudenzi wrote. “The review is focused on identifying a model that gives the discipline a sustainable long-term future, works effectively for tournaments and fans and supports the wider player pathway.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Maurene Comey was illegally fired as federal prosecutor, judge rules
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Daughter of ex-FBI director James Comey, a Trump foe, was dismissed in 2025 despite her work being widely praised

Maurene Comey, the daughter of the former FBI director James Comey, was unlawfully fired from her job as a federal prosecutor in New York last year, a federal judge ruled on Monday.

Judge Jesse Furman said that Comey, who was an assistant US attorney for a decade, was illegally fired in July 2025 despite her work on some of the nation’s highest-profile cases and consistently receiving “the highest accolades from supervisors and peers alike”.

After her firing, Comey sued the justice department and others, saying her termination violated the constitutional separation of powers, the first amendment and the due process clause of the fifth amendment.

She asserted that she was fired because she was the daughter of James Comey, a longtime foe of Donald Trump, or because of her perceived political affiliation and beliefs, the judge noted.

Furman rejected the government’s claim that Comey could be fired because federal prosecutors exercise the president’s “conclusive and preclusive” powers.

He said the government’s claim that Congress is barred from regulating the removal of federal prosecutors “flies in the face of nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent”.

Furman added: “Indeed, to accept Defendants’ argument would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation’s constitutional system.”

The judge granted Comey retroactive reinstatement and back pay from the date of her firing through 20 December to “make her whole” and ensure that she doesn’t suffer adverse employment consequences for the “unlawful termination”.

Comey’s lawyers – Ellen Blain, Nicole Gueron, Deepa Vanamali and Margaret Donovan – lauded the ruling.

“This hard-earned victory belongs to Ms Comey, to all civil servants, and to all fighting for the rule of law,” they said in a statement. “As the Court correctly held, to accept the government’s argument about unlimited executive power ‘would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation’s constitutional system.’ This decision reaffirms our bedrock system of checks and balances: the President is not above the law.”

The justice department did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment.

Under the Trump administration, the justice department has fired scores of career employees, including prosecutors and FBI agents, who participated in investigations of the president or who were perceived as opposed to the administration’s agenda. Some of those firings have also resulted in federal lawsuits.

The firing of Maurene Comey was seen as particularly personal, given her father’s longtime adversarial relationship with Trump.

The president fired James Comey as FBI director in May 2017 as the bureau was investigating ties between Russia and the Republican’s successful 2016 campaign for the White House. Trump in the years since has repeatedly called for Comey to be jailed, and his justice department has worked with mixed success to make that happen.

An earlier criminal case accusing James Comey of having lied to Congress in 2020 was dismissed by a judge who concluded that the prosecutor who filed the charges was illegally appointed.

A separate pending indictment charges the former FBI director with threatening Trump through an Instagram photo of seashells in the numerical arrangement of “8647,” a case he has sought to dismiss that some legal experts have greeted with skepticism.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Southern California prepares for flooding amid forecast of ‘record-breaking tides’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Dani Anguiano
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Residents of coastal communities told to avoid beaches during high tides and keep further away from the ocean than usual

Southern California coastal communities are preparing for days of flooding amid potentially “record-breaking tides” this week.

The National Weather Service warned that significant coastal flooding is expected in San Diego and Orange counties through Thursday that could close roads and inundate homes, businesses and critical infrastructure. To the north, a wide swath of the coast from San Luis Obispo county to Los Angeles county could see “minor to moderate” coastal flooding with tides as high as 8ft.

“Avoid the beaches during high tides, keep farther back from the ocean than usual (waves will run much farther up the beach that expected), stay off rock walls/jetties, and make sure flood-prone property is protected this week,” the NWS office in San Diego said in a statement.

More than a week before the exceptionally high tides were forecast to arrive, the Orange county city of Newport Beach declared a local emergency to prepare for flooding. Staff were deploying across the area to inspect infrastructure, reinforce beach berms and install sandbags and other equipment, the city said. Newport Beach is providing free sandbags and advised residents to inspect vulnerable areas around their properties.

Due to El Niño and the Kelvin wave, ocean water levels in the region have already been about 15 to 22in higher than expected, Newport Beach city manager Seimone Jurjis said in a statement.

“A foot and a half may not sound like much, but in a coastal community like ours, it can mean the difference between water staying below a seawall and water spilling into streets, garages and homes, especially during some of the highest tides of the year,” Jurjis said.

This month has already brought extreme weather in the region, including flooding that overtook city streets and large waves that struck beachside homes. The remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel left a trail of destruction in California, significantly damaging homes, destroying a boardwalk and forcing residents to evacuate.

With a historic El Niño unfolding in the Pacific, California is expected to face severe storms this winter.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Father pays tribute to son, six, killed by truck on Kansas soccer field
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Richard Luscombe
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
At funeral service Chris Adrian remembers son Cole as ‘capturing the heart’ of everyone, after tragedy killing two

The father of Cole Adrian, a six-year-old boy killed when a woman drove through a soccer game at a park in Wichita, Kansas, on 17 October, paid an emotional tribute to his son at his funeral service on Monday.

Chris Adrian, of McPherson, Kansas, spoke through tears while he remembered Cole as an energetic, fun-loving child who loved life and “captured the heart” of everyone he met.

“Cole often told us this was the ‘best day ever’, even on days when nothing really special happened,” Adrian said during the eulogy, which was livestreamed. “He found joy in the simplest things, and had a way of making ordinary days feel extraordinary.

“The world would be a much brighter place if we all had a little bit more of Cole’s heart.”

The service for Cole at McPherson Free Methodist church was his family’s farewell to one of two victims from the tragedy at the Stryker Sports Complex that remains under police investigation.

Nicholas Schafer, 35, a soccer coach and middle school teacher also from McPherson, about an hour north of Wichita, was also killed when a pickup truck with a 34-year-old woman at the wheel reportedly sped from a parking lot and across the pitch where a game was under way.

Ten other people were injured, including girls aged five and nine, two boys aged eight, and one five-year-old boy.

The suspected driver, from Garden City, Kansas, who reportedly had two of her own children in the car with her, according to police, was arrested at the scene. She was released a day later without charges pending further investigation, including the results of toxicology testing as well as an examination of her truck.

At Monday’s service, Adrian said the family had taken comfort from the support of the Wichita youth soccer community, whose players wore tribute shirts bearing the letters “LLCA” at a game days after Cole’s death.

“At first, we didn’t know what it stood for,” he said, clutching the hand of his wife, Natalie, Cole’s mother.

“And so we sat up there in the press box, and it was ‘laugh like Cole’ – oh no, no, it could be ‘love like Cole’, ‘live like Cole’, ‘long live Cole’.

“Every one felt perfect. They’re more than words on a shirt now. They’re a reminder of who Cole was, and who we can all strive to be.”

“Monday morning, there was a double rainbow over our town of McPherson – and for me, it was an answer, it was a promise, it was a reminder from heaven that Cole and Nick are there together, and that someday we will see them again,” he said.

“We miss Cole more than we could ever express, and there are no words that can make this hurt less. There’s no pep talk that can make any of this make sense or be OK. There’s one thing that brings us comfort, that last week Cole ran through those gates of heaven just like we’ve seen him run across that soccer field so many times.

“I could see him running full speed, wrapping his arms around Jesus and giving him one of those famous squeeze hugs. Saying those words we were so lucky to hear so many times: ‘best day ever’.”

Investigators have urged the public to be patient as they continue to work through the circumstances of case in search of a cause.

Wichita’s police chief, Joe Sullivan, released a statement defending the release of the driver the day after the tragedy.

“We know that this case has captured the attention of people all over the country, and many of those people have strong opinions even though they do not have direct knowledge of what occurred,” he said, as reported by Kansas NPR affiliate KCUR.

“We recognize that the decision the law and constitution required us to make on [18 October] may not be popular. We swear an oath to support the laws of the state of Kansas and the constitution of the US, and no one in the Wichita police department takes that oath for granted.”

https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.title: Walter Koenig, actor best known as Chekov on Star Trek, dies aged 90
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.author: Adrian Horton
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.text:
The actor appeared in the cult 1960s show as well as many of the films but also worked as a writer

Walter Koenig, the actor known for playing Pavel Chekov throughout the Star Trek franchise, has died, his representative confirmed to the Hollywood Reporter. He was 90.

Koenig died at his home in north Hollywood surrounded by his daughter and niece, according to a Facebook post by Zachery McGinnis, the founder of Galactic Productions, an appearance agency that counted the actor as one of its clients. His death was attributed to “old age”, with no other details provided.

“Today we mourn the passing of Walter Koenig, whose talent, warmth, and unforgettable performances left a lasting mark on generations of fans around the world,” McGinnis wrote. “Walter’s legacy extends far beyond the screen. Through countless convention appearances and interactions with fans, he shared his kindness, wit, and appreciation with everyone fortunate enough to meet him. He understood what Star Trek meant to people and embraced the community that grew around it.”

The post concluded: “Thank you, Walter, for the memories, the inspiration, and for boldly going where few have gone before.”

“My heart is heavy,” wrote Koenig’s Star Trek costar George Takei on Facebook on Monday. Takei first met Koening in the 1960s, “on the bridge of the Enterprise” and remained friends for six decades; Koenig served as Takei’s best man at his wedding in 2008.

“Walter was more than Chekov. He was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man, and a loyal friend,” Takei wrote. “To the fans who loved him for so many years, thank you. He loved you too. Rest well, my dear friend. Keep navigating a steady course.”

Jesse Thorn, the host of the NPR show Bullseye, also confirmed the news on Bluesky, citing his friend Danielle Koenig, the late actor’s daughter. “Something I was struck by knowing Danielle, her husband and her late brother Andrew (and talking with George Takei) was the very sincere love those Star Trek cast members had for each other,” he wrote. “That whole thing was thrust upon them and their obvious deep friendship was so clear. What a gift.”

Born in Chicago but raised in Manhattan as the child of Lithuanian immigrants, Koenig began his acting career in 1962, with an uncredited role as a sentry in Combat!. He joined Star Trek for the start of the second season and appeared in 36 of the 50 episodes that aired between 1967 and 1969.

He continued his role as the Russian Chekov in the first seven Paramount movies derived from the show, released between 1979 and 1991, as well as in a two-part crowdsourced Renegades series that debuted online in 2017. He most recently reprised the voice of Chekov in a 2023 episode of the animated series Star Trek: Picard.

Koenig also worked as a writer, penning episodes for such series as The Powers of Matthew Star, Family, Land of the Lost and The Incredible Hulk. He wrote, produced and starred in the 2010 sci-film InAlienable, starring Richard Hatch.

Koenig was married to actor Judy Levitt, with whom he appeared in three Star Trek movies as well as another acclaimed sci-fi series, Babylon 5, which ran from 1994 until 1998. The couple were together from 1965 until her death in December 2022 at age 83. Their son Andrew, who played Richard “Boner” Stabone in the ABC sitcom Growing Pains, died in 2010 at age 41.

Koenig is survived by his daughter, the actor and screenwriter Danielle Koenig.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: iPhone Duo owners report cracks in Apple’s first foldable handset
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Dan Milmo Global technology editor
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Company says small number of devices affected by display glitch after posts appear on Reddit and social media

Owners of the new foldable iPhone are reporting cracks in the device’s screen, as Apple confirmed an issue with a “small number” of units.

Reports of cracks have emerged on Reddit and social media platforms since the handset went on general sale globally on Friday. Experts said there had been too few examples to determine whether therewas a more serious problem with Apple’s first foldable device, which retails from $1,999 (£1,499).

“We are aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units. If users experience issues with their iPhone Duo display, they should contact AppleCare for a replacement,” it said.

One user in Australia reported that their Duo had cracked within six hours of taking ownership of it and posted their experience on Reddit.

“I was showing it to a friend, and as I opened it, I felt something around the internal hinge, underneath the screen,” they wrote alongside an image of the phone showing an apparent display malfunction where a white strip of light ran along one half of the screen.

“As I continued opening it, I heard an audible crack, and the screen broke right along the hinge.”

They said their local Apple store had replaced the phone immediately. The Guardian has been unable to verify the user’s claims. Another user in Australia posted that they had heard “almost a cracking noise” on their handset, which resulted in a similar screen malfunction.

A report by the Bloomberg news service also highlighted similar issues among users in the US and India.

Apple believes the affected units are showing defects quickly after use. It said the response from early users had been “incredibly positive”.

The company said demand had been “nothing short of extraordinary” for the iPhone Duo, its most high-profile product launch under the company’s new chief executive, John Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook in September.

The device has sold out and the next round of shipments is not expected until January, according to a report in the Economic Daily, a publication based in Taiwan, the home country of Foxconn, Apple’s main device manufacturer.

Francisco Jeronimo, the vice-president of data and analytics at IDC, a tech research company, said it was too early to tell whether the screen issue was significant.

Citing similar problems at Samsung in 2019 with the company’s Galaxy Fold phone, he said: “What matters now is how the company responds … Samsung experienced problems with the original Galaxy Fold in 2019, but it also showed that a fast and transparent response can contain the damage to a category.

“Apple said that any customer with problems should ask for a replacement, which is the right first step.”

Ben Wood, the chief analyst at the research firm CCS, said he was taking a very cautious view of the Duo screen problem and that there was as yet no evidence of a more widespread issue with the device.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: As students we never sought power – here’s how we reclaimed Serbia | Novak Simin
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Novak Simin
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
After freedom, we want to give our people something radical: a normal, functioning state

Two years ago, I harboured no political ambition whatsoever. I was a student at the faculty of technical sciences in Novi Sad, my home town, pursuing a PhD in human resources and simply living my life. That was until the canopy collapse at the newly renovated train station in Novi Sad in November 2024, which killed 16 people. I took part in street protests and rallies in response to this shocking event, and like many others, realised that it needed to be a turning point.

This was not an unavoidable tragedy. Systemic corruption and a culture of entrenched impunity were obvious factors in the collapse. But instead of ordering a full and impartial investigation and coming clean on official failings, the authorities began pushing back against us for demanding justice. We were vilified and attacked in the streets but law enforcement did nothing. So we took refuge in our lecture halls and schools, barricading ourselves inside faculty buildings, ready for a long haul.

Democratic principles have long been ignored in Serbia but we made sure we observed them in our gatherings. As our coordination developed, we made sure we had the same clear goal for every demonstration we organised: pressuring a corrupt government to meet our demands. And these were demands that in any free country would have been accepted automatically. We wanted, for example, all the documentation concerning the renovation of Novi Sad railway station to be made public, without redaction, and that everyone responsible for the works be held to account. We demanded that those who assaulted us in the streets be arrested and prosecuted. Instead of agreeing, state officials began branding us fascists and traitors.

I was personally targeted for speaking out. As I handled media relations and communications, this often meant giving interviews to the country’s few remaining independent outlets. For this, I was accused by the regime’s propaganda machine of money laundering “millions” and conspiring with foreign powers. Others had to leave the country after being accused of high treason; some spent months in detention on manufactured, illegally obtained evidence. Many of us were placed under surveillance, our parents threatened, and many were fired from jobs and dragged through the mud in the pro-government popular press.

But none of that intimidation broke us; rather it hardened our resolve. And eventually, when it became clear the regime would never concede, we opted to enter the electoral arena ourselves. That was the genesis of the Student List. Through open, democratic plenary sessions, we nominated individuals of integrity and competence, people who were committed to justice and freedom for a silenced society.

Our aims were clear and never wavered: we wanted Serbia to be governed by the rule of law, independent public institutions, transparency and solidarity in a fractured nation. We marched thousands of kilometres across Serbia, campaigning relentlessly and in doing so helped, I believe, to rekindle hope among the broader public. State propaganda could not hope to drown out that much unfiltered grassroots momentum.

Now the regime has fallen, our collective effort to rebuild Serbia begins. True, sceptics may argue that we have filled parliament with political novices. The truth is that we have filled it with people eager to serve and willing to learn. Our newly elected representatives are professors, doctors, lawyers, farmers and scientists, all experts in their fields. Each has an established record of honest work and civic integrity. They may lack traditional political backgrounds, but they have spent the past two years studying the realities of governance and public trust. That very lack of direct political involvement is why the Serbian people have placed their faith in us: they did not vote for slick rhetoric or cynical manoeuvreing. They voted for clean hands.

We are neither promising, nor expecting overnight miracles as a result of this victory; rather we hope for something fundamentally radical for Serbia: normal, functioning institutions.

This mandate must first of all dismantle the culture of impunity. That requires verifiably independent prosecutors, fully transparent public procurement processes, and legal accountability for anyone who treated state resources as private spoils. For too long our teachers, healthcare workers and civil servants have seen their expertise subordinated to party loyalty cards. We want to restore the dignity of these dedicated public servants.

We have taken our country back, and are proud to stand as free citizens of Serbia. If this historic turning point proves anything, it is that this country does not belong to an untouchable ruling elite. It belongs to all of us. We have proven that dignity is non-negotiable. Now, the real work begins. This victory marks the end of institutional fear. For the first time in years, we can breathe freely.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Guardian view on Lula’s comeback: a victory for Brazil and the world, as well as a Trump rebuff | Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
A fourth presidential victory gives Lula another chance to defend democracy, protect the Amazon and deliver for Brazil’s working people

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s win in Brazil’s presidential election is a triumph for him, his country and the world. The 80-year-old incumbent snatched victory from the jaws of defeat, blocked the rise of the far right and saved the planetary air-conditioning system of the Amazon from irreparable destruction. Known universally as Lula, he made history by becoming the first candidate to win a presidential run-off after finishing second in the opening round. In triumphing against Flávio Bolsonaro, the leftist stopped what could have been the most dangerous consolidation of authoritarian rule in Brazil since military rule ended. A Bolsonaro presidency could have used a rightwing Congress to extend presidential terms and pack the supreme court, entrenching power for generations.

Lula seemed to have been energised by his first-round defeat by Mr Bolsonaro. The three-time president initially pitted his extraordinary life and record against a 45-year-old senator married to controversy. But voters wanted answers to economic insecurity, rising prices and poor public services. Lula reversed course in the second round, offering immediate relief from everyday costs and indebtedness – including to the rising number of self-employed voters whom his rightwing opponent had been courting. Popular mobilisation transformed the runoff into a race to stop a Bolsonaro restoration with student protests, mass demonstrations and a 10 million-strong “Lula’s Army” WhatsApp channel. It seemed to work. Nearly 5 million more people voted in the second round of the Brazilian election than the first.

Mr Bolsonaro’s desperate refusal to concede follows his father’s playbook. In 2022 then-president Jair Bolsonaro did the same, claiming fraud. The elder Bolsonaro’s attempted coup saw him jailed for 27 years. This time Lula’s margin of victory – 4.4m votes – over the younger Bolsonaro was twice that achieved over the father. His win has also been recognised by rightwing regional leaders, conservative newspapers and even a prominent evangelical ally of the Bolsonaros. It may be significant that defeat denied Mr Bolsonaro a presidential shield from allegations of corruption and money laundering. Whether he remains in Brazil after his term as senator expires in February remains to be seen.

After the Bolsonaro clan, the next biggest loser from the results of the Brazilian election is Donald Trump. Lula’s win broke a run of seven rightwing presidential wins across Latin America, a regional advance for which Mr Trump had claimed credit. While rightwing leaders in Chile, Paraguay and Peru congratulated Lula on his victory, the White House remained silent. The US president has only himself to blame: he tried to use tariffs to pressure Brazil over the elder Bolsonaro’s prosecution and its courts’ enforcement actions against American tech companies. Mr Trump’s meddling handed Lula a winning argument for Brazil’s sovereignty.

Brazil remains divided, with a rightwing Congress ready to obstruct Lula – particularly on the environment. But few are better placed to negotiate than the former trade unionist who founded the Workers’ party. Lula’s victory provides an elected counterweight and that matters for labour rights, public services, Indigenous communities and global climate policy. The win shows the wider democratic left that a broad coalition can defeat the right. Can governing produce the secure livelihoods, strong state provision and meaningful opportunities that make that coalition durable? The next four years in Brazil may provide an answer.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Guardian view on Serbia’s student revolution: from principled protest to power | Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Two years after the Novi Sad tragedy gave birth to a youthful political movement, Sunday’s remarkable election has taken the country into a new era

This weekend it will be two years since the collapse of a shoddily constructed train station canopy in Serbia’s second city, Novi Sad. The tragedy, killing 16 people, was swiftly attributed to state corruption and failures of regulation, sparking student-led protests across the country.

Some of those demonstrators dared to imagine that they could become the catalyst for a democratic revolution.

On Sunday, that is more or less what happened. After sustaining their protests and turning them into a political movement, the students resoundingly defeated Aleksandar Vučić’s autocratic government in a snap legislative poll called by the president himself. Their victory constitutes one of the most remarkable election outcomes in recent European history.

For well over a decade Mr Vučić and his Serbian Progressive party (SNS) have exerted a domineering grip over civil society and the media, ruling through a combination of cronyism, patronage and bullying authoritarianism. As a report by international observers confirmed on Monday, the government made full, unscrupulous use of such tactics to ensure there was no level playing field for the vote. That it was nevertheless routed by a leaderless movement of 20- and 30-somethings will have been noted across a continent in which youth protest is challenging political priorities.

As in Hungary, where a focus on corruption helped the opposition to unseat Viktor Orbán after 16 years in office, the students’ campaign for basic democratic renewal struck a deeper chord than perhaps even they thought possible. Posing the choice for voters as “Serbia or mafia?”, they put forward a Student List of civic candidates dominated by academics, but also featuring farmers and well-known athletes. A turnout of almost 70% – the highest in a Serbian election since the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1992 – delivered them a comfortable majority.

What comes next will necessarily be an experiment in doing things differently. By standing apart from established structures of politics, the student insurgents embodied a freshness of approach and won the trust of the public – including in rural areas presumed to be bastions of Vučić support. In the immediate future, the new government is likely to function as a kind of constituent assembly, dedicated primarily to cleaning up civil society and rolling back the abuses that saw Serbia plunge towards the bottom of European corruption rankings.

Politically, the priority will be to consolidate this domestic agenda by winning the forthcoming presidential election. which is due by late December. But in the longer term there will be less straightforward debates to be had. Mr Vučić’s defeat is good news for the western Balkans as a whole, where he has been a consistently disruptive presence. But on foreign policy issues such as joining the European Union and relations with Russia, opinion across the student movement is divided.

As a new government seeks to re-establish the rule of law and a properly functioning and accountable state, Brussels must do all it can to assist that process while outlining a plausible and attractive path to EU membership. Mr Vučić’s Serbia, like Mr Orbán’s Hungary, became a soft autocracy where power was so entrenched that it was hard to imagine how it could be dislodged. But now there are new and better possibilities. In extraordinary fashion, the students’ inspiring journey from principled protest to power has shown just what the art of politics can deliver.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/liv.title: Ballon d’Or 2026: updates from 70th edition in London – live
https://www.theguardian.com/football/liv.author: Daniel Harris
https://www.theguardian.com/football/liv.text:
⚽️ Ballon d’Or updates from 8pm GMT ⚽️ Ceremony returns to England in nod to Stanley Matthews ⚽️ Women’s power rankings: will a new winner be crowned? ⚽️ Send your thoughts to Daniel via email

I can’t for the life of me get on board with the line we’re now hearing: had Argentina somehow snaffled the World Cup, the award would have to be Messi’s. He’s still got plenty, of course, but a stuffy set-piece goal, say, or a 0-0 and penalty triumph wouldn’t have somehow made him the best in the world. It’s not a lifetime achievement award.

Talking of UK winners, it’s absolutely insane to think that, in 1968, three winners – Denis Law, Bobby Charlton and George Best – played in the same Manchester United team. Now, though, despite the money in the Premier League and with the exception of Erling Haaland and Bruno Fernandes, the best attackers are found in La Liga and Ligue 1. That looks likely to change only in the next generation and only if English clubs develop their own elite talent
