With the discovery of natural selection, it seemed obvious to Galton that “what nature does blindly, slowly, and ruthlessly, man may do providently, quickly, and kindly”, as he put it in his seminal 1904 essay, Eugenics: Its Definition, Scope, and Aims.

An enduring image from the early decades of the movement is the “eugenics tree” commissioned for the Second International Congress of Eugenics, held in New York City in 1921. Growing from roots labelled with disciplines across the natural sciences, social sciences and humanities, the tree is surrounded by the words “eugenics is the self direction of human evolution”. In that image, the accumulation of knowledge as well as biological processes are provided with a teleology. But what are their goals? What is all the control, management and optimisation really for?

To Galton, and to the generations of committed eugenicists who succeeded him, eugenics was politically and morally necessary in order to prevent societal disaster due to degeneration. Following earlier thinkers such as Thomas Malthus, they worried that too many poor and undesirable people were reproducing. In a short time, the superior peoples, whether defined as the upper class or as “Anglo-Saxons”, “Nordic types” or “Aryans”, would be outbred and outcompeted by their natural inferiors.

Eugenics’ proposal of wholesale management of the population was thus made in service of a particular ideal of humanity, where the universal “best” was defined in a strikingly narrow way. Through the notion of “hereditary genius”, Galton presented the privileges of wealth and class as innate qualities; while he explained undesirable traits such as “vagrancy” and “criminality” as the causes, rather than the consequences, of poverty, deprivation and marginalisation. Galton’s eugenic utopia was an idea that reflected the prejudices of a particular place and time.

The same is true of liberal eugenics in our own time. We may question whether the genomics companies’ promises of “best babies” are credible. But it may be more important to ask what their notion of the “best” is. What do they see as valuable and worthless in a human life?

Liberal eugenics accentuates the positive. In an attempt to distance itself from the forced sterilisations of the past, it prefers to focus, as Nucleus does, on human improvement and enhancement. But as Rutherford notes, in biology you cannot select for something without selecting against something else. Positive eugenics and negative eugenics are two sides of the same coin; without an idea of what is undesired, there can be no notion of the desirable.

For the Victorian eugenicists, the “best” was an amalgam of racial fantasies about “Nordic” or “Aryan” types conflated with the privileges of the upper classes, defined against the undesirable character of brown and black people, and the underclass. For the new eugenics in its liberal form, positive qualities coalesce around productivity and competitive advantage. The ideal human is strikingly close to the ideal worker, someone who is smart, efficient and unlikely to ever take a sick day.

Against this ideal stand the unwanted lives of people with disabilities and chronic illnesses. Intellectual disability was among eugenics’ biggest bugbears, but a range of other conditions recur as targets to be eradicated. In a way, this is unsurprising. Disability really does mean disadvantage. That is something I know in my bones – and my muscles. Disability, as the scholar Tom Shakespeare has written, is a predicament. It means limitation and restriction; it can mean pain and suffering. There are simple reasons why I longed so deeply for a cure. The reasons why and how that longing began to fade are more complex.

As it turned out, medical genetics really did produce an effective treatment for spinal muscular atrophy. About a decade ago, a drug called nusinersen was being developed. Some studies suggest that if it is administered early enough, it can wholly counteract the symptoms of the condition, while arresting its progression in adults. But medical genetics also proved that I didn’t have SMA after all. The original diagnosis was made on the basis of muscle biopsies and clinical guesswork. When a test for the genetic markers for SMA became available, mine came back negative. Instead, I was shown to have an even rarer condition – rarer, and less likely to attract research funding. I am tempted to quote Franz Kafka, who once remarked that there is infinite hope in the universe, only not for us.

But, in truth, that isn’t quite apt. Losing both the original diagnosis and the possibility of a treatment felt like a wave of sorrow, tinged with relief. Strange as it may seem, it also gave me a greater sense of freedom, that my life was really my own.

Don’t get me wrong. If there was an actual cure for my condition, I would take it. But there won’t be one, at least not for me. Too much time has passed; too much of my life is behind me. It is my life as it unfolded, and I try my best not to compare it to lives I didn’t live.

It is easier to think this way in your forties than in your teens. In the company of my nondisabled friends, I see plenty of injuries, illnesses and vaguely defined aches. We all have the markings of life. It’s not exactly that my disability ceases to matter as I grow older. In one way, it’s quite the opposite, as I feel the physical impact of the world on my muscles and joints. But I do feel a sense of convergence with my kith and my kin about the tenuousness and frailty of it all, about the need to take care of each other, as we hurtle towards what is coming.

Call it a kind of realism. Those of us who have kids know another side of it. If you plan to have a particular kind of child, you are setting yourself up for failure. Every parent I know has had to abandon their notions of what they thought their children would be for the reality of their particular children. I don’t think any one of them subscribed to the idea of an ideal baby. I hope they didn’t. Such an ideal is a terrible thing for parents as well as children to live up to.

This is the most corrosive effect of liberal neo-eugenics: in positing that an individual ideal of embodiment is something that can be specified, quantified and realised, it creates a framework for torturing both our children and ourselves. Why are we not this perfect thing? Why are we not fitter, happier, more productive? I’m not particularly sentimental about the value of disability in any particular case, but I think it is crucial to acknowledge disability as part of human variation. In treating ever more traits and qualities as things to be measured, ranked and diagnosed, we are doing the opposite – turning variation itself into something like disability.

For me, hope comes from working to change the world so that it accommodates imperfection. One of the reasons I dislike liberal eugenics is that its individualist ethos runs counter to political measures that have mattered immensely in my lifetime. I believe we should direct our efforts toward making better societies rather than making better people.

During the postwar era, in parallel with the eugenic shift from the population level to the individual level, disability began to become a socio-political issue rather than a medical one. What the sociologist Mike Oliver once called the “personal tragedy theory” of disability was challenged by a social model that explained how people with a range of different impairments and illnesses were made disabled by societal structures.

Essentially, what constitutes “disability” varies with place and time. Although dyslexia can be hugely disadvantageous in the modern world, in a nonliterate society it amounts only to neurological difference. The kind of mobility impairment that I have – that is, being unable to walk for more than a few steps, or get up from the floor – is restricting under any circumstances. But it is orders of magnitude more disabling in a society without wheelchairs, or wheelchair accessibility. In between these extremes, there are conditions, illnesses and impairments that amount to disability in some contexts but not in others.

The goal is not to abolish cures, but to abolish the idea that only cures, or the prenatal optimisation of an embryo, can make for a life worth living. For the disability movement, the aim has always been to make a better world for everyone: a world where people with all kinds of bodies can thrive and flourish. That includes both people who were born disabled and people who had disability thrust upon them. It is a project that accounts for human variation, and the variability of life.

That is why it stands opposed to the neo-eugenic notion that there is a “best baby”; the best, in the singular, is not something the human species should be striving towards at all. It also bears remembering that the majority of disabilities do not stem from wholly genetic causes, but from an interaction of human genetic variation with the wear and tear of the world. There are good reasons to research cures, treatments and interventions whenever possible; there are equally good reasons to temper our expectations for how the human species may be perfected.

Rosemarie Garland-Thomson, a scholar of disability and bioethics, has put forward the “case for conserving disability”. It is a provocative case, for the obvious reason that disability, and chronic illness, are qualities which entail vulnerability and dependence on others. But, then again, so does the human condition. We are born helpless, and we age into helplessness. Even if we come into the world equipped for perfect health, we are always at risk of illness and injury. Neo-eugenics offers a vision of total independence, of a disconnect from society. Measured against such an ideal, all of us fall short. However strong and self-reliant we may think ourselves to be, we are a social species, with few prospects of surviving, let alone thriving, on our own.

The aim of control, and so of predictability, is intrinsic to eugenics’ notion of the ideal society. But who wants to live in a fully controlled, fully predictable world? A world where an external entity tells you how to live your life down to the last detail, what to eat, when and where to move, what to watch, all in the name of becoming your best possible self? Oh, right.

Against this vision of total algorithmic control, we must appeal to the unpredictability of the human condition. Shortly after the second world war, Hannah Arendt wrote her magnum opus The Origins of Totalitarianism, in which she traced the construction of “superfluous people” – whole swathes of the population made disenfranchised and killable by states that saw them as useless at best and dangerous at worst. Eugenics was central to this idea of superfluousness: of people who were incidental to the future of the species, or the nation, or the race.

Arendt described totalitarianism as, among other things, a vision for the absolute closure of the future, against all alternatives. In a subsequent book, titled The Human Condition, she laid out the alternative principle, by which human societies could grow and develop. That principle was plurality – the encounter with difference. Only this encounter provided the possibility for what Arendt saw as humanity’s highest calling – namely action: something with unforeseeable consequences and unpredictable results.

With her notion of plurality, Arendt was not referring to disability as such. But the concept can be extended to human embodiment. As humans, we are very much alike, but we are not the same. We may share the same bodily needs that must be met if we are to flourish, but our varying capabilities, talents and preferences mean that flourishing may look very different from one case to the next. Against the narrow-minded eugenic idea of “the best baby”, we can perhaps set another concept of Arendt’s: what she called natality. With each birth, with each new person, something wholly unique comes into being. And the world is made anew.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: The fight for Jaysley Beck: how her grieving mother turned detective – and took on the military
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Anna Moore
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
In 2021, the young soldier took her life after being sexually assaulted by a sergeant major, then sent thousands of messages by her line manager. She was just 19. Five years on, Leighann McCready is still searching for answers

When Leighann McCready phoned her 19-year-old daughter, Jaysley Beck, on 15 December 2021, she got no reply, but brushed away her worries. “Jays always, always answered her phone, but it was early, eight in the morning,” she says. Beck, an army soldier in the Royal Artillery, had been at a party the night before at her Wiltshire barracks. She was probably asleep.

It was a busy time, the Christmas countdown. Soon, Beck was expected to be back home in Cumbria, where her parents – McCready and Anthony Beck – own a village pub. McCready had already bought matching Christmas pyjamas for Beck and her older sister Emilli to wear on the day.

Beck had been preparing for the holidays, too. She had been Christmas shopping two days earlier, calling and consulting throughout the day with her mum, who was transferring the cash to cover it all. She’d bought presents for herself and her sister: a Gucci bag, a belt and a purse. For her dad, she’d bought tickets for a James Blunt concert for the two of them to attend together in February. At the end of the spree, Beck had messaged her mum: “We’re two so lucky girls aren’t we, Mum? Thank you, thank you, thank you. I love you with all my heart!”

Despite all this, as the hours passed that Tuesday in December, with still no word from Beck, McCready began to feel a deep foreboding. She knew that, in the preceding weeks, her daughter had been struggling through a strange and intense period of escalating harassment from her line manager. With this in mind, Emilli offered to call one of Beck’s friends at the barracks, who assured them that Beck was probably fast asleep. “He said he was five minutes away and he’d go and wake her,” says McCready. “That five minutes just seemed like forever. I continued ringing Jays’ phone – until somebody else answered it. The voice said: ‘Hello, can I ask who I’m speaking to?’ And I just knew. They didn’t even have to tell me.”

Gunner Beck had taken her life, alone in her bedroom. Her suicide threw a spotlight on the British army and the treatment, safety and protection of female recruits. For the last five years, ever since Beck’s death, McCready has fought for answers and accountability. She has found some, but believes there is still far more to uncover. At every step – the service inquiry, the inquest and a subsequent police investigation – McCready has been in the public eye, talking to the press, advocating for her daughter. Now, she features in a Stacey Dooley documentary, Death in the Barracks, which follows the family’s continued search for justice. She still can’t quite believe that any of it is real.

“Grief is not what you see on TV, where you instantly fall to the floor and break down in tears,” says McCready, who has worked for 30 years in the care sector, much of it as an end-of-life nurse. “The moment I found out, I automatically went from being a mum, a partner, a daughter, to quite literally feeling as if I was putting my uniform on. It was about protecting a family and guiding them. No matter how many interviews I do or how many times I see Jays’ photo in the news, it doesn’t register. That isn’t my daughter – and this isn’t my life. I call it my ‘invisible uniform’ and I have never taken it off.”

Beck had joined the army at 16. “As a child, I used to call her my baby muck-magnet,” says McCready. “She was a cheeky little chops – pulling out her pigtails, collecting snails. She loved helping her dad with DIY. You always knew when Jays was around.” Aged 15, she’d returned from a school careers day intent on joining the army. McCready wasn’t keen. “I hadn’t expected that in a million years,” she says. “I thought it was a phase, but she was determined. She put her heart and soul into it. I remember her running round the village wearing backpacks weighted with bricks to build her strength up. She was only tiny – probably a size six in clothes.”

After Beck’s initial military training, her family attended her passing in parade at Army Foundation College Harrogate. “It was magical,” says McCready. “I was a proud mum.”

Beck settled happily into army life – but in her final six months, that changed. In July 2021, at a training exercise, Beck was sexually assaulted by Michael Webber (then 39, married, and a battery sergeant major). She escaped, then spent the night hiding in her car. When Beck reported the incident to senior officers, she was advised not to be “a female troublemaker”, and was urged to think of Webber’s career, and his family. Eventually, after she reported it a second time, Webber was asked to write Beck a letter of apology. He was promoted shortly afterwards. This meant that, three months later, when her line manager, bombardier Ryan Mason, 32, began showing an obsessive interest in Beck, she had no faith in any complaints process, and nowhere to turn.

McCready had known all this as it happened. “Jays told me everything,” she says. Her daughter had even shared Mason’s messages on a family WhatsApp – he sent more than 4,600 in two months. The family had tried to advise and support her, but they were hundreds of miles away, and military protocol was a strange, sealed world. “When she was assaulted by Michael Webber, she’d said: ‘Get off me, sir.’” says McCready. “I remember my first reaction was: ‘How, Jays, did you call him “sir”?’ Some of it was over my head.”

In the days after Beck’s death, as their home filled with military personnel, McCready became determined to bring all she knew to light. “Jays was not going to be another statistic. She was not another ‘sudden passing’,” she says.

“I was not a ‘grieving mum’. You have to be stronger than that,” she continues. “I had to keep going for Jays and also for Emilli. What would she do if I broke? She’d crumble, she wouldn’t be far behind me.” Christmas was days away, so McCready asked Emilli how they should spend it. Should they even get a tree? “Emilli said: ‘Lets do the tree, and let’s still go to Auntie’s as planned for Christmas Day.’ So that’s what we did,” says McCready. “It didn’t feel right, but nothing would have felt right. I printed up a big picture of Jaysley and asked if I could put it in the tree so she’d be watching.” McCready didn’t touch any alcohol – in fact, she hasn’t had a drop since losing her daughter. “I don’t want alcohol to affect my emotions,” she says. She doesn’t watch TV either. “I don’t think it’s good for my mindset. I remember trying to settle down one night – I think it was [with] Gogglebox – and the first thing that was shown was a mortuary. I couldn’t turn it off quick enough.”

Her “invisible uniform”, her years in end-of-life care, guided all her decisions in those first weeks. “I knew I needed to be kind to my mind, to bubble-wrap it and protect it,” she says. “I chose not to see Jays after her passing and I don’t regret it. I know from my work that it’s just a shell left behind, and do I want to see my daughter’s shell? Instead, I can close my eyes and she’s that happy little girl – she’s smiling, she’s singing, she’s running round the block with her backpack on. I didn’t deal with the coroner – I didn’t want to know details.”

What she did want, instantly and urgently, was to visit Beck’s room in Larkhill garrison. She had to push for access. “I was told I was not allowed, so we had a meeting. I explained how much I needed this moment. I wanted to lie on my daughter’s bed. I wanted to know the last bit of music she played – Jays loved music, we always shared songs and playlists. What was the last bit of laundry she put in her laundry basket? How do her clothes smell?”

The family were finally allowed entry on 28 December, although they were initially informed that they had to be accompanied. “I said: ‘Absolutely not.’” McCready had another motive, too. “I needed to gather as much information to find out what happened,” she says. “I wanted the letter of apology from Michael Webber – I knew exactly where she’d filed it. I wanted her smart watch and her laptop. I got all of them. I did want her phone, too – but Wiltshire police had already taken that.” Months later, when the police had done nothing with the phone, McCready returned to Wiltshire to collect it, having argued successfully that she had paid for it – so it was in fact hers, not Beck’s.

“Not only had I put my invisible uniform on, in my mind, I was also becoming a detective,” McCready says. “I sat down with a roll of wallpaper and I did a timeline.” She also found a lawyer through the Centre for Military Justice. “We’ve been on this journey together and we’ve had to push for every single inquiry and investigation since.”

There have been some answers. After the inquest, the coroner’s summing-up report found Mason’s “intolerable harassment” and “the daily barrage of messages, calls and face-to-face encounters” to have been a significant factor in Beck’s suicide. As her line manager, Beck found Mason possessive and manipulative, setting the rota so that they were always together. He said that he loved her, composed messages that ran to essays, called her at night and engaged in lengthy conversations, sometimes until 4am (when she had to be up at 6am).

On 7 December 2021 – a week before Beck’s death – Mason and Beck had been staying in a hotel for a recruitment event when Beck left suddenly in the night, after calling a friend while in tears, who drove over and took her back to barracks. At the inquest, giving evidence, Mason said that he did not know the reason for Beck’s sudden departure that night. (He left the army the day after the recruitment event.)

The summing-up also found that the earlier mishandling of Beck’s sexual assault complaint against Webber had left her “with a feeling of injustice but, more importantly, [a loss of] faith in her ability to complain effectively”. After the inquest, Webber was charged with sexual assault and, last October, pleaded guilty. He was sentenced to six months.

Other factors were identified as “significant” by the coroner, foremost Beck’s “turmoil” around her intimate relationships. In November 2021, she had separated from her long-term boyfriend – although the two remained friends. She’d then embarked on an affair with a married sergeant. She was a 19-year-old girl, says McCready, making some mistakes and finding her way – and none of this explains why her daughter, who had never reported any mental health problems, should so suddenly end her life.

“Truth be told, there are still so many unanswered questions,” says McCready, “but I’m trying not to let them into my head. It won’t change anything for Jays. Instead, I’m trying to focus on changing things for the next people.” She welcomes MoD plans to tackle “unacceptable behaviours” in the military, including a Violence Against Women and Girls taskforce and a tri-service team, covering the army, navy and RAF, which will take serious complaints out of the single chain of command.

“It’s going in the right direction,” she says, “but it’s not enough. The reporting system has to be independent, separate from the army. I’m still contacted daily by soldiers, veterans and their families who have their own stories of rape, assault, bullying, harassment – and it’s not just females.” She hopes the Dooley documentary will encourage more to come forward, and she’s in the process of establishing a formal organisation, Jaysley’s Voice, to advocate on their behalf.

Meanwhile, Christmas – that most difficult anniversary – is coming. This year, McCready and Anthony are flying out to Thailand to meet Emilli and her partner, who now live in Australia. “We’ve promised each other that we’ll always be together at Christmas,” says McCready. “Emilli went travelling 10 months after we lost Jaysley, so we’ve met her in Vietnam, Singapore, Thailand, Bali. She keeps us busy, living the best life possible, which is exactly what Jays would have wanted for her. She’d have wanted that for all of us.”

Sometimes, McCready wonders if she has left any time and space for grief. She has rarely cried, she says, and opted against counselling. Could it all come crashing down? “I do ask: ‘Is this it?’” she says. “What am I waiting to feel like? Am I in denial?” Usually, though, she prefers to believe that Jaysley is close by, holding her together, protecting her from the worst of it, still on guard. “Maybe she’s saying: ‘This is how it will be for you, Mum, I’m not going to let you be hurt,’” says McCready. “For me, she’s still here.”

Stacey Dooley: Death in the Barracks screens Tuesday 27 October at 9pm on BBC Three; 10.40pm on BBC One; and iPlayer

https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2026/o.title: Cheer up, Scrooge! The merriest Christmas theatre shows, from musketeers to a penguin party
https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2026/o.author: Arifa Akbar
https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2026/o.text:
The festive season brings swashbuckling adventure, heartwarming Antarctic antics, a yuletide spin on Pride and Prejudice and Matthew Bourne’s Cinderella

Selina Cartmell is sending in the clowns this Christmas, directing Stephen Sondheim’s fairytale musical about mismatched couples. Originally inspired by an Ingmar Bergman film, it has some of the most exquisite songs of Sondheim’s magnificent oeuvre and is choreographed by former Strictly judge Arlene Phillips.

Buckle up for some swashbuckling: the RSC’s version of D’Artagnan’s duelling adventures alongside Athos, Porthos and Aramis is co-produced with Told By an Idiot, a company known for its visual comedy. It is billed as a “wild” new adaptation of Alexandre Dumas’s novel and features an international company of performers.

In George Stiles and Anthony Drewe’s musical drama for all ages, Ugly is a plucky wee duck, teased by siblings and friends alike for his idiosyncratic looks. We find him undertaking a perilous wild goose (duckling?) chase in his quest to discover the beautiful drake within.

Birmingham Rep until 1 November, then Peacock theatre, London, 21 November to 3 January 2027

Raymond Briggs’s gorgeous snowman goes walking in the air again in a new version of the Christmas classic, about an unlikely friendship that takes delightful flight. Featuring Howard Blake’s timeless score, it is now directed and choreographed by Will Tuckett and features puppets designed by Tahra Zafar, who recreated Michael Bond’s Paddington Bear for the West End musical.

The Robin Hood story is relocated and respun to place a female outlaw at its centre. Now it is Maid Marian of south Wales, whose resistance against the king’s men will be accompanied by familiar faces from the legend. Performed by a band of actor-musicians and directed by Lee Lyford.

Here’s a south pole show filled with icy wildlife, from tripping penguins to cheeky albatrosses. There are clowns, puppets and the promise of some magical surprises in this tale of what lies at the bottom of our planet. A winter wonderland for children, aimed at three- to seven-year-olds.

Amid the season’s flurry of fairytale princesses in glass slippers is Matthew Bourne’s 30-year-old ballet, twirling back for an anniversary tour. Set during the second world war, it situates the romance in blitz-torn London. Hannah Kremer and Katrina Lyndon share the role of Cinders, who meets an RAF pilot. The show travels to 17 venues over 24 weeks.

Another spin on the heroic outlaws of Sherwood folklore. This Robin Hood hails from E15 and hits east London in a hoodie, along with his merry band of “mandem”. Nottinghamshire’s forest is swapped for housing estates, retail jungles and the Central Line commuter rush as Robin’s men take from the undeserving rich to give to the area’s poor.

A child befriends a flamboyant, poetry-reciting dragon and embarks on an intrepid campaign to save it from a slayer who mistakes it for a fire-breathing fiend in Kenneth Grahame’s book. A David and Goliath story in reverse, now told as a musical family show.

The elves want old Saint Nicholas to take five from shimmying up and down chimneys and drink in some yuletide spirit himself in this adaptation of Mac Barnett’s book. Directed and choreographed by Olivier award-winner James Cousins, it has songs by Harry Blake.

The National Theatre’s Christmas shows have hit the mark in recent years. This one reimagines Rudyard Kipling’s classic tale of Mowgli and friends’ adventures through the mangroves of the Sundarbans. It’s adapted by Anupama Chandrasekhar and staged by the NT’s artistic director, Indhu Rubasingham, with puppetry by Nick Barnes and Finn Caldwell.

Just when we thought Neverland was safe! Captain Hook strikes back in this continuation of JM Barrie’s story about the pirate’s feud with the forever young leader of the Lost Boys. Here it comes in the form of a pantomime, complete with songs and aerial stunts.

The hot new takes on Pride and Prejudice keep on coming. This festive permutation by playwrights Lauren Gunderson and Margot Melcon finds the Bennets reuniting at the family estate, and centres on bookish middle sister, Mary, and a Christmas visit from Lord Arthur de Bourgh.

What’s Christmas without this classic about moral wrongdoings, ghostly reckonings and redemption, featuring the stingy Ebenezer Scrooge? Charles Dickens’ Victorian London is swapped for Edinburgh in the Lyceum’s production, adapted by Deborah McAndrew and directed by James Brining. It might be comfy Christmas fare, but it still contains resonant messages for our times about the duty to be charitable.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: A leaderless revolution has swept Serbia. The world should be watching | Aleksandar Matkovic
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Aleksandar Matković
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
I saw a remarkable experiment take shape in Belgrade. Its lessons should be studied by other European countries struggling with unrest

More than a decade ago, the WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange told an interviewer in Belgrade that Serbia was “a country where the future happens first”. The phrase circulated widely on Serbian social media in the weeks before Sunday’s election, but in a way that could not have seemed possible 10 years ago. Who would then have imagined that Serbia today could be at the forefront of global democratic change?

The images from Belgrade on Sunday night – people dancing and crying in the streets, while in Novi Sad, the city that sparked the student movement, a flag bearing the image of the convicted war criminal Vojislav Šešelj, which had hung from a building since the 1990s, was torn down – reinforced the feeling that the future had truly arrived.

Watching my home country from abroad, I found it hard not to share in the excitement and emotion. I became involved with the student movement behind this electoral earthquake and was an election candidate for it, for about six months before moving abroad. My involvement began while lecturing in Belgrade at the university’s blockaded faculties in 2024 and 2025. During these extraordinary blockades, something happened that was not widely discussed in the western media: the emergence of a collective sharing of intelligence and a process of shaping opinion that would become key to Sunday’s outcome.

For almost two years, students debated almost every aspect of Serbia’s economy and society – from lithium mining and resource exploitation to the economic power of local oligarchs, as well as issues such as healthcare and education. Sometimes discussions lasted six hours. All of this happened before the students developed any joint programme or formed an organisation capable of outmatching the traditional liberal parties. In a sense, knowledge came first, and organisation followed.

Sunday’s election victory for what became the Student List, therefore, emerged from a novel political culture: a leaderless movement based on collective self-governance and political education, unseen in the Serbian political arena since the collapse of Yugoslavia.

Given Serbia’s recent history, how was this remarkable democratic experiment even possible? One answer lies in the movement’s ability to rally a wide range of people who, despite different political convictions, wanted to counter the perceived corruption of Aleksandar Vučić, the authoritarian president. With the economy dependent on foreign direct investment after the destruction of Yugoslavia, the political leadership formed close ties with foreign-owned corporations. Vučić’s name was often intertwined with the activities of multinationals such as Rio Tinto, the Anglo-Australian mining giant that sought to extract the country’s lithium.

In this context I received death threats following the publication of a critical scientific paper on the contested lithium issue; many of my colleagues faced similar intimidation. But the mistreatment of Serbian citizens who challenged large-scale investment projects also began to shape public consciousness in Serbia. Vučić’s party was accused of standing by and even participating, while opposition parties offered only lacklustre responses.

From the students’ standpoint, party leaders were seen as easy to corrupt when confronted with the financial power of international projects. And so, to change the system, you had to start by changing the political structures that enabled it.

In this sense, this was not just another election; it was a monumental struggle between the old, which was dying, and the new, which was struggling to be born – to paraphrase Antonio Gramsci. In Serbia, the new movement has arisen out of the old: it began with faculty occupations, blockades and plenary assemblies, before evolving today into the largest political force in the country.

By winning the parliamentary election, the Student List has broken the monopoly of political parties. It has become more popular than both the rightwing government and virtually all the opposition parties across the spectrum, most of which did not even win enough votes to meet the electoral threshold. Thus, the “old”, in Serbia’s case, at least, is confirmed as dead.

And what the Serbian people chose was not another party but a list of 250 candidates, 134 of whom hold PhDs, 44% of whom are women, and 135–140 of whom are now projected to enter parliament. Behind them stood an organisation unlike anything seen in traditional, leader-based political parties. In this way, “a bunch of students”, as the Economist described them, has created something that should be studied as it goes beyond the traditional ways of doing politics.

Will a leaderless movement be able to govern? This is where things get tricky. In the context of what the historian Adam Tooze calls the world’s “polycrisis”, a collective intelligence based on self-organisation may be a tempting answer. After all, the student protests in France, Italy and Belgium, along with protests in Spain and Albania, have emerged in response to interlocking crises of housing, education and environmental destruction. For these crises elsewhere in Europe, so evidently mismanaged by governments, the lessons of the Serbian experiment may become crucial.

On the other hand, one should not idealise the situation. The list comprises ideologically opposed blocs, from rightwing adherents to leftwingers and liberals. Most of those elected have never before held political office, and the parliamentary system will require them to nominate a prime minister and, in future presidential elections, a presidential candidate. Will the Student List bring the same energy to the national assembly without jeopardising the very method that made it so strong? Moreover, for Vučić, losing the election does not necessarily mean losing the system. On the contrary, his concession of defeat may also have been a strategic move, allowing him to keep the party apparatus intact for a comeback.

Whatever happens, one question has been put on the table: to what extent are self-organisation and decentralised decision-making a basis for government? For the time being, people are celebrating on the streets of Belgrade, Novi Sad and many other cities and towns across Serbia. But the real fight has only just begun. The world should be watching closely: it may be witnessing the start of a very different kind of politics.

Aleksandar Matković is a postdoctoral researcher at the Institute of Environmental Science and Technology in Barcelona and a fellow at the Transnational Institute in Amsterdam. He works on environmental history, political economy and the history of Yugoslavia

https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.title: Macklemore’s Free Palestine tour review – a triumph of a show with performances from Hozier, Kneecap and more
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.author: Alexis Petridis
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.text:
3Arena, DublinSeveral unannounced guests feature on the first European date of the rapper’s sold-out benefit tour, including video messages from Mark Ruffalo and Cynthia Nixon

“We’d like to thank Ed Sheeran for organising this concert,” offers a member of Kneecap, one of several unannounced guests who have turned up for the first European date of Macklemore’s Free Palestine tour. It’s a characteristically two-fisted approach to the matter in hand from a band who have seldom shied away from controversy, but it has more than a grain of truth in it.

The events of the last six weeks are quite something, and perhaps not what Robert Kraft, the billionaire owner of the New England Patriots, had in mind when he led efforts to pressurise Sheeran to remove Macklemore from his summer US tour, after the rapper made a speech about Palestine on stage at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium. Macklemore was duly removed from the tour, but the rapper saw his profile rise dramatically as a result – in fairness, he was hardly unknown, but his biggest hits are a decade old – while every other artist on Sheeran’s tour quit in solidarity. Sheeran’s tour limped on amid much opprobrium, while Macklemore was able to translate the publicity into a tour of his own, in noticeably bigger venues than he played on his last European tour, with proceeds donated to organisations assisting Palestinians. Dublin’s 13,000-capacity 3Arena is sold out, as is every other date on the tour.

Accordingly, a certain infectiously giddy excitement attends the event itself: the audience receive everything – speeches from activists; video messages from actors Mark Ruffalo and Cynthia Nixon and the Strokes frontman Julian Casablancas, among others; sets of Arabic-themed dance music from Palestinian American DJ Habibeats; and an appearance by longstanding political US hip-hop duo Dead Prez.

They go nuts for Lina Makoul, the first Palestinian to win the Israeli equivalent of The Voice: her brief set opens with a wordless vocal protesting censorship and ends with a song admonishing late-stage capitalism that comes complete with a glancing reference to Guy Debord’s La Société du spectacle, which really isn’t what one would expect from a TV talent show winner. They receive Beoga, the County Kerry folk band who performed on Sheeran’s Galway Girl, but left the singer’s tour alongside Macklemore, like returning heroes. It turns out they’re founding members of an organisation called Irish Artists For Palestine, which does rather beg the question of what Sheeran thought they might do under the circumstances. “You don’t fuck with the Irish, lads,” offers drummer Eamon Murray.

There’s something very striking about the fact that the local artists who’ve heeded Macklemore’s call to help out are evidently committed to the cause behind it: you never get a sense of anyone rocking up in order to grab brownie points or reflected glory. Backed by a string section, Hozier’s performance is heavy on audience-pleasing hits – Take Me to Church, Too Sweet – and takes in a rendition of a remarkable 19th-century folk ballad called The Prayer of Shields, which he apparently learned from Ian Lynch of Lankum. The screens behind him display a QR code that links to a petition in support of 55 students from Gaza who have not had their visas approved to study in Ireland. He goes down a storm, but the real bedlam is caused by Kneecap, who know a thing or two about how controversy can impact an artist’s profile. Their brief set opens with a film that proceeds in a frantic blur of images – The Troubles, Sinéad O’Connor ripping up the pope’s photo on Saturday Night Live – causes an outbreak of moshing and ends with DJ Próvaí struggling to maintain his balance in the midst of the audience: it’s splenetic, chaotic and remarkably powerful.

When Macklemore finally appears, it’s hard to miss the effect of recent events upon him, not least because his opening track, Chant – a 2022 single about his struggle with addiction – now sounds remarkably like a defiant comment on them: “This is my moment … you can’t take my voice from me.” He has a point: he’s been writing about Palestine since 2024’s Hind’s Hall, but as he rolls out his old hits – Thrift Shop’s hymning of limiting one’s spending rather than splurging in grandstanding rapper style; Same Love’s backing for same-sex marriage – a fresh sense of energised purpose about his approach is hard to miss. Between songs, he assiduously shifts attention from himself to the cause he’s advocating, but notes that the show itself “makes me feel glorious”. Understandably so: he mentions that he’s “called up a lot of people in the last six weeks” and notes that Kneecap and Hozier were the first to agree to perform alongside him, which makes you wonder how successful his efforts have been elsewhere. But in Dublin at least, the Free Palestine show feels like a worthwhile triumph.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Eagles’ nightmare season deepens as Cowboys hand Philadelphia fifth straight loss
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
Dak Prescott threw for 212 yards and three touchdowns, two to CeeDee Lamb, and the Dallas Cowboys beat Philadelphia 38-21 on Monday night to hand the Eagles their fifth straight loss.

Javonte Williams ran for a career-high 155 yards and a touchdown, and the Cowboys (3-4) remained in contention for the NFC East title. The New York Giants lead the division at 4-2-1.

The Eagles (2-5) are spiraling into a disaster of a season with their longest skid since 2016.

Philadelphia quarterback Jalen Hurts is expected to miss the rest of the season because of blood clots in his lungs. Tanner McKee provided little encouragement that he can turn the season around, completing 23 of 35 passes for 211 yards with one touchdown and one interception.

With Dallas trailing 21-20 late in the third quarter, Lamb hauled in his second touchdown on a beautiful 16-yard floater from Prescott in the corner of the end zone. Prescott ran in the two-point conversion for a 28-21 lead.

Brandon Aubrey kicked field goals of 55, 27 and 24 yards. The final kick extended Dallas’ lead to 31-21. Williams capped the scoring and the first 150-yard rushing game by a Dallas player since Ezekiel Elliott in 2018 with a two-yard touchdown. The Cowboys finished with 204 yards rushing.

McKee had a pass intercepted by linebacker DeMarvion Overshown late in the fourth quarter.

McKee orchestrated the Eagles’ first touchdown drive in the third quarter this season when they ran almost 10 minutes off the clock and he hit rookie Makai Lemon for a four-yard touchdown and a 21-20 lead.

The Eagles didn’t score again and are running out of time to salvage their season.

The Cowboys got a field goal on the opening drive, and the Eagles came right back and made it 7-3 on Saquon Barkley’s eight-yard touchdown run. Barkley returned after missing the last two-plus games with a hamstring injury and had 37 yards rushing on the drive.

Barkley entered with 36 yards rushing all season. He still seemed bothered by the hamstring and had to visit the sideline medical tent. Barkley also missed long stretches getting treatment for his back on the sideline and finished with 62 yards on seven carries.

Prescott threw touchdown passes of nine yards to Lamb and 21 yards to George Pickens that helped the Cowboys stretch their lead to 20-14 at half-time. Pickens’ catch was particularly impressive, as he escaped tight coverage by safety Andrew Mukuba in the back of the end zone and dragged his left foot sideways for the score.

At half-time, Eagles owner Jeffrey Lurie was inducted into the team’s Hall of Fame.

Lurie bought the Eagles on 6 May 1994, and since the turn of the century they have been one of the top franchises in football. The Eagles are one of three teams to play in four Super Bowls since 2004 and have won the only two titles in franchise history under Lurie’s ownership.

Lurie was flanked by Eagles Hall of Famers including Brian Dawkins and Donovan McNabb and gave a brief speech. However, unlike other Hall of Fame inductees, Lurie did not hold a pre-game news conference. Coach Nick Sirianni remained the only team representative addressing Hurts’ condition since he was injured.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: ‘It’s the smell of freedom’: Belgrade cleans up after Student List triumph
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Guy de Launey in Belgrade
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Binbag-wielding volunteers clear encampment used by thugs to intimidate opponents of deposed government

Student List cleaned up at Serbia’s parliamentary elections. So it was only fitting that the morning after a night of raucous celebrations, the movement’s supporters were gathering, bin bags in hand, at Pioneers Park, opposite the national assembly building in Belgrade.

For the previous 18 months, this small patch of greenery – with its established trees and playground – had been a no-go zone. A pro-government camp known as Ćaciland had taken over the space with convicted criminals living there in white tents, happy to attack journalists, or anyone else who came too close. Police stood by but did nothing to prevent the violence.

On election night, it seemed that thuggery might be on the cards again. Half an hour before the polls closed, large numbers of masked, black-clad men started gathering in and around Pioneers Park. Their intimidating presence gave credence to pre-poll predictions that the governing Serbian Progressive party (SNS) would not hand over power without a struggle.

What happened next took almost everyone by surprise. Shortly after the polls closed – and before any projections of the results had been published – Aleksandar Vučić told supporters at SNS headquarters that they had suffered a comprehensive defeat to the Student List. As cheers rang around the heart of Belgrade, he added that he did “not want unrest” or “anything like that on the streets”.

The riot police stood aside and the barriers blocking access to the area around Pioneers Park were removed. The goon squad made a rapid exit – and Student List supporters joyfully ransacked Ćaciland, setting fire to some of the tents.

But this is not a movement that likes to leave a mess. Over the two years of anti-corruption protests that led to the Student List’s victory, participants have always cleaned up after themselves. So the call went out for volunteers to restore Pioneers Park to something approaching its previous state.

Hundreds of people answered the appeal and joined municipal workers to remove the remains of Ćaciland. Some dismantled the mangled white tents, while others painstakingly cleaned and disinfected the climbing frames, swings and slides in the children’s playground.

Radomir Dalic painstakingly combed over the grass to remove cigarette butts and other rubbish. Apparently relishing his labours, he said he was overjoyed that the park was finally rid of “criminals with violent intentions towards us”.

“Yesterday was a big victory, so today is the smell of freedom,” he added. “We are in garbage, but it’s the smell of freedom.”

Tamara Tomic wore yellow rubber gloves for the occasion – and radiated similar pride in taking part. “Gathering here and cleaning this place just shows that we want to live nicely,” she said. “We want to enjoy the city, enjoy a normal life without violence and without anyone torturing us.”

For now, nobody is asking too many questions about how the Student List will govern. In fact, Serbian voters have taken something of a leap into the unknown – because this is a movement that operates unlike a traditional political party. It has no hierarchy and no leader. Its candidates were chosen by a series of student assemblies, with nominations ranging from academics to athletes, economists to engineers.

The Student List did publish an 11-point plan. Most of these points deal with anti-corruption measures – ironically, the pitch that secured victory in 2012 for Vučić and the SNS. Other commitments include judicial reform, media freedom, affordable housing and improved access to healthcare, with the promise of “a doctor in every village”.

But beyond the domestic priorities – in essence, a clean-up for public institutions – little is clear. The Student List went into the elections without naming a candidate for prime minister, let alone a possible cabinet.

Kurt Bassuener, co-founder of the Democratization Policy Council, said he was concerned about what that might mean when the euphoria of victory died down, and the serious business of forming a government began.

The thinktank chief added: “I’m hoping that there is a dream scenario plan here – they have portfolios and people who have credibility in particular issue areas and they can hit the ground running. Because the danger of a broad coalition like this is that the fissures will show soon after victory.”

Ilija Srdanović, the candidate ranked first on the Student List, has played down the potential for strife. A cardiologist at the university in Novi Sad, the city where a deadly roof collapse sparked the student protests, he has protested alongside the students since the early days. However, he was keen to emphasise that his ranking on the list did not mean he would become prime minister.

“The student movement is fully democratic,” he said, adding that the aim was to buck Serbia’s history of “creating the cult of personality or leadership”.

The 250 candidates on the Student List were “equal subjects in this struggle”, Srdanović insisted, with “numerous candidates who can be chosen for the prime minister position or any other position”.

But his confidence does little to reassure those who have noticed that the broad spread of views held by Student List candidates could lead to trouble. Despite Vučić’s warnings that a Student List government would impose sanctions on Russia and recognise Kosovo’s unilateral declaration of independence, the movement’s foreign and regional policy remains opaque.

“We have not seen seas of EU flags at demonstrations by students or the marches across Serbia,” said Michael Davenport, a former EU and UK ambassador to the country.

“There are massive policy areas where there is no consensus among the Student List or those have been elected. The approach towards accession to the European Union is not clear, nor is the position with regard to regional issues like Bosnia and Herzegovina and, very particularly, Kosovo.”

Many people are happy to leave these concerns for another day. Vučić and the SNS have fallen – and the cacophony of car horns continued throughout Monday as drivers passed the clean-up crew in Pioneers Park.

One visible symbol of the old regime has been swept away. The Student List voters are hoping more will follow.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: G Flip and Chrishell Stause have broken up and like many in the queer community, I’m in mourning  | Rebecca Shaw
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Rebecca Shaw
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Love may not be dead, but it’s had a difficult morning. As much as I’d like a full investigative report, I will instead be getting on with life, as they will

In this current bummer of a world, we often wake up to bad news. This morning, it was devastating. I picked up my phone and saw multiple texts asking me how I felt about the fact that … Chrishell Stause and G Flip have broken up.

If those names seem like some sort of gibberish to you, I won’t expect you to understand the seismic shift. While I was sleeping soundly in Australia in the knowledge that love exists, Strause, from the LA “real estate” show Selling Sunset, posted a vulnerable and deeply sad video where she revealed that she and Australian drummer G Flip have parted ways after being married for several years.

Her clear, genuine sadness, her talk of feeling like a failure – it moved me. I posted about it on Instagram and in came the flood of responses: Nooooo. Love is dead. Love isn’t real. Whose fault is this. I’m devastated. I’m in mourning. And so on and so forth. Many queer people in particular have been sliced in the heart by this news. Every group chat I’m in is talking about it (not all instigated by me).

I’ve started seeing comments under posts about the breakup such as “Who?” or worse, “Who cares?” and I have to tell you that I care. We care. To me, and people like me, this relationship was a beautiful queer success story.

Chrishell comes from a poor background, and her previous marriage ended in a brutal public dumping by actor Justin Hartley. She joined Selling Sunset as a real estate agent and soon became the main character as she compellingly rebuilt her life. During the process she met and fell in love with a non-binary drummer from Australia.

Watching someone from such a hyper heterosexual world like Los Angeles real estate, from a hyper heterosexual show like Selling Sunset, begin to dip her toe into the queer world was amazing. Watching her experiencing a truly fulfilling romantic relationship and falling for someone who loved her back and encouraged her to be her true self was a balm. Bringing that queer dynamic to the world of reality TV was also deeply enjoyable.

I think everyone tuned into this public relationship was happy to see Chrishell glowing. She and G Flip travelled together, their love always seeming to become stronger and more joyous. Chrishell seemed to love Australia, and in fact became part of Australia, endearing herself by travelling to all sorts of places G Flip’s music took her, such as Wollongong. When she ordered a flat white in a Selling Sunset scene at a cafe, I felt national pride. When the show introduced wide American audiences to their relationship, and to Chrishell’s hyper femme love for the non-binary G Flip, the couple received homophobic hate. But their love endured.

Of course, we don’t know what happened. We know that Chrishell seems heartbroken, posting a video because she felt she owed it to the fans of their relationship, the ones who have been so supportive. We know that she seems confused, saying it won’t be hard for her to be respectful of G Flip “because I am in love with this person”, and adding she doesn’t “have all the information and the reasons” for the breakup.

We know that G Flip posted, saying that their head and heart feel very heavy. Ultimately, as much as I would love a full investigative report, a timeline, perhaps a podcast series, we are strangers to these two people and their relationship. Their love seemed genuine and real, and as we all know, that sometimes isn’t enough. Chrishell also said she is “definitely never doing this again”. I hope she doesn’t mean true love, I hope she means that after her public marriage breakup with Justin Hartley and her very visible relationship with G Flip, she won’t be bringing an audience along with her next time.

It must be pretty exhausting to have your romantic life turned into a spectator sport, even if the spectators are mostly well-meaning strangers, such as lesbians who love your love.

So for now, I and many others will be in a short period of mourning. It’s yet another loss of a nice thing. I will be lighting a candle and accepting condolences. And then, I will be trying to get on with my life, just as Chrishell and G Flip will. Love may not be dead, but it certainly had a difficult morning.

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: The pest I’ll never forget: the rats stood six or seven deep on the lawn beside my dormitory
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Bim Adewunmi
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
All it took was one or two careless teenage girls giving the vermin a taste of their snacks and they became the most well-fed animals imaginable

I’ve written a fair amount about my boarding school years in Nigeria in the 90s, but never about the rats that accompanied my school experience. Picture it: thousands of girls from across the country, each bearing a suitcase or two of a term’s worth of “provisions” – cornflakes, sugar cubes, powdered milk, hot chocolate powder, and so on. All it took was one or two careless girls giving the rats a taste of the exotic and they became among the most well-fed rats in the country, enjoying a steady stream of delicious teenage-girl snacks.

I will never forget the sight of rats – six or seven deep – congregating at dusk on the scraggly lawn next to my dormitory, like an illegal gathering of political dissidents. They were large (what with their rich diet), thick tails twitching, noses pushed together, damn near whispering. At first, they would scatter when humans approached. Then we had to clap and stomp to get them to shift. Like the proletariat, the rats began to understand their power, and stand their ground. They were no longer pests but now a sort of predator. If this sounds like the beginning of a highbrow horror, that’s how it felt.

Stories circulated – rats that seemed irritated and bemused when you shouted at them; rats that strolled rather than scurried. The most fantastical stories came from people who alleged they’d woken up to a rat nibbling on their toes, and that the rats were dastardly enough to blow cool air, between bites, to soothe their victims back to slumber. I have a specific memory of being actively chased by the two large rats I’d disturbed when I went to fetch a bucket of water one night. I remember telling that story, still breathless, to wide-eyed roommates. A friend in another house came back to her dorm one evening to find a mother rat and her newborn pups – pink and devoid of fur – under her pillow.

These rats were of course in their own habitat, perfectly at home, and adapting to our unwelcome presence. We were the interlopers, with our classrooms and dormitories, and daily assemblies and annual sports days. I can now recognise that dealing with a certain kind of pest is a fact of life in places where nature has not yet been completely decimated. The rats were the price of a kind of freedom. But years later, post-pandemic lockdown, when the rats attempted to colonise New York, I had searing flashes of the rats of my childhood. Yup, still traumatising.

https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2026/.title: ‘The view from the Mournes was CS Lewis’s idea of Narnia’: how Northern Ireland inspired a magical kingdom
https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2026/.author: Graham Little
https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2026/.text:
Ahead of Netflix’s Chronicles of Narnia dropping early next year, we discover the fantastical landscapes that fired the Belfast-born author’s imagination

On the gable walls of the tough, working-class streets of east Belfast, the mystical beasts of Narnia vie for brick space with balaclava-wearing loyalists. The murals of the city have long projected the power of paramilitaries, but in recent years they have also begun to reflect the more positive contributions made by other local people, including the author CS Lewis.

Lewis was born in Dundela in 1898 in an attractive terrace house that has sadly since been demolished to be replaced by rather unattractive flats. But elsewhere in this part of the city, the Lewis connection is being built on and celebrated. CS Lewis Square is in the Holywood Arches neighbourhood and has a short walking trail featuring metal sculptures of Mr and Mrs Beaver, Mr Tumnus and other beloved characters from The Chronicles of Narnia. The centrepiece is a gigantic Aslan, towering over all from atop a circular mound.

About 15 minutes’ walk away, St Mark’s church on the Holywood Road is the proud custodian of a much smaller lion that may have inspired Lewis’s creation of Aslan. His grandfather, the Rev Thomas Hamilton, ministered here, living in the rectory for 13 years, and his front door was decorated with a beautiful brass lion’s head doorknob. The original has been removed for safekeeping, but an exact replica attracts thousands of Lewis pilgrims each year.

Leafy Circular Road, half a mile away, is where the Lewis family moved in 1905 to a large, redbrick house that, back then, was on the outskirts of the city. The road has since been subsumed by the growth of the town, but remains the realm of the prosperous. The house, called Little Lea, is privately owned, but can be seen from the iron gates at the end of the drive.

“To a child, it seemed less like a house than a city,” Lewis wrote of the family home in his autobiography, Surprised By Joy. “I am a product of long corridors, empty sunlit rooms, upstairs indoor silences, attics explored in solitude.”

Little Lea appears in the opening two Narnia books, first when a boy exploring a large attic in The Magician’s Nephew finds a way into another world, and then in The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe when a game of hide and seek leads a group of inquisitive children to that same magical world a generation later.

Although it was close to east Belfast’s industrial heartland, it was also just a fence clamber away from the fields, hills and woodland glens that fringed the city like a vast adventure playground. As children, Lewis and his elder brother Warnie seem to have had a freedom to wander that would terrify modern parents. They would trek for hours up into the hills between Belfast and Strangford Lough, and travelling that way today still evokes a sense of romantic escapism.

The Belmont Road takes you up, climbing dramatically out of the city and into the expansive high ground that towers over Belfast, Bangor and Newtownards. There are many viewpoints up here. Lewis didn’t record the exact spot that inspired the following ethereal description of the views he loved, but for this writer, the crags of the Whitespots country park on the hill above Newtownards are a pretty good bet, especially as this place also chimes loudly with his descriptions of the stone table on which Aslan was sacrificed in The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe.

“Looking south with a little east in it, a different world,” he writes in Surprised By Joy. “And having seen it, blame me if you can for being a romantic. For here is the thing itself, utterly irresistible, the way to the world’s end, the land of longing, the breaking and blessing of hearts. You are looking across … the plain of Down, and seeing beyond it the Mourne Mountains.”

Lewis once told Warnie that the view from the Mournes above Rostrevor looking down over Carlingford Lough was his idea of Narnia. The statement is now stencilled on a bench at a viewpoint in the town’s Kilbroney forest park. Sitting there, in the majesty of this area, it is easy to imagine, as Lewis later wrote in an essay, that a “giant might raise his head over the next ridge”.

Rostrevor is an hour’s drive south of Belfast, and an hour’s drive in the other direction will take you to the equally spectacular north coast, where Lewis holidayed with his mother as a young child. There’s an ongoing debate among Lewis scholars and his many passionate fans about whether it was Dunluce Castle or Downhill Demesne that inspired Cair Paravel, the castle capital of Narnia.

The ruins of Dunluce perch precipitously on the coast east of Portrush, while Downhill Demesne, near Castlerock, contains what remains of the old Downhill House but also the iconic Mussenden Temple, which much better fits the description of Cair Paravel looking “like a great star resting on the seashore”.

Lewis was writing his autobiography at the same time he was producing the seven Chronicles of Narnia. The experiences and landscapes he was remembering for his memoir very likely bled into the creation of his magical kingdom. And so the heavenly, pastoral landscapes of Narnia on the murals of east Belfast might feel familiar even to those locals who haven’t read the books or watched the screen adaptations. The wholesome images of his imagination being sandwiched between paintings glorifying terrorism is an unusual setting for a tribute to the world’s most famous Christian apologist, but perhaps in Belfast, as in Narnia, good will win in the end.

The first of Netflix’s new The Chronicles Of Narnia adaptations, Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew, will be released in cinemas on 12 February 2027 and on Netflix on 2 April. Surprised by Joy by CS Lewis © 1955 CS Lewis Pte Ltd, The Lion, The Witch and The Wardrobe by CS Lewis © 1950 CS Lewis Pte Ltd

https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.title: The One About Matthew Perry review – the star of one of TV’s biggest ever shows gets a loving tribute
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.author: Lucy Mangan
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.text:
This intimate, warm, thoughtful three-parter about the Friends actor speaks to his friends, family and ex-girlfriends – and their adoration for him is overwhelming

“God, you can do whatever you want to me, just please make me famous.” So prayed Matthew Perry when he was a young unknown actor auditioning in LA, enjoying the partying and the friendships but struggling to find work. Many have offered up such a fervent wish, of course; few have had both sides of it fulfilled in such a spectacular way as the man who became part of one of the most successful sitcoms in television history and who died after relapsing into drug addiction in 2023 at the age of just 54.

The three-part, three-hour documentary – titled, perhaps inevitably, The One About Matthew Perry – charts the whole of the actor’s rise and fall. It is an exhaustive but never (quite) exhausting film. Three hours is a long time, for sure, to tell what is in essence a sad but very simple tale, and some tiny trims could undoubtedly have been made, but it avoids tedium because of the quality of the interviews and the interviewees. The latter include his half-sister Mia and his best friends since his first days in LA, Roger Castillo and David Pressman. They all talk about the brother and the man with such love and such despair at the addictions he could not beat that it becomes at points not just a moving tribute to Perry but also to the thousands upon thousands of addicts and the people who love and despair of them, but whose stories don’t make international headlines.

Perry’s parents divorced when he was a baby and he lived with his mother in Canada but flew frequently to California (his memoir details his terror, at five, of making the trip alone with a strap reading “Unaccompanied minor” around his head) to see his father, the actor John Bennett Perry. Mia was born to John and Matthew’s stepmother when Matthew was 16 and it is clear from family photos and video footage that they adored each other from the beginning. She talks about “Matty” and the good times they shared and the bad times he put her through with the warmth and grief that is the mark of the truly loved – and the loving ones left behind.

His friends do likewise. So too do a handful of ex-girlfriends. Normally the presence of exes not only makes you fear the worst but delivers it too, but here there is no mud slung, no sense of producers glorying in a “find” who turns out to have nothing to say. They all give fond, eloquent accounts of the man they knew – focusing, like Mia, on the good things but not skipping over the bad stuff and his failings, paying us and him the courtesy of providing a portrait of the man entire.

After a childhood that may have been slightly peripatetic but seems to have been loving and essentially stable, Perry – the class clown from an early age – went out to LA to see if he could parlay his comic talents into a career. It worked. Director William Richert saw him making a group of companions laugh in a restaurant and cast him as River Phoenix’s best friend in A Night in the Life of Jimmy Reardon, which I think makes Matthew Perry, however unexpectedly, the Lana-Turner-in-Schwab’s-drugstore of the 90s, though as he noted in an interview with another friend, Kevin Pollak, years later (for a laugh – always for a laugh): “It would have been a better story if anyone had seen the movie.”

Then, in 1993, a script for a new show called Friends Like Us began circulating. By the time Perry got a call to audition, he was already knew the lines because so many of his peers had asked him to help prep for theirs; this guy in it, Chandler, was so like him they felt Matty could really help.

The programme gives the phenomenon of Friends its due but, like the decision to keep mawkishness at bay, rises above expectations by not dwelling on it or letting it overwhelm the subject – even if, at points in real life, it did the man.

Then come the years of addiction – to booze first, then pills, then the ketamine that initially promised to lift his depression but which eventually killed him – and the many, many efforts to get sober. They are described in his memoir, but it is here that you see the pain on his family and friends’ faces as they remember his and their frustration as each attempt ended, never more than a year later, in relapse. Mia notes in her interviews that their father supported his son through everything, probably partly out of guilt for not being fully around as a parent in his childhood, and that he would have loved to have contributed to this film but that he is now too ill to do so. It’s a mixture of honesty and an evocation of a close, if complicated, family background that characterises all her contributions.

It remains at heart a simple, sad story. But this unexpectedly candid, thoughtful, genuinely intimate film gives it nuance and depth, and gives a voice to wider sorrows – including what a shame it was that Perry could not enjoy his talent or appreciate the joy it gave as fully as his audiences always did.

https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2026/o.title: ‘A dog would get treated better than a drag queen in Hollywood’: Alaska on prejudice and leading Oh, Mary!
https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2026/o.author: Owen Myers
https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2026/o.text:
The RuPaul’s Drag Race alum on queer visibility, politics and starring in Cole Escola’s smash comedy

Alaska may be starring in the most subversive comedy in American theater today, but she carries herself with the poise of a 40s movie star. On a brisk September afternoon, the actor, comedian and RuPaul’s Drag Race alumnus is in a small rehearsal room in New York’s midtown, sipping hot tea from a flask while perched on a hard-shell travel case. She sits bolt upright, as if she has spent her life balancing books on her head.

It has been a madcap time for the actor as she prepares to play Mary Todd Lincoln in a new touring production of Cole Escola’s Tony award-winning comedy Oh, Mary!. She is amid a few weeks of rehearsals in the city before the show’s four-month sprint across the US. When I ask how she is handling the upheaval from her Los Angeles home, she smiles indulgently. “I mean, I would go to the planet Remulak for this show,” she says, referencing the home planet of the Coneheads. “I didn’t even think about it. I was just like, ‘Let’s make this happen.’”

Alaska (AKA Alaska Thunderfuck 5000, born Justin Honard) is on the brink of her biggest career moment yet and is determined to make every moment of it count. Since competing in season five of RuPaul’s Drag Race in 2013, the self-described “extraterrestrial phenomenon from the planet Glamtr0n” has released five electro-pop albums with titles like Anus and Vagina, taken to the high seas for drag-themed cruises and co-written and performed in the off-Broadway hit Drag: The Musical, produced by Liza Minnelli. Her live performances showcase the art of drag at its high-concept creative peak; a recent performance of Taylor Swift’s The Fate of Ophelia was a delightfully dizzying hurricane of hairstyles, props, frills and feathers, with three costume changes in as many minutes.

With Oh, Mary!, Alaska is stepping away from nightlife stages and into the shoes of a character already played by actors including Maya Rudolph, Jane Krakowski and Jinkx Monsoon as well as Escola. A London production opened in 2025, while a live-recorded special of the show will air on HBO next year. The character of Mary Todd Lincoln, in Escola and director Sam Pinkleton’s vision, is stifled by her duties, drinks to escape the unbearable company of her (closeted) husband, and longs to return to the life as a cabaret star that she gave up to be first lady.

Director Pinkleton first encountered Alaska over a decade ago when she played Nomi Malone in a Showgirls tribute show at San Francisco’s Castro Theatre. “It was electric,” he tells me. “I was like, ‘This person is a star; you can’t take your eyes off her.’”

Pinkleton cast Alaska in a 2021 Los Angeles production of Head Over Heels, which reimagined the Broadway musical as a queer rave. “I couldn’t believe how much she cared and how great she was technically,” he says. “I have since worked with a lot of drag queens, and I’ve had exclusively great experiences because they are really hard workers. You know, they make everything happen on their own.”

After an initial Zoom workshop with Pinkleton and Escola this March, Alaska was offered the role of Mary this summer. She was particularly struck by the purity of the character’s ambition, even as she resorts to increasingly bizarre tactics to get back on the cabaret stage where she belongs. “This isn’t a comedy show to me,” Alaska says. “This is deathly serious. It’s very real, and I think that’s why so many people can step into the role and make it seem like it’s written for them.”

“I feel like I can make sense of this role,” she adds. “I can’t name any other role where I feel like I make sense. I mean, being a weird drag queen person, queer-bodied person existing in society … that’s exactly what I felt like when I grew up.”

Raised in Erie, Pennsylvania, she was a shy and watchful kid. “I wish that I had the confidence to be like, ‘You know what? I am something and I do deserve more than like being scared to go out of my fucking room,’” she says. “It wasn’t until many years later, when I discovered theater and drag, that I was able to find that in myself. But it is a feeling of like, ‘Fuck, I can’t be.’”

She was introduced to the world of performance while on school trips: she caught a touring production of The Phantom of the Opera while in Canada, and saw a version of Cats at SeaWorld. (“Maybe they should do Oh, Mary! on water skis in Florida,” she muses.) She was especially drawn to the over-the-top femininity of film characters like Jessica Rabbit and Michelle Pfeiffer’s Catwoman. “Not real people”, she notes.

As a theater major at the University of Pittsburgh, she starred in a 1922 Czech expressionist drama called The Insect Play (she played a murderous wasp) as well as in Brecht’s Mother Courage and Her Children. Importantly, the program taught every aspect of mounting a production, including directing, playwriting, set design and costume – crucial skills for a drag superstar in the making.

After a few years of gigging around LA, Alaska won a slot on RuPaul’s Drag Race season five. For many fans, it’s still the best season, with a cast that also included Jinkx Monsoon (now a Broadway star in her own right) as well as much-loved comedy queens Detox and Alyssa Edwards. Alaska was the rare queen that could do it all; she finished as runner-up and after the season aired in 2013, she found herself as one of the most famous drag queens in America. “It was being shot out of a fucking cannon. I was in my late 20s, but still mentally I was still a child.”

Alaska and her then-partner Sharon Needles (who had won season four of Drag Race) went from being broke and scraping together money for a 12-pack of beer to being the most famous drag queen couple in America. “Our lives changed a lot really fast, and we made every single mistake that you can make,” she says. “There was no gameplan. There was no roadmap. We suddenly had money and we never had a fucking penny before. It was do every drug, drink every thing.”

After reading a book by the Buddhist nun Pema Chödrön, who she says “does a really good job of talking about meditation and consciousness in a way that a dumb American can understand”, Alaska became sober for two and a half years. These days, she has a more moderate relationship with alcohol, which has set her up to be in fighting shape for Oh, Mary! “The rehearsal has been really intense,” she says. “It’s like doing cardio every day. Which is great, because I hate cardio.”

Despite its financial successes in New York (Oh, Mary! was the first show of the 2024-25 season to recoup its costs), the show is perhaps not the most natural choice to tour a politically divided country, with dates in smaller cities including Hartford, Connecticut, and Saint Paul, as well as Los Angeles and Boston. “I think it’s pretty great,” Alaska says. “It’s going to be interesting because there are going to be people seeing the show who don’t go see Broadway shows all the time. I’m excited to shock people.

“I mean, it would even be important even if we didn’t have a piece of shit in the Oval Office,” she says. “But I think it’s always worth being who we are – loudly, fiercely and hilariously. That’s always a good thing.”

The pipeline from drag superstar to grande dame of theatre hasn’t always been so well established, and Alaska credits Jinkx Monsoon’s arc from Drag Race to Broadway as an inspiration. “She’s slammed open so many doors for so many people,” Alaska says. “And she continues to do so. I’m glad to walk right through, honey.”

Does she face stereotypes because of her background in drag? “It’s definitely better now. I mean, I’ve been doing drag for almost 20 years. On a Hollywood set, a dog would get better treatment than a drag queen. And that’s not even an exaggeration. That’s hard, and that shit still exists and still happens.”

I’m curious if Drag Race feels far away to Alaska now. It’s been 10 years since she was crowned the winner of All Stars season two. “Yes and no”, she says. “My job as a podcaster is talking about Drag Race. I still work with all the girls from Drag Race all the time. Yes, it’s in the past, but still it’s very much a part of my life. I wish I was more in that universe, but they won’t fucking invite me. So if they read this, maybe they could call me. I would love to have been in Stop! That! Train!” So RuPaul and the film’s producers never got in touch? “No”, she says crisply. That’s a shame. “I agree.”
