The Nobelists note that the California’s proposed billionaire tax was sneaked in to prevent billionaires from fleeing to avoid it: “Some affected taxpayers may have tried to leave between the time they learned about the proposed ballot initiative – in late November 2025 – and January 1st of 2026,” they wrote. “But the window was so short that it is unlikely any significant number of billionaires successfully cut ties with the Golden State in such a short period of time.”

In fact, between January and October the number of billionaires living in California grew by 20. Elon Musk may believe that welfare recipients are the “parasite class” and empathy is “the fundamental weakness of western civilization”. But perhaps California’s billionaires feel enough empathy for less fortunate humans to part with a paltry $110bn, especially since their wealth has grown by a cool $400bn so far this year.

Not all billionaires move to avoid taxes. Trump’s 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, which capped the state and local tax deduction, was expected to prompt the rich to flee high-tax blue states in droves, as they could no longer deduct their state and local tax payments on their federal tax returns. But a study by a Cornell sociologist and an economist at the treasury department found almost no impact on the migration rates of the affluent, at least in the first year following the change.

Indeed, the rich in New York City are hit by a top city income tax rate of 3.9% on top of a 10.9% state tax, compared with zero in Miami. Still, there are 154 billionaires in New York state, according to a report by Oxfam. Nine of the 10 richest live in the city. The only state with more billionaires than New York is, wait, high-tax California.

Still, Newsom and Becerra have a point. California’s richest billionaires have gone feral over Prop 40. Google’s Sergey Brin has helped coordinate some $200m to oppose it and promote two countervailing propositions, 41 and 42 that, if passed, would emasculate the tax. One would bar retroactive taxes – putting wealth accumulated in the past off limits – and forbid new taxes on financial assets or other personal property.

The opposition is gaining traction. A poll in September found that Prop 40 falls just short of majority approval. Just in case, the fast money has tried to flee the state, to make it out before deadline. In the run-up to Christmas of 2025 Brin and Google co-founder Larry Page moved many of their business interests out of California. They also bought homes out of state. Travis Kalanick, former CEO of Uber, left following Musk to Texas. Paypal and Palantir mogul Peter Thiel moved his residence to Miami last year.

While some of the more optimistic analyses assume that avoidance tactics by California billionaires will reduce the taxable pot of wealth by only about 10%, others are less sanguine. Even if it passes, the tax will be taken to court, including on grounds that retroactive taxation violates due process, and may not survive litigation. Some assets – real estate, notably – will not be taxed. Foreign billionaires may wiggle out under double taxation treaties. And more billionaires will leave, assuming that though it was billed as a one-time affair, the new tax will become permanent. This will hit future income tax revenues.

Altogether, economists from Stanford University concluded that the new tax would raise only around $30bn, while the flow of lost income tax revenue would cost state coffers nearly $39bn, in net present value. The estimate fits with results from studies of attempts to avoid wealth taxes in Swiss cantons. It also checks with behavioral responses of the rich to other forms of taxation. For instance, Enrico Moretti, an economist at the University of California Berkeley, and Daniel Wilson of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, found the location of the very rich is highly sensitive to estate taxes.

These should be the most American taxes of them all, a good fit for a democratic nation that conceives itself as a meritocracy; a tool to prevent the emergence of a hereditary aristocracy passing economic and political power down the generations. Still, the rich don’t much care for them.

In 2001, George W Bush did what Republican presidents do: he cut taxes. But his Economic Growth Tax Relief and Reconciliation Act included an annoying twist: it eliminated the credit offered by the federal government to offset the estate tax burden imposed by states on the ultra-wealthy. All of a sudden, billionaires’ estate tax liability became dependent on which state they lived in. Dying as a resident of New York, Pennsylvania and Connecticut, which had estate taxes, abruptly become way more costly than dying in a state with none, like Texas, Florida … or California.

By 2010, over a fifth of billionaires in the Forbes 400 list who originally lived in a state that levied an estate tax state had moved to a non-estate tax state, while only about 1% had made a move in the opposite direction. Moretti and Wilson estimated that by 2017 states with estate taxes had lost 23 of 72 Forbes 400 billionaires who lived there in 2001. Altogether, Forbes 400 wealth subject to state estate taxes fell from some $203bn in 2001 to about $122bn 16 years later.

States with estate taxes didn’t just lose the income tax revenue of their departing billionaires. Extra losses not considered in Moretti and Wilson’s analysis include the effect of plutocrats relocating their businesses. Moreover, estate taxes could well deter other billionaires from moving into the state, or encourage those who remained to try more aggressive tax avoidance strategies than usual.

In light of the difficulties in taxing billionaires and even the lesser rich, there is an argument out there that a less progressive, flatter tax structure could do better at raising money. European countries fund a large share of their generous welfare programs with value added taxes on consumption, which are more difficult to avoid but place a heavier burden on lower-income people who consume a larger share of their paychecks.

And yet the idea of letting plutocracy off the hook seems unacceptable. Brin has said Prop 40 reminds him of the Soviet Union, which he fled with his parents in 1979. Apparently he prefers a social arrangement more like the one that prevailed in the Czarist Russia in which a narrow few amass vast riches unencumbered by a responsibility to contribute to societal wellbeing. That’s the America we all live in now.

If American democracy is to survive this moment, it must figure out a way for billionaires to contribute more. It is essential not just to fund the public goods the nation needs to function. It’s indispensable to restore a sense of fairness to the American experiment. Democracy cannot endure without it.

Let’s see what happens next month in California. But the hard truth for blue states eager to raise more revenue to fund the social safety net and pay for public goods is that they are not up to the task, given competition with Republican-run states where taxes are anathema. As Moretti points out, the tax gap between red states and blue states has become enormous. California’s top marginal rate is 13.5%. Florida’s is zero. The temptation for the next Czarist plutocrat to move from the first to the second is not insignificant.

Indeed, Moretti and Wilson have another research paper that looks at what top scientists and engineers do when states raise income taxes. “People do leave,” Moretti told me. “These are not billionaires, but only highly paid workers.”

The good news is that while there are many ways in which California’s attempt at taking a nibble out of billionaires’ wealth may fail, it is not technically impossible to tax the oligarchy. There are various options available. Federal estate tax rules could be cleansed of the myriad loopholes that allow dynastic wealth to accumulate, such as those allowing unrealized capital gains to accrue forever tax free and bequeathed to heirs with the gains reset to zero. Taxes on capital income could be raised to restore fairness between taxation on capital and labor.

Economists Erick Zwick of the University of Chicago and Owen Zidar of Princeton propose that restoring the tax schedule to where it was in the Clinton administration 30 years ago would raise $5tn over a decade and do wonders for America’s public finance. The main challenge to that is political: it requires an overhaul of a political equilibrium that over the last 50 years has largely revolved around cutting taxes.

But restoring fairness and efficacy to the American state is in the end not a task for the states. Altogether, the government collects almost 3% of GDP less in taxes than it did at the turn of the century. Over 2% of that decline was about federal revenues. The average central government in the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development today raises twice as much in taxes, as a share of GDP, as the US federal government.

Fixing this is, of course, a political problem, one that will remain intractable as long as half of the political spectrum believes its only job on this earth is to cut taxes. But it would be helpful for the fleet-footed billionaires to give some thought to the social contract in which they want to live; whether they are interested in broad-based prosperity or, rather, they are happy to slink into their castle, raise the drawbridge, and hope societal upheaval does not interrupt dinner.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: The US urgently needs more bilingual healthcare workers. This clinic might have the solution
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Cecilia Nowell
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
In New Mexico, where a shortage is acute, Casa de Salud trains college and high-school health apprentices who understand the communities they serve

“I’ll be getting a little bit closer to you to put the cuff on,” Gisselle Martinez said, demonstrating how to take a manual blood pressure in a trauma-informed manner. “It might be a little tight. Let me know if you feel any discomfort and I can take it off.”

She’s not a doctor or a nurse – at least, not yet – but a 21-year-old college student. Between classes, Martinez works as a bilingual health apprentice at Casa de Salud, a primary care clinic in Albuquerque, New Mexico. On top of taking vitals, Martinez is certified in harm reduction – she can run a needle exchange and give out fentanyl test strips. And she understands how a patient’s trauma and past neglect can show up in an exam room.

“My entire life I had to pretty much translate for my parents whenever they would go to the doctor,” said Martinez, whose parents speak Spanish. That responsibility sometimes felt overwhelming, like when she didn’t know how to translate certain medical terms, or when she herself had to go under anesthesia and explain the risks to her parents.

Now through Casa’s de Salud’s apprentice program, she is working toward becoming the certified nurse anesthetist she wishes she and her parents had access to.

“As a bilingual first-generation student, I aspire to help my community,” she said.

While states across the country face a healthcare workforce shortage, the need is particularly high in rural areas and within Spanish-speaking communities; in New Mexico, 32 of its 33 counties face a shortage. Although they make up 20% of the population, Latinos account for only about 6% of the US physician workforce.

To provide that care, not just for the community, but from the community, Casa de Salud’s year-long apprentice program has trained more than 300 bilingual high school and college students since its founding in 2005. The aim is not only to help students from marginalized backgrounds get into medical programs, but to keep them in the community. At least a third of the students Casa de Salud has tracked have gone into the healthcare field, with more than half of those attending medical school.

“You’re more likely to work in a community if you grew up in the community,” said health apprentice program developer Colette Village Center, who is from the Standing Rock Sioux Nation. “We want to see more representation of lower-wealth individuals, under-represented individuals in healthcare, because that saves lives.”

Casa de Salud opened in 2004 when a local physician approached a group of promotoras – trusted liaisons between the community and healthcare workers – in Albuquerque’s predominantly Hispanic and Latino South Valley neighborhood.

“There were a few of us women who called themselves the promotoras tradicionales, who would do limpias,” said Lorraine Cordova, one of Casa de Salud’s founders, describing a spiritual cleansing common in the Mexican folk healing tradition of curanderismo that often uses herbs, prayer and intention-setting to process emotional stressors.

The group met every few weeks at a gym in the South Valley, where they offered limpias, massage, reiki, accu-detox and other treatments. Seeing the need for connecting culturally grounded caregivers to the healthcare system, Casa de Salud soon after launched its health apprentice program.

Alejandra Casarrubias was among the program’s first students. Today she’s a registered nurse, a sexual assault nurse examiner and clinical manager at Casa de Salud.

“You don’t only have to be bilingual, but bicultural,” she said, describing the importance of training healthcare providers who understand the communities they serve. According to the Association of American Medical Colleges, “patients from minoritized races tend to fare better with doctors of the same race”, across metrics like infant mortality and compliance with healthcare plans.

Casa de Salud provides care to a patient base that is predominantly Spanish-speaking and 80% uninsured. Because of the health apprenticeship’s bilingual requirement, Village Center says 100% of the apprentices are themselves Latino, and many like Martinez are also first-generation college students. She’s thoughtful about recruiting students not only from local colleges, but through the college assistance migrant program, and the nearby high school, where students have historically undergone the same training.

“I already knew about Casa de Salud because my family, back in the day, used to use it,” said Sebastian Hernandez, a 19-year-old health apprentice, who’s currently studying biochemistry and film production and hopes to become an internal medicine physician.

Many of the clinic’s patients continue to use alternative medicines like those its founding promotoras offered. “A lot of the times when those people go to the doctor, they get disrespected for having those kinds of traditions,” said Village Center, who added that the clinic still tries to teach health apprentices about those practices.

When new apprentices arrive at Casa de Salud, they work their way through different stations at the clinic, starting at the front desk, then moving to taking vitals, and ending in the clinic’s lab, where they process tests and learn how to draw blood and run EKGs. While at Casa, apprentices also help with the clinic’s syringe exchange program and learn about its gender-affirming care program.

Alongside their formal training, apprentices also participate in workshops about healthcare history and receive mentorship from their peers and alums. Between patient rooms, the clinic also keeps a bookshelf well-stocked with study materials for university entrance exams and a cabinet full of free scrubs. There are also bulletin boards filled with scholarship opportunities, financial aid advice and information about the local university’s pre-med society.

“Any type of grad school that I had seen, whether it be CRNA [certified registered nurse anesthetist], PA [physician assistant], MD, medical school, all of them are so competitive to get into, so it’s intimidating,” said Fabian Corral, an alum of the program who’s currently enrolled in school to become a physician assistant. “But when you’re surrounded by other people who also want to do that stuff, it’s encouraging.”

Corral and two other students in his Casa apprenticeship class are now enrolled in the same physician assistant program at the University of New Mexico, where they meet for study groups together. They’re among 16 Casa alums who’ve gone to school to become physician assistants, advanced practice providers who are increasingly filling healthcare gaps in rural communities.

“I don’t know what my future holds, but if it has to do with serving the community, then I would feel like I made the right choice,” said Corral.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Trump reopened an LGBTQ+ suicide hotline. But the department that runs it vows to ‘restore biological truth’
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Melissa Hellmann
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
While organizations celebrate the reinstatement of the ‘press 3’ option by Samsha, details about rollout and training counselors remain secret

For nearly three years, counselors through the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline for LGBTQ+ individuals answered more than 1.5m calls, texts and online chats – until the Trump administration terminated it in July 2025. But now, more than a year later, the service is back online.

The federal agency that oversees the lifeline, Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (Samhsa), shuttered the specialized national lifeline service known as the “press 3” option for financial reasons last year, though critics cited political motivations. After pressure from activists, LGBTQ+ organizations, and politicians, Congress approved legislation to allocate more than $33m to services for queer youth, including to the specialized lifeline. While suicide prevention and LGBTQ+ rights groups celebrate the reinstatement, details about the rollout and how the counselors will be trained remain shrouded in secrecy.

According to Health and Human Services (HHS), the department “remains fully aligned with President Trump’s Executive Orders to defend women from gender ideology extremism and restore biological truth to the federal government”, a spokesperson said in a statement to the Guardian. But LGBTQ+ rights groups and allies question how the department’s directive will affect the service’s inclusivity. HHS did not respond to repeated requests for details about policy changes to the service. The Guardian messaged the press 3 option through its live chat function following its reinstatement, during which a counselor offered gender affirming sentiments, asking questions such as: “what makes you feel most yourself and affirmed in your identity?” Toward the end of the chat, the counselor encouraged remaining in “spaces where you feel seen, heard and most definitely the safest”.

Members of Congress such as Senator Tammy Baldwin and Representative Seth Moulton, who pushed for the press 3 option, applauded its reopening, stating their intention to continue fighting for its preservation. Following the shutdown of LGBTQ+ services last year, the 988 national lifeline remained, with counselors continuing to offer specialized services for veterans and field calls from all populations. Queer youth are more than three times more likely to attempt suicide than their heterosexual and cisgender peers, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 2023 survey data.

“For 14 months, ‘Press 3’ was shuttered because President Trump and RFK, Jr. made a choice to put politics over people and cut off life-saving services for young Americans. I worked hard to force the Trump Administration to do the right thing and follow the law that I wrote to restore specialized services for LGBTQ Youth,” Baldwin, a Democrat from Wisconsin and the first out gay person elected to the US Senate nearly 15 years ago, said in a statement to the Guardian. In 2020, she authored the legislation that created the national lifeline, and has helped lead the congressional push to reinstate the service for LGBTQ youth over the past year. “While ‘Press 3’ is back online, I’ll continue fighting to protect and strengthen 988 to make sure that when Americans are in crisis, the help they need and deserve is available.”

The Trevor Project, a nonprofit focused on suicide prevention for queer youth, was at the forefront of the shutdown last year as one of several groups contracted to field calls from LGBTQ+ people. The nonprofit helped pioneer the service a few years ago, offering training to counselors on supporting callers’ gender and sexual identities. However, the Trevor Project was shut out of the most recent iteration of the press 3 option because the organization was considered an inactive member of the 988 network.

Upon the termination of the service last year, the Trevor Project lost a $25m federal contract and let go of more than 200 counselors. But the organization’s privately funded suicide prevention lifeline continued amid the shutdown, partially through a campaign that raised more than $20.4m from about 26,000 donors. Mark Henson, the organization’s vice-president of Advocacy & Government Affairs, said that it was impossible to ascertain how the press 3 closure affected the privately funded lifeline’s call volume.

“While we can’t directly speak to what the new services look like, we know from our nearly 30 years of providing crisis intervention services for LGBTQ+ youth that best-practice care requires continuous improvement and clear standards,” Henson said in a statement to the Guardian. “We have seen statements that HHS remains in alignment with anti-transgender executive orders. We are uncertain about whether or not the executive orders in question impact the inclusivity of services being provided.”

Along with its own fundraising efforts, the Trevor Project also launched a petition to protect the press 3 option that garnered more than 54,000 signatures. The organization also partnered with agencies in Illinois and California to train 988 Lifeline counselors in supporting queer youth in those states.

The sustained advocacy over the past year “speaks to the support and the recognition of communities that are disproportionately at risk for suicide, and ensuring that when they call or text 988, or when they’re in crisis, they have trained counselors that are culturally responsive, and affirming to their unique needs”, Laurel Stine, the nonprofit American Foundation for Suicide Prevention’s executive vice-president and chief advocacy and policy officer, said.

“The restoration is not the end point. It’s not the end of the conversation. That advocacy continues because of the sustained investments that are needed in 988 and specialized services that people can rely on when they reach out and need help in a crisis.”

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: I struggled to come to terms with my mum’s death. Then I swam in the sea and suddenly felt connected to her
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Angela Giuffrida
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
My mother was a keen swimmer, and she lived with depression. I wonder if she found the same respite in the water that has helped heal me since she passed away

It was early morning in late September, off the coast of Kaş in Turkey. Watching the slightly choppy sea from a boat, the last thing I felt like doing was embarking on another 5km (3-mile) swim. Mind fog had sapped my energy, and my mood was decidedly Eeyore-like. But as I pulled on my cap and flippers, adjusted my goggles and took the plunge, something shifted.

Head in the water, the knotted feeling in my throat began to loosen. Breathing came properly. There was respite.

My swimming is far from sophisticated – my strokes are messy and I am mostly kicking from the knees. Still, I manage to move forward, albeit slowly, hugging the coastline of Turkey’s Lycian Way, turning a corner and entering an area of calm. The water is blue-green. Fish glide purposefully beneath, and I’m uplifted when I see a turtle navigating around a rock on the seabed.

I came to Turkey with SwimTrek, a Brighton-based company offering guided open-water swim tours. The plan is to complete 25km over five days. On the one hand, it is a holiday; but for me, the combination of swimming and the sea has become something more than that.

It began in Croatia in June 2024, eight months after my mother died unexpectedly, when a friend persuaded me to sign up to swim 3km a day for a week.

I had been feeling lost as I tried to come to terms with my mum not being here any more, and generally anxious, made worse by sleepless nights. Even on calm days, at times it felt difficult to breathe, the tightness in the throat unrelenting.

The only thing that seemed to help was swimming, especially with the focus on the Croatia challenge. My preparation was mostly in the pool, pretty much all of it breaststroke.

I had a rude awakening on the first day of the trip when I tried to swim either breast or backstroke – the latter steering me wildly off course. On day two I was kitted out with flippers and one of the SwimTrek guides taught me the basic front crawl technique. From that point, my confidence in the sea grew.

The sensation of being immersed in the open water is difficult to describe, but it brings me instant relief. I feel weightless yet anchored by the buoyancy. The rhythmic movement while watching the sea life helps to clear my mind of clutter.

This is a far cry from my early experience of swimming. Growing up in the south London town of Croydon, the closest I got to the water was a municipal pool. I was taken there by my mum. I would bob around in the freezing water of the children’s pool while she would swim laps in the adult one.

Going swimming in those days – the 1980s – was synonymous with verrucas and posters featuring cartoon images warning against “bombing” and “heavy petting”. The latter made me and other children giggle although none of us really knew what it meant.

The changing rooms were grim and you would travel home with wet hair, laden down by a damp towel and stink of chlorine for days. The highlight was a post-pool Curly Wurly from the snack machine.

On a hot summer’s day, my mum would take us on the train to Brighton. I would go reluctantly, more enthused by amusement arcades than the sea.

But I was lucky. There were glimmers of the sea winning me over. With an Italian father, every two years we would go on holiday to Italy, travelling by train from the UK to see relatives in Turin and then along the Mediterranean coast to see those in Sicily, where my dad was born.

When we were at the beach, my mum would swim up and down, seemingly for hours. I would look out for her now and then from the shore.

It is only now, since I have started swimming myself, that I wonder what those swims meant to her.

My mum lived with depression and anxiety, and I believe the sea might have given her the same kind of respite it has given me.

I don’t know because we never spoke about it. The only time we really talked about her swimming was when she called needing help to buy a cap, which had to be of a particular variety, or goggles, online.

My mum, who was 73 when she died, did other things to keep active, too – going to the gym every morning, at least until Covid, and she loved playing tennis and walking.

After years of talking about it, my parents moved to Bexhill-on-Sea in East Sussex a few years before she died. So now, whenever I return to the UK from Italy, Bexhill is where I go. I appreciate the UK coastline much more and find that walking by the sea when there, or even just listening to it for a few minutes, helps to centre me. Now and then, I brave a cold-water dip.

But it is the swim tours that have become a powerful source of all-round wellbeing, helped also by a welcoming swimming community and new friendships made. A year after Croatia, I did a 4km-a-day trip in Greece, where I celebrated my 50th birthday.

I managed to complete the Turkey one, too, feeling a huge sense of achievement and absolutely no shame about being the slowest in the group.

I’m already planning next year’s swim. And even though I’m sad that I can’t tell my mum about it, the sea makes me feel connected to her.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.title: Reader Q&A: After Lula’s sensational victory in Brazil’s presidential election, post your questions for the Guardian’s Latin America correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.author: Tom Phillips, Michael Hubbard and Guardian moderators
https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.text:
Having lost the first round of Brazil’s presidential election to far right rival Flávio Bolsonaro, incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva spectacularly triumphed in the second. What comes next for Brazil? The Guardian’s Tom Phillips will be answering your questions from 15:00 GMT today.

Ask a question: log in or sign up here to comment, or email conversations@theguardian.com

After losing the first round of Brazil’s presidential election to far right rival Flávio Bolsonaro, incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, better known simply as Lula, pulled off the most stunning political fightback in modern Brazilian history by winning the second, in so doing securing a fourth presidential term. It will see him become the country’s longest-serving leader.

The result – 51.79% to Lula, 48.21% to Bolsonaro – was delivered after a supreme court judge had extended polling time by two hours, and after Lula’s camp accused their opponents of sabotaging public transport in an attempt to keep their voters from the polls. It was the first time in Brazilian electoral history that a first-round verdict had been overturned.

But Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro who is serving a 27-year jail term for his part in an attempted coup after the last presidential election, refused to accept the result – just as his father had done, four years before. He called Lula’s victory “sacanagem”, a Portuguese word that roughly translates as “bullshit”.

Brazil remains a deeply divided country and Lula will have to navigate a hostile Congress, packed full of Bolsonaro allies, if he is to make significant legislative changes in his fourth term. His options are also constrained by a gloomy economic outlook, with Brazil experiencing soaring debt and entrenched structural problems. As he turns 81, will the re-elected president have the energy to face down the far right opposition for another four years and to lay out the ground for a credible successor?

And what does Lula’s latest victory mean for the wider region, and for the country’s relationship with Donald Trump’s administration? In the Guardian’s Opinion pages columnist Jordana Timerman wrote that “Lula’s victory shows that the rightward shift is neither inevitable nor irreversible. But the movement retains substantial electoral support, influence over the political agenda and a powerful ally in Washington.”

The Guardian’s Latin America correspondent Tom Phillips will be answering your questions on the election result, what it means for Brazil and the wider region, and what the country’s future may hold, here from 15:00 GMT on Tuesday 27 October. Comment with your question below, or email conversations@theguardian.com

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Want to know what you’re really like? Just ask the people who see you twice a year | Zoe Williams
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Zoe Williams
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Apparently, I’m the person who turns up soaking wet, sucking Haribos. Who needs lifelong friends who know you inside-out when acquaintances tell it like it is?

The worst kind of professional relationship is with the person you see twice a year, in a variety of different locations, because whatever they notice about you from that tiny observational sample, that’s what you’re like. So on the first rainy day in folk memory, the opening bars of Storm Austen, I turned up to a job with a photographer, soaked. I’d been on my bike and had tucked my trousers into my socks, so the accumulated water in the ankle area had seeped upwards, giving me a confusing wet leg-warmer effect, then a couple of dry inches, then an unbelievably wet rest of body. I was so wet that when I went to hug the studio’s labrador, he backed away from me like I was trying to give him a bath.

“You were really wet last time!” the photographer exclaimed, remembering our previous meeting back in March. “Well, it’s a wet country,” I replied, before the person we were there to shoot chipped in: “It’s actually in unprecedented drought, but fine.” Then the photographer asked, “Have you thought about getting some wet-weather clothes, if you’re going to cycle?” and I said, “Obviously this is the first time that’s occurred to me, otherwise it would have happened at some point between March and now,” except she didn’t hear me because I had my mouth full of Haribo chewy sours.

“You ate all the Haribos last time,” my colleague observed, and I’ll skip the denials because even though I can’t remember that, it sounds true. Something about getting soaked on a bike makes me powerfully hungry – I think the sense of grievance messes with my blood sugar. “Have you ever thought of having breakfast?” came the next bolt of blue-sky thinking. It’s a great ice-breaker, making such a fist of your life choices that you become a human suggestions box, everyone mucking in with some basic improvements. But this, I insist, was two freak days of 2026; all the others have panned out fine.

The Guardian’s year in review 2026 On Tuesday 1 December 2026, join your favourite Guardian writers for an evening of candid conversations, witty remarks and surprises as we look back on the year-defining stories of 2026. With Zoe Williams, John Crace, Pippa Crerar, Jonathan Liew and Lucy Mangan. Book tickets here or at guardian.live

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Kane’s Ballon d’Or triumph a glorious riposte to celebrity fawning of ceremony | Barney Ronay
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Barney Ronay
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
The England captain spoke movingly on night of deserving winners and unintentional hilarity in London

Well, there’s something new. Football: now available in new, genuinely heartwarming flavour.

There was a lovely moment at London’s Palladium theatre, with the clock creeping towards 11pm at the end of a startlingly shrill and bloated evening of never-ending awards and never ending award-related excitement.

Not just for Harry Kane, who is now the 2026 men’s Ballon d’Or winner, and in the process placed indelibly in that lineage of elite footballers. But also, frankly, for anyone watching, as Kane stood on stage gazing a little shyly at his golden orb, and kicked off his speech by thanking everyone, paying tribute to everyone, everywhere, then finally cracking into tears and a strangled croak as he thanked his parents for sacrifices made, his wife for always being there, and even, in slightly jarring vibe-shift from the warm honeyed tone, José Mourinho.

Even Kane’s biggest advocates will rarely claim their man is one of a kind, sui generis, in the mode of the Ronaldo-Messi godhead. But Kane is exactly this in his own admirably humble way.

Not just an exceptional footballer, the best, most deserving men’s player in the world this year, a European golden boot, scorer of 89 goals since August 2025, Bundesliga champions, World Cup semi-final captain, model of extreme professionalism and care. He’s also quite clearly the nicest man, if not just in football, then possibly the world.

Or at least it felt like that as he walked off in that very dear and tender way, the centre of the world in that moment, but also just keen to get off the stage and let everyone get on with clearing up.

It would be wrong to say Kane’s victory in the final vote of the night redeemed the grotesqueness of the ceremonies itself. There was a roomful of hugely deserving winners here. But Kane hits particularly hard.

And the Ballon d’Or is, let us be clear, a horrendous event, albeit a supremely popular horrendous event. There was the usual pomp around the ceremony, staged this year at a fancy theatre close to Oxford Circus.

This isn’t sport. It’s celebrity culture, red carpet fawning, the worship of images and people, and fame. Football isn’t supposed to be cocooned this way, to send the message that there are barriers and ropes and special people. Yeah, well, good luck with that.

The night kicked off with French Montana in spotless white tuxedo performing on an open-air double-decker bus. He definitely speaks, clearly, carried well, seemed enthusiastic. If it all goes south from here, the evidence suggests French Montana could, at the very least, get a job as a London tour bus operator.

Before long Thierry Henry and Kate Scott glided on stage, half an hour late, to add a little deft and easy charm to a furious schedule of pots and prizes.

And the awards came thick and fast. The Spain manager, Luis de la Fuente, won coach of the year. “I hope in the future I will become in English better,” were his first words at the lectern, throwing his hat in the ring for a disastrous pension-padding six months at Manchester United two years from now.

There was a lovely moment as Burna Boy came on to present the Socrates award for charitable works to Bukayo Saka. He was asked if there were footballers who had inspired his love for the game. At which point he looked at Thierry Henry and said, “definitely, one of them’s standing right there”, and of course he said it in his Burna Boy voice, looking Thierry deep in the eyes so smooth and deep, just almost an impossibly sexy moment.

The Ballon d’Or can be unintentionally hilarious at times like these. There were just so, so many video tributes, so much excitingly portentous music. This is a stage where everyone happening at every moment is very clearly the most important thing ever to happen, superseded only by the next thing to happen on that stage, and then the thing after that.

The degree of fawning is startling at first, but glazed by familiarity before long. At one point Cristiano Ronaldo appeared very briefly in a fact-cut big-screen montage and the crowd shrieked a song, clutched its hand to its fevered throat, collapsed into the aisles in sheer priapic excitement.

Although by the time the original Ronaldo emerged onstage at 10.44pm, there was a sense of the genuinely vertiginous company Kane was about to join. Ronaldo read out the name inside the envelope, and the hall collapsed into cheers and yells and roars as Kane appeared onstage.

And yes the Ballon d’Or is a fundamentally silly thing on its own terms. As a concept it jars with the basic concept of team sport, promoting instead the opposite of sport, the opposite of team culture, the modern disease of fawning parasocial engagement with star names.

In many ways the world would be a better place if the Ballon d’Or was simply abolished, as an example to all who pore over reels and clips and the imagined qualities of their celebrity paramours.

But it is also fascinating, unignorable, and endlessly moreish. All the more so this time. Kane as the Ballon d’Or 2026 is a genuinely fine, uplifting, instructive moment in the spotlight.

It is always tempting to talk about the journey these players make. Everyone has a backstory. Most footballers come from adversity. Kane has this, in his own way, 16 years into a professional career, which has names like Leyton Orient, Millwall, Leicester and Norwich on the timelines. He was unexceptional as a junior, didn’t stand out as particularly skilful or big or outstanding in his numbers. He played as a holding midfielder for a bit while Spurs decided what to do with him.

Kane worked relentlessly. He was Millwall young player of the year 2012, fitting bookend to the Ballon. He made it because he simply refused to go away, to stop working, honed instead the deeper skills in his quiver, the purity of his shooting, the range of his passing long and short

And Kane is exceptional in other ways. Without ever peacocking around promoting his brand, without really trying he remains the most likable, authentic, role-model-ish modern-day England player. For a man who never talks big or acts big he has a happy knack of becoming the key player wherever he goes. Perhaps Kane has become cool now. He has always been likable, with that mild-mannered air of a kindly Victorian chimney sweep with a hamster in his waistcoat watch pocket. In the Bayern years, Kane has become leaner, more glossed and handsome, jawline, tan, iconic Vampire hairline.

Mainly he expresses a common confusion about what talent really is. Talent isn’t simply moments. Talent is also application, focus, craft, the ability to work, to make others better.

And yet his elite career has also been oddly grudging. Somehow the idea has always been out there that Kane is undeserving of these accolades, despite his own mildness and humility, his obvious team qualities, his relentless delivery of goals, effort, leadership. It is a genuinely odd conclusion given the opposite is so manifestly true, that this is an entirely uplifting story of overachievement, of hard work and applied intelligence, as opposed to the kind of talent that just needs to be flame-throwered in the right direction.

It is undeniably true that Kane’s levels can drop dramatically when he can’t perform at his full physical capacity. There have been moments where it has been tempting to wonder if he’s gone far enough as England’s captain in the last few years, if his body and his talent deserve a little care.

https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.title: Fears grow for Iranian athletes on death row as mountaineer latest to be hanged
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.author: Ed Aarons
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.text:
Two sportspeople have been executed in the past month and at least six more face the same fate, says activist group

Fears are growing for more Iranian athletes facing execution after mountain climber Ali-Sina Mostafavi became the latest in a string to be killed by the regime.

Mostafavi – who documented his ascents of some of the world’s highest peaks, including Mount Everest – was executed on 14 October having been arrested in April after the anti-government protests a few months earlier. His death followed the killing of Siavash Jamshidi Kheirabadi, a taekwondo athlete, at the start of October, and the mixed martial arts fighter Gholamreza Khani Shakarab, who was hanged in May.

Now Human Rights for Sport – a group of former Iranian athletes based in Oslo that has been documenting the growing number of cases – has warned that at least six more are facing execution after having their sentences upheld by Iran’s supreme court. They include the swimmer Ali Pishevarzadeh and the footballer Ehsan Hosseinpour, who were both arrested during the January protests, and Mohammad Javad Vafaei Sani – a boxer arrested in 2020 for taking part in protests a year earlier. He saw his request for a retrial rejected last year.

Another MMA fighter, Benyamin Naghdi, equestrian athlete Taraneh Rahimi and the climber Maryam Siri have also been condemned to death this year.

Human Rights for Sport said six athletes have already been executed in cases linked to the January protests or earlier political charges.

Dr Zohreh Abdollahkhani of Human Rights for Sport, said: “The Iranian sporting community is under enormous pressure.. For one of those sentenced to death, we managed to raise attention and awareness through other organisations and they halted his execution. But it was only temporary and I’m very concerned about all of them.”

Human Rights for Sport believe that athletes have been targeted to send a message to the wider community, with the deaths of prominent sportspeople often given widespread coverage in the state-run media. They include Navid Afkari Sangari – a wrestler who was executed in September 2020.

“He was a role model and very famous in the whole community. What happened to him was also a warning to the whole population: look what we can do to someone like this,” Abdollahkhani said.

Mostafavi’s death sentence was upheld by the supreme court at the end of September and he is believed to have been subjected to physical violence during his detention in Kerman before being transferred to solitary confinement. He was accused of being an “armed agent of the American-Zionist enemy” and was arrested for allegedly opening fire on civilians in Azadi Square in Kerman on 24 March and taking part in January’s protests. Mostafavi’s family are thought to have been summoned to the prison hours before his execution.

Abdollahkhani said that making contact with those facing the death sentence is a challenge, as some members of their families are also being targeted by security services.

“In one case, his sister and brother-in-law have been arrested and the whole family’s phone lines are under surveillance. So it’s simply impossible to make direct contact,” she said.

Overall, Human Rights for Sport has found that 217 Iranian athletes were killed by direct gunfire in January, and more than 100 others detained. Four members of the European parliament also wrote to Fifa before the World Cup concerning Iranian athletes facing execution but Abdollahkhani said they received no response.

“Fifa is aware of the concerns raised regarding the situation of Iranian athletes and thanks all stakeholders for their continued collaboration and dedication to raising awareness of these critical matters,” a spokesperson for football’s governing body said.

Abdollahkhani also criticised the International Olympic Committee (IOC), saying changes in staffing had made it difficult to raise cases through its human rights and safeguarding structures. The IOC disputed her account, saying it had “fully functioning human rights and safeguarding teams”. It said it was deeply concerned about athletes affected by events in Iran but lacked the authority, as a non-governmental organisation, to change a sovereign country’s laws or political system.

“Within our remit, we work tirelessly with all stakeholders of the Olympic movement, including national Olympic committees and international federations, to support the creation of a safe sporting environment for all athletes. We will continue to work with our Olympic stakeholders to support all athletes globally through sports diplomacy, and we remain in touch with the Olympic community of Iran.”

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Kylian Mbappé dropped by Chinese brands for ‘offending national sentiments’
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Agence France-Presse
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Kylian Mbappé has been dropped by two major brands in China after a video circulated online in which the France striker apparently joked about the former leader Mao Zedong. In China jokes about Mao, the founding leader of the People’s Republic of China who died in 1976, are considered disrespectful and remain a social taboo.

“Our company firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any behaviour that offends national sentiments,” the drinks company Dongpeng said in a statement on Tuesday, adding that “with immediate effect we are terminating all cooperation with Kylian Mbappé”.

Adverts showing AI-generated images of the 27-year-old France captain drinking a Dongpeng sports drink were regularly shown in China during this year’s World Cup.

Mengniu, China’s largest dairy producer, also cut ties with the Real Madrid forward, who has been hugely popular among Chinese fans with millions of followers on social media. Mbappé is fondly nicknamed “Guigui”, the Chinese translation of “Turtle”, due to his popularity as a character in a Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles meme.

“With immediate effect our company is terminating all cooperation with Kylian Mbappé,” Mengniu said in a statement. “Mengniu firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any words or actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people,” it added.

The announcements came after a video emerged online with Mbappé saying that the funniest internet meme he had seen was of his face photo-shopped on to that of “some guy – I think he’s a Chinese dictator”.

This was an apparent reference to a meme of Mbappé superimposed on an image of Mao, one of several using the footballer’s face and other historical figures. The authenticity of the video could not immediately be verified by AFP Fact Check.

“Dongpeng Beverage ends cooperation with Mbappé” was the top-trending topic on the Chinese social media site Weibo. One Weibo user said that the “extremely serious wrong remarks … crossed the red line. They are completely unacceptable”. Others urged Dongpeng to remove Mbappé’s image from their energy drink bottles.

Dongqiudi, one of China’s biggest online football outlets, said in a statement on Monday evening that Mbappé’s remarks were “offensive to China and the Chinese people” and “have hurt the feelings of Chinese football fans and the Chinese people”.

Mbappé in September addressed a previous meme depicting him as a military dictator, in an interview with the French sports newspaper L’Equipe. “There’s a part of it that’s funny. You can tell that, for some people, it’s all in good fun. But there is another part that’s a bit less funny because of the damage such people have caused throughout history,” he said. “Being compared to individuals who murder others, or who have brought misery to millions upon millions of people – well, I don’t think I’ve ever done anything like that in my life,” he said.

The furore in China came a day after Mbappé lost out to Harry Kane for the Ballon d’Or, the most prestigious individual award in football.

Global sports stars who have commented on sensitive topics such as Taiwan, Tibet and Hong Kong have previously caused controversy in China and been dumped by sponsors there. The former NBA player Dwight Howard referred to Taiwan as a country in 2023 as he appeared in a video with the island’s vice-president and current president, Lai Ching-te, sparking fury on Chinese social media. Beijing claims Taiwan is part of its territory and has threatened to use force to bring it under its control.

The Houston Rockets general manager, Daryl Morey, posted a tweet in 2019 supporting Hong Kong protests, leading to China suspending sponsorship deals with the NBA and pulling games off Chinese television for a year.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.title: Silicon Valley parents want the tech they help build out of their childrens’ schools
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.author: Robin Buller in San Francisco
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.text:
Both private and public schools in tech regions are limiting the use of tech in classrooms. But will low-income districts be able to follow suit?

German Gil spends most of his waking hours looking at screens. Since moving to the San Francisco Bay Area in 2015, the software engineer has bounced between start-ups and giants including Netflix, Facebook and GitHub.

But when it came to the education of his daughter, Victoria, he wanted her to have a different experience, one in which his “kid could be a kid”.

Gil and his wife enrolled Victoria at the San Francisco Waldorf school, a private school built around nature-based play. Now in fourth grade, Victoria spends her school days free of screens. Instead of working on Chromebooks, the students in her class are binding books by hand.

This sort of experience doesn’t come cheap. Kindergarten tuition at the school, which sits in San Francisco’s affluent Pacific Heights neighborhood, just two miles from the headquarters of AI giant Anthropic, runs $40,000 a year; high school, close to $60,000. But the program is intensely popular.

It may seem a contradiction, but in the past years, many well-paid tech workers in Silicon Valley have paid a premium to keep their children away from the platforms they help build. Applications for early childhood enrollment at San Francisco Waldorf have grown notably, according to the school’s executive director, Lauren Smith, and many of the new parents work in tech.

Now, parents in the region are pushing for changes beyond private school campuses to public districts, where screens have become a ubiquitous part of life in the classroom. Parents in California tech enclaves such as Mountain View, San Mateo and others want public schools to re-embrace the emphasis on human connection over screen time that schools like San Francisco Waldorf offer. They are organizing, and they are making a dent, with some public schools banning phones or rolling back their use of computer-based tests and assignments.

As evidence mounts of the damage social media and other platforms do to young people – and as courts have begun to agree – parents, and governments, have started to re-evaluate kids’ relationship with tech, and its role in education. Major US school districts such as New York City and Los Angeles have recently embraced tech rollbacks. Parents in other countries, too, are increasingly scrutinizing tech’s encroachment into education.

“There is much more buzz around this today than there was a few years ago,” said David Monahan, campaign director of Fairplay, a US advocacy organization fighting to limit screen use among children.

Silicon Valley parents bring something to this fight that many other communities don’t have: firsthand knowledge of the industry. When San Mateo union high school district put together a taskforce last year to examine the role of AI in schools, at least two of its volunteer members worked at large tech companies, including one in Google’s AI division, according to Jennifer Jacobsen, a school board trustee.

“These professionals know more than the average community member about the products,” Jacobsen said. “They can see a longer runway of where these products are headed and their potential impact on education.”

Many American public-school parents are dismayed to learn how early screens enter the classroom.

Jillian Kolonski, a writer in San Mateo, was stunned when her five-year-old daughter was sent home with a Chromebook for math practice. “I was like, what?! She’s in kindergarten!” Kolonski recalled.

Candice Wei, a Palo Alto college counselor, was similarly shocked to learn that her kindergarten-age son was using screens in class with few guardrails. It prompted her to dig deeper into what local high schools allow. “YouTube isn’t banned. Generative AI isn’t banned. It’s almost criminally negligent,” she said. “I don’t allow this in my house. Why is it allowed in schools?”

In its early days, ed tech was viewed as a sign of a more equitable and accessible digital future. The pandemic made it an essential part of remote learning, and many tools stayed once students returned to classrooms. In 2025, 99% of school teachers surveyed by the New York Times said that their students received school-issued devices, and 81% said that their school gives students screens by kindergarten.

But experts, and a growing number of parents, are worried about the omnipresence of tech in day to day learning. Half of US teens spend four or more hours a day on screens, not counting schoolwork. Monahan, of Fairplay, sees classroom screen time as reinforcing those trends. “What sorts of habits are we fostering at school if students spend hours staring at screens with the seal of approval of their teacher?” he asked.

Research suggests that students retain what they learn with pen and paper better than what they learn on screens. Critics also say excessive ed tech replaces, or at least stunts, the student–teacher bond that is critical to emotional learning and strips away the productive struggle that fosters learning.

“You as a human being are much more likely to put in effort for a teacher you love or a parent you love than for a computer that is not really going to give you love,” explained Yvonne Kao, senior director of learning sciences and technology at the nonpartisan educational research non-profit WestEd.

Kao points out that the use of technology can vary widely across US school districts. She describes hearing about rural districts that lack the staff to vet technology or keep up with best practices for buying it.

Silicon Valley parents are in a different position: “There’s a savviness around tech that I think you acquire from being immersed in the tech environment,” Kao said. “You know better what it is good for and what it is bad for, and you can kind of try to thread the needle.”

It’s pushed many in the arms of private schools. Unbound by state and local bureaucracy, private schools in California are able to more quickly change direction, are free to enact policies that limit tech and have more money to spend on teachers instead of apps.

Wei, who started her local chapter of parent advocacy group Schools Beyond Screens, said classroom screen time is an increasingly common cause for leaving the public system that she hears about. “I’ve been approached by parents who considered [our public school], toured it, saw kids on screens, and were like, ‘I guess I’m going private,’” she said.

But it has motivated others like her to push public school districts to vet the companies landing multimillion-dollar contracts with schools and to demand proof that their products improve on learning. “That means asking for data about what specific outcomes they’re looking for that this tech is supposed to help with, and knowing what the plan is if they aren’t seeing those outcomes,” said Kolonski, whose husband works for an AI company. “A lot of these companies have really sexy pitches, but then on the ground, the work doesn’t quite bear out.”

Amid pressure from parents, public schools in San Mateo have stopped sending Chromebooks home with students in kindergarten through second grade, and high schoolers are subject to a blanket ban on cell phones. In Mountain View, schools are moving away from using i-Ready, an adaptive reading and math program used in school districts across California that has drawn criticism for repetitive lessons and been accused of sharing students’ data without consent. Palo Alto public schools, meanwhile, have prohibited the use of a technology developed just next door in Silicon Valley: “smart” glasses.

While proponents of human-centered learning are heartened by the progress, they are concerned that less-resourced districts will be left behind, stuck with the digital learning tools wealthier ones are abandoning.

The “techlash” is broad, said Jon Valant, director of the Brown Center on Education Policy, and parents across income levels want the same thing – high-quality, human-to-human education – for their kids. The difference is who can pay for it. Staff salaries are the biggest expense at any school, Valant explained: “The reason [private schools] cost a lot of money is that they have a lot of adults in those buildings … It’s when budgets get tight that the temptation to replace people with technology is especially hard to resist.”

The gap could only widen: the Trump administration has thrown its weight behind school choice programs, which give families some or all of the public money that would have been spent on their child’s education through vouchers or education savings accounts to use on private schooling. It means that when parents take their children our of public schools and into the private system, they take the funding with them.

“I am worried about this technology rolling out in ways that are very unequal across communities,” Valant said. “What we end up seeing is it’s the kids who are in the lowest income areas that find themselves spending a whole lot more time on screens, even if their parents don’t want them to be.”

San Francisco Waldorf offers financial aid to families who can’t afford the price tag. But Antero Garcia, a professor at Stanford’s Graduate School of Education, too, worries that in some regions private schools are the only route to a screen-free education, and that every student who opts out of public school takes funding with them. “What that looks like is fewer teachers, maybe a longer commute if a school were to close, and larger class sizes,” explained Garcia.

The parents with the means to leave, Garcia argues, are also the ones best equipped to change public schools for everyone else. “They have the social capital and resources, and they probably understand how to work within the bureaucratic system,” he said.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: North Carolina legislators closed their on-campus voting sites. HBCU students marched miles to vote anyway
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Adria R Walker
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Last year, the state’s board of elections removed several polling sites from local colleges – and students have taken it upon themselves to organize voting

On 15 October, the first day of early voting in North Carolina, mostly Black students from North Carolina Agricultural & Technical State University (NC A&T), Bennett College and University of North Carolina at Greensboro (UNCG) marched from their college campuses to their nearest polling sites for the first day of early voting.

Previously, students were able to vote on their respective campuses; however, late last year, with Republicans at the helm, the North Carolina board of elections removed several polling sites from local colleges: UNCG, NC A&T, Western Carolina University (WCU) and Elon University. As a result, students have taken it upon themselves to organize voting. The marches – two, so far – took about two hours round trip, but to the students, protecting their right to vote, they say, is worth it.

“I think that a lot of students wanted to come and march because they knew that it would make a statement,” said Dihanna Williams, a student at NC A&T. “It would show them that, despite y’all taking away something that should be a right to us, we’re still going to go out and vote because that’s also a right for us and that’s something that our ancestors fought so hard for us to accomplish. I don’t think that anything would have gotten in the way of A&T students voting.”

College Democrats of North Carolina, from NC A&T, UNCG and WCU, sued the North Carolina state board of elections over the early voting sites back in January. According to the lawsuit, without a polling place on campus, WCU students without cars (more than 60% of the student body) would have to walk nearly two miles – in parts along a four-lane highway with no sidewalks or guardrails – to reach the nearest polling site. Indeed, in February, some WCU students marched that distance to reach their new early voting site.

The suit noted that NC A&T is the country’s largest HBCU, while WCU’s polling place served more Black voters than any other polling site in its county during the 2024 election.

“State and county officials brushed aside urgent warnings that their decisions would disproportionately burden young and Black voters and denigrated students who advocated for their rights,” the lawsuit said.

The marches are part of broader efforts to combat voter suppression, organized both by students and by national organizations, such as the Michelle Obama-founded When We All Vote. During the second march, which took place on 22 October, hundreds of students were joined by the actress Marsai Martin, a co-chair of When We All Vote, a nonpartisan initiative to increase young and minority voter turnout, and the recent Love Island USA winner Trinity Tatum, who’s also an ambassador for the organization.

“I’ve realized that if we want things to change, we’ve got to show up together. It’s hard to think of another campus showing up as hard as North Carolina A&T,” Martin said to the crowd. “We are here to celebrate something that this campus has made very clear. Y’all do not back down.”

Shia Rozier, a senior at NC A&T and a co-founder of Protect Ours, a student-led organization that helps run shuttles to the polls, has been working with other students to mobilize around voting. Since her freshman year, Rozier has gone to state board of election meetings in Raleigh and protested for polling sites.

“It has been a continuous back and forth trying to make sure we have on-campus polling sites, which is really essential at a campus,” Rozier said.

While some students may have responded to the removal of polling sites with apathy or taken it as an excuse to not vote, Alexis Cox, a junior honors political science student, said that it only fired the students up.

“Students feel even more motivated to get out and vote,” Cox said. “That’s why we were so enthusiastic about marching in the heat to our polling site, showing other students how to vote and offering rides to each other and we’ve also organized different shuttle services to the polls.”

During NC A&T’s homecoming last week, campus leaders held Votecoming: Party at the Polls, a voter mobilization effort, as part of When We All Vote’s efforts. When We All Vote’s Party at the Polls has been associated with a two to four-percentage point increase in voter turnout. Rozier said that student organizers are also hosting voting-centric cookouts and events.

“It really brings back a culture where voting is engaging after a time where you’re fighting for your rights,” she said. “It’s unpleasant to be told by your representatives that your voice doesn’t matter. We’re pivoting and just deciding, ‘If it didn’t matter as much, you guys wouldn’t be working to take it away.’”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Not registered to vote yet in the US? There’s a good chance you can still cast a ballot | Laura W Brill
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Laura W Brill
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Twenty-two states and Washington DC let voters register on election day. Why aren’t politicians doing more to reach young people?

With election day just a week away, candidates are ignoring millions of young Americans who could still cast a decisive ballot but have not yet registered to vote.

By contrast, my mailbox has been full of political flyers: the various campaigns gleaned my name from the voter file, recognized that I am a regular voter who hadn’t cast a ballot yet, and assessed through their targeted analysis that it’s worth spending on printing and postage to get their message to me.

Honestly, they are wasting their money on me – I have voted now and would have done so anyway, with or without their glossy mailers. What they should be doing is targeting people who are probably way more persuadable than I am, yet are routinely ignored: the millions of Americans who will be old enough to vote for the first time this November.

In California alone, for example, there are nearly 300,000 eligible 18-year-olds who can legally show up through election day and cast a provisional ballot. Their votes would count the same as mine. So why are their mailboxes empty?

It’s not just the 18-year-olds. We estimate that more than 1 million young Californians ages 18-24 who have not yet registered and are therefore not in the voter file still have a right to vote on election day or during early voting. And it’s not just California. More than half of US states allow eligible voters to cast provisional ballots either on election day, during some part or all of their early voting period, or both.

We estimate that 1.7 million 18-year-olds live in the 22 states (plus Washington DC) that allow voters to register on election day. Voter files show that almost half of them have not yet registered, so are probably not receiving mail from campaigns.

Across the country, only 45% of 18-year-old Americans are registered to vote, compared with 82% of the over-45s. It’s not apathy or laziness that stops them – it’s more often that no one bothered to ask them or explained how to do it and why it matters – including the candidates.

That’s despite the more than $10bn already spent in this campaign. Imagine if just 0.01% of that were spent building the on-ramp to democracy instead of on throw-away mailers and tune-out ads.

Four other states allow provisional voting during all or part of their early voting period for those who aren’t yet registered, but don’t allow it on election day itself: Massachusetts, Nebraska, New York, North Carolina.

You might wonder: does election day registration really matter for first timers? The answer is – absolutely. We looked at the voter files for a sample of four states with same-day registration on election day and they all see far more 18-year-olds making it into the voter file on that final day versus any other day of the year.

And this really should not be a surprise, but turnout correlates positively with allowing voting for eligible voters who haven’t signed up in advance.

Young people – because they are registered at such low rates and therefore aren’t targeted by candidates – often become aware of elections in the final weeks of campaigns, as more and more money is spent on advertising. In many states though, that is well after early registration deadlines. Plus they are highly mobile compared with other age groups, making early registration more challenging for them. The result is millions of voices left unheard, cycle after cycle.

We need to rebuild the systems that bring young voters in and that will take time, money and vision. But in the next few days leading to 3 November, we can all reach out to the people we know in the same-day states and encourage them to register and vote. It’s not too late for them to have their say and it’s never too early to start the habit of voting.

Laura W Brill is the founder and CEO of the Civics Center, a non-partisan non-profit with a mission to make voter registration a core part of high school

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Police called to Florida soccer game after parents say three-year-old benched for being too good
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Guardian sport
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Police were called after a dispute involving the parents of a three-year-old player at a soccer game in Florida over the weekend.

The boy’s parents can be heard on police body cameras saying their son, Nevada, had been kicked out because he was too good at soccer and was embarrassing the other children. However, an organizer at the game said Nevada had pushed other children and his parents had become argumentative when their son was taken out the game.

In police body camera footage the organizer of the event, who works for i9 Sports, a youth sports group, can be heard saying Nevada’s parents had caused a disturbance.

“The kid is good. He’s great. Really good,” the organizer says in the footage. “He’s very advanced compared to the other ones, so he’s scoring a lot of goals. But he’s pushing the kids ... So, I try to tell him, don’t push; we want to play without pushing, right?”

Nevada’s parents posted a clip of their son at the event in which he can be seen dribbling around older children with ease. The video has since gone viral. Nevada cannot be seen pushing any other children in the footage posted by his parents.

“They’re mad at my son because he actually plays soccer. They’re literally kicking him out of this place because he’s good at soccer,” his mother says in the body camera footage. “First, they said he’s not passing, but nobody’s catching the ball when he’s passing.”

The i9 Sports worker told police they were willing to give Nevada’s parents a refund if they left.

“I just want him out. Immediately,” the organizer told police. “Just give me their names so I can give them their refund.”

The Winter Park Police Department said the family agreed to leave the event and no one was arrested.

“The family stated the game was over and they were leaving. The family was cooperative with the officers,” the department wrote in a statement on its website. “No one was arrested, trespassed, or forced to leave the park.”

i9 Sports said it was reviewing the incident and had contacted Nevada’s family.

“We are aware of concerns being shared regarding an incident at a local i9 Sports program, and we take them very seriously,” i9 Sports said in a statement. “The respectful treatment and well-being of every child and family matter deeply to us. We have reached out to the family and have begun a review that includes speaking with those involved. While we work to understand the circumstances, we will not speculate or share unverified information. We appreciate everyone who has brought their concerns to our attention.”

One officer appeared to want to see more of Nevada though. “I kind of want to see him play. I bet he’s good,” he can be heard saying to another officer on body camera.

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.title: Elon Musk’s AI Odyssey: the dullest, most pointless riposte possible to Christopher Nolan’s brilliant epic
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.author: Peter Bradshaw
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.text:
It is hardly a shock that Grok AI’s interpretation of Homer is as meaningless as a laptop screensaver. The only surprise would be if Musk accepted defeat graciously. Which he won’t

Think back. Do you remember when Elon Musk, in a weird online tantrum, and without having seen the film, condemned the supposed wokery in Christopher Nolan’s, The Odyssey, for getting Elliot Page to play Sinon and Lupita Nyong’o to play Helen of Troy? As the plaudits and the box-office receipts for Nolan’s Odyssey piled stratospherically up, Musk showed that being a good loser is not among his qualities. He petulantly exclaimed that he could do his own better and more authentic Odyssey on Grok AI. And now he has released the first online seven-minute “episode” to a world that has long since forgotten about this claim and didn’t care in the first place.

In Musk’s version, as the tale begins Odysseus is – off screen – pretending to be mad to avoid fighting in the Trojan war. Grim-faced Palamedes and Agamemnon are shown testing this ruse by taking his baby boy Telemachus and placing him in the harm’s way of a plough in a field; Odysseus instantly rushes to save his child, showing that he isn’t mad, and agrees to fight. We see him join the armada, with Penelope and Telemachus (soon to grow to a little boy) left behind. This, effectively, is a prologue sequence that is not in Nolan. The expeditionary force arrives at Troy, and an intertitle tells us we have cut to a 10-years-later flashforward; the siege is about to escalate into the fake-horse attack.

As ever, the AI footage is ponderous and inert, demonstrating its familiar uncanny-valley stock-footage quality with classical-age Call of Duty graphics. Every single dramatic moment – Odysseus’s cod-insanity and his agreeing to fight, taking leave of his family, the hardship and adventure of the sea journey and the climactic decision – is all as motiveless and meaningless as the movement of shapes on a laptop screensaver. The ships are lined up on the sea like a row of high-def space invaders. Perhaps the worst thing about it is the deadly audio and digital-robot voice work. Every character speaks with that even, over-emphatic, declamatory tone.

Who cares? Certainly not Musk. He has no passion to tell us this story, only to win an argument that he long since lost. Perhaps he will now do his Grok AI version of Digger, in which Tom Cruise’s oil baron in fact saves the universe by drilling for more and yet more oil. Or maybe he will release his own Grok AI version of You Can See Everything in which glassy-eyed Elizabeth Holmes will prove her little blood-diagnosis box actually does work before she zooms off with Elon in his flying car.

Of course, as we are always being told, AI is continuously improving. With succeeding episodes, this boring and pointless series may look better. But if Elon’s AI-Odyssey is of any value at all, it is to underscore the basic truth: nobody believes AI has any artistic merit, only financial merit. In terms of quality, it is a pitiful fraction of the real thing, but a zillionth of a zillionth of a zillionth of the cost. It is time for Elon to make his own inglorious retreat from this phoney AI Dull-yssey.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Carrick given chance to save job as he stays for Manchester United’s game at Chelsea
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Jamie Jackson
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Michael Carrick has been given the chance to save his job by turning Manchester United’s results around, with the head coach remaining in place for Saturday’s visit to Chelsea.

The decision by Jason Wilcox, the director of football, and Omar Berrada, the chief executive, can be viewed as a surprise given United’s dire form.

Sunday’s abject 3-0 league home defeat by Bournemouth followed Wednesday’s equally dire 4-1 reverse at Como in the Champions League.

Carrick’s side have won twice in 12 games and were eliminated from the Carabao Cup by Brighton. United are 16th in the Premier League, a point above the relegation zone.

Yet Wilcox, who has driven the retaining of Carrick, wants to give the 45-year-old a chance to transform form and results. Whether Carrick could survive another poor performance and result at Stamford Bridge is in the balance.

United host Roma in the Champions League three days later, then Aston Villa in the league the following Saturday. Carrick’s reprieve may also be a move to allow time for Wilcox to secure a replacement should the decision be taken to sack him.

United will have to pay Newcastle about £3m in compensation if they want Eddie Howe. He is Wilcox’s prime candidate if a change is made and wants the job. When he left Newcastle in July a deal was struck on the remaining terms of his contract which means the club would be due compensation.

United would also have to pay Newcastle a minor sum for Howe’s staff, headed by his assistant, Jason Tindall.

Manchester United’s director of recruitment, Christopher Vivell, has been pushing the case of Julian Nagelsmann, the former Germany and Bayern Munich head coach.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Illinois man arrested after allegedly sending suspicious powder to Congress members using his return address
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Richard Luscombe
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Matthew Unglesbee admitted to sending the letters to four unidentified politicians, officials say

An Illinois man accused of sending letters containing suspicious white powder to four members of Congress has been arrested after he allegedly wrote his own name and return address on the envelopes, according to authorities.

Matthew Unglesbee, 36, of Quincy, remained in the custody of US marshals on Tuesday on federal charges of perpetrating a hoax and sending threatening communications through the mail.

In an eight-page criminal complaint unsealed on Monday, Charis Hobbs – a taskforce agent with the FBI’s Springfield office – said Unglesbee admitted during an interview on Sunday that he sent the letters to the four unidentified politicians.

Unglesbee told the agent that the substance he placed inside the envelopes was salt – because it “kind of looks like” anthrax, the complaint said. Preliminary testing did not reveal the presence of any biological or chemical toxin.
