“Each letter contained a white granular substance and a handwritten letter which read ‘ha ha’,” the court filing said. A letter to an unnamed US senator also contained granules and read “Hah enjoy the gift”.

On each of the four white, letter-sized envelopes, the agent said, Unglesbee wrote his name and home address in Quincy.

None of the staffers who handled the letters at any of the four Congress members’ offices in northern Illinois opened the envelopes, the complaint said. The offices had alerted each other to look out for mailings with Unglesbee’s name on them.

FBI personnel “trained in handling weapons of mass destruction, and threats of biochemical toxins” were sent to three of the politicians’ offices on Wednesday after staff called authorities, and hazardous materials (hazmat) response teams attended two of them.

Having retrieved the communications with Unglesbee’s address on them, FBI agents visited his home, where they discovered another envelope – empty and addressed, but not sent, to one of the same Congress member’s Washington DC office.

The suspect told investigators that he mailed four letters “after hearing someone in a restaurant mention the news story of other letters being sent”, the filing said. Earlier in October, the FBI and US Postal Inspection Service said they were investigating multiple reports of suspicious letters sent to state officials and election offices across the country.

Unglesbee denied participating in the other suspicious mailings. But he allegedly told investigators that he anticipated the Congress members would “take it serious” because the powder he sent could be perceived to be anthrax, which he said he knew was dangerous and would cause hazmat teams to have to respond.

“Unglesbee claimed he was joking but recognized the recipients would not know he was joking and could perceive it as a threat,” the complaint said.

In a justice department press release on Monday announcing Unglesbee’s arrest, Ryan Presley, special agent in charge of the FBI’s Springfield field office, said authorities were focused on “keeping our public institutions safe from intimidation”.

He said: “Mailing unknown substances to congressional offices creates fear and disrupts the public institutions vital to our democracy. We, along with our partners, will remain vigilant in identifying and holding accountable those whose actions threaten to intimidate public officials or disrupt our democratic systems.”

Unglesbee was tentatively scheduled to appear for a detention hearing on Wednesday afternoon in federal court in Springfield.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Four takeaways from Anthropic’s potentially record-breaking stock market filing
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Johana Bhuiyan
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
The AI company’s first public financial disclosures reveal explosive growth, huge costs and risks ranging from cyber-attacks to the limits of safeguards

Anthropic has filed to go public on the US stock market, revealing for the first time the AI research lab’s financials and all the risks – more than 90 pages of them – that might negatively affect its business.

The company’s investor prospectus, released on Monday, veers from hyperbolic predictions about AI’s “incredible potential” to existential risks of the technology to the reality of its current business: explosive but incredibly expensive growth. The filing to US financial regulators, known as an S-1, provides the public’s first look at an audited version of Anthropic’s finances.

Here’s what you need to know: Anthropic is making a lot of money. It’s also losing a lot of it. The five-year-old firm has been valued between $1.5 and $2tn by some investors but did not list a target valuation in its S-1. Founded in 2021, the company has seen explosive growth every year of its existence.

Anthropic brought in $16.3bn in revenue and lost $80bn in just the first half of 2026, though much of that was due to a $72.4bn one-off charge. In 2025, the company brought in $4.585bn and lost roughly $33.9bn, per the filing.

Securing computing power accounts for the vast majority of Anthropic’s costs. The company spent nearly $9bn on AI infrastructure in the first half of this year, up from $2.3bn in the same period last year.

Anthropic, unlike OpenAI, has made it clear that its customers are largely other businesses. “Frontier AI is most valuable in real-world settings, as deployment across enterprises is where economic impact is greatest,” the company executives wrote in the filing.

The company said its top five customers account for 25% of its business – which makes it risky business.

Anthropic says there is considerable potential for AI to reach levels of intelligence that would be akin to what its executives called “‘a country of geniuses in a datacenter’ – millions of virtual agents with the ability to revolutionize every area of human endeavor: software, physics, math, biology, medicine, finance, economics, commerce, robotics, military and intelligence capabilities”. Noticeably, the company mentioned military capabilities despite being embroiled in a standoff with the Trump administration over its refusal to limit restrictions on the way the Department of Defense could use Claude.

The company highlighted four specific categories of opportunity at the start of the filing: Acceleration of progress in biology and medicine; economic growth; spreading said growth globally; and streamlining government services (such as social services and medical programming).

The company said it was already working with several pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies and improved the process for clinical trials, which is “cutting the time it takes to write clinical trial reports from months to minutes”.

The company’s executives claim they have also made biological discoveries with Claude, including a “molecular machine” that has the “potential to be developed into a novel biotechnology tool”. One purported use case: gene editing.

The company discusses risks in two contexts: the dangers that AI itself poses to society and human beings, and the ways Anthropic’s business could go awry.

Risks that AI poses were broken down into four main categories: misuse by bad actors, loss of control, authoritarian abuse and economic disruption. While Anthropic put a great deal of emphasis on the guardrails it has implemented to block attempts to misuse its models, it also includes one big caveat later in the filing: those safeguards may not work.

Anthropic’s most capable models are capable of providing “meaningful assistance to malicious actors seeking to develop chemical, biological, or other dangerous weapons”, the company’s executives wrote in the filing.

The company deploys technical safeguards, “but such safeguards are incomplete, may be outdated in light of evolving threat models, have been and may in the future again be circumvented, or may fail to operate as intended”.

Already, Anthropic has detected what it believes is the first documented case of a large-scale cyber-attack with little human intervention. The company believes a Chinese state-sponsored hacking group manipulated a Claude code tool “into attempting infiltration into roughly 30 global targets, including large technology companies, financial institutions, chemical manufacturing companies, and government agencies”, per the prospectus.

The company said it recognized AI may be used by authoritarian governments to “deepen repression” and develop “high-tech surveillance states”. Anthropic presented less of a defense or potential safeguard against those uses and instead said it was committed to working with “free societies to provide a counterweight to authoritarian abuse and to promote freedom and democracy”. The firm seems to suggest that its work with what it describes with scant details as “free societies” will cancel out in some way the AI-enabled repression of authoritarian regimes.

The company had a falling out with the Trump administration after the firm said it would not change its restrictions to allow its models to be used to build domestic surveillance or autonomous lethal weapons.

Anthropic goes into detail in laying out 92 pages of risks to its business. Investors are making sense of a type of company that is fairly new to the public market in a highly competitive space with everything to lose.

The company acknowledges that much of its success is tied to its top executives and whether they stay at the firm, being able to edge out its main competitors Google and OpenAI, navigating the tumultuous regulatory landscape around AI and datacenters and surviving any public relations fallout over its AI models being used to do things they are not supposed to do, like create bioweapons.

The company’s focus on enterprise customers means that if any of its top buyers leave, the company could take a huge hit.

Anthropic’s structure as a public benefit corporation – which is a designation for a for-profit company that balances financial interests with achieving a stated social good – may make it harder to achieve its short – or medium-term financial goals, the company said. The firm is obliged to report on its progress in meeting its public benefit goals in the same way it has to report its financials.

There’s also all the risk related to any AI-enabled catastrophic event – the sort of doomsday scenario Anthropic employees have been warning about. Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, has called for a pause on AI development to ensure firms are developing it responsibly to avoid any such catastrophe. In addition to the public harm and potential fallout over a scenario where Claude went rogue, Anthropic said they worry they will be subject to a great deal of liability, especially considering insurance options for AI are still evolving.

“We may be unable to obtain coverage for certain AI-related liabilities on commercially reasonable terms, or at all, leaving us exposed to potentially significant uninsured losses,” the filing reads.

The bedrock of Anthropic’s AI infrastructure is concentrated in the US, making it extremely vulnerable to regulatory changes, power grid constraints, natural disasters and opposition to AI or datacenters. The filing specifically calls out datacenter moratoriums that have been passed or are being considered as among the big issues they are concerned about.

“We are expanding our data center capacity internationally as part of our efforts to diversify our infrastructure footprint and reduce concentration risks,” the filing reads.

The company, which says a big part of its value proposition is its talent, also said it worries about US immigration policies affecting its ability to recruit and retain highly qualified employees. The Trump administration has targeted H-1B visas, a tool tech firms have come to rely on to attract and hire from the global pool of tech and engineering talent.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: ‘Sloppy gruesomeness’: reviewers slate Musk’s AI-made Odyssey film
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Dan Milmo Global technology editor
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Tesla tycoon launched Grok project after criticising Christoper Nolan’s diverse casting for his Homeric blockbuster

Elon Musk has released an AI-generated rival to Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey after pledging to make a version “true to the art of Homer”.

Having criticised the hit movie in the summer, the tycoon said he would use Grok Imagine to make a “historically accurate” adaptation.

The initial results have been released on X in the form of a seven-minute episode made in conjunction with Wonder Studios, a London-based startup.

Musk had objected to Nolan’s casting choices – such as black actor Lupita Nyong’o as Helen of Troy – and used the blockbuster as a vehicle for reciting his views on diversity, equity and inclusion.

The Tesla tycoon had promised to make a “full-length movie” version of Homer’s poem before the year ends but is sticking to a film released in episodes.

The first episode starts with Odysseus agonising over whether to join the Greek forces in their attempt to sack Troy. He then sails from Ithaca, his home island, with his men crying out for “vengeance” before they make land and start fighting.

The episode ends after 10 years of conflict, with Odysseus holding, ominously, a wooden figurine of a horse.

Xavier Collins, the co-founder of Wonder Studios, said the first episode was made in less than two weeks with a creative team of three, including the US-based director Dev Walker. It is understood to have cost tens of thousands of dollars. Nolan’s version cost $250m (£188m) and was shot in multiple locations over 91 days with a vast crew. It has made $1.8bn at the box office.

Despite Musk’s criticisms of Nolan’s film, the creative team behind the latest take on Homer are supporters of the summer blockbuster.

Collins said he was a “huge fan” and told the Guardian: “We were not given any direction to make it [Musk’s version] anti-woke or anything like that. We were given the opportunity by one of the world’s best frontier labs to work on one of the best stories ever told.

“The brief was ‘help us understand the technology, where it’s strong, where it could use improvement’.”

Peter Bradshaw’s review in the Guardian gave it one star, saying: “Every single dramatic moment – Odysseus’s cod-insanity and his agreeing to fight, taking leave of his family, the hardship and adventure of the sea journey and the climactic decision – is all as motiveless and meaningless as the movement of shapes on a laptop screensaver.”

The episode on the Grok Imagine X account has received 7.3m views and some harsh feedback, with a reviewer in the Telegraph saying: “You can feel your eyeballs twitch as it unfolds in all its sloppy gruesomeness.”

Collins said Wonder aimed to make the next episode an improvement on the first and would address criticism, including the historical accuracy of its boats and rapid pacing.

“We are going to take a look at all of the comments and all of the things we could have done better and see if we can improve it. The goal is that the next episode we make is radically better than the last,” he said.

Wonder has also worked with Google DeepMind to produce an AI-generated video for the Lewis Capaldi track Something in the Heavens.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.title: Trump and Rubio head to Texas to stump for Ken Paxton as midterms campaign enters final week – US politics live
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.author: Chris Hippensteel (now) and Tom Ambrose (earlier)
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.text:
President and secretary of state to flaunt oil tanker filled with Venezuelan crude bound for Texas refineries

President Trump is set to headline back-to-back campaign events in Texas on Tuesday, as Republicans look to bolster Senate candidate Ken Paxton in the face of a strong challenge from Democrat James Talarico.

Trump will rally in Corpus Christi this afternoon, then head to Lubbock for an evening event. He’ll be joined on the campaign trail by Secretary of State Marco Rubio – a highly unusual move for the nation’s top diplomat.

Together, the pair are set to flaunt an oil tanked filler with Venezuelan crude bound for Texas refineries, according to officials familiar with the plans.

Trump has frequently touted the oil deal his administration struck with the new, US-backed Venezuelan leadership after deposing its former leader, Nicolás Maduro, earlier this year, as a windfall for the nation. Rubio, a chief architect of Trump’s foreign policy, especially in Latin America, has been deeply involved in those negotiations.

The stunt also comes at a moment when surging oil prices, an aftershock of the war in Iran, have kneecapped the Republican party going into the midterms, countering Trump’s 2024 election promises to bring down prices.

Those grievances have put states once considered reliably Republican into play for the midterms, and Texas may be chief among them. The state hasn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate in decades, yet recent polling has found a closely contested race between Paxton (a divisive candidate dogged by scandal) and Talarico.

Speaking to reporters on the tarmac before departing for a campaign event in Michigan, JD Vance responded to a question about President Trump’s remarks branding Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed as a “jihadist.”

Vance, who has sparred with the progressive El-Sayed repeatedly on the campaign trail, took a somewhat softer tone. But he didn’t walk away from Trump’s remarks.

Vance said that El-Sayed had identified himself with a segment of Democrats “who seem to align with people who justify violence against the United States of America.”

“I don’t know what’s in the guy’s heart,” Vance said. “I just know he has a lot of weird friends.”

On 3 November, millions of Americans will vote in midterm elections to decide control of the House of Representatives and Senate, as well as the governorships in 36 states.

In an October poll by the New York Times/Siena College, Donald Trump’s approval rating sank to 36% with most respondents expressing frustration over his handling of the US economy, cost of living and Iran war.

We’d like to hear from all Americans of voting age about their thoughts on the midterm elections. What are the main issues that will decide your vote and why?

Since President Trump first proposed the installation of a monumental new arch in Washington, critics have argued it would detract from another important site nearby: Arlington National Cemetery, the nation’s largest military cemetery, which sits just across a nearby bridge.

But a new analysis by The Washington Post has found that the arch would, quite literally, cast a shadow over the hallowed burial ground.

On 284 days out of the year, the arch would block sunlight from portions of the cemetery, its shadow passing over the graves of more than 75,000 people, as well as several notable memorial sites. Those include the eternal flame honoring former president John F. Kennedy and the Military Women’s Memorial.

The shadow would also pass over the grave sites of several Supreme Court Justices, including Thurgood Marshall and Ruth Bader Ginsburg, the Post found.

Israeli voters are going to the polls today to decide the future of prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who president Trump has strongly backed and who worked with him to launch the ongoing war with Iran.

Early turnout in the election, branded by some as the most consequential in Israeli history, was the highest it’s been in decades, according to data released by Israel’s Central Elections Committee.

Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, faces his first true election test since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks on Israel and the beginning of the war in Gaza. That conflict touched off a wider regional conflict that increasingly drew in the US, culminating in the current US-Israeli war on Iran, which Trump and Netanyahu jointly launched earlier this year.

That war and its economic aftershocks (the soaring price of fuel, in particular) have loomed large over the US midterm election. Today’s election in Israel will help determine the future course of that war, and what Israeli leadership will be working with the US to see it through, as well as implement Trump’s peace plan for Gaza.

Follow along the Israeli election as it unfolds here, with my colleague Yohannes Lowe.

While Donald Trump is heading to Texas, JD Vance, his vice president and a top MAGA campaign surrogate, will be in Howell, Michigan, campaigning for Republicans in the state.

The stop in Michigan is part of a campaign blitz that just yesterday took Vance to Montana and Kansas. The latter of those two states has become the site of an unexpectedly competitive Senate race, with Democrat Adam Hamilton mounting a strong challenge against the Republican incumbent Roger Marshall.

Vance has already made multiple midterm stops in Michigan, where the Senate race between Abdul El-Sayed, a Democrat, and Mike Rogers, the Republican, has seen some of the fiercest campaigning of this election season.

Vance and El-Sayed have repeatedly sparred over campaign remarks. The vice president has called El-Sayed “very evil,” and El-Sayed, a Muslim who has faced frequent GOP attacks on his faith, has accused Vance of Islamophobia. We’ll see if that back-and-forth continues today.

Three tankers carrying Russian diesel are en route to the United States, with a fourth expected to depart Wednesday, Moscow has said, part of a deal that triggered a fierce Ukrainian and European backlash.

US president Donald Trump this month struck an agreement with Russia’s president Vladimir Putin to ease sanctions in exchange for Moscow releasing diesel onto global markets.

The measure was seen as an attempt to lower fuel prices for American consumers ahead of the US midterm legislative elections on 3 November and drew sharp criticism from Ukraine and its allies.

“At present, three tankers” with Russian fuel are on their way to the United States, Russian deputy prime minister Alexander Novak told reporters on Tuesday.

Social media feeds are awash with an unprecedented flood of AI-driven disinformation ahead of November’s US midterm elections, according to experts, who warn many posts are likely “slipping through the cracks”.

As tens of millions of Americans prepare to cast their vote, social media companies have scaled back their efforts to protect voters from lies meant to manipulate elections.

While the backlash against Facebook after the Cambridge Analytica scandal prompted social media giants to bolster their trust and safety operations, a counter-backlash from the right over fears of speech restrictions – which intensified after Elon Musk’s takeover of X, formerly Twitter, and the election of Donald Trump in 2024 – has led to significant layoffs from relevant teams.

Artificial intelligence has made it easier than ever to launch a disinformation campaign. And platforms are increasingly relying on AI, rather than human intervention, to respond.

“You can run an information operation now with quality that was impossible in 2016 for super, super cheap,” said Frances Haugen, a former Facebook data engineer turned whistleblower and advocate for transparency and accountability in Big Tech. Operatives playing dirty tricks can get around content moderation rules “because you can just keep tweaking the post a little bit each time you create them, and some of them are going to get through”, she said.

President Donald Trump and secretary of state Marco Rubio on Tuesday plan to show off a newly arrived oil tanker filled with Venezuelan crude to be processed in Texas refineries, according to a congressional aide and two US officials.

The visit to Port Arthur, Texas, comes on the same day that Trump is campaigning in the state for Republican candidates in the midterms, AP reported.

The president has rallies scheduled in Corpus Christi and Lubbock. Trump is trying to shore up support for US Senate candidate Ken Paxton, who is locked in a tight race with Democratic candidate James Talarico.

It’s not clear whether Rubio, who also serves as Trump’s national security adviser, would take part in any campaign events. But it’s the first time that he’s hitting the road with Trump as the president barnstorms the country.

The two US officials and the congressional aide spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss Rubio’s plans before they were publicly announced.

It’s highly unusual for the nation’s top diplomat to participate in political travel. Rubio’s trip would be the latest example of how Trump’s second presidency has blurred the lines between governing and campaigning. Attorney-general Todd Blanche has already been appearing at rallies alongside Republican candidates.

Rubio previously ran for president in 2016 and is considered a top prospect in 2028. He has not said whether he will run, and his political activities have been limited since becoming secretary of state.

Donald Trump has called the former FBI director, James Comey, a “dirty cop”, Reuters reports. The US justice department is attempting to prosecute Comey for a third time, on the grounds of sharing sensitive national security information in ⁠2016, according to court documents ⁠made public on Monday.

The case was revealed in a court document known as a “criminal information” that the justice department said ⁠it filed to stop the 10-year statute of limitations on the offense from expiring earlier this month.

The document, filed in Washington federal ⁠court, charges Comey with transmitting and conspiring to transmit national defense information. It alleges he shared classified information with a reporter from ‌the New York Times ‌in October 2016.

“I think he’s a dirty cop,” president Trump told reporters at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, when asked about Comey. “I don’t know much about ‌it,” he said.

Comey said in a video on Instagram that “they’re back again” and ‌referenced the Justice Department, but did not provide further details. “I’m still innocent,” he added. Comey’s lawyers have already asked a judge to dismiss the case, arguing it is legally improper.

Donald Trump campaigned in Corinth, Mississippi in support of Republican senator Cindy Hyde-Smith and told the crowd his rallies have “totally changed the dialogue”. “Nobody’s ever campaigned like I have for midterms,” he said.

A vocal protester then attempted to engage the president in some dialogue, on the subject of his ballroom, and where it might be most appropriately located.

Trump lashed out in racist terms at his predecessor, Barack Obama, for joking over the weekend that his renovation of the White House, with “gold everywhere”, has “the White House looking like Saddam Hussein open a Cheesecake Factory.”

Trump told reporters that Obama “doesn’t notice dirt and filth” of the White House before he rehabilitated it. Trump said then that he was “a very clean person” but, “you have to explain that to Obama” because the former president doesn’t understand and is “not smart at all.”

Trump said that the comeback victory of Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, over his far-right opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, “looked like another rigged election, frankly.”

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Arise, Sir Harry? Downing Street hints at Kane knighthood after Ballon d’Or win
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Jessica Elgot Deputy political editor
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Downing Street has hinted that Harry Kane deserves a knighthood, praising the footballer’s “extraordinary achievement” as the first English winner of the Ballon d’Or in 25 years.

The prime minister’s spokesperson said Andy Burnham sent praise and congratulation to the England captain, who was announced as the men’s winner of football’s most prestigious individual award at a ceremony on Monday night.

Number 10 said they hoped it would be the prelude to a trophy to celebrate with England “before too long” – alluding to hopes of an England win when the country co-hosts the Euros in 2028 with Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.

The Bayern Munich player is the first Englishman to win the award since Michael Owen in 2001. “The PM would like to congratulate Harry Kane on winning the Ballon d’Or,” the spokesperson said. “To be the first Englishman to win it in 25 years is an extraordinary achievement, and what a moment to do it here at home.

“Seventy years after Sir Stanley Matthews won the inaugural award, it caps a remarkable season and Harry continues to set a brilliant example to young players across the country, and the PM knows the whole nation will be incredibly proud of him. And, hopefully, there’s another trophy to celebrate with England before too long.”

Asked whether Burnham would like to see Kane receive a knighthood, she said: “I think everyone would agree, Harry Kane has given an enormous amount to English football, and this is a very special moment for him and the country, but, as ever, I’m not going to pre-empt the honours process.”

Kane received the award at a ceremony at the London Palladium on Monday night, beating Kylian Mbappé of Real Madrid and Barcelona’s Lamine Yamal.

He is the fifth English player to win the award, the list also including Kevin Keegan and Sir Bobby Charlton.

Burnham cannot decide whether to hand Kane a knighthood, but ministers and departments can make recommendations to the honours committee, as can private individuals. The sport committee includes the presenter Sue Barker and the chief executive of the Football Foundation, Robert Sullivan.

Kane holds an MBE, awarded after England’s success in reaching the semi-finals in the 2018 World Cup. Players are often not awarded knighthoods until after retirement. The former England captain Sir David Beckham received his knighthood last year, as did the former England player and manager Sir Gareth Southgate.

Before those awards, the most recent was the Scottish player and Liverpool manager Sir Kenny Dalglish. Owen, also a former Liverpool player, has not received a knighthood, and nor did Keegan, the former Newcastle player and manager who was also England’s captain and manager.

https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.title: Elizabeth Holmes mania: how the buzziest film of the year has resurrected a gut-twisting TV drama
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.author: Hannah J Davies
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.text:
The Theranos fraudster is the subject of Nathan Fielder’s mind-bending You Can See Everything documentary. It is now driving audiences to watch Disney/Hulu’s 2022 series, The Dropout – and they’re seeing it in a whole new light

There are surprise smash hits, and then there’s You Can See Everything, Nathan Fielder’s documentary-cum-psychodrama about the disgraced US entrepreneur Elizabeth Holmes. It arrived in US cinemas with much buzz: this was, after all, an A24 production, helmed by one of TV’s leading performance-art pranksters. But You Can See Everything has surpassed all expectations to become an undeniable hit, and is now the highest-grossing US documentary in 15 years just two weeks after its release.

Co-directed by Lance Oppenheim, it is a surreal and masterly epic; at a press screening in London, the audience appeared to be alternately spellbound by its comedic elements and repulsed by the sheer grossness of some of its characters. That grossness, it should be mentioned, doesn’t pertain only to Holmes, who was sentenced to more than 11 years in prison (this has since been reduced several times) for defrauding investors, after the collapse of her sham blood-testing startup Theranos). It has also – perhaps unsurprisingly – led audiences towards other media inspired by Holmes’s downfall. Journalist John Carreyrou’s book, Bad Blood, has returned to the bestseller lists; the ABC News podcast The Dropout, hosted by Rebecca Jarvis reported a 900% surge in listeners; while the Disney/Hulu TV series of the same name enjoyed a 700% bump in viewers, and is now ranked #47 on IMDb’s “Most popular TV shows” list, despite having been released in 2022.

As Holmes mania abounds, I decide to fire up the podcast, a show I listened to when it was released in 2019. Unlike You Can See Everything – which explores whether Holmes can convince us of her innocence, as much as whether she is innocent – The Dropout podcast takes us back to her halcyon days, when she was named America’s youngest self-made billionaire. This was a time when her Steve Jobs-esque black turtlenecks, apparently bogus baritone voice and talent for wooing super-rich investors was a large part of the story (the first episode is titled Myth-Making).

But it wasn’t just about Holmes the person – it was about what her company did (or rather, didn’t do) and offered a stark reminder that the claims that she made never matched reality. In one episode, we hear Holmes declare that it is possible to run “any lab test from a drop of blood from a finger”, juxtaposed with a clip from a deposition hearing where she is asked just how many tests her machine was capable of carrying out: “I-I-I don’t know exactly what the number was … I think there were probably tens of tests …” (If this sounds like a straightforward lie, Holmes offers her own explanation of her claims in You Can See Everything.)

The TV adaptation of The Dropout recycles the story that the podcast so thoroughly investigated, albeit with a little more artistic licence (Holmes dances like a robot to Lil Wayne, and there’s an entire plot point that’s reverse-engineered to incorporate the Katy Perry song Firework). It’s entertaining, sure: I find myself strangely captivated by the stilted professional relationship/romance between Holmes (Amanda Seyfried) and Sunny Balwani (Naveen Andrews), 19 years her senior, who are obsessed with one another but suggest a cold indifference, too (see also: a real-life text exchange between Holmes and Balwani, where she wrote: “You are the breeze in the desert for me. My water. And ocean. Meant to be only together tiger,” to which Balwani replied: “OK”).

But for the first few episodes at least, The Dropout is mostly like watching a campus drama that occasionally morphs into an episode of Law and Order. Seyfried is great – all bulging, marble-like eyes, unsettling jaw placement and off-kilter speech patterns – but there is a sense that this is an almost meme-esque endeavour, gleefully ripped from the headlines (You Can See Everything does, in its own way, ask whether that might have indeed been the case). At the end of episode one, Elizabeth stares at her finger, and – deus ex machina – the idea for Theranos arrives.

But The Dropout series, like the podcast before it, was built on inescapable facts and what the Guardian described at the time of release as the “gut-twisting mental gymnastics” of it all – the technological inadequacies of Theranos’s equipment; the surveillance culture that meant employees felt they couldn’t speak out; the third-party machines the company used in place of its own hardware; false positives for HIV, cancer and other serious conditions. It might sound facile, but it’s a reminder of the sheer weight of what Holmes’s company did, and of her ability to fight off the most legitimate of concerns. It touches, too, on the suicide of Ian Gibbons, the company’s former chief scientist, who took his own life before he was due to testify against the company. It would be irresponsible to lay the blame for this death solely on Theranos. But it’s clear, amid the jacked-up comedy, that there was plenty of pain for its writers to mine.

Holmes’s story first gripped the world during what was a big moment for scammers, from the phoney heiress Anna Delvey to Fyre festival, with its schadenfreude-inducing story of influencers stranded in the Bahamas under disaster relief blankets. In the years since, the conversation around such grifts has become less cut and dried: Delvey has gone full-on media caricature, while – conversely – many Fyre attenders were revealed to have been normies who got their tickets on Groupon.

Aptly, perhaps, for a moment that was so focused on untruths, the narrative of the “golden age of the grift” is now being rewritten again, in real time. Fielder and Oppenheim have done something daring and brilliant with You Can See Everything, incorporating a new era of technofascism and AI in the process, and meeting Holmes not as a Silicon Valley sweetheart but as a mother and soon-to-be-convict. But the facts – be it on TV or on a podcast – remain as unsettling as ever. “The world believes a reality about me that isn’t true,” says Holmes in the film. And yet so much of it is hard to ignore.

https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.title: Jon Stewart on the midterms: ‘Republicans running for Congress can’t defend Trump’s reckless record’
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.author: Guardian staff
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.text:
Late-night hosts discussed Trump’s distraction tactics and crass comments on Nicki Minaj’s derriere as he campaigns

Late-night hosts mocked Donald Trump’s bizarre rally with Nicki Minaj as the clock ticks down to the US midterm elections.

With just a week to go until the US midterm elections, voters “are, for some reason, fixated on the economy, cost of living, the war in Iran”, said Jon Stewart on Monday’s Daily Show. “And Donald Trump is actually back out there on the campaign trail to make his closing arguments.

“I imagine the president will be laser-focused on the issues that matter most,” the host deadpanned before playing a clip of Trump talking about the physical form of the Ohio Senate candidate Jon Husted: “I looked at his ass, and I’ve never done that with a man before. A man’s ass, his ass, the ass. His ass was like a big piece of muscle.”

“And by the way, don’t feel left out, ladies, Trump’s got plenty of ammo left for you,” Stewart continued before playing another clip of Trump at a weekend rally in Michigan, where he introduced the rapper Nicki Minaj: “By the way, I looked at one hell of a beautiful ass before – Nicki Minaj. That’s hard to miss.”

“How the fuck is this real?” Stewart exclaimed. “‘Stand up, Nicki. Twirl around. Give us a look at that.’ Talk about inflation, my God!

“Look at Trump’s face when Minaj is talking,” Stewart added. “Look at what he’s doing. He’s transfixed. He’s staring at her ass. He’s like Yogi Bear floating towards a pie on a windowsill.”

Later in the segment, Stewart touched on Barack Obama’s roasting of the Trump White House. At a rally in Michigan for Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, the former president joked that Trump’s renovations “got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory”.

Stewart said he knew immediately that the joke would cause a firestorm: “As soon as I heard him say it, you can feel it already, what a shitstorm this is going to set off on the right, for Barack Obama to compare anything that Trump does to the brutal dictatorship of Saddam Hussein?”

He was right … sort of. Fox News host Martha MacCallum was indeed angry, but on behalf of the Cheesecake Factory. “The Cheesecake Factory comment … goes exactly to why Democrats lost the middle class, why they lost blue-collar voters,” she said. “He doesn’t respect your way of life and say: ‘That’s a nice night out.’” Network contributor Kaylee McGhee White called the comments “condescending to a popular food chain restaurant”.

“The part of the comparison that bothered you was the Cheesecake Factory part? Not the Saddam Hussein part?” asked a bewildered Stewart. “You know the Cheesecake Factory is not an actual factory, right? We did not ship cheesecake jobs to China.

“There’s a reason why Donald Trump and anyone representing his Republican Congress are distracting you,” he added. “Republicans running for Congress can’t defend Trump’s reckless record or their refusal to do anything to check his worst impulses.”

On Late Night, Seth Meyers checked in on the midterm campaign trail. “Usually, this is when candidates try to cement their closing message with something simple and hopeful that leaves voters with a sense of optimism and motivates them to get to the polls, he said, citing the famous example of Obama’s closing message in 2008, where he offered voters a chance to “turn the page”.

“The GOP’s closing message is, let’s say, slightly less elevated,” he noted. “In Ohio, they’re running an ad exploiting the childhood trauma of a gubernatorial candidate. In Michigan, they’re calling the Democratic Senate candidate a jihadist. They’re using an anti-trans slur against the Democratic Senate candidate in South Carolina. And in Texas, they’re making gross, homophobic jokes like this.”

Two weeks ago, at a campaign stop in Texas, JD Vance told the crowd: “I love you too, sir, in a totally platonic way … I’m the vice-president, not James Talarico.”

“Hold on, I’ve gotta tell all my friends at the fifth-grade lunch table about that one,” Meyers mocked.

“This is how desperate and gross they are,” Meyers added. “They’re stooping to gutter bigotry and homophobia.”

And in Los Angeles, Jimmy Kimmel looked at potential malfeasance with the election process this year. “There are shenanigans afoot this time around,” he said, as Trump filed a lawsuit in California to interfere with vote counting in the state, “as if he has any chance of winning”.

Trump also ordered the Department of Justice to block certification of the Senate race in Alaska in the event that the Republican candidate loses. “It would go like this,” Kimmel said. “If the Democrat, Mary Peltola, wins in Alaska, the election was rigged and the result would be overturned, but if the Republican wins, never mind. All is good. Remember when the Russians were the ones trying to interfere with our elections?”

The shenanigans were another distraction tactic, Kimmel argued, because “Trump has failed on every count. He’s kept none of his promises. Not only has he made a mess of this country, he’s made a mess of the whole world. So what do you do when your presidency crashes and burns and may very well take Congress down along with it? You make a phone call to the totally stable Nicki Minaj.

“Horny Donald is my least favorite Donald of all of them,” Kimmel said after the clip of Trump praising Minaj’s “beautiful ass”.

“Can you imagine what would happen if Joe Biden said that?” he added. “How would Fox News handle Joe Biden saying: ‘Nicki Minaj has a beautiful ass?’ Steve Doocy would have to eat the Bible on camera.”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: In Gaza, no privacy, no peace: this is what our lives look like a year after the ‘ceasefire’ | Akram al-Sourani
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Akram Al-Sourani
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
I look at myself and my neighbours queueing for water, and dream of a lost normality. We are now strangers even to ourselves

Every morning, I look at myself and my neighbours standing in the queue for water, and remember how each of us once had a life of our own, our privacy, our own toothbrush, our own home and our own bathroom. How we used to wash our faces and drink clean water without ever imagining that a day would come when these simple routines would become a battle with ourselves and with every drop of water. Even standing beneath a hot shower has become a dream postponed until further notice.

A year has passed since the announcement of the “ceasefire” in Gaza, yet the spectre of war, bombardment and death has never left our lives.

War is not simply the bombing of buildings or the evacuation of a residential neighbourhood. There are small wars inside this one enormous war. The tent is a war. The surveillance drone – the zannana, as we call it, for its incessant buzzing – is a war. Queueing for water is a war. Waiting to use the toilet is a war. The death of privacy is a war. Thirty people crammed into a single room is a war.

Every morning, the same question follows me: what will happen today? Will my children return from what remains of their school to what remains of our home, having walked along what remains of a street, when bombardment could take them from me at any moment?

They walk long distances because transport is difficult and expensive amid fuel shortages, repeated border crossing closures and the trickle of essential supplies into Gaza. It is as though life itself is being rationed to us, drop by drop.

In Gaza, waking up alive is not enough. You must also make sure that the place where you slept is still somewhere you can spend the following night. You must hope that your children can dream of an ordinary day – one in which obtaining a loaf of bread, an education or medical treatment is not an achievement worthy of celebration.

It is as though the ceasefire never happened. The sounds of bombardment, explosions and surveillance drones have continued to accompany our days and nights. What remains of our homes and tents trembles – and so do our hearts.

In Gaza, to be alive is to live on the edge of death. As though we are still trapped in October 2023, when the course of our lives was redrawn into a new geography, and evacuation became a matter of Israeli orders dropped from the sky on leaflets – orders to flee from one place to another, from one tent to another disappointment, from one dangerous patch of land to a corner that seemed slightly less dangerous.

On the morning of Friday 13 October 2023, the skies over Gaza rained down evacuation leaflets ordering us to leave our homes and head south.

We left, but we have never truly returned to ourselves. We lost the people we were before the war. We are no longer who we used to be. The war has turned us into strangers, unfamiliar even to ourselves.

We left the stairwell, the curtains and the windows. The sofas, the router, the 55in television, the pressure cooker on the stove, the unwashed dishes – and half a lemon that, for some ridiculous reason, we always insisted on keeping in the fridge door.

We left behind conversations, arguments, disagreements, embraces and unfinished secrets. Stories told after dinner. A bunch of keys, and a never-ending chain of household troubles.

We left our photo albums, our wedding pictures, and the hairstyle that irritated me on my wedding night because of all the hairpins; the clutter in the storeroom, the gas lighter, the bathrobe hanging behind the bathroom door, the dining table, the backgammon table, and the water, electricity and internet bills.

And we left behind a precious set of drinking glasses, imprisoned in the display cabinet since 1997 on the charge of being “far too good to bring out for guests”.

And it turned out we had been wrong to punish our little boy for breaking a cup.

Three years have passed, yet we still fear hearing again the announcement that changed our lives: “Leave your homes immediately and head south.”

Three years of displacement, tents and fear. Three years in which school years have begun and ended without our children experiencing anything resembling a normal education.

For the first time, school years are no longer measured in grades and certificates, but in the number of years children have spent displaced.

It is as though the words I wrote years ago had been waiting for me in the present. As though I had written an early warning that I myself failed to take seriously.

I never imagined that the words I had written in satire would one day become the details of our daily lives.

From Gaza to Khan Younis, to Rafah, to al-Mawasi, to al-Zawayda, to Deir al-Balah, from a tent to what remains of our home, we have arrived safely in the unknown.

Our dreams have yet to arrive. Our hopes have yet to arrive. I fear they may have evaporated somewhere along the way.

And today, a year after the announcement of the “ceasefire”, I am still standing in queues: for aid, for cooking gas, for water – and in the endless queue of those waiting for the unknown.

I wait for my children to return from school, and I try to recover something of the life we left behind.

There is more to tell – if there is anything left of our minds, or our lives, to tell it.

Akram Al-Sourani is a writer and poet from Gaza City, and the author of A Homeland Out of Coverage, Half-Baked Homeland and What’s That

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Epstein files are a sledgehammer for the US midterms | Katie Phang
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Katie Phang
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Voters have a chance to break America’s two-tiered system of justice and hold powerful people accountable

When Americans go to the polls a week from now, accountability will be front and center.

The Jeffrey Epstein files are emblematic of a corrupt system. And the fish rots from the head down. Beyond the grifter-in-chief and his spawn are billionaires profiting from pay-to-play relationships and predatory corporations rewarded for choosing profits over people, machines over humanity.

As many as 88% of Americans who plan to vote in the midterms prioritize candidates who have promised to hold powerful people to account, including by releasing the full Epstein files, according to a September GBAO poll, which also found that what the files represent – sexual exploitation of children; government corruption; abuse of power and powerful people escaping accountability – was a bigger concern than many of the everyday issues the pollsters tested. The finding echoed a poll from Reuters/Ipsos earlier this summer which found 69% of Americans believe the Epstein files show that “powerful people in the U.S. are rarely held accountable for their actions”.

Before he was elected president, Donald Trump sat down with Fox News’s Rachel Campos-Duffy, who, during yet another softball interview typical of that network, posed the following question: “Would you declassify the Epstein files?” Trump answered: “Yeah, yeah I would.”

Kash Patel, Dan Bongino, JD Vance and the president’s son, Donald Jr, all sang in the chorus that demanded the files be released. But as soon as Trump became president, and Patel took over at the FBI, the tune changed dramatically. Now that Trump was in a position to actually do something about it, suddenly there was nothing to see. The FBI, under the direction of Patel and joined by Pam Bondi, the then US attorney general, even released a memo stating there was no client list, no evidence to pursue investigations against third parties and that “no further disclosure would be appropriate or warranted.”

Trump went on to declare the Epstein files a “Democrat Hoax” and tried his damnedest to distract the public from demanding justice. As is well known, Congress eventually passed the Epstein Files Transparency Act (EFTA), requiring the attorney general to release the files with very limited grounds for redactions and withholdings.

We all saw the botched rollout of the 3.5m pages of materials and how egregiously it reviolated Epstein survivors by releasing confidential personal information. The EFTA was supposed to protect those survivors, but Trump’s Department of Justice blacked out the names of those with money, means and influence but exposed victims and survivors. If you think that was an accident, I’ve got some swampland in Florida to sell you.

Then in January of this year, Todd Blanche, then the deputy attorney general, declared that Trump’s Department of Justice was done. Just done. In my long career as a trial lawyer and journalist, I’ve been reading documents for what they say and what they leave out, and have personally reviewed tens of thousands of the released Epstein files. I never thought I would see our Department of Justice conceal the crimes of a small, moneyed elite.

So, I sued for the transparency the law required. On 27 April, I filed Katie Phang v Attorney General Todd Blanche in federal court in Washington DC, arguing that Blanche violated the Administrative Procedure Act when he illegally redacted and withheld documents pursuant to the EFTA. Blanche’s illegal conduct was making it impossible for journalists to do their jobs; to bring the truth and transparency that the American people demanded and deserved.

On 25 June, the presiding judge in my case, Emmet Sullivan, found that Blanche had failed to respond substantively to my arguments and that therefore “the Attorney General has conceded that he is in violation” of EFTA. Judge Sullivan also ordered Trump’s justice department to begin producing specific unredacted documents. Since then, Blanche has violated court orders, refused to comply with the law and rules of procedure, blown deadlines and made cheap, insincere excuses. Instead of enforcing the law, the attorney general of the United States has been busy subverting it.

double quotation markInstead of enforcing the law, the attorney general of the United States has been busy subverting it

Here’s the thing, though: voters have noticed. They’re angry and candidates are seizing the day. More than 160 unique Epstein-related campaign ads worth more than $35m in airtime have aired leading up to the midterms. In Ohio, Sherrod Brown has been hammering the incumbent Republican senator Jon Husted over his acceptance of donations from the billionaire Les Wexner. (Epstein was Wexner’s financial adviser and Wexner has denied knowing about or participating in any of Epstein’s crimes.) In Georgia, Jon Ossoff has positioned himself as someone fighting Washington corruption and the “Epstein class”. In Texas, James Talarico has stood in solidarity with Epstein survivors and called on his opponent, Ken Paxton, to do the same. (So far, he hasn’t.) Sky Roberts, the brother of Virginia Giuffre, an Epstein victim who died by suicide last year, and Giuffre’s sister-in-law, Amanda Roberts, appeared in an ad backing Colorado Democrat Jessica Killin in a House race against Republican Jeff Crank, who refused to meet with Sky and Amanda and declined to sign the bipartisan discharge petition to force a vote on the EFTA.

Just this week, a new staff report from Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee alleged that a “growing body of evidence demonstrates that Donald Trump was an active participant in Jeffrey Epstein’s sexual abuse of young women during the mid-to-late 1990s,” and that DOJ and the FBI “are doing everything they can to keep the American people in the dark about it.” (Trump denies any wrongdoing in connection with Epstein.) Although the report mostly cites previously reported allegations against Trump, it reflects the outsized importance of the Epstein Files in the election.

For decades, some version of “just the way it is” has protected corrupt actors such as Epstein, his friends and associates. Epstein got a sweetheart plea deal while his elite circle was spared investigations or the ignominy of publicity, allowing them to continue to perpetrate their offenses and live their rarefied lives. And the people who were supposed to protect the survivors and hold the bad actors accountable turned a blind eye in what appears to be an exchange for access and privilege.

But survivors refuse to be silenced. A federal judge has told the top cop to stop breaking the law. And voters across party lines are rebelling. “Just the way it is” won’t cut it any more.

The Epstein files have become a sledgehammer to break America’s two-tiered standard of justice. That, to me, is the beginning of accountability. That is how we win, and how we build a better future.

Follow them on Substack: Stacey Abrams, Robert Reich, Paul Krugman, Naomi Klein, Mehdi Hasan, Bernie Sanders, Rebecca Solnit, Katie Phang, Judd Legum, Margaret Sullivan, and Wajahat Ali.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Elon Musk says he has ‘cyber psychosis’. Do you too? | Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Whether using chatbots for childcare or taking up smoking, a new affliction is sweeping through the tech world. Here are the signs

In the least surprising news you’ll hear all week, Elon Musk has said he’s not entirely right in the head. “I’ve got a little bit of cyber psychosis,” the world’s richest and most irritating man explained during an event this month. “Maybe a lot actually.” Musk added that, over “various points this year”, he’s had “AI or SI psychosis probably half a dozen times”. SI, in case you missed the super-important memo, stands for “superintelligence” and it’s what Donald Trump wants everyone to call AI now, for reasons too stupid to explain.

While the phrase SI is still being used 0nly by weaselly tech bros desperate for Trump’s approval, you’ll probably have heard the term “AI psychosis” bandied around a lot. On the most serious level, it refers to delusional thinking induced or exacerbated by sycophantic chatbots. People who have ploughed their life savings into a ridiculous business idea, for example, because computer code told them they were the next Jeff Bezos. But the phrase has also been used more jokingly to describe overexuberance around artificial intelligence, and that seems to be how Musk was using it. The comments about his self-diagnosed bouts of cyber psychosis came as the tech mogul waxed lyrical about how great AI music videos have become, and how he believes artificial intelligence now “understands beauty and harmony”.

I don’t know if Musk gushing over the beauty and harmony of AI slop is down to cyber psychosis or possibly his widely reported enthusiasm for the benefits of ketamine and psychedelics. But I can tell you that large swathes of Silicon Valley are dangerously high on their own supply of AI bullshit. And the sickness is rapidly spreading to the populace. So, I’m taking it on myself to help you spot a couple of signs that demonstrate someone has become over attached to AI or grown too credulous when it comes to the puffery around the industry.

A sudden cigarette habit is one of the more unusual signals something is afoot. This month, Palantir chief technology officer Shyam Sankar told CBS that numerous AI researchers “have started smoking as a way of signaling to other researchers” that they believe AI is going to cure cancer soon. Sankar provided no data to back up this extraordinary claim, which he said was emblematic of “this mass psychosis, social delusion” around AI. But tech executives don’t need to prove things any more, do they? They just make grandiose statements and watch the investor dollars roll in.

Another signal your brain may have been fried by AI? An inability to interact with your small children without the help of a large language model. “I cannot imagine having gone through figuring out how to raise a newborn without ChatGPT,” OpenAI CEO and new dad Sam Altman said on Jimmy Fallon last year. Try to imagine, Sam! People have been doing it for a while. Earlier this year, Altman also informed us that AI is a great way to bond with your kids. “cool use case of chatgpt work i heard last night: connect your family calendars and explain your kids’ interests,” Altman tweeted. “every morning for the drive to school, have it make a podcast that talks about one kid’s soccer game that afternoon, one kid’s upcoming birthday, some news, etc.”

While Altman’s parenting tip didn’t land well with normies, Marissa Mayer probably appreciated it. Mayer made her name (and tons of money) as the first female engineer at Google and the CEO of Yahoo; now she’s flogging an AI assistant called Dazzle. In a new interview with the New York Times, Mayer told a story about how, when her daughter Marielle was turning 10, her teacher wanted three bullet points about what made Marielle special. Mayer “felt overwhelmed”, and asked Dazzle for help. “It came back and was like, your daughter is empathetic, creative and an animal lover,” Mayer told the Times. I don’t know how much AI Kool Aid Mayer has drunk, but it’s clearly enough to have made her believe asking AI for insights about your kid is sweet, not downright dystopian.

Unfortunately, I do not have the cure for AI psychosis. But as the gold rush continues, let me point you to a sobering reality check from American asset management firm Apollo Global Management. “Despite massive investments and widespread hype … [AI] has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech,” stated an insight it published on Saturday. While AI is obviously a transformative technology, I suspect we’re in the middle of a bubble that’s about to burst. After all the mass exuberance, we’re due a very nasty comedown.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Are seed oils unhealthy? Why are so many influencers speaking out against them? | Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Randomised trials of omega-6s do not show an increase in inflammation caused by the fatty acid

If you’ve been online lately, you’ve probably been bombarded with the discourse about seed oils. Once a completely innocuous food that no one really talked about, they have become the enemy of the moment. Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of health and human services in the US, has called them “toxic” and vowed to act against them. There are countless activewear-clad influencers online saying that nothing harms your health more than these products.

Which is odd, because the Australian dietary guidelines say seed oils are basically fine. You should limit them because they’re high in calories but otherwise there’s no major reason – according to the guidelines and most experts – why you should avoid them. As Prof Lauren Ball, director of the University of Queensland’s Centre for Community Health and Wellbeing, says: “There’s no convincing evidence that eating seed oils like canola or sunflower oil in normal dietary amounts harms our health. In fact, these oils contain unsaturated fats, which are generally beneficial for cardiovascular health.” Dr Jason Wu, a professor at the University of New South Wales, agrees: “The evidence base consistently points to health benefits of eating seed oils.”

Seed oils are a group of cooking oils that are, unsurprisingly, extracted from seeds. They’re generally quite highly refined – although you can get less refined versions of many of them – and include canola oil, sunflower seed oil, rice bran oil, soya bean oil and corn oil. Most of the time vegetable oil is composed of seed oils – it’s often a mixture of sunflower seed and canola oils.

The concerns about seed oils boil down to one thing: inflammation. It is asserted that the omega-6 fatty acids contained in most seed oils such as linoleic acid can be harmful in large doses and may cause the body to become more inflamed over time. This isn’t entirely crazy – there is some evidence from rodent studies that omega-6s cause inflammation, and that having too many of them can have long-term negative outcomes.

The problem, of course, is that lab rats and mice aren’t people. Very high levels of omega-6s can cause liver dysfunction and gut issues in rats but that doesn’t mean that a bit of sunflower seed oil is going to destroy your intestines.

Data from humans doesn’t really show this connection. People who eat more linoleic acid have substantially lower risks of cardiovascular disease than those who eat more. Studies looking at supplementing seed oils in people’s diets have shown no major impacts – and sometimes even modest benefits – compared with placebos.

Human studies also don’t support the inflammation link. Randomised trials of omega-6s do not show an increase in inflammation caused by the fatty acids. A randomised crossover study in which the same people were randomly given either omega-3 or omega-6 fatty acids found that there was no difference in how they affected inflammatory markers. Evidence from careful analyses of genetics and causality in humans show little indication that omega-6 fatty acids are inflammatory. As Wu puts it, the pro-inflammatory effects of omega-6 fatty acids are “not supported by evidence”.

On the other hand, we know that animal fats are probably bad for you. They contain high levels of low-density lipoprotein – bad cholesterol – which goes on to clog arteries and cause heart attacks. Ball notes: “Replacing saturated fats, such as those in butter, with unsaturated fats in oils like canola and sunflower can lower LDL cholesterol, an important risk factor for cardiovascular disease.”

In other words, the scientific perspective is simple: seed oils are fine. They’re high in calories but otherwise perfectly healthy, and if you’re eating them to replace saturated fat then they’re probably going to improve your health. So why are there crazy-eyed men yelling at canola oil in the supermarket aisle on Instagram?

The story here is mostly about dietary fads. Favourite diets online now are quite high in animal fats. If you’re promoting your new book about keto diets, it’s not great for sales if everyone thinks that eating too many steaks is going to give them heart disease. Yes, there were some scientific concerns but those have been largely disproven in the literature already.

There are a lot of people scaremongering about seed oils online, which makes sense. You get a lot more attention for yelling that we’re all being poisoned than by calmly explaining the science. I doubt the furore about seed oils is going away any time soon.

But from a health perspective you’re probably better off eating seed oils than any other fats. You should limit consumption, because too many calories is not great, but whether you’re frying, making mayonnaise or whatever, it’s likely that the healthiest choice is a seed oil of some kind.

Dr Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz is an epidemiologist and science communicator and a senior research fellow at the University of Wollongong

Antiviral is a fortnightly column that interrogates the evidence behind the health headlines and factchecks popular wellness claims

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Trump-appointed CDC deputy director to resign after six months on the job
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Jessica Glenza and Michelle R Smith
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Jennifer Shuford is expected to leave her post after midterm elections ‘to spend more time with my family’

The deputy director and chief medical officer of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) will resign after six months on the job, according to an agency email obtained by the Guardian.

Dr Jennifer Shuford was appointed by Donald Trump in April as part of a four-person senior leadership team.

The appointments were meant to stabilize the agency after the previous CDC director, Susan Monarez, left less than a month into the job – publicly describing the directives of the health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, as “unscientific”.

“I am leaving to spend more time with my family,” Shuford said in a statement, sent via email by the CDC director, Dr Erica Schwartz. “I am so thankful to President Trump and Secretary Kennedy for giving me the opportunity to help lead CDC. It has been an amazing experience, and I will be forever grateful for it.”

Shuford is expected to leave her post on 12 November, after the midterm elections.

The deputy director was appointed as part of a four-person team in April, alongside Schwartz and two other top leaders. Shuford’s appointment was cheered by public health leaders, such as Association of State and Territorial Health Officials (ASTHO), who would have known her work as Texas health commissioner.

Trump described the team as “Highly Respected Doctors of Medicine [who] have the knowledge, experience, and TOP degrees to restore the GOLD STANDARD OF SCIENCE at the CDC”, in a social media post.

In the time since Shuford has worked at the agency, Kennedy has made significant changes that undermine vaccine trust and access. In just a few recent examples: Kennedy fired all 17 of the CDC’s expert vaccine advisory panel members and replaced them with ideologically aligned appointees, slow-walked death updates to the agency’s measles dashboard, and forced the CDC to publicly contradict scientific consensus on vaccines and autism – a change the Autism Science Foundation said left it “appalled”.

At the same time, the agency has lost one-third of its workforce and 48 distinct measles outbreaks have roiled the US, particularly in Pennsylvania. The overwhelming majority of Americans – including Maha supporters – trust vaccines.

“I am deeply grateful for Dr Shuford’s outstanding leadership and commitment to CDC and public health, especially as she has navigated an exceptionally demanding, high-profile, and constantly evolving environment over the past several months,” said Schwartz in the email announcing Shuford’s departure.

Dr Satish Pillai will serve as acting deputy director and chief medical officer as the team searches for a successor to Shuford.

https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/202.title: ‘I was so sick’: is running a marathon while on a GLP-1 a bad idea?
https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/202.author: Lauren Gould
https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/202.text:
As the weight-loss drugs become more common, some runners find the side-effects challenging. Here’s what experts say

This feeling couldn’t be chalked up to inexperience. Keri, who asked us to omit her full name due to the sensitive subject matter, has completed dozens of half marathons and four full marathons.

She ran the 2024 Philadelphia marathon fast enough to earn a coveted spot in this year’s Bank of America Chicago race, one of the eight world marathon majors.

But this half marathon felt different. It was the first time she had raced on a GLP-1. Less than a week beforehand, she had taken her first 2.5mg standard starting dose of tirzepatide, commonly sold under the names Mounjaro and Zepbound, for weight loss.

Throughout the race, Keri felt nauseous, struggling to keep down the energy gels many endurance runners rely on for fuel.

“After that half marathon, I was so sick,” she said. Keri had a “severe” reaction to the 2.5mg dose and, in hindsight, wishes that she had started at a lower dose.

The number of people taking GLP-1s to lose weight has grown from 3% to 11% in the past two years. A 2026 cohort study found that 15 times more people use them for non-FDA-approved reasons compared with five years ago. The study also found that 35% of users are not considered overweight according to the BMI chart.

Meghann Featherstun, an Ohio-based registered sports dietitian, has worked with multiple marathon runners who use GLP-1s; they are more accessible now than when they first came on the market and fewer clinical criteria are required for a prescription, she said.

Some experts, such as Heidi Skolnik, a fellow of the American College of Sports Medicine and author of Your GLP-1 Game Plan, believe it’s possible to run longer races while taking GLP-1s.

“If you can eat enough to fuel your workouts and your runs and drink enough, then go for it. Good for you. But if you can’t, then don’t. Then you’re working against your health and wellbeing,” she said.

GLP-1 side-effects such as nausea and loss of appetite can negatively affect running performance. Some athletes use strategies such as microdosing to achieve their weight loss goals while still training for half and full marathons. In one subreddit, “Zepbound athletes”, users exchange advice for training and performance while on the drugs, such as skipping doses and how to get enough fuel for races.

Some researchers, such as Emily Lundstrom, an assistant professor of clinical physical therapy who studies low energy availability, believe endurance athletes focused on performance should wait until they have finished preparing for a race to use a GLP-1. “Even microdosing is not a good idea,” she said.

As the number of people who take GLP-1s for weight loss grows, so has the controversy surrounding these drugs.

When Serena Williams, a decorated female tennis player, became a spokesperson for Ro, a telehealth company that sells GLP-1s, it opened up a debate over who should take these drugs and if they have a place in sports. Some accused her of promoting thinness and unnecessary weight loss. Others argued that her openness may help reduce the shame surrounding GLP-1s. Yet despite the pushback, runners relate to her journey.

Steve, a 44-year-old from Oregon, who asked to be identified by only his first name because of the deeply personal topic, has always considered himself active. Even when he wasn’t training for a long-distance race, he went for casual runs, boxed and lifted weights.

“No matter how hard I trained, no matter how much I tracked my macros and stayed on plan, I just kept gaining weight,” he said. He noticed Williams had a similar story of turning to a GLP-1 because she couldn’t reach her desired physique through diet and exercise.

Steve started a tirzepatide compound in July 2026 and soon began training for an October half marathon. Initially, runs didn’t feel great. Five miles usually came easy, but now required multiple breaks and spiked his heart rate higher than usual.

Steve cut his 2.5mg dose in half after four weeks, a tip he saw on Reddit. He can now train without a heart-rate spike. “I don’t feel as exhausted any more,” he said. His weight loss has stalled, but he said it wouldn’t be worth taking the drug if he couldn’t train properly on it.

Dr Melanie Jay, a professor at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine, said GLP-1s can cause a two to 10bpm increase in resting heart rate, but further increases are possible during exercise. However, Jay noted that there weren’t many studies on how the second generation of GLP-1s (such as the tirzepatide Steve takes) affect exercise and heart rate. Other common side-effects of GLP-1s are gastrointestinal, including nausea and constipation, which Jay said can improve with time.

Long-distance runners should exercise caution when it comes to these drugs, said Claire Shorenstein, a board-certified sports dietitian.

“Typically, I would not want someone to be on a GLP-1 while actively training for a marathon or any other type of endurance event,” she said.

Because marathoners and other endurance athletes are already at risk for underfueling, Shorenstein says taking a GLP-1, which suppresses appetite, can lead to a chronic state of low energy availability, where the body doesn’t have enough energy left for “all the other functions that our body needs so that we can stay alive and be healthy”.

Low energy availability is not permanent, but over time, it can cause Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (Reds), which may reduce bone density and decrease immunity. In women, it can cause hypothalamic amenorrhea (loss of the menstrual cycle). Reds is treated through adequate nutrition and exercise adjustments.

“I was definitely at risk for Reds because I was underfueling,” said Keri, the runner who was training for the 2026 Chicago Marathon. She has stopped and restarted her GLP-1 use during training, due to harsh side-effects, weight gain and appetite loss. “I’m not doing another dose until after the marathon,” she said.

Kylie Keeton, a 32-year-old based in Texas, lost 170lb without a GLP-1. However, when she increased her running mileage, she noticed the number on the scale began to rise. Despite feeling “super embarrassed” about it, she decided to try semaglutide at the end of 2025 and eventually switched to a tirzepatide.

But side-effects such as nausea made it hard to hit her mileage, and she had to drop out of a half marathon.

Keeton felt torn about whether to continue taking the drug. It was hard to decide whether weight gain or not being able to run was worse, she said. Keeton tried various strategies to integrate GLP-1 use with her fitness practices, such as breaking up her weekly dose into two smaller doses.

But this is not recommended because “it is not how the drug was studied in any of the clinical trials”, said Dr Nidhi Kansal, who specializes in GLP-1 treatments at Northwestern Medicine.

Kristy Baumann, a Minnesota-based registered dietitian who works with endurance runners, said she doesn’t personally see clients take doses in this way. However, she notes athletes should time their doses after a long run or race day: if you take it the day before, “you’d have a greater chance of GI issues”, she said.

Eventually, Keeton stopped taking the drug. She had lost about 5lb in six months of taking GLP-1s and didn’t think it was worth continuing given the expense. Now she can run without feeling nauseous and hopes to improve her personal record by 45 minutes at the 2026 BMW Dallas Marathon.

Overall, there is little research on using GLP-1s while long-distance running. The experts I spoke to expressed caution over energy levels and dosage tweaks, and urged users to heed any adverse symptoms or difficulties. The only thing that’s clear is that long-distance runners who use GLP-1s can have varying experiences.

Nikki Thornton, a 47-year-old marathon runner based in Taree, Australia, started a GLP-1 in 2023 to lower her blood sugar levels, which were reaching pre-diabetic ranges, and lose weight. At first, Thornton noticed she struggled to run more than 5km (about 3 miles). Eventually, completed the sweltering Sydney Marathon, but experienced gastrointestinal issues. “It was the worst one I’ve ever done,” she said.

About six months after starting a GLP-1, she said her body adjusted. In 2025, she improved her Sydney Marathon time by three hours.

While Featherstun, the sports dietitian from Ohio, works with marathon runners on GLP-1s, she said they rarely stay on them for long.

“Every single person who’s been on it, I’ve got an email from them. ‘I’m done with it. I’m off it. I can’t handle this.’ So I do think it’s a really tricky combination,” she said.

https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.title: ‘We did everything wrong!’ The tragedy of the hit-free band behind Blondie’s Hanging on the Telephone
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.author: Alex Deller
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.text:
They gigged wildly, helped other groups to fame and their songwriting brilliance gave Blondie a signature track. Could a deathbed wish now see the Nerves finally making it big?

The Nerves should have had it all. Formed in 1974 and gifted with earworm melodies, good looks and a painstaking work ethic, the trio of Jack Lee (guitar, vocals), Peter Case (bass, vocals) and Paul Collins (drums, vocals) wrote, rehearsed and gigged as if their lives depended on it. Not quite punk and dismissive of the description “power pop”, they aimed to cram epic brilliance into effervescent, two-minute songs.

When the music industry ignored them, the Nerves opted to make their own luck, pressing their own EP and booking a gruelling nationwide tour that saw them share stages with Devo and the Ramones. After they split in 1978, a bittersweet coda to their brief career swiftly followed: Parallel Lines, Blondie’s smash-hit third album, opened with a cover version of their song Hanging on the Telephone. Previously a Nerves calling card, the Blondie take seemed to scrub them from history.

“I figured it would be two weeks, or a month tops, before we were famous,” smiles Paul Collins from his New York home today. A Juilliard student with a bohemian upbringing and an overriding love of rock’n’roll, Collins dropped out and headed for the west coast. “I was barely 18, I had 80 bucks in my pocket and I was scared to death,” he recalls. Within three days of arriving in San Francisco, he found an ad tacked to the wall of a record store which led him to the enigmatic Jack Lee, a transplant from Sitka, Alaska.

Peter Case proved harder to woo. Baling on school at 15 and ditching Buffalo for San Francisco, he played blues and country standards on the street to pay for food. “I slept in a beat-up van parked down by the water,” says Case. “It wasn’t even my van.” Lee and Case struck up a friendship when the latter was busking. When Collins came on board, the Nerves were transformed from idea to actuality. “You just couldn’t find people that wanted to do something that was that out of joint,” Case recalls. “There was nobody else like Jack around – someone who had a vision, wanted to go with it and could write.”
