The movie also marks a personal breakthrough for the pair, who first met when they were actors. “Friends who read the script said to us, ‘Oh, you’re going there?’” recalls Ambrossi. “We’ve been writing together for 13 years about LGBTQ+ characters but it has always been, like, lesbians, trans women …” Previous collaborations include their 2017 debut film, Holy Camp!, which they adapted from La Llamada, their stage musical about a summer camp staffed by nuns. In one scene, God materialises to sing I Will Always Love You. Their 2023 series La Mesías (now streaming on Mubi) is a hypnotically bizarre tale of Christian pop stars, extraterrestrials and bad parenting. But no gay men.

What took them so long? “Sometimes you don’t want to talk about yourself,” offers Calvo, speaking up at last. “Many queer creators have projected themselves into other characters. Pedro Almodóvar, Lorca with The House of Bernarda Alba, Michael Patrick King with Sex and the City.” He flashes a rare smile. “Good show.”

Ambrossi identifies a psychological dimension to the delay: “It’s true you don’t want to be too on-the-nose. But you start wondering if there is also another reason.” In the 1932 strand of the film, the elite casino members use a system of black and white balls to vote on admitting newcomers. The black ball for no– la bola negra – becomes a symbol of queer generational shame and rejection that must be wrestled with. Is it shame, then, that kept Ambrossi from addressing his own sexuality in his work? “In my case, yes. I wasn’t ready to talk about desire or sex because I felt ashamed in some way.”

He and Calvo were already friends with their compatriot and hero Almodóvar, whose company El Deseo, meaning Desire, co-produced La Bola Negra. “I told Pedro, ‘I don’t deal well with desire.’ He looked at me and said, ‘You need to start.’ That’s when it clicked: if you don’t deal explicitly with desire, you are missing life.”

Perhaps that is why the word “explicit” crops up several times in Ambrossi’s conversation today: having been out as a gay man but under the radar in his work, he is eager now to emphasise the ways in which La Bola Negra is defiant or unequivocal. One aspect is the casting of gay actors in gay roles, most notably the Bambi-eyed singer Guitarricadelafuente, who makes his screen debut as the lovestruck soldier.

“It’s not that straight actors can’t play gay,” says Calvo. “There are no rules in art. But …” Ambrossi jumps in: “We like to do it this way. When I was 10, I watched Rupert Everett in My Best Friend’s Wedding. I wasn’t sure I was gay, but I knew he was like me. There was a truth in his eyes that I want to get in my movies.” He sighs. “Rupert Everett was so brave. He should have been James Bond.”

Calvo had an unhappy experience as a young gay actor. “I was a teenager playing a gay role on TV,” he says. “When it finished, I didn’t get many auditions. I was advised to cut my hair, not paint my nails.” A short back and sides didn’t help, though. “I guess people could still tell. So I decided to write roles for actors who don’t have space in the industry.”

Once the pair began dating as well as working together, the two-headed queer celebrity phenomenon of Los Javis was born. They were playwrights, film-makers, actors and reality TV participants, including regular judges on the Spanish version of Ru Paul’s Drag Race. Being an indispensable part of Spanish cultural life came at a price. Calvo points to this now as one of the reasons he and Ambrossi separated during the making of La Bola Negra. “People would talk to me in the plural all the time, ‘It was nice to meet you guys.’ I’d be like, ‘Huh? I’m standing alone here.’ I felt I’d lost my individuality.”

Spain didn’t cope well with the breakup. “It was a big deal,” Calvo admits. “There were cameras outside my door for a month.” Keen to move on, Ambrossi displays a flicker of irritation: “I think we’ve passed through this conversation. Imagine everyone talking about your ex forever! We love to write and direct together and we’re going to keep doing that.” The matter is closed.

After all the diversifying and cross-platforming, Los Javis have reached their Pokémon-style final evolution. “From now on, we want to focus on movies,” says Calvo. No regrets, though. “The other things were important in making a statement,” Ambrossi points out. “I grew up thinking directors should be serious and monolithic. We represented a new way.” Calvo lifts a finger: “A non-binary way,” he says. “We don’t see life as stiff. We mix genres. A more flexible time is coming. Take the work seriously but not yourself.”

Before they go, there is a line in La Bola Negra that I ask them to unpack. When the modern-day researcher Alberto asks the Lorca scholar played by Glenn Close for advice on what he should do with the pages of that incomplete story, she tells him: “You’ve inherited something and you don’t know what to do with it. You are truly a Spaniard.”

Calvo is happy to help. “In Spain, we always have to be reminded by foreigners that we have a rich, interesting culture and history,” he says. Ambrossi elaborates: “It is as if pride is shameful. When someone is doing well and winning awards all over Spain, people are like, ‘Hmm. That’s not very Spanish.’ Unless it’s football.” Where does that attitude come from? “Maybe religion,” muses Calvo. “Maybe dictatorship.”

Does it apply to them? Are they destined to underplay their triumphs for ever? They offer their best you’ve-got-to-be-kidding looks, then answer in unison: “Not us.”

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.title: Gulliver fans celebrate three centuries of Jonathan Swift’s classic satire
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.author: Rory Carroll Ireland correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.text:
Events in Ireland explore origins of Gulliver’s Travels, the Dublin clergyman’s book that became an instant hit in 1726

In March 1726, an Irish clergyman visited London and arranged for a courier to deliver a manuscript to a publisher under cover of night. The dean of St Patrick’s Cathedral in Dublin knew his novel would cause trouble and wanted to publish it anonymously.

His name was Jonathan Swift and the story was called Travels into Several Remote Nations of the World. The satirical work was published that October and is better known 300 years on as Gulliver’s Travels.

An immediate sensation, it skewered Georgian pretensions and entered popular culture through translations, children’s versions, comics and films. The anniversary is now being celebrated at Swift’s alma mater, Trinity College Dublin, and at events around Ireland.

Exhibitions, festivals, seminars, art competitions and workshops are exploring the origins of Swift’s masterpiece, its retelling through a feminist lens, and its prophetic depiction of a society in thrall to a form of artificial intelligence.

“Lemuel Gulliver’s first voyage to the land of Lilliput is the one most familiar to audiences today,” said Stephanie Breen, an assistant librarian and co-curator of the exhibition at Trinity. “This exhibition, however, brings viewers on a journey to all of the lands Gulliver encountered – Lilliput, Brobdingnag, Laputa and beyond and the country of Houyhnhnms.”

The exhibition, which runs until December and is available online, draws on the university’s collection of hundreds of editions and popularisations of Gulliver’s Travels, including engraved illustrations, pop-up versions, a 1976 Marvel comic and the only known surviving copy of an abridgement printed in 1761.

The voice of Gulliver’s wife, Mary, who is neglected and left at home “big with child” until his eventual, grumpy return, was imagined through contemporary works such as Alison Fell’s The Mistress of Lilliput and Lauren Chater’s Gulliver’s Wife, said Aileen Douglas, a professor of English and exhibition co-curator.

Gulliver’s experiences in Laputa, a floating island dedicated to arts and science, resonated with our era’s anxieties about technology, said Douglas. Its inhabitants seek to extract sunbeams from cucumbers and obtain knowledge via an “engine” of wires, handles and paper that can produce tracts on philosophy, poetry and mathematics “without the least assistance from genius or study”.

In the kingdom of Luggnagg, Gulliver is at first enchanted and then horrified by the Struldbruggs, a race that is immortal but continues eternally to age and sicken.

A panel discussion about the role of art in challenging power, and Gulliver’s attacks on human vanity and scientific arrogance, is to be held at Trinity on Wednesday. At the cathedral, a children’s choir will perform the premiere of a work by the composer Seán Doherty, along with organ recitals and extracts of Gulliver’s Travels read by the Swift scholar Brendan Twomey. An exhibition and lecture series at the Robinson library in County Armagh runs until December.

Born in 1667, Swift combined posts in the Church of Ireland with pamphlets and essays that pioneered deadpan, savage satire, including A Modest Proposal, which suggested alleviating the plight of the Irish poor by selling their children as food to the wealthy.

He wrote Gulliver’s Travels in Dublin and at an estate in County Meath, where it is said that some very tall and very small farm workers inspired the storytelling.

When shipwrecked on Lilliput, Gulliver discovers diminutive inhabitants who are waging war against a rival kingdom in a dispute over which end of a boiled egg should be cracked – a satire on Europe’s sectarian conflicts. Gulliver captures the Blefuscudian fleet and douses a fire at a Lilliputian palace by urinating on it.

Marooned among giants in Brobdingnag, Gulliver’s stories about his “own dear native country” inadvertently reveal its corruption and cruelty, prompting the Brobdingnagian ruler to pillory humanity as “the most pernicious race of little odious vermin that nature ever suffered to crawl upon the surface of the earth”.

Swift’s publisher, Benjamin Motte, did not know his author’s identity but the book’s success, and Swift’s literary record, enabled many to guess, said Douglas. “People sort of knew it was him.”

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Rays rally in 12th inning to beat Brewers and stave off World Series sweep
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
Jonny DeLuca and pinch-hitter Ben Williamson singled home runs in a stunning 12th-inning rally, and the Tampa Bay Rays staved off World Series elimination with a 4-3 win over the Milwaukee Brewers on Tuesday night that forced Game 5.

Cooper Pratt hit a tiebreaking home run off Ian Seymour in the top of the 12th for his fourth hit of the game as Milwaukee neared a sweep and their first World Series title.

But the Rays, also seeking their first championship, rallied in the bottom half after a throwing error by third baseman Joey Ortiz on Junior Caminero’s leadoff grounder against reliever Antonio Senzatela.

Liam Hicks singled off Shane Drohan, who relieved in his first appearance since 15 October, and DeLuca’s single to center drove in pinch-runner Cedric Mullins to tie the score at 3.

Fri 23 Oct Game 1: Milwaukee 3, Tampa Bay 2Sat 24 Oct Game 2: Milwaukee 5, Tampa Bay 4Mon 26 Oct Game 3: Milwaukee 10, Tampa Bay 1Tue 27 Oct Game 4: Tampa Bay 4, Milwaukee 3 (12 innings)Wed 28 Oct Game 5: Milwaukee at Tampa Bay, 8pm (Fox)Fri 30 Oct Game 6: Tampa Bay at Milwaukee, 8pm* (Fox)Sat 31 Oct Game 7: Tampa Bay at Milwaukee, 8pm* (Fox)

In the US, all World Series games will air on Fox and Fox Deportes, with streaming available through Fox One. In the UK, the series will be carried by TNT Sports. In Australia, fans can watch on ESPN, with streaming available through Disney+ and Kayo Sports.

Chandler Simpson’s single loaded the bases and Milwaukee employed a five-man infield with the infield in.

Williamson, who had been 1 for 15 in the postseason, hit a chopper over first baseman Jake Bauers and into right field.

Tampa Bay became just the fifth of 26 teams that fell behind 3-0 in the World Series to win Game 4. The previous four lost Game 5.

Of 43 teams to trail 3-0 in any best-of-seven postseason matchup, the only one that rebounded to win was the Boston Red Sox against the New York Yankees in the 2004 American League Championship Series.

Tampa Bay ended an eight-game winning streak by the Brewers, who were bidding to become only the second team to sweep a League Championship Series and the World Series.

David Hamilton also homered for the Brewers. Jackson Chourio had a single and double, improving to 10 for 20 in the Series.

Pratt, a 22-year-old rookie whose go-ahead hit sparked the Brewers to a 5-4 win in Game 2, drove a slider into the left-field seats against Seymour. Pratt had tied the score at 1 with an RBI double in the second.

Milwaukee players bounded out of the dugout to greet Pratt, who debuted in June and became the first rookie to hit an extra-inning homer in the World Series.

Milwaukee fans in the crowd of 40,514, many waving yellow towels and some wearing cheeseheads, brought a Badger State feel to Tropicana Field.

Tampa Bay returned to their white home jerseys, a day after playing in Devil Rays throwbacks.

Simpson hit an RBI double off starter Dustin May in the second, but Milwaukee tied the score in the fourth against Griffin Jax when Frelick hit a two-out single and came around on Pratt’s double.

Caminero singled leading off the bottom half to chase May and advanced on a groundout. DeLuca hit a hard grounder to Hamilton and Caminero twisted toward the grass to avoid the third baseman’s tag, then came home when Hamilton bounced his throw past Bauers for an error.

Hamilton, Milwaukee’s No 9 hitter, drove an 0-2 fastball at the letters from Jax into the right-field seats for his second home run of the postseason – half his regular-season total and just his second since 6 June.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Rise of Palestinian parties in Knesset will redraw Israel’s political landscape
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Julian Borger in Nazareth
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Exit polls indicate opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot will have to work with Arab-Israeli leaders to have a hope of governing

Full report: Coalition talks loom as Israel exit polls suggest Netanyahu and Eisenkot blocs tied

The big gains made by Palestinian parties in Israel’s general election pose an urgent and fundamental challenge to the country’s mainstream opposition: either cooperate with Arab Israelis or hand Benjamin Netanyahu a roadmap to political survival.

In the wake of Tuesday’s exit polls, the leader of the opposition bloc, Gadi Eisenkot, declared them a victory for “Israel’s Zionist national majority” but the real outcome looks as if it will be far more complex than that.

The greatest change between the new Knesset and the old will be the dramatically increased representation of Palestinian parties, which are projected to win 17 to 18 seats, up from 10. That redraws the battle lines on Israel’s political landscape. Arab Israelis will not so easily be sidelined and ignored.

The exit polls placed Eisenkot’s opposition bloc and Netanyahu’s governing coalition tied. Though the prime minister’s Likud party could still be the strongest single party, neither side has enough to get 61 seats in the 120-seat parliament for a majority.

If confirmed by actual results, that would give Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, discretion over who he asks first to try to form a government. If one candidate cannot succeed in six weeks, the challenge is passed on to the next option. It could be an extremely long process, and all this time Netanyahu’s coalition would stay on in a caretaker role.

Eisenkot could argue he has a chance of negotiating his way to a Knesset majority. To do so, however, he and his partners in the “change” bloc would be obliged to sit down to talk with the Palestinian groupings, the Joint List and Ra’am (an acronym for the United Arab List).

They would probably find Ra’am and its leader, Mansour Abbas, easier to talk to. Abbas has already participated in a right-leaning government of Naftali Bennett, now a junior partner in the Eisenkot bloc. Abbas has a Jewish Zionist deputy, he has shown willingness to make political compromises and stated emphatically on Tuesday that his priority is to “bring down Benjamin Netanyahu, [Bezalel] Smotrich, and [Itamar] Ben-Gvir in this election”.

However, most estimates based on the exit polls show Ra’am as the smaller of the two Palestinian groupings, with seven projected seats in the new Knesset and it is not clear that would be enough, even if a pact was made with the consent of the other members of Eisenkot’s bloc, to produce a majority government.

Negotiations with the Joint List, with 11 or more projected seats, would be tougher. Eisenkot has laid down four conditions: recognise Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, accept the values expressed in Israel’s declaration of independence, accept conscription for Palestinian Israeli citizens, who are exempt, and denounce Hamas as a terrorist organisation.

Speaking on Tuesday as the votes were being counted, Amjad Shbita, the general secretary of Hadash, the socialist party that is the biggest faction in the Joint List, said Eisenkot would be in no position to impose terms for coalition talks.

“Laying down conditions won’t work with the Joint List,” Shbita said. “We will negotiate as equals because we need each other.”

In the absence of an agreement with one or both of the Palestinian groupings, it is possible that Eisenkot could try to govern as a minority government, with informal vote-by-vote agreements that would keep the new coalition afloat.

It would be an unstable solution, making another election more than likely. That would provide Netanyahu the opportunity to rally support among conservative Israeli Jews and claim to have been vindicated in his campaign slogan, “the Right or Palestine”, which rhymes in Hebrew.

Netanyahu has looked beaten before over his three decades at or near the top, and staged a comeback each time with the aid of his unparalleled tactical skills as a dealmaker. No one is yet ruling out another breathtaking political escape. But this time, if he does bounce back, he would owe his resurrection to his avowed political enemies for dropping him a lifeline rather than make historic compromises across Israel’s deep racial divide.

Speaking from the Joint List victory party in Nazareth in the early hours of Wednesday, one party official said: “The Zionist opposition will have to choose between supremacy and building democracy.”

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: A moment that changed me: I was always a pushover – until I stood up to some teenagers
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Ellie Violet Bramley
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
On the eve of my 40th birthday, I was doused with cold water at a train station. Before, I would have shrugged it off. But suddenly I realised it was time to assert myself

It was the evening before my 40th birthday – a freezing cold night in March – and I was travelling across London to meet some old school friends for dinner. As I walked down the stairs into the tube station, I spotted a few teens leaning over the balustrade above me. I thought nothing of it; teens hanging about aimlessly is as classic a combination as Archers and lemonade. That was, until they each threw a few KFC paper cups’ worth of icy water over my head.

I noticed it in slow-motion and, at first, kept walking. Then I realised that my hair was wet and so was my back. Without thinking, I ran back up the stairs and followed the teens, who were marching off down the main road. People on the street were watching me, obviously intrigued to see what I was going to do. What was I going to do? A few people looked at me with pity and pointed me in the right direction.

When I caught up with the teenagers, they pretended it wasn’t them. The two girls strode quickly ahead, but one of the boys hung back – perhaps also intrigued to hear what I was going to say. What was I going to say?

Still drenched, I sputtered the kind of fangless inanity I might say to my five-year-old as she pours rice all over the floor or starts drawing on the walls. Why, I asked, had they done it? The boy said nothing. I asked again and he denied they’d done anything, all adolescent swagger and smirks.

Eventually he changed tack, telling me that it was, to be fair, funny. He said it a few times, as if to hammer home his point. Eventually, after more back and forth, I remember saying, simply: “It’s upset me. You’ve upset me.” To my surprise, it prompted a mumbled but seemingly heartfelt: “Sorry, bro.”

It might not sound like much, but I felt genuinely appreciative that this teen had uttered his low-key but nevertheless disarming apology. And after spending a lifetime as a pushover, this moment was a breakthrough for me.

Historically, my kneejerk reaction to being wronged would have been to pretend that all was well, that I hadn’t been rattled; the wind hadn’t been knocked out of my sails. All good! But here I was admitting to this stranger, who would no doubt have preferred that I had quietly scuttled off to the tube, that I was upset. I couldn’t simply shrug it off – I was too damp and too shocked. Plus, I had made a promise to myself that I wouldn’t be such a walking wet wipe.

Previously, I would have done anything to avoid public confrontation, or even just discomfort. I would hide terrible food in a napkin and smuggle it out of restaurants rather than say anything to the waiting staff. I would allow myself to be overcharged, elbowed in the head on public transport, or worse, groped, and not say a thing. On one occasion I found myself saying yes to a flower subscription service in the street, despite being overdrawn and not in the market for weekly gladioli. All because it was less embarrassing than saying “no thanks”. With friends, I struggled with emotional honesty.

When I’d turned 30, at a particularly low ebb, I had pledged to change my ways. But despite my determination at the time, the results were not instant and I’d spent another decade being broadly incapable of sticking up for myself – or others – in moments that mattered, and even in moments that didn’t.

But that night something changed. In truth, it had been stirring for some time. As a new mum, I’d been forced to find my voice for the sake of my tiny baby, who was still without one of her own. I managed to stick up for her in a way that I wouldn’t have been able to do for myself, holding her place in the queue for the slide against bigger kids, or declining roughhousing from well-meaning toddlers at soft play – these were baby steps.

Back outside the tube station, I thanked the boy for his apology and, in my mind’s eye at least, we shared a quick smile by way of closure. I made my way back to the tube, boarded my train, and a few tears of shock ran down my cheeks, as I messaged my friends to say that I was going to be late.

When I arrived at dinner, they asked why I was so wet. I explained what had happened and felt a twinge of pride at their surprise. By the time I got to them I felt calm, but in a past life, I would have turned around and gone home, convinced that my soaking was evidence of something lacking in me – and the embarrassment would have stayed with me long after I’d changed into dry clothes. This, I realised, as I took a sip of victory wine, was progress.

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.title: Post your questions for Alex Cox
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.author: Rich Pelley
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.text:
As the cult director of Repo Man and Sid and Nancy prepares to release his final film, Dead Souls, he takes your questions

Everybody has their swansong, whether they know it or not. But for Alex Cox, his latest film Dead Souls – a darkly comic western loosely based on Nikolai Gogol’s 1842 novel – is billed as his final film.

If it really is his last film, the fiercely independent British film-maker can look back on a helluva run. He broke through with 1984 punk classic Repo Man, then went on to direct Gary Oldman as Sid Vicious in Sid and Nancy. He made the political “western” Walker in 1987, starring Ed Harris – then from 1988 to 1994 introduced viewers to cult and overlooked films as the original presenter of BBC Two’s Moviedrome, essentially doing film nerd YouTube decades before YouTube existed.

He ended up making films in Mexico in the 1990s, including the brilliant Highway Patrolman, then returned to his home town of Liverpool for Three Businessmen and The Revengers Tragedy. Back in the US Cox made Searchers 2.0 (an update of the classic western), Repo Chick (a sequel) and sci-fi comedy Bill the Galactic Hero.

In Dead Souls, Cox also stars as Strindler – or is it Swindler? – a mysterious drifter roaming the American west offering to buy the names of dead Mexican labourers, before becoming tangled up with outlaws, crooked officials and his own increasingly tall tales. The cast also includes Edward Tudor-Pole – punk frontman, actor and former Crystal Maze host – so at least there’ll be someone around to tell Cox when his time is running out.

So is Cox about to do a Tarantino? Post your questions below by midday on Wednesday 4 November, and we’ll print his best answers as part of our Readers’ Interview series.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Trump is in a corner and likely to lash out at Iran again. Here’s how to avert that disaster | Simon Tisdall
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Simon Tisdall
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Once the midterms are over, Trump will be free to pursue vendetta politics. But with will and diplomacy, he can be reined in

As another Iran catastrophe looms, one question matters more than any other: how to stop it before it’s too late? Whatever the eventual outcome of Israel’s election and next week’s US midterm polls, Donald Trump, playing the Lone Ranger, and Benjamin Netanyahu, his badass Tonto, appear hell-bent on resuming the illegal war of choice they began in June last year and expanded in February. Like a Shakespearean tragedy moving inexorably to a bloody denouement, the worst is yet to come. And yet three things seem certain: the US and Israel will again fail to totally destroy Iran’s largely hypothetical nuclear capabilities; its regime will survive; and millions of ordinary people, there and around the world, will pay the price for this unjustified, reckless aggression.

Ducking and weaving, Trump is desperate to dodge the blame for the Republicans’ anticipated midterm meltdown, largely triggered by war-related fuel and consumer price inflation. He claimed Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries were responsible, but that didn’t wash. He cut a treacherous diesel deal with Vladimir Putin but, as usual, Russia’s smirking mafioso conned him. He urged US allies to tap their strategic reserves but, unsurprisingly, vilified and sidelined European leaders, who view his war as an unmitigated disaster and declined to bail him out. Trump also reportedly rebuffed last-gasp, electorally driven pressure from Netanyahu to hit Iran this month, fearful it would unleash a Democratic tsunami.

Yet once the midterm polls close, and whatever the results, all these considerations fall away. What voters think will no longer matter to Trump. At that point, he can do more or less what he wants, in foreign and defence policy, for his final two years. And what he wants has little to do with imaginary Iranian nukes, a democratic uprising in Tehran, or any of his other bogus justifications for waging war. Trump will be free to do what he does best: vendetta politics. Iran’s greatest sin is to have defied the imperial will. He wanted an easy Venezuela-style, regime-altering victory (and sweetheart oil deals). What he got was a middle digit, burnt fingers and a forever war. Just as he vengefully pursues opponents at home, so he now victimises Iranians. It’s not rational or ideological. Like everything with Trump, ultimately it’s personal.

Netanyahu’s reasons for wanting another bash are thoroughly dishonourable too, but in a different way. Given his myriad, chronic failures before and after the 2023 Hamas massacres, his trashing of Israel’s international reputation by his criminal actions in Gaza and Lebanon, and his Trump-ish slide into bigoted, ultra-nationalist authoritarianism, Netanyahu is fighting for his job and, potentially, his freedom. He insists, despite his record, that only he can ensure Israel’s security. He suggests, outrageously, that opposition victory could pave the way for Israel’s destruction in a second, nuclear Holocaust. Israel’s military chiefs suspect he may restart the Iran war in order to dominate and manipulate the inevitable post-election coalition talks – hoping to stay in power and out of jail.

The likely, mortifying consequences of a renewed US-Israel onslaught after 3 November should be fully understood. For starters, the price of oil will spike again, perhaps to unprecedented levels, negatively affecting people all around the world. Pentagon officials, possibly peddling disinformation, suggest Iran is preparing to retaliate with missile and drone attacks against Saudi and other Gulf oil refineries, infrastructure and underwater internet cables, while reinforcing blockades of the strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea’s Bab al-Mandab strait. The impact on international energy supplies, transportation and international trade generally could be far worse than last spring.

Trump reportedly plans a shock-and-awe, time-limited assault – primarily on the mountain complex where Iran’s stockpile of enriched uranium is supposedly stored, plus its missile bases and energy grid. If this sounds familiar, it is. Trump’s chief gunslinger, Pete Hegseth, and his air-force cowboys claim to have destroyed many of these targets already, some more than once. Total success will probably elude them again. What’s more likely is that the war’s duration will lengthen, and more Iranian civilians will suffer the fate of over 100 schoolgirls killed in a Tomahawk missile strike in Minab in February. For that atrocity and others, Trump and Hegseth have never admitted responsibility.

Other foreseeable consequences include: the spread of related conflicts, involving Iranian allies and proxy militias, to Yemen, Saudi Arabia, Iraq and Lebanon; attacks on US embassies and personnel from Jordan to Kuwait; intensified, opportunistic settler violence and land grabs in the West Bank; stepped-up Iranian freelance assassination and sabotage operations in Europe; further undermining of US and Israeli democracy from deliberate obstruction of war-zone accountability, official cover-ups and blatant lying, and restrictions on independent media reporting; another hugely damaging split between Washington and its reluctant European allies; and another geopolitical free lunch for the west’s anti-democratic challengers, Russia and China.

Here are two more questions. By what right does the US, in particular, presume to behave in this way? Forget, if you can, Trump and Netanyahu. What does the American public (or at least, those who vote Republican) say? Have they not learned by now, after so many disastrous interventions that the world does not want, and does not need, to be saved by the US? In the age of Maga, this vulgar exceptionalism has surely had its day. Second, reformulated question: how may this looming catastrophe be prevented? Resumed warfare, leading to a wider, globally destabilising conflagration, is not inevitable. But urgent action is necessary now.

A talks process, mediated by Qatar, though neglected and boycotted by the White House, has not completely collapsed. Negotiations could yet produce viable outcomes if given a chance, Badr Albusaidi, Oman’s foreign minister, told the Guardian this week. A longer-term solution, he suggested, could be a non-aggression pact involving all six Gulf states, plus Iran and Iraq, acting on the premise that they, not the US, would be the primary, joint providers of future regional security. As Albusaidi spoke, top officials from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey were in Tehran on a last-ditch mission to pre-empt resumed hostilities. All power to them. At least they’re trying.

It would be reassuring to think Trump and Netanyahu are listening. But the bottom line is that, for their different reasons, both men probably want this war. A firm, united course of rapid, preventive action is required to head them off. Britain, its European allies and like-minded governments took a tentative, defiant step in Istanbul last weekend, urging diplomacy over violence. Now they and all the world’s democracies must stand as one and, in a formal demarche, tell the US and Israel they risk a permanent rupture with immediate and long-term negative economic, diplomatic, commercial, military and security consequences if they ignore global opinion and go to war again.

Trump is not king of the world. And Netanyahu cannot do as he likes with impunity. It’s high time they were told.

https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.title: How rebuilding old mosques is bringing Sikhs, Hindus and Muslims together in Punjab
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.author: Cheena Kapoor
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.text:
Many Muslims saw their places of worship destroyed or abandoned during the sectarian violence of India’s partition in 1947. Now villagers of many faiths are coming together to revive them

Gajju Khan is smiling as he sits in an unfinished building in the northern Indian state of Punjab in the late afternoon. The 87-year-old is hopeful that before he dies he will hear the azaan, the Muslim call to prayer, echo across his village once again when the mosque is completed.

The last time he heard it here was when he was eight years old, living with his parents in Tira Maloya, a village in Chandigarh, not far from where he lives now.

He is also excited because the mosque has been funded almost entirely by the Sikhs and Hindus living in his village of Jakhiwal, in Fatehgarh Sahib district. Even though he fondly remembers how Sikh neighbours sheltered him and his brothers when brutal sectarian violence erupted during partition in 1947, he never expected a house of worship to be rebuilt for the 18 Muslim families who remain in the village.

“This was my maternal home. My parents sent my two brothers and me here to save us from the bloodshed – they were killed back in our village,” says Khan. “Sikhs hid us from the patrols of men with sticks and burning torches.”

Khan reserves his deepest gratitude for Bibi Rajinder Kaur, 77, a Sikh villager who persuaded her grandson to donate a parcel of their farmland to build a mosque. She did so, she says, because every other faith had a place to gather, while local Muslims had none.

“There is no deed better than giving someone a place to worship,” Kaur says. “Also, it felt like we needed to appease God for the blood this land had seen. The Muslims in our village had to travel 4km [2.5 miles] to another village just to pray.”

Bibi Rajinder Kaur, a Sikh, donated family land to build a mosque in her village. ‘There is no deed better than giving someone a place to worship,’ she says

Gajju Khan, who hopes to live long enough to see the mosque in his village completed

During the partition of British India, the border severed Punjab in two, unleashing catastrophic communal blood-letting and forced migrations that virtually emptied the eastern, Indian side of the region of its Muslim population. Hundreds of village mosques were abandoned, desecrated or turned into cattle sheds and storage units.

But over the past decade, several rural Sikh and Hindu communities have quietly stepped forward to restore these places of worship. Even in villages without a Muslim population, people have invited Muslim farmhands and clerics from nearby districts to pray in these newly revived mosques.

About 50 miles fromJakhiwal, in Sangrur district’s Punawal village, Jaspal Sharma, who comes from a family of Hindu priests, donated his land for the construction of a new mosque and hosted a feast for the entire village at its inauguration in February.

Sharma, 48, says the donation was about neighbourly duty. The village has 550 households, of which just a very small proportion are Muslim.

Jaspal Sharma says donating some of his land to build a mosque was a neighbourly duty

The new mosque in Malerkotla, Punjab, welcomes worshippers for evening prayers

“It’s right opposite our house, so the sound of prayers five times a day creates a lively atmosphere. We like it,” says Sharma. “And it wasn’t just us; everyone in the village, Hindus and Sikhs together, contributed what they could. Some gave money; others donated bricks and cement.”

For Sukhjinder Singh Pandher and his brother, restoring a local shrine in Malerkotla’s Umarpura village was an act of filial reverence. Their grandfather fled west Punjab during partition to settle in India.

“Nobody is treated as different here,” says Pandher, sharing a cup of tea with his Muslim neighbours on the bare floor of the restored mosque. “Eid and Gurpurab [Sikhs’ most holy festival] are celebrated by both communities with the same fervour.

Sadna Qasai, one of the many mosques in Punjab that fell into ruin after partition

“We live as one and no matter what happens in the rest of the country, the mood here is that of love and unity. Punjab’s conscience cannot tolerate cruelty against a being, irrespective of caste and religion,” he says.

Pandher points to the syncretic traditions and blending of cultures that are deeply rooted in Punjabi history, noting the popular belief that the 16th-century Sufi saint Hazrat Mian Mir was invited to lay the foundation stone of Sikhism’s holiest site, the Harmandir Sahib, or Golden Temple, in Amritsar.

Inspired by the former shahi, or chief, imam of Punjab, Maulana Habib-ur-Rehman Sani Ludhianvi, non-Muslim villagers have contributed to more than 165 such mosques in the past nine years.

Sikh men in Punjab’s villages have been coming together to fund and help build or revive old mosques

“Partition tore at the natural fabric of Punjab,” says the current shahi imam, Maulana Muhammad Usman Rehmani Ludhianvi, who succeeded his father in 2021. “This state itself is an inquilab [revolution]. Online, there is immense polarisation, but on the ground in our villages, ordinary people are still choosing to protect each other.”

https://www.theguardian.com/fashion/2026.title: Jess Cartner-Morley on fashion: to nail this year’s British heritage look, just study Rivals
https://www.theguardian.com/fashion/2026.author: Jess Cartner-Morley
https://www.theguardian.com/fashion/2026.text:
Thanks to Jilly Cooper, tartan and tweed, waxed jackets and wellies are a style vibe right now

British heritage, in fashion terms, is a country where it is permanently October. A conker-brown and pleasant land, if you will. Brand Britain in the style sense comes into its own in autumn: roaring fires, muddy lanes, damp dogs. Waxed jackets and chunky knits, tartan and tweed, jaunty scarves to banish draughts. Clothes for going on a hearty walk, but with a hip flask in your pocket. Fashion has been mining this seam since long before Brideshead Revisited made battered evening dresses and Oxford bags look romantic, and it keeps returning, because trad British style is satisfyingly utilitarian while also being loaded with enough backstory (class, history, eccentricity) to be intriguing and reinventable.

Also: Rivals. It has taken considerable restraint for me not to mention Rivals in the whole of the first paragraph, because it is now a matter of mere weeks until we get our next Jilly Cooper fix and I, for one, cannot wait. Cannot wait for Cameron stalking the corridors in her foxy power suits, for Taggie in her cute jeans and jumpers, for Valerie in head-to-toe tweed and an aggressive amount of blusher. The success of Rivals has done for old-school British dressing what Emily in Paris did for the beret, only with better jokes and more adultery. Jolly hockey sticks style is the new French girl chic. This fantasy is homegrown, which makes it both more embarrassing and harder to resist. Just as Emily and her friends and frenemies are a camp send-up of fashionable Paris, Rivals is a fond, nostalgic semi-parody of the British wardrobe. The show’s costume designer, Ray Holman, has drawn on original 1980s pieces from Dunhill and Mulberry for inspiration. With Liberty fabrics, nods to polo uniforms and sturdy waxed coats, he has brought the Sloane ranger back into the fashion conversation for the first time in years.

British heritage is a style vibe right now. Barbour and Mulberry joined Burberry in stepping up to the style plate and taking part in London fashion week this season. Kate Moss is in her wellies for Hunter’s latest advertising campaign, while Sienna Miller and Idris Elba star in Barbour’s. Barbour also features a cameo from some sheep, which says something about how countryside-coded the British heritage look is at heart. Fair Isle knits and Argyle diamond-pattern sweaters are worn draped over the shoulders, shown off as trophies. Waxed or tweedy jackets are taking over from urban puffer jackets. The neutral of the season is brown (mud) rather than black (asphalt).

There is plenty of glamour, too. Pearls, silk scarves, jewel-toned velvets. Polka dots, which have broken out of the village fete and are now in their baddie era. The key is to let the fancy stuff rub up against the practical stuff. A waxed jacket over a party dress is a core British look, whether you are going to a rave, a festival or a hunt ball. There is something deeply British in the irreverence of putting a battered coat over a hot dress. A silk scarf is a retro touch that works equally well in a gale and a paparazzi shot. Tweed is surprisingly versatile, because it looks great out of context: with baggy jeans, or over a band T-shirt.

One of the best things about British heritage style is that – unlike the high maintenance of Emily in Paris – it is only improved by looking a little lived-in. A waxed jacket benefits from the creases it develops after a few adventures. Cashmere has more soul when the neckline is a little looser. Wellies are nothing without mud. It’s a style that often looks more appealing when you find it in a charity shop than when it’s box-fresh off the catwalk.

The twist? One element of metropolitan polish. An urban girlie, slicked-back bun and a gold hoop. A pointy shoe, or trousers with a crease down the front. That way it works whether you have a labrador at your heel or a laptop on your knee.

Styling: Melanie Wilkinson. Model: Imogen May at Milk. Hair and makeup: Sophie Higginson using Sam McKnight and Makeup by Mario. Blazer, £65, and trousers £40, both Marks & Spencer. Trench, £269, and top, £75, both Aligne. Shirt, £125, Me+Em. Heels, £99, Dune. Rings, model’s own. Earrings, £34.99, Pilgrim

https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2026/.title: Cycling in the wild heart of the Netherlands: an autumnal break in the Veluwe
https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2026/.author: Suzanne Bearne
https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2026/.text:
The untamed, magical landscape takes in a vast national park, palatial houses and a sculpture garden and museum stuffed with Van Goghs – all easily accessible by bike

One minute I’m cycling through an expansive dusty pink stretch of heathland with sloping sand dunes in the distant horizon, the next I’m winding through a fragrant Scots pine forest as sunlight filters through the branches of red-barked trees to make a kaleidoscope of white shapes on the trail floor ahead.

I’m in Hoge Veluwe National Park, a 5,400 hectare (13,000 acre) nature reserve in Gelderland, about an hour and a half from Amsterdam. It’s crisscrossed by 25 miles (40km) of cycling paths, and around 2,000 free-to-use white bikes are available for visitors to explore the ever-changing scenery.

I’ve been flitting back and forth to the Netherlands for years and have lost count of the times friends there have raved about the park and the wider Veluwe region, a forest-rich ridge of hills and diverse landscapes, stretching 37 miles, north to south. Finally I’ve come to see for myself and explore on foot and on two wheels over a few days – adding in a dash of culture at some of its historic towns and museums too.

My trip starts at Natuurcentrum De Ginkel, a charming nature and visitor centre near Ede outside Arnhem. Here I meet nature guide Hanna Pol who takes me into the forest. “Veluwe is very biodiverse,” says Pol quietly as we walk past verdant oak, pine and birch. Trees with autumnal tawny-coloured leaves line one side of the path and wildflowers, with pops of bright yellow sunflowers and vivid red poppies, the other. Pol reels off some of the wildlife here: roe deer, five types of woodpecker, beavers, wild boar and wolves. As we crunch through a carpet of fallen leaves, we spy a small brown frog on a log, a woodpecker dancing around a tree, and the outline of two rust-red deers in the distance.

We make our way to the wildlife observation area, an enclosed building with curved windows and a theatre-style set of wooden chairs. “The deer pass this way every night to eat,” says Pol. “Once we saw a really big fight break out.” She’s seen wolves too – they returned to the country in 2015 after about 150 years and it’s a controversial topic, with farmers worried about their livestock. We don’t see the elusive creatures, just a solitary bright white buzzard perching on a tree. On the shelves behind us, an assortment of skeletal remains includes antlers, skulls, the teeth of a wild boar and the foot of a deer.

That night I stay in a stylish and sleek cabin with floor-to-ceiling views of the forest at Buitenplaats Petersburg on the edge of the park. It’s a peaceful haven of lodges with fairy lights strung around the woods and an enchanting Italian restaurant, Il Lupo, with an outdoor terrace.

Besides its unspoilt natural wonders, Veluwe has plenty of other attractions. I visit Paleis Het Loo, a 17th-century royal palace in Apeldoorn, once the summer residence and hunting lodge of William of Orange III and his wife Princess Mary II Stuart. It’s an impressive building with ornate rooms, a staircase with the second biggest mural in the Netherlands, formal symmetrical gardens and an underground museum which tells the story of the Dutch royal family.

Hotel de Echoput, a family-run modern hotel nearby, surrounded by the forest, is my home for the night. Its Grand Bistro Echo is a treat, with a menu that focuses on local ingredients – I enjoy fried mushrooms with a creamy Dordogne sauce and a vegan cheesecake with basil and white chocolate.

The next morning, after a brisk walk in the woods with barely a soul around, I visit the historic Hanseactic city of Harderwijk, on the shores of Wolderwijd lake. I wander the narrow cobblestone streets, medieval city walls and Old Town Hall with guide Marianne van Limbeek. “Harderwijk means hiding place for shepherds,” she tells me. We bump into Hendrik Kaper, a local street organist wearing a flat cap who treats us to a rendition of Bohemian Rhapsody on his portable wooden organ.

But it’s in Hoge Veluwe national park that I find the greatest sense of serenity – though one day a small adder with a dark zigzag stripe stops me in my tracks. Come outside peak times, as I have, and you might have some of the trails to yourself.

Within the park lies Kröller-Müller Museum, a revered national art museum and sculpture garden founded by art collector Helene Kröller-Müller, who along with her husband, shipping magnate Anton Kröller, bought vast amounts of land in Veluwe (their private estate was later donated to the state). My timing is great as all 88 of its Vincent van Gogh paintings are on show together for the first time since 1984 (until 3 January). The sculpture park is one of the largest in Europe, and I stroll around the surrounding open grass and into the forest and stumble across various artworks (there are about 200 pieces dotted around). A short cycle away is Jachthuis Sint Hubertus, the former country residence of the Kröller-Müller family with a watchtower more than 30m tall (apparently Helene loved afternoon tea at such lofty heights) surrounded by a lake with a very athletic bunch of jumping carp.

I stop at Restaurant De Hoge Veluwe at Park Paviljoen for an early pasta dinner on the terrace before the sky turns a moody grey and rain looks imminent. Fortunately it’s only a 15-minute cycle to Otterlo, a pretty village with clusters of fairy lights and bunting decorating red brick houses and Vakantieoord Het Lorkenbos, a charming holiday park surrounded by trees. My bungalow is cute and, feeling as if I’m in a twinkling winter wonderland, I light a candle and look up the Dutch word for cosy. It’s gezellig – a perfect description of how I feel after my nourishing break in this wild and restorative part of the Netherlands.

The trip was arranged by Visit Veluwe. Entrance to Hoge Veluwe national park €13.85 per adult. Cabins at Buitenplaats Petersburg from €110. Camping at Het Lorkenbos from €23 a night, bungalows from €320 for two nights. Double rooms at De Echoput from €169. Omio provided train travel: Eurostar runs from London to Amsterdam

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: ‘Ferritin face’: are social media claims about iron deficiency fact – or fiction?
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Nicola Davis Science correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
Experts say symptoms such as dark circles under the eyes, grey skin, cracked lips and hair loss can be a warning sign – but there are other factors too

TikTok is rife with influencers warning of “ferritin face”, a term they use to describe the pallor, dark circles, dry skin, and hair loss claimed to indicate low iron stores. But is this based on fact or fiction, and when is it time to head to the GP?

Iron is not made in the body, so typically we consume it in our diet. Ferritin is the protein responsible for storing iron in the body, particularly in the liver, and releasing it in a controlled manner.

By measuring ferritin levels, which can be checked via blood tests, it is possible to get an snapshot of the body’s iron reserves, although experts warn such levels are not always a reliable guide.

Blood ferritin levels of less than 30 micrograms/L indicate an iron deficiency, according to guidelines from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence.

However “a level below 50 might be a pointer of iron deficiency,” said Sue Pavord, professor of practice in medical haematology at Oxford University hospitals.

The symptoms influencers describe, such as dark circles under the eyes, grey skin, cracked lips and hair loss, can be caused by a variety of factors, including genetics, stress and dehydration. But experts say low iron stores can have an effect.

“Iron is needed for every single cell of the body. So if you are iron deficient, you will be very fatigued, have brain fog, your skin will look dull and saggy, you’ll look pale and tired,” said Pavord. “While we can’t diagnose iron deficiency from the face, it might be a suggestion that there is iron deficiency.”

Prof Toby Richards of the University of East London and the Iron Clinic added such changes were particularly pronounced in people with very low iron stores. “They tend to be the really sick patients,” he said.

“Periods and pregnancies are the most common [causes],” said Pavord, but others include not getting enough iron – either from dietary choices or because of poor absorption, as can occur with coeliac disease.

Low ferritin levels can also arise as a result of blood loss linked to gastrointestinal problems, such as gastritis or polyps.

“We also sometimes see it in athletes because of the high demand for iron on their bodies,” she added.

Richards said those who are at high risk of low ferritin – such as people who have heavy periods, are pregnant or have had children, or are vegetarian or vegan – should ask for a blood test, adding that should include a full blood count, ferritin level check, and test for levels of B12 and folate.

“This is a proper disease, and to put it into perspective, it’s the leading cause of disability in women of reproductive ability,” he said.

Pavord also said those who are concerned about their ferritin levels should ask for a blood test, adding it was important to understand the cause of iron deficiency.

“Older people suspecting iron deficiency would need a proper clinical assessment and investigations to look for a source of bleeding from the bowel,” she said.

Pavord said it is possible to buy iron tablets over the counter at a pharmacy.

“Taking iron tablets without confirming iron deficiency is not really going to do you any harm, particularly if you’re a young woman, because you’re losing a lot of iron with periods,” she said.

But Richards noted many products do not necessarily contain the appropriate dose. “If you are iron deficient, you need to be on a full treatment dose … and then repeat your blood results in three months’ time,” he said. “What’s marketed is normally the lower dose supplements

“We need to stop normalising iron deficiency,” she said. “Many women are just exhausted trying to cope with their periods, cope with their pregnancies, cope with their young children and their busy jobs, and we need to stop normalising fatigue.”

Richards agreed. “ Anything that raises the plight of women in this area is a good thing,” he said.

However Dr Asiya Maula, a GP from the private firm The Health Suite, was cautious. “The risk with social media trends is that people may see themselves in a list of symptoms and assume they have a deficiency without checking whether that is actually the cause,” she said.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The climate crisis will destroy our economies – we learned this 20 years ago. When will we act? | Fiona Harvey
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Fiona Harvey
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The radical Stern report showed that a low-carbon future is also good economics. But it seems that capitalism needs a reminder

Saving the only planet we have makes good economic sense. There is, after all, no money to be made on a dead Earth. There may be costs involved now, but they are worth paying to protect our children from certain destruction.

These propositions seem self-evident now. But two decades ago, mainstream economists had very different ideas. They had proved that the climate crisis would be a mere economic blip, easily absorbed by growing economies and therefore not worth spending money on. In their accounting, they considered ice caps and glaciers functionally worthless, that trees only add to GDP when they are cut down, and that a livable climate shouldn’t even merit a line on a spreadsheet.

What changed? Twenty years ago this week an earth-shaking report was published by Nicholas Stern, a former World Bank chief economist turned adviser to Gordon Brown. His review, The Economics of Climate Change, upended conventional wisdom among economists and dragged them into a new century. It set out, for the first time, in clear and bold terms, why investing in a low-carbon future makes economic sense.

The Stern review, in 700 dense pages full of graphs and data, is a model of transformative thinking. Using standard economic tools and methods, and in ways that other mainstream economists could understand, Stern made three key, and at the time radical, conclusions: that the costs of inaction on the climate were greater than the costs of action; that the climate crisis was a market failure; and that economic growth was compatible with cutting greenhouse gas emissions.

Stern’s crucial insight, the revolutionary idea on which his whole thesis turned, was that future generations have as much right to be born as we did. Traditional economics mistrusts anything that could happen in the future, applying a “discount rate” to it. Likely future profits are reckoned as lower in value than those of the present, as are likely future losses.

That might make sense when compiling companies’ accounts, as it prevents them over-selling themselves on optimistic assumptions. But applying a discount rate where the climate is concerned is a gross distortion – effectively, it means future lives are assigned less value, and so taking actions now that protect children when they grow up are made to appear uneconomic.

To gauge how startling this proposal was at the time, consider William Nordhaus, former professor of economics at Yale, whose work was the previous standard for climate economics. He confidently asserted in the early 1990s that countries should budget for “moderate” global heating, of about 3C to 4C above preindustrial levels, because below that the cost of cutting greenhouse gas emissions would outweigh the damage of climate change. In order to reach these conclusions, Nordhaus’s work relied on the same “discounting” assigned to future damage and future lives that Stern set out to challenge.

The vitriol poured on Stern by fellow economists – including Nordhaus – was intense. I covered it at the time for the Financial Times, and I remember the spluttering outrage of traditional economists, fuming that the discount rate – a central tenet of Treasury forecasting around the world – could be meddled with. The ethical point appeared to elude them. Ethics have little place in GDP.

But Stern stuck to his analysis, and in the 20 years since it has been found sound – if anything, he underestimated both the rapidity of heating and economic consequences, and overestimated the cost of renewable energy. Stern’s work liberated many governments: they could now justify bold climate strategies to investors, aid donors and the ever-present bond markets. Conversely, laggard administrations could be challenged at the ballot box and, increasingly, in court.

Today, Stern says, if he were re-doing the review, he would place more emphasis on the role of nature, as the collapse of biodiversity around the world is a key economic and national security threat that has been grossly underestimated, and neglected as a result.

It might seem, in 2026, as if Stern has won the argument. But traditional economic approaches to the climate refuse to go away. In 2018, even after a deluge of science showing that 3C heating would leave coastal cities under water and swathes of agricultural land as desert, Nordhaus published a paper claiming that 3C would reduce global GDP by just 2.1%, and even a 6C increase would incur just 8.5% GDP loss. However, other climate scientists have indicated that at 6C widespread famine could leave billions of people, in economic terms, suboptimally productive. Or, as the rest of us might say, dead.

In 2018, Nordhaus was awarded the Nobel prize. His work on the climate was prominent in the citation and his prize lecture. In hundreds of universities around the world, economists are still being trained today in those same traditional growth models he used. And sunny predictions that the climate crisis could shave just a few per cent off GDP are still in use, shockingly, among governments, businesses and international institutions, even as temperatures shatter records and the supercharged El Niño threatens trillions of dollars in damages.

The results are plain to see: governments refusing to act, markets over-valuing fossil fuel companies, investors punishing businesses that dare to prepare for a low-carbon world. Many insurance companies, supposedly the enforcers of probity in capital markets, are alleged to knowingly be fudging their figures to massage climate risk away, as the Guardian revealed this month.

If we are to have a thriving future economy, as well as a living planet and robust human societies, we need a new system of economics that values these things. Stern showed the way. Twenty years later, the rest of the world must catch up.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Jay-Z is the perfect Super Bowl shill for a league of billionaires
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Lee Escobedo
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
The rapper lends the NFL a veneer of credibility but is unlikely to push back on the establishment figures who run the league

On Monday the NFL named Jay-Z as the headliner for this season’s Super Bowl half-time show. His company, Roc Nation, produces the show under a 2019 deal reportedly worth $5m a year, and the agreement was extended for another five years in 2024. NFL commissioner Roger Goodell said his one request when the partnership began was that Jay-Z “take the stage himself one day“.

Goodell’s wish makes total sense: Jay-Z is the perfect choice for the half-time show, and that’s not a compliment. The NFL wants a shill who can still pass for a rebel, and nobody in American music plays that part better than Jay-Z.

Jay-Z’s origin story has become an American legend. Years before he sold records, Shawn Carter grew up in Brooklyn’s Marcy Houses and sold crack as a teenager. When labels passed on him, he hawked CDs from the trunk of his car on college campuses. Then he put out Reasonable Doubt in 1996 on his own label, Roc-A-Fella. “Nobody would sign me,” he said later. The money followed. In 2013, he performed Picasso Baby, a track about the paintings he wanted to own, for six hours straight at a Chelsea gallery, and Marina Abramović joined him. By the time of The Story of OJ in 2017, he was handing out financial advice. Forbes puts his fortune at about $2.8bn. He raps for the rich now, a Black oligarch who seems about as cut off from the rest of the country as the rest of the billionaire class.

His bootstraps story mirrors the platitudes Americans have been told for decades – work hard and you’ll get what you deserve. On paper, he’s the perfect avatar for America’s polluted ideas of capitalism. But the country Jay-Z is rapping to is in terrible shape. How many of us can relate to his lyrics in 2026? Gas and grocery prices have rocketed. SNAP enrollment fell more than 13% in a year as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act tightened the rules. Only 63% of adults say they could cover a surprise $400 expense.

You can see why the NFL would use Jay-Z as someone who can give the appearance that the league, with its huge conservative fanbase, is actually progressive. He wore Colin Kaepernick’s jersey on Saturday Night Live in 2017 after the quarterback had sparked a protest movement against police brutality by kneeling for the national anthem. Jay-Z then dedicated The Story of OJ to Kaepernick onstage. A year later, on Apeshit, he bragged about turning down the Super Bowl and told the NFL it needed him more than he needed it.

In June 2019, Forbes named him hip-hop’s first billionaire. A few months later, Roc Nation signed its deal with the NFL. But at the news conference announcing his NFL partnership, Jay-Z no longer appeared as receptive to Kaepernick’s approach to protest. “We’ve moved past kneeling,” he said. That same year, Kaepernick settled his collusion grievance against the league after he said his protests had effectively ended his playing career.

The 2019 deal also put Roc Nation to work on Inspire Change, the league’s social justice initiative. It’s safe to say that Kaepernick was unimpressed. “I just want you to know, one, you’re serving the culture up to a bunch of racists and, two, they don’t care about you,” Kaepernick later recalled saying to Jay-Z. “You’re the music guy to them. They quite literally need a Black face – and have said as much.”

Seven years later, Jay-Z is still battling Kaepernick, the man who says he was blackballed by the NFL. This summer, Jay-Z linked up with Target, which had been boycotted by many Black customers after it rolled back its diversity and inclusion policies. Kaepernick, on the other hand, said he would not allow his memoir to be sold at any of the chain’s stores. At a concert in July, Jay-Z rapped that Kaepernick had allowed himself to be silenced by signing his grievance with the NFL (sources close to Kaepernick have denied this). “Buddy took a check, I ain’t even mad at him, but along with that check you have to sign a non-disparagement. I’m the one [the NFL] can’t control,” Jay-Z rapped to the crowd at Yankee Stadium.

Maybe that’s true, but it doesn’t appear that Jay-Z is doing much to control – or change – the league either. In 2021, USA Today’s Mike Freeman wrote: “There isn’t a single, tangible thing you can point to that shows Jay-Z helping with the league’s social justice efforts.” That’s a little unfair; through Inspire Change the NFL has funnelled millions into charities across America. At the same time, the NFL is mostly run by the same old, rich conservatives it always has been. There is still no Black majority owner of a team, and Forbes now puts the combined value of the league’s 32 teams at more than $300bn. In 2025, Donald Trump, who once called NFL players who protested during the national anthem “sons of bitches”, became the first sitting president to attend a Super Bowl, and that same week the league pulled “End Racism” from the endzones in New Orleans. That slogan had been on NFL fields since 2020 as part of Inspire Change.

Conservatives have noticed. A Daily Wire column hailed Jay-Z as a “legend” and told readers there likely wouldn’t be any anti-ICE activists onstage at this season’s halftime show, adding that “after last year’s Bad Bunny debacle, Jay-Z offers a compromise.”

That’s about right. Jay-Z won’t have anybody to push against at the Super Bowl. The NFL is Roc Nation’s client, and the team owners are its partners. As we saw with the Target debacle, whatever Jay-Z says up there, he’s unlikely to go against the people who pay him.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Spain train crash: at least 10 feared dead after collision in Toledo province
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Sam Jones in Madrid
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
High-speed service reportedly runs into back of another train, knocking two carriages off track

At least 10 people are feared dead and many more injured after two high-speed trains collided in Toledo province in central Spain.

Spain’s state rail infrastructure authority said services between Madrid and the southern region of Andalucía had been suspended “⁠following a rear-end collision between two trains” on Wednesday morning.

A spokesperson for the regional government of Castilla-La Mancha region, where the crash occurred, said the cause and ‌ number of injuries were yet to be determined.

Government sources told El País at least 10 people had been killed, and that the crash could be worse than the Adamuz rail disaster in January in which 45 people were killed.

Spain’s state broadcaster, TVE, reported that the crash happened after a high-speed train ran into the back of another service, knocking two carriages off the track.

Manuel Galán, the mayor ​of ​Urda near the ​city of Toledo, said he had ​been ‌asked by ​emergency ​services to prepare a sports hall to accommodate the injured.

Spain’s main political parties, which are gearing up for next month’s general election, suspended their planned activities for the day.

The prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, expressed his shock at news of the crash. “I remain in constant contact with the transport minister, and with the president of Castilla-La Mancha,” he said in a post on X. “Emergency services are working on the ground to assist those affected and ensure their safety, in coordination with all the involved administrations. My love, solidarity, and support to all the victims and their families.”

https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2026/o.title: ‘Fear is contagious’: why horror shows are taking over the New York stage
https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2026/o.author: Benjamin Lee
https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2026/o.text:
Hit London plays 2:22, Paranormal Activity and A Ghost in Your Ear are now spooking audiences on and off Broadway amid high demand for communal experiences

As we escaped the restrictions of the pandemic, with many also trying to escape the smartphone addiction that was exacerbated by it, there was widespread desire for the in-person communal experience. It was a slow crawl back with casualties along the way but as the Hollywood and Broadway box office return to pre-pandemic levels this year, our craving for IRL thrills appears to be stronger than ever.

It’s why Imax and 4DX formats are breaking records, concert attendance is at a new high according to a mid-year report and the most recently tracked season of New York theatre grossed more than the previous. It also helps to explain why the hottest tickets of the fall are for plays in the most communal genre of all: horror.

The giddy sensation of watching, gasping and shrieking at something scary is why horror has remained so reliable on the big screen (that and its low stakes, low-budget nature) and why a film such as May’s breakout shocker Obsession was something audiences simply had to see in a sold-out cinema. Last year horror films made a record $1.4bn at the US box office with this year’s figures suggesting another historic rise.

As A-list names, established musicals and retooled IP continue to score the highest grosses on Broadway, three spine-tingling transfers are hoping to lure horror nuts away from the screen and into the theatre.

The shows all started out in London, apt given that the West End was home to The Woman in Black, a jumpy bumps-in-the-night ghost story that became the second longest-running play in the city’s history and one that has become something of a blueprint for how to invite in a wider audience to a genre often viewed as “for fans only”.

“I’ve got a really sort of seminal kind of trace memory of watching Woman in Black in a theatre and just feeling totally exhilarated the moment that the entire audience screamed together,” British writer Danny Robins tells me over Zoom. He’s here in New York as his hit Olivier-nominated play 2:22 opens at the Lucille Lortel theatre in the village. It’s a four-person supernatural chiller that’s become known for its unusual viral casting, launching the acting career of Lily Allen when it started back in 2021 and since welcoming in everyone from ex pop group members (Girls Aloud’s Cheryl, The Saturdays’ Frankie Bridge, Busted’s Matt Willis) to TV hosts (Love Island’s Laura Whitmore and Stacey Dooley) to Inbetweeners (James Buckley).

It has gone everywhere from London to Los Angeles to Melbourne to Wolverhampton and its New York debut arrives at the same time as a transfer of headphone horror A Ghost in Your Ear also opens just blocks away while a screen-to-stage adaptation of Paranormal Activity has become a Broadway blockbuster further uptown.

“Fear is contagious,” A Ghost in Your Ear writer Jamie Armitage says. “At a time when theatre’s like: ‘Ooh, how do we stand out? How do we do something specific?; I think giving that collective emotional experience is so theatrical and it’s also just so much fun. And I think that’s why these horror shows are doing well and finding an audience.” (He too sees The Woman in Black as the “gold standard”).

His play combines the classic – we’re being told a literary ghost story taking place in a mysterious old house – with the contemporary – it’s via an audiobook recording and each audience member has to wear headphones throughout. The Guardian’s Arifa Akbar called it “a good, old-fashioned ghost-train of a story” when it opened in London at the end of last year.

Similarly, 2:22 uses some flashy light design and a supporting role for an Alexa device to update the framework of an old-fashioned thriller with a sting in its tail. The unconventional casting also helps (in New York, Pitch Perfect’s Anna Camp stars alongside Iron Fist’s Finn Jones) as does a healthy amount of savvy self-awareness from the team behind it. They’ve seen the memes that have cropped up, jokes online that either Peppa Pig or Liz Truss would be joining the cast, and they know who their audience is. “I remember sitting outside a restaurant next to the theatre where we opened on the first night and there were gangs of young women who were coming to see Lily Allen,” says the show’s longtime director Matthew Dunster. “They had party hats on and they were singing: ‘We’re going to see a play!’” He told me he wants the Duchess of Sussex next.

At the Noël Coward theatre in London, the show didn’t just break the box office record but the bar one as well. “I loved that,” Robins says. “I thought that was people having a fun night out, that you were having a great time, you were having one or two drinks to kind of steady your nerves.”

Dunster adds that “[theatre] can be very po-faced, very issue-based”. He remembers a “snobbiness” prior to 2:22 about putting on a horror show and he recalls chatting to figures within the theatre world before it opened with the “audible sharpening of knives” in the background.

When I went to see Paranormal Activity, the ornate lobby of the August Wilson theatre was soundtracked by Soundgarden and My Chemical Romance with neon cocktails and pretzel bites on sale. It felt less like a crowd waiting for a Broadway play and more like one lining up for a rollercoaster.

Armitage noticed a difference in the type of audience too for both the London and New York productions of A Ghost in Your Ear, something that “excites” him. “I always think that is essential for theatre particularly at the moment to find what are ways of drawing in these audiences whether that be from who’s in the show or what the show is itself,” he says. For a US audience, he also cast Lucas Iverson, an actor from the phenomenally popular medical drama The Pitt, in the lead (vocal young women near me had bought tickets purely because of him).

For Robins, keeping ticket prices for 2:22 low was also something of an “ethical mission” for him, saying that a ticket should be closer to “the cost of a meal not the cost of a holiday”.

Party hats, pretzel bites and booze might not be what many expect from a night out at the theatre – and the success of these shows comes at a time of tension. Stars such as Rosamund Pike, Cynthia Erivo and Lesley Manville have spoken out about phone usage from audience members while the availability of alcohol at shows such as the most recent Broadway restaging of Cabaret has led to a backlash over how inebriated they might also be.

“I think often that rowdiness comes from not knowing how to behave and being put in a situation where you feel a bit uncomfortable,” Robins says. “I think theatre can be really bad, really clinically effective at making people feel uncomfortable.” He believes that 2:22 does the opposite and gives a “sense of belonging” to those in the audience. “I think if you create an environment where people feel comfortable and where it feels accessible and if you are exciting and stimulating people, you’re not going to be rowdy and disruptive because you’re really enjoying what you’re watching,” he adds. “I like a little bit of noise!”

Robins also says that it’s “weird” that within a “middle-class theatre community”, a vocal response is seen as inappropriate whereas in other communities it would be “absolutely welcomed and championed”. He also shares that when the show was in LA, with Constance Wu as Jenny naturally, audiences clapped for everything. “If theatre wants to survive, it’s got to feel fun,” he says. Armitage too noticed a difference in the US where he found audiences more “vocal” than they had been in the UK. “If they want to, like, scream and sort of hoot and do whatever they like during the show, I kind of love that because it means they’re having a good time,” he says.

It’s too early to tell how well 2:22 and A Ghost in Your Ear will do in New York (although both performances I attended were close to being sold out), yet Paranormal Activity has become an unqualified smash, extending its run by eight weeks after already making more than $8m. For Halloween, the August Wilson theatre will celebrate by screening the original movie with the franchise heading for an inevitable big screen reboot next year.

Horror remains frighteningly popular business and what better than watching it in a theatre where everyone else can hear you scream?

“Audiences are hungry for experiences which feel truly live,” Armitage says. “I think it’s a beautiful fluke of timing that three shows which all seemed to catch a wave in London and find an audience are all arriving in New York at the same time. Hopefully they can recreate that attraction for audiences to come and be scared together, to come and see something which is truly live. I kind of feel that’s what’s behind it: it’s matching the audience’s hunger.”

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.title: In One Brief Moment All Eternity by Elif Shafak review – what Madame Bovary thought of Flaubert
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.author: Lara Feigel
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.text:
This audacious portrait of the French author through the eyes of his women is Shafak’s love letter to literature in dark times

In Frantumaglia, her collection of essays on writing and reading, Elena Ferrante writes that she has sometimes dismissed Gustave Flaubert as a “misogynist”, angered by his invention of as callous a mother as Emma Bovary. In other moods, however, she has wondered whether Flaubert allows his female characters to say what “women truly think and say and live but do not dare write”.

Ferrante’s ambivalence is, I think, the most fitting feminist response to Flaubert’s novel. It’s tempting to castigate him as a male writer who kills his female character because he can’t imagine any other end for a transgressive woman; to reproach him for not giving Emma Bovary the profundity of emotion with which Tolstoy imbues Anna Karenina. But this isn’t the whole story, because Flaubert was so complex a figure: restlessly self-doubting even as he more than held his own in an age of cocksure egos; ecstatically happy in his solitary states of aesthetic creation precisely because they could throw him outwards into other people’s stories and minds.

Elif Shafak’s audacious new novel is written out of this ambivalence. An opening chapter shows a devastated Flaubert killing what the narrator styles as “the only woman he has ever loved with heart, mind and soul”, by writing the end of Madame Bovary. The book then shifts briskly to Emma’s own voice, angry with her creator for denying her the freedom to learn from her mistakes (“Could it be because I am a woman?”). These two visions of Flaubert, teeming with creative passion for his own protagonist on the one hand and an exasperating misogynist on the other, become the twin poles of a vast 600-page novel exploring his life from every possible perspective. Thankfully, Shafak doesn’t attempt to ventriloquise Flaubert himself, master of the mot juste. Instead, she has Emma summon the voices of 30 feminine figures, human or otherwise, encountered by Flaubert between birth and death, and alternates their accounts with that of the third-person narrator.
