This is the ideal vehicle for Shafak, who delights and often excels in giving voice to anyone and everyone, including, memorably, the tree protagonist in The Island of Missing Trees. I have always admired Shafak’s storytelling verve while not quite falling for her whimsicality, and I balked slightly at the fancifulness of the chapters voiced by Opium (“Let me lighten up your load, ease the burden. I shall cradle you in my warm embrace”) and Syphilis (“I will damage your cells, burrow into your brain, penetrate your dreams”).

But Flaubert himself might have been drawn to these extremes of literary inhabitation, which are a sort of extreme realisation of his own famous statement to Louise Colet: “It is a delicious thing to write. Today, for instance, as man and woman, both lover and mistress, I rode in a forest on an autumn afternoon under the yellow leaves, and I was also the horses, the leaves, the wind.” Certainly, I fell for Jamilah the camel (“I smile all the time. I cannot help it”), who comes at a point when the reader has either thrown the book aside in exasperation or been carried away by its abundance. “I saw those knives – and I smiled”: Shafak imbues Jamilah’s death with genuine tragedy, at a time when the inhabitants of defeated Paris are murdering zoo animals for restaurants to serve up as gourmet dishes.

Throughout, Shafak powerfully evokes the minute-by-minute sensory experience of a sensitive child, and then of the adult still tragically caught up in his childhood world. She is astute and often moving on the main players in Flaubert’s life: the eventually overbearing mother who she suggests couldn’t quite bring herself to love him as an infant after losing several children before him; the sister whose death he never recovered from; the adored niece he allowed to be pushed into an unhappy marriage, despite understanding more profoundly than anyone in his century quite how unhappy such marriages could be; the lover who “thought I could help him, gently peeling off his loneliness like wallpaper lifted from a tired wall”.

It’s with the invented minor characters that Shafak’s gift for storytelling finds its fullest expression. It’s as though she has tunnelled through Flaubert’s refined stylisation back into 19th-century chaos and exuberance, giving us a female murderer whose sister, passing as male, turns up to tutor the unteachable young Gustave; and the wife of the prosecutor who brought Madame Bovary to trial, laughing here at her husband’s secret hobby of writing pornographic poems. . By the end, Shafak’s powers of narrative invention become a kind of bravura performance, as unexpected, splendidly unlikely connections emerge between minor characters and disparate scenes.

In an author’s note Shafak describes the novel as her “love letter to literature”. Certainly she shares Flaubert’s often idealistic sense that literature can help us even when everything else in our lives and world becomes bleak. “Without stories, without art, our descent into savagery would be even swifter,” she has Flaubert just about convincingly muse. Occasionally, I yearned for more of Flaubert’s cold analysis and sheer vitriol alongside the idealism. But this is unashamedly Shafak’s Flaubert, and I am glad of her faith in storytelling as a shaky light guiding us in dark times, even if I can’t always confidently share it.

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.title: Everest: The Other Side review – couple’s climb on the mountain’s toughest face comes with tricky moral questions over their lofty ambitions
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.author: Leslie Felperin
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.text:
Immersive portrait of mountaineers Jim Morrison and Hilaree Nelson as they seek to become the first people to ski down Everest’s north face

With some of its showings in the huge Imax format, this National Geographic-backed documentary feels like a callback to the early, glory days of large-format cinema when it was all about spectacle and scale, turning footage of natural-world wonders into an immersive experience. Those with a fear of heights or prone to vertigo may find this all a bit too immersive, in fact. That’s even more the case considering the point of the movie appears to be to provoke anxiety in the viewer for nearly the entire running time as we watch the subjects scale the steeper, far less travelled north face Mount Everest and then, for reasons never quite adequately explained, ski back down it again.

Such was the mission of experienced mountaineer Jim Morrison, an amiable-seeming fellow who, like all of those who pursue extreme sports, seems to feel a compulsion to put himself in the kind of grave danger that, should things go wrong, would put other people in danger rescuing him. His partner Hilaree Nelson shares his passion, and the two of them set off to be the first people to ski down Everest’s north face, and the first third of the film tracks them as they plan and eventually do practice runs to achieve this goal. Neither seems able to adequately explain why they’ve chosen to take such a risk, although Nelson tries a bit to articulate her mountaineering life almost as if it’s a career choice that her two teenage sons should simply accept as her choice to make, and maybe even thank her for – even if that means that should she be injured or lost they and Morrison (who is not the boys’ biological father) would also have to deal with the aftermath.

We don’t want to give away what happens, but these moral questions hang over this film in a much more obvious way than they do in most other mountain-climbing films. (Interestingly, this is also a work co-directed by another couple, Jimmy Chin and Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi, who appear on screen to thrash out their own feelings on risk and reward.) Meanwhile, there’s some thoughtful footage of the various Nepalese guides who assist in Jim and Hilaree’s adventures, local men who have been climbing these mountains all their lives because they have far fewer career choices than the western tourists who come through town with camera crews, swathed in brightly coloured, prominently logo-bearing sports equipment.

The lurid palette of this kit does in fact become a bit distracting when we get back to the mountain climbing stuff, and if you want to just relax and look at the stunning landscape you need to train your eyes to ignore the fluorescent jackets obstructing the view. That’s not criticising the cinematography itself; it is pin-sharp thanks to the most advanced kinds of lenses and drone technology. But it’s safe to say the ethics aired here are a far murkier affair.

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.title: Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It? by Judi Dench review – whatever you do, don’t call her a ‘national treasure’
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.author: Fiona Sturges
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.text:
The actor waxes lyrical on directors, dildos on why she hates being referred to as though she’s a dusty old relic

In the late 1950s, Judi Dench was invited to meet a major Hollywood producer about a possible career in the film business. The producer looked at her for a long time and said: “Very nice to meet you but you’ll never make a movie because you have every single thing wrong with your face.” As she left his office, Dench – who was 23 and about to make her professional debut as Ophelia in Hamlet at the Old Vic – breathed a sigh of relief and resolved to concentrate on theatre. Though she dabbled in film and TV, it wasn’t until the 1990s that she became a bona fide movie star, playing M in the Bond films and winning an Oscar for her portrayal of Elizabeth I in Shakespeare in Love. Yet, she notes: “Being onstage is where I feel safest. Yes, I’ve appeared in films, but I’d never consider myself a film actor.”

Dench’s reflections on her working life form the backbone of Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It?, a memoir built around her conversations with the actor and theatre director Brendan O’Hea, Dench’s friend with whom she also collaborated on 2023’s Shakespeare: The Man Who Pays the Rent. This book confirms much of what is already known about Dench: that she is impishly funny, swears like a sailor, and that, despite that film producer’s unkind comments, she has “no hang-ups about what I look like on camera … Acting for me is not about looking glamorous. It’s whatever’s needed for the story.” We also learn that Dench, who is 91, can’t resist a prank: while playing Brecht’s Mother Courage at the Barbican in London, she replaced the drinks her character serves to two soldiers with cider vinegar – “It was a joy watching them knock it back, made even more glorious by the fact they had to ask for a top-up.”

In keeping with her previous book, this one is delivered in a question-and‑answer format. The chapters are thematic and cover faith, animals, directors and directing, comedy, choosing a part, which means the chronology is all over the place. While the book starts quite reasonably with Dench’s early life in York as the daughter of a GP, it ends, oddly, with a chapter called Starting Out, in which we learn what she did after her A-levels. And while she has an easy chemistry with O’Hea, there are times when his line of questioning gets tediously granular, as in: “What’s your favourite dressing room?” Such are the perils of having an actor interview an actor.

But despite the shoptalk and the haphazard structure, there are enough witty anecdotes and oddball facts to keep it clipping along. We learn that Dench has a waste-collection truck named after her: “Dame Foodie Dench”; that she had a cat called Bernard the Duck Fucker (though O’Hea neglects to ask how he earned his name); and that, on the opening night of Madame de Sade, Dench’s co-star Frances Barber gave her a double-ended, bendy dildo which she wore as a scarf when the company gathered for director’s notes. Elsewhere, Dench pays touching tribute to departed friends including the late Maggie Smith, whom she says was “a very complex person – intensely private, and I suspect quite lonely at times; she’d occasionally erect an electric fence around herself”.

The whole project is kept afloat by Dench’s rare humour and warmth which long ago elevated her to national treasure status (an appellation she loathes as it makes her sound “like a dusty old relic”). Her eyesight is now poor, but her memories are pin-sharp, relayed through a prism of amused self-deprecation and passion for her job. The book’s title references Dench’s professional nerves, which lead her to keep her bag by the rehearsal room door in case she is compelled to do a runner. Learning lines may have become more difficult, but she has no intention of stopping work. “Take the keys out of the ignition and the car will conk out,” she cautions. “Don’t retire, do not go gentle, and don’t even think about going quietly.”

Spain’s rail system operator ADIF said the crash occurred Wednesday morning in the province of Toledo

At least 10 people are feared dead and many more injured after two high-speed trains collided in Toledo province in central Spain.

Spain’s state rail infrastructure authority said services between Madrid and the southern region of Andalucía had been suspended “⁠following a rear-end collision between two trains” on Wednesday morning.

A spokesperson for the regional government of Castilla-La Mancha region, where the crash occurred, said the cause and ‌ number of injuries were yet to be determined.

Government sources told El País at least 10 people had been killed, and that the crash could be worse than the Adamuz rail disaster in January in which 46 people were killed.

At least 10 people are feared to have died after two high-speed trains collided in the province of Toledo in Spain, with concerns the death toll could be much higher.

The number of people affected is expected to rise, local authorities said, with growing concerns about a “major tragedy” (11:03).

The affected trains are understood to be Iryo 7076 with 146 passengers plus one baby on board, and AVE 2080 with 397 passengers on board, making it 544 people in total on board of both train (10:46).

The incident comes less than a year after a similar crash in Adamuz, the province of Córdoba, which killed 46 and injured 152 in January this year (11:00).

Spain’s high-speed railway network ranks as the largest in Europe and the second biggest in the world after China, carrying 25 million passengers in 2024.

Spain’s prime minister Pedro Sánchez said he was “shocked” by the accident (11:05), with transport minister Óscar Puente working at the emergency control centre to “obtain all possible information about what happened” (11:16).

Spain’s transport minister Óscar Puente has only issued a brief holding statement for now:

“In the [emergency] control center since 9:40 trying to obtain all possible information about what happened.”

The two affected trains are understood to have been travelling on the high-speed Madrid–Seville line.

Esther Padilla, spokesperson for the Castilla-La Mancha region, told RTVE it appeared that one of the trains may have stopped before the incident.

“Shocked by the serious train accident in Toledo. I remain in constant contact with the Minister of Transport, @oscar_puente_, and with the president of Castilla-La Mancha, @garciapage.

Emergency services are working on the ground to assist those affected and ensure their safety, in coordination with all the involved administrations. My affection, solidarity, and support to all the victims and their families.”

“Very concerned about the information we are getting about a new rail accident. The priority now is to attend to the victims and support their families. My full support to the emergency teams working on the ground.”

Spain’s health minister Mónica García just appeared on RTVE Noticias with a brief update on the incident.

She said there are no further details regarding the number of fatalities and affected, as the focus is on ensuring proper care to all injured, with hospitals freeing up resources whenever possible to allocate them to this incident.

But she conceded – and repeated twice - that it was “a high-impact accident, and we fear this will turn out to be a major tragedy.”

Today’s accident evokes grim echoes of this January’s tragedy in Adamuz, where 46 people killed and 152 were injured after two high-speed trains crashed in Adamuz, the province of Córdoba.

A few days later, a driver was killed and 37 people injured when a train was derailed by the collapse of a retaining wall near Gelida in Catalonia.

Following the Adamuz train crash earlier this year, Spain’s largest train drivers’ union called for a three-day nationwide strike as it demanded more thorough safety checks and “the restoration of safety standards on the railway system.”

But with almost 4,000km of track, Spain’s high-speed railway network ranks as the largest in Europe and the second biggest in the world after China, according to the Spanish infrastructure administrator Adif.

The network is tremendously popular, competitively priced and generally considered a safe mode of transport. In 2024, Renfe said more than 25 million passengers had travelled on its high-speed trains that year.

But in another major incident in 2013, 80 people died after a train derailed in the country’s north-west near Santiago de Compostela. An investigation concluded the train was travelling at 179km/h on a stretch of the line with an 80km/h speed limit when it left the tracks.

Local government spokesperson told TVE that the death toll “will almost certainly rise.”

“We know that the number of fatalities and injuries will continue to rise. We are prepared to provide the best possible care as quickly as we can, but the situation … is likely to worsen.”

She said the affected trains are likely to be Iryo 7076 with 146 passengers plus one baby on board, and AVE 2080 with 397 passengers on board, El País reported.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: Fed set to hold interest rates steady in last decision before midterms
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Gaya Gupta
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
US central bank last month raised rates for first time since 2023, in move that infuriated Donald Trump

The US Federal Reserve is expected to leave interest rates unchanged on Wednesday during its last rate-setting meeting before the midterm elections, keeping rates at one of the highest pre-election levels seen in over 20 years.

Last month, Fed officials raised rates for the first time since 2023, citing rising inflation. Inflation has hovered for years above the Fed’s target rate of 2%, and for most of this year, the annualized inflation rate has remained above 3%.

The move infuriated Donald Trump, who said that “interest rates in the United States should be 1% or less”.

Though inflation rose higher in September, going from 3.4% in August to 3.7%, a pause would signal the central bank is taking a wait-and-see approach ahead of the midterms next week.

Interest rates determine the cost of interest for loans, including for credit cards, mortgage and some savings accounts. During times of high inflation, raising rates can slow price increases.

Multiple Fed leaders have suggested in recent weeks that the central bank has room for a pause, even if most Fed economists are predicting one more rate hike before the end of the year.

“The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time,” Fed governor Christopher Waller said earlier this month.

The proximity of the election also makes it more likely that the Fed will “not take any radical action,” said Nicholas Economides, a professor of economics at the NYU Stern Business School.

“Even if the Fed were to do something radically different, the economy would not have time to adjust before the elections,” he said.

Rising prices this year have largely been driven by war in the Middle East with Iran. Oil prices have soared with the closure of the strait of Hormuz, a crucial passageway for trade. Inflation rose last month to its highest level since the spring, while oil traded briefly above $117 a barrel earlier this week, its highest price in more than six months.

The higher cost of living is expected to play a crucial role in the upcoming midterm elections that will determine which party will control Congress. Across multiple polls, the economy has been cited as the top issue for voters.

By itself, hiking interest rates cannot solely address inflation caused by supply shocks, Economides said. Raising rates is helpful for when the economy is too hot, or when demand outpaces supply, but can be counterproductive otherwise.

“If inflation is caused by supply factors, it doesn’t make sense to try to cure it by increasing interest rates because it won’t work,” he said. “It will slow down the economy at a time in which you don’t want it to slow down.”

Fed chair Kevin Warsh has suggested, however, that present-day inflation has persisted beyond the war, and the central bank’s decision to raise rates was to prevent prices from creeping up further.

“We cannot affect any individual price, whether it be oil prices, whether it be foodstuffs at the grocery store,” Warsh said at the Fed’s September meeting.

“But what we can do, and will do, is ensure that any change in relative prices don’t broaden out, don’t have second and third-order effects on the economy. That’s what we’re tasked to do, and that’s what we will do.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: A US woman feared dead was reported alive in Mexico. But cops now say that isn’t true
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ramon Antonio Vargas
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Mexican police had said they found Shayna Feinman in Tijuana, raising the hopes of missing Arizonan’s family

Arizona authorities say their Mexican counterparts were resoundingly mistaken when they publicly claimed recently that they found alive a woman who was feared slain after disappearing in 2024 – a turn of events that her sister has called “turmoil” and “heartbreaking”.

The case in question centers on Shayna Feinman, who was reported missing in rural Yavapai county, Arizona, in March 2024 at age 38.

Authorities believe she was walking to an acquaintance’s home when she was last seen – but she never arrived or returned to her dog, as the Arizona news outlet KSAZ reported. An ensuing search turned up Feinman’s car abandoned near where she had been staying with her boyfriend, Cavett Richards, according to the station.

Her wallet and identification reportedly were inside the vehicle, and her cellphone was ultimately recovered on nearby land.

Although Feinman had not been found, the Yavapai county sheriff’s office subsequently charged Richards as well as a man named William DalCerro with second-degree murder, conspiracy and concealing a corpse in connection with her disappearance. But the charges were dismissed, a $20,000 reward being offered for information as authorities kept investigating the case.

The secretariat for security and citizen protection in the Mexican municipality of Tijuana then delivered what initially appeared to be a startling update in Feinman’s case on Saturday, saying in a statement that she had been located in the city’s Encino neighborhood the previous day.

The statement from the secretariat had a picture of the woman sitting in front of a desk atop which was a missing poster with Feinman’s information. It asserted without elaborating that investigators had confirmed Feinman’s identity, noting that her physical characteristics matched those listed in her missing person report.

The woman had been put in protective custody while Tijuana authorities arranged for her to speak with the Feinman family and US consular officials, the statement said. The agency went so far as to post a link to its Saturday statement on a social media page belonging to Feinman’s sister, Kara.

But both Kara Feinman and the Yavapai’s sheriff’s office met the Tijuana officials’ statement with evident skepticism.

Kara told KSAZ in a story published on Monday that she was waiting for the Yavapai sheriff’s office “to know for certain” that Shayna had been found.

Though she acknowledged the woman in the picture released by Tijuana officials had “similar physical attributes” to Shayna, Kara struck a cautious tone, telling KSAZ: “I can only hope and pray [for] good news – but right now, we have to be realistic.”

Meanwhile, a sheriff’s office spokesperson told KSAZ that the agency was “aware of reports indicating that Shayna Feinman may have been located in Mexico” – but “at this time, the information remains unconfirmed”.

“There is insufficient evidence to verify her identity,” Yavapai sheriff’s office spokesperson Paul Wick added to KSAZ. Wick said the sheriff’s office was “actively investigating the matter” and would provide an update as soon as one could be “confirmed and … released”.

The Yavapai sheriff’s office published that update on Tuesday, when it said in a statement: “Today, US authorities confirmed to [office] detectives, utilizing physical evidence, that the individual located is not Shayna Feinman.”

The sheriff’s office alluded to prior media reports “regarding the alleged discovery of Shayna Feinman” that “were published without official law enforcement confirmation” – before saying its “detectives continue to work diligently with [her] family during this stressful time”.

Tijuana’s security and citizen protection secretariat did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In an interview with the Guardian on Tuesday, Kara Feinman said she believed the confusion about her sister possibly being in Tijuana initially stemmed from at least one concerned citizen who became convinced that she was there and made that known on social media.

She described being guarded about that possibility, reluctantly opening her mind in light of the Tijuana secretariat’s claims – and then enduring cyberbullying online by users who harshly judged her for not reacting effusively enough to the ultimately false news that Shayna had been found alive.

As she processed the reality that the search for the truth about her sister’s disappearance continued, Kara Feinman said her hope now was for those passionate about such investigations to realize how harmful it can be “jumping to conclusions without having all of the information” and then directing harsh words at the people most affected by those cases.

“Words are stronger than people think, and kindness can go so far,” Kara Feinman said. “It’s been turmoil going through this.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Loves me, loves me not: Trump and allies target Fox News over coverage
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Jeremy Barr in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
In social media posts, president has said network is ‘doing little to help’ Republican party in midterm elections

Donald Trump has always viewed conservative media as a tool to help him and his party achieve political victory and stay in power. But with polls flashing red for his party ahead of next week’s midterm elections, the president and his allies have trained their fire on the most prominent player in the space: Fox News.

For years, the president has criticized Fox’s non-partisan polling operation, and in recent weeks he has called out the network for not sufficiently airing his midterm rallies – even when they are not particularly newsworthy.

The president has also repeatedly taken aim at the network for interviewing Democratic candidates, viewing the presence of the candidates on the channel – even for contentious sit-downs – as disloyal. “FoxNews is spending far too much time putting on the OPPONENTS of Republican Party Candidates, people that love our Country, and have Great Policies and Ideas,” he wrote in a Truth Social post on Sunday. “These American Patriots are being absolutely ‘blurred out’ by the Media, and Fox is doing little to help. That’s the only reason this Race is close, if it is indeed close.”

Trump’s admission that he expects Fox News to “help” is striking, even as his expectations have been thinly veiled over the years.

In another Truth Social post last week, Trump rationalized that Fox News is featuring Democratic candidates “to be Politically Correct”, encouraging his fans to watch an upcoming rally on all Trump, all-the-time conservative media company Right Side Broadcasting Network.

Trump has been particularly angry at Fox News for interviewing Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan. “FoxNews spends more time covering the Jihadist and Dumocrat candidates than they do the good old fashioned Republicans, the people that have saved America, and are making it great again,” he wrote in a third Truth Social post. “All they talk about is Dumocrat Jihadists like El-Sayed, with his softball interview by Martha MacCallum, and the like. She never interviews me like that. They don’t show my record breaking Rallies the morning after, but others do, and that’s what MAGA is watching. Fox is promoting the Dumocrats, not the Republicans and MAGA. They have totally lost their way!” (El-Sayed has played up some of the light praise he’s received on Fox, including some compliments from host Jesse Watters, in a recent advertisement.)

Laura Loomer, one of Trump’s most reliable boosters, wrote in a post on X earlier this month that “@FoxNews should be exposing jihadists…not platforming them and whitewashing their terrorist agenda.”

Peter Navarro, the president’s senior counselor for trade and manufacturing, has encouraged Trump supporters to turn off Fox News. He has been particularly livid at the network’s decision to part ways with longtime Trump backer Maria Bartiromo early last month, after she reportedly shared Fox’s internal guidance about how to cover a Trump speech.

During an appearance last week on the extremely pro-Trump Real America’s Voice network, Navarro said that Fox News “is supposed to be our side”. Instead, he said, the network “is trying to destroy the signature piece of the Trump agenda”, referring to on-air criticism of the president’s tariff plan. He ended his attack on the network by encouraging viewers to “turn Fox off … You don’t need Fox”.

In July, Steve Bannon, a former Trump White House chief strategist and a longtime critic of the Murdoch family, criticized the network for not playing up claims of election fraud made in a primetime speech by Trump. “The [Murdochs] hate Trump, they hate Maga” he said. “If you watch Fox and support that crap, you are part of the problem.”

But, as has been true throughout Trump’s political career, his occasional criticisms of Fox News are offset by the personal relationships he has with many of the network’s hosts – and the positive coverage they offer him.

Chris Stirewalt, an anchor and political editor for the center-leaning cable network NewsNation, spent more than a decade at Fox News before being pushed out as part of the fall-out from the network’s early-but-correct call of the state of Arizona for Joe Biden on election night in 2020. The call drew a massive wave of backlash from the Trump faithful and the president himself, but Stirewalt noted that the network is still at the center of the conservative media world.

In the event that the Republican party faces a wipe-out next Tuesday, Stirewalt says: “I think the president will definitely be chippy about it and say stuff, but I think one of the lessons is that [Fox News] survived and the symbiotic relationship goes both ways.”

In perhaps the clearest example yet of the closeness between Trump and Fox, predicated on decades of friendship, Fox News anchors Sean Hannity and Ainsley Earhardt chose to host the rehearsal dinner for their wedding at the president’s Mar-a-Lago Club – with him in attendance – on 23 October. Their wedding a day later was also reportedly attended by both Fox and Trumpworld royalty, including Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff, Dan Scavino, White House deputy chief of staff, and Karoline Leavitt, who recently left the Trump administration after a successful stint as press secretary to serve as an on-air contributor for Fox.

Despite his complaints about the network not covering his rallies, Fox News sends a reporter to each of them, and has aired many of his recent rallies, including one in Texas on Tuesday and more than an hour of the president’s rally in Michigan on Sunday. Trump’s rallies are also aired live on the streaming service Fox Nation.

Trump also still receives favorable interviews on Fox. On Sunday morning, Trump was interviewed on Fox News by Larry Kudlow, his former director of the national economic council, who has temporarily picked up Bartiromo’s weekly time slot.

Through the nearly 25-minute interview, Kudlow mostly let Trump rant about his accomplishments, talk up Republican candidates and denigrate Democratic ones. In an unconventional move for a news interviewer, he also suggested campaign messages for Trump: “Sir, will you end this campaign on a optimistic note? On a pro-growth note. Freedom. Free enterprise. We don’t want socialism. We want to keep the borders closed. We want the culture to be consistent with western traditional values.”

But before he even began his questioning, Kudlow said he wanted to lead off with a “thought” about his presidency that was akin to an endorsement.

“I think you’re on a roll,” he said. “I mean, you’ve been relentless. You’re campaigning. It’s herculean. You’re turning the tide, you’re getting voters out, you’re raising enthusiasm. The economy is booming. We’re the hottest in the world. Stocks are doing great. Drug prices are coming down. Oil is flowing through the Persian Gulf. I mean, I think in the last month, you may have turned this whole thing around.”

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.title: ‘There is no inevitable dystopia’: Jeanette Winterson on AI and the future of humanity
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.author: Aida Edemariam
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.text:
The author believes we are at a turning point as a species – and even in the shadow of big tech it’s up to us how we want to proceed

‘I am a storyteller by trade,” writes Jeanette Winterson on the first page of her 2021 book 12 Bytes, an idiosyncratic and thought-provoking series of essays in which she considered just how artificial intelligence might change everything about our lives. “And I know everything we do is a fiction until it’s a fact: the dream of flying, the dream of space travel, the dream of speaking to someone instantly, across time and space, the dream of not dying – or of returning.”

She had already been thinking about our possible futures for at least 15 years – her 2007 novel, The Stone Gods, for instance, imagined a post-climate catastrophe world populated by robots and humans who never age, while 12 Bytes was preceded by Frankisstein: A Love Story, which alternates a recreation of the summer Mary Shelley wrote Frankenstein with a trans doctor’s travels among present-day cryogenecists and AI-enabled robots.

When we meet, Winterson is just back from China, where, she tells me, her first novel, Oranges Are Not the Only Fruit, a fictionalised account of her childhood, has sold more than a million copies in the past six years; more than 200,000 mostly young women tried to come to see her speak. She thinks this is because, in a world of long work hours and looming AI-engendered precarity, this fictionalised account of her own escape from an entrapped childhood gives readers permission to imagine a different future for themselves. She has since written 13 novels for adults, as well as nonfiction, short stories, children’s books and screenplays. Now she wants to persuade the production company Goalhanger to give her a podcast. “I want to do one called The Rest is Human,” she says, sitting at a bare wooden table in her home, a Georgian set of rooms above a shop – which she also owns – in Spitalfields, east London. “To see what we retain for ourselves in this absolute scramble to outsource everything we thought we were.”

Because we are, she argues, at a turning point in our story as a species. Until the Industrial Revolution, change was all about “Mother Nature and the slow process of becoming”, but then we “massively intervened. And that’s a decisive moment.” Computing, 70 years ago, was another step. Artificial intelligence – which she would prefer to call alternative intelligence – is next, and “an evolutionary leap. That’s what this is. AI is much more than a tool.” Given this, a certain understanding of the irreducibly human – our feelings, our imaginations, our centuries of study of who we are and what we have done – must be central to how well or badly things might go.

She’s often strikingly optimistic about it. She imagines a relationship with AI, for instance, where you can “have a chat to your system. It’s going to look at everything. It’s going to go at such speed. It’s going to look at transport. It’s going to look at utilities. It’s going to look at employment, going to look at job hours, going to say, ‘What do these weird things called humans thrive on? What do they like? And have they always liked it?’ We could do this in a genuinely utopian way and say, ‘Right, we’re going to make it better.’” We are at a deeply significant moment of choice, she believes, that mirrors the choice we had in the Industrial Revolution – namely, “What future shall we build?”

But in failing to distribute its gains fairly, the Industrial Revolution ushered in an era of unprecedented wealth for the few and unprecedented levels of misery for the many – a state of affairs many predict is not only already echoed but will be dwarfed by the fallout from AI: a permanent underclass, entire continents left behind and starved of current sources of income. Not to mention the environmental impact of datacentres at a time when the world can least afford it.

The problem is not AI, she insists, but us. “There is no inevitable dystopia.” If things go wrong, it will be because of “old-fashioned thinking laid over this brand-new reality”. Specifically, “the idea of meaningless endless work being good for the soul is a 19th-century madness designed to keep people in their place. Most of what we fear about AI and jobs comes down to the political and economic choices our masters will make, just as they did in the Industrial Revolution.” She isn’t blindly optimistic. She does know that, “Yes, we are on track to mess up this chance to fundamentally change our relationship to the world of work” – but that’s because “our masters are using out-of-date, not-fit-for-purpose economic models”.

But it isn’t only the old winner-takes-all, “rational” ends-justify-the-means economic models that are the problem. Our flawed assumptions, and our prejudices, being the material on which large language models (LLMs) are trained, are built into the very fabric of AI. Not to mention the characters and the moral imaginations of those developing it. When we meet, Winterson is reading Jill Lepore’s The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State, and reiterates Lepore’s argument that we are now living “the sci-fi books that these [men who are] ruling the world read when they were 13. And she said, ‘We are now all under the covers with these boys and their flashlights. And the thing is, they didn’t read them as warnings about how to preserve what’s good in us. They read them as instruction manuals.’ It’s absolutely terrifying.”

One big thing they seem to have taken from these books, and Winterson cannot help but be fascinated by, is “the ultimate goal of Silicon Valley … to get out of the body and off the planet” – not least because she is so aware that humanism, in which everything is brought back to ourselves, our perceptions and our bodies, is historically so recent. People say, “These are machines, you can’t have relationships with them,” she says. “I look at them and say, ‘billions of people on this Earth right now are having their most profound relationship with a non-biological entity they call their sky god.’ Right? It’s always been so! We are absolutely primed not to worry about biology being everything about us. That’s why religion was invented – it is the world’s first disruptive startup. It’s there to say, this is not it. This is not the end, this doesn’t matter, this is a transition.”

So we’re literally making our own gods? “Totally! What tech is doing now is what religion has always wanted,” which is, at its most basic level, a solution to the problem of death. “I mean, has there ever been a time where religion and science are asking the same question, since the Enlightenment? They’re both saying, ‘Is consciousness obliged to materiality?’ And religion has always said no. And science has always said yes. And now science is saying, ‘Um, noooo.”’ You know, to me, where I come from” – a childhood of fundamentalist Christianity in 1960s Accrington, and training as a preacher – “this is completely fascinating.” Later, on email, she adds, “I love my body, but I would be happy to shape shift. Happy to slip out of it into pure consciousness one day and of course people say there is no consciousness without a body, and that was the scientific belief. But now? Haha.”

I would, I have to say, argue the opposite, that advances in neuroscience, immunology and psychotherapy mean it is more the scientific belief than ever. Not to mention the fact that AI is also entirely dependent on a physical system, otherwise known as datacentres. Although, as she points out it’s important to remember that “the machines don’t have a limbic system. They’re only neural networks. But we’ve got two systems – we’re like a hybrid car with two powertrains, so we’ve got the neural network, our rational processing self, and we’ve got the limbic system, which is much older and that’s the fight-flight-freeze, and where all our feelings come from.” Perhaps detaching from the limbic is the next stage, she says, and it definitely isn’t all good. “Maybe we’ll decide that we don’t need this feeling machine … that is where the tech bros are heading. I don’t know if you’ve ever sat in a room with some of these bigger guys, because it’s very interesting. They are not connected to their feelings. They find them kind of bothersome.”

This tech-enabled possibility of a kind of transcendence seems to have arrived alongside a requirement for faith – in the technology, in the future it is making, in the people building that future, in its predictions both of utopian heaven and various shades of hell, all by high priests who jealously guard access to what’s actually going on. “What we know about humans is they love monopolies,” says Winterson, “because it’s a concentration of power. Of course it can be corporatised, monopolised to such a degree that it becomes the worst prison imaginable,” as told in Joanna Kavenna’s brilliant 2019 dystopian novel Zed. “That is a real possibility,” she says. “And that’s why we need people who are sort of free-range humans, who can think.”

The problem then is how we support – or develop – such humans. “There are basically two ways to know you have a future,” claimed Alex Karp, the CEO of Palantir, recently. “One, you have some vocational training. Or two, you’re neurodivergent.” Daniela Amodei, the president of Anthropic and herself a literature graduate, when asked more or less the same thing, had a different take. “I actually think studying the humanities is going to be more important than ever,” she said, because “the things that make us human will become much more important instead of much less important.” Which makes the bonfire of the humanities in the UK somewhat concerning: in the year to December 2024, 4,000 jobs in the social sciences, humanities and arts were lost. Exeter University recently announced it would be cutting 150 roles, affecting eight in 10 academics in the faculty of humanities, arts and social sciences, while last month Nottingham said it would be ending its modern languages and its music degrees. At some universities the humanities, according to a report in this paper, risk being “extinguished” altogether.

Why save the humanities? One answer might be that they teach a sense of where we come from and who we are, which also feels threatened. “Massive numbers of students are going to emerge from university with degrees, and into the workforce, who are essentially illiterate,” one professor told New York magazine, responding to the first tranche of AI natives arriving in higher education. “Both in the literal sense and in the sense of being historically illiterate and having no knowledge of their own culture, much less anyone else’s.” It risked, a report from MIT claimed, being a kind of generational “cognitive surrender”.

Another is the processes by which people should be taught – reading, and being critical of what is read, and then having to write cogent defences of those critiques. Having to tussle your intuitions into an essay helps you to discover what – and how – you think, and how the ideas of others work. Winterson, who studied English at Oxford, and has been professor of new writing at the University of Manchester for 14 years, as well as teaching “a free-thinking class about creativity”, agrees. But she is dismissive of much of the current system. “Maybe I’m controversial here but I do think higher education needs a top-down restructure. I don’t think it’s viable and I don’t think it’s delivering in its present form.” The thing is, “We’ve got a market that doesn’t really know what education is for. Is it for jobs? Is it for personal growth? There are a lot of worthless higher education courses which are not helping, either. I think it’s always better, being a practical northern girl, to face the facts to start with.”

We need to think, she says, about “what’s reserved to us that isn’t going to be done bigger, better, faster, stronger by the machines. And that’s where higher education really comes in. The question that’s sitting on top of all these things about, ‘Why are these jobs going?’, ‘What’s happening in these courses that aren’t getting any applicants any more?’, is ‘What sort of humans will we need in the world to come? What are humans for? What are we going to do with us?’”. And that “takes us back to the idea of, well, OK, how do you develop a mind? How do you protect a mind? Because the mind is this massive, monstrous place where anything can happen.”

And for this, “a humanist education is essential. We have to centre the human here. By changing how we educate our kids from the start we can foreground creativity, play, problem-solving, thinking, because it’s fun to think, the arts because humans are naturally creative. Show me a child that doesn’t want to hear a story or do a dance or paint a picture or have an imaginary friend. This isn’t imposed and it isn’t elitism. It’s us.”

Even an hour a week, she thinks, would make a difference. “Let’s ask what you think about the world. ‘Why do you think that?’ It’s not costly. It’s actually about will.” Teach maths and arts and science, she suggests, at least to A-level, even if they aren’t examined. “Of course we will specialise. We need doctors and chemists but we also need what used to be called well-rounded people. Everything is interesting! Humans are born with a big brain. Mostly we don’t use it.”

Once past formal education, she would embed artists and public intellectuals at every level. “The arts aren’t a leisure industry,” as she puts it in 12 Bytes. “The arts have always been an imaginative and emotional wrestle with reality – a series of inventions and creations. A capacity to think differently, a willingness to change our understanding of ourselves. To help us to be wiser, more reflective, less frightened people. Artists make something out of nothing every day.”

We meet before Jacob Coxon quit his job at Anthropic to warn of a 10% chance AI might erase humanity, sending a wave of panic across the world. Afterwards, I check in about how positive Winterson is feeling now. The worst “could happen”, she repeats. But “the immensity of the good outcome is just as real as the totality of our failure to get this right”. Above all, “this is a human decision and a human predicament. This is our big chance. Maybe our last chance, just like Turing’s colleague Jack Good said when he called AI our last invention. It’s all to play for.”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: A bitter night in Israel for all who craved a fresh start. Netanyahu survives – and we are more divided than ever | Dahlia Scheindlin
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Dahlia Scheindlin
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
After an exit poll that gave the opposition hope, reality dawned. With all the votes on the right, the prospects for the left and centre now look bleak

Following Israel’s nail-biting election, nearly every political community in the country experienced triumph and despair. The initial results swung wildly from the first exit polls to the slow real-vote count; the bloc of parties loyal to the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, might yet win, and each side feels that its fate hangs in the balance.

So far, only one certainty remains: Israel’s bitter divisions are deeper than ever.

At 10pm Jerusalem time, three television stations published their exit polls by veteran pollsters showing a stinging loss for Netanyahu’s current government. In all three, his current coalition won just 50 out of 120 parliamentary seats, with 70 for the opposition. It was small consolation for Netanyahu that his Likud party held a slight lead over the main challenger, the Yashar party led by former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot.

Millions of Israelis who voted for opposition parties felt exhilarated. Together, four Zionist lists within the opposition ran a two- or three-seat lead over Netanyahu’s bloc, though neither of those groupings was close to a 61-seat majority. Eisenkot gave a passionate speech about the defeat of the “coalition of failure”, by a “larger and stronger Zionist majority”. Former prime minister Naftali Bennett, another leading opposition figure, declared that the “alliance of those who served” had won – referencing Israelis who have served in the military, while Netanyahu’s government had shielded Israel’s ultra-Orthodox Jews from service during Israel’s longest and bloodiest war.

Those first polls also showed an unprecedented gain for parties representing Arab-Palestinian citizens of Israel, with 17 or 18 seats out of 120. That community, about one-fifth of the population, had a powerful turnout of more than 75%. In earlier years, their turnout rates had lagged behind those of Jewish voters. Many Arab citizens preferred to avoid legitimising elections in a country that has discriminated against them since its founding, alongside ongoing occupation and now full-blown war against Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza.

But the community was seized by the urgency of ousting ultra-nationalist, anti-Arab extremists in the current government. Calls to boycott elections nearly vanished, and the first results made Arab parties look like kingmakers for coalition bargaining.

Netanyahu’s camp would have been dejected at first. To be sure, two additional exit polls showed more flattering results for his bloc, but these were commissioned by right-leaning channels that many viewed as biased. Throughout the campaign, their poll findings had been outliers.

Then the counting began. Within hours, Netanyahu’s bloc staged a reversal, pulling significantly ahead of the four opposition Zionist parties many hoped would replace him. The Arab parties retained a strong showing but lower than the original heady projections. But three of the four Zionist parties preferred to exclude them for coalition-building purposes. As a result, even if the total opposition vote outweighs support for the outgoing government, Netanyahu might have done it again.

It is not yet clear if any one group of parties can reach a 61-seat majority. Negotiations to form a coalition will take dizzying twists in the coming weeks; maybe a minority government or a stalemate will be the unsatisfying result.

But one thing is certain. Israel’s divisions have never been more profound. Blocs, camps and tribes have never been more irreconcilable.

The majority of Israelis who voted for any opposition party cannot fathom how they will survive under another extremist, anti-democratic, pro-war coalition led by Netanyahu and his theocratic allies.

Yet the clear majority of the voters supported ideologically rightwing parties, who hold perhaps 74 seats at present, including Netanyahu’s bloc and at least two clearly rightwing opposition parties led by Avigdor Lieberman and Bennett. The centre and left wing in Israel cannot fathom how they will survive under these nationalist, militarist, illiberal lawmakers with a firm majority in Knesset, regardless of the government.

Arab citizens could suffer the most severe disappointment. In return for their greatest-ever political participation, with the singular aim of ousting a government that loathes them, their efforts may have gone for nought.

Israel’s moderately leftwing Democrats party appears on course to reach around nine seats, more than twice the parliamentary strength of an equivalent party in the last Knesset. But for roughly 20% of all Israelis who call themselves leftwing, who dream of a country that no longer lords it over Palestinians and still dares to hope one day for peace, there is little horizon for hope.

Israel has always been famously divided, yet managed somehow to hold together. Now, the lively disagreements of the past have given way to fundamental, even existential questions about whether the people of Israel have anything in common with each other; and whether some will simply give up and go.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: We are seeing the rise of psychopatriarchy everywhere | V (Formerly Eve Ensler)
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: V (formerly Eve Ensler)
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Psychopatriarchy is jet fuel to racism, colonialism, imperialism and capitalism

For those of us who have spent our lives trying to dismantle this endlessly destructive paradigm of patriarchy, it has become increasingly clear in recent months that something more terrifying is afoot.

The wheels are off the cart. We are in the midst of a chaotic, demented acceleration of the most violent and cruel aspects of this system which has evolved into what I am calling Psychopatriarchy.

Psychopatriarchy is a reaction, a backlash against the progress we have made on all fronts: women’s rights, civil rights, immigrant rights, workers rights, trans rights etc.

It has birthed an authoritarian fascist reality, poisoning our social and psychological environment with terrorizing violence, cruelty and precarity. It has consolidated the billionaire class who are driven by the mindset summed up in the slogan “move fast and break things.” Or, one might say, grab things, rape things.

Psychopatriarchy is found in the 120 people who own more money than half the population on earth, in the systems of oppression, surveillance and violence which become more and more sophisticated and widespread, in the few mainly white men with extreme wealth and power who are now merged with the government and own the systems of communication, AI, police or state militias like ICE.

Psychopatriarchy is a sanctioning of extreme hatred and violence against women from the top, many of whom are rapists, batterers, pedophiles and abusers or men who openly support them.

The president of the US is a civilly adjudicated sex abuser and has not only flippantly dismissed allegations of sexual violence made against others in his orbit, but made it fashionable and popular attitude for the men in his delusional cult.

He has created a suffocating atmosphere of misogyny and predation. We only have to look to the manosphere, or the rape academies online where millions of men exchange best practices for drugging and raping their wives, girlfriends, sisters or deepfake pornography which is destroying thousands of women’s lives or sex robots.

Or rape islands where some of the most powerful men in the world are alleged to have raped underage girls and not one has been prosecuted. Or universities where young men allegedly gang-rape an incapacitated woman or where young women can’t put down a drink at a party without fear of being drugged, where they are blamed for being assaulted.

Psychopatriarchy is women dying preventable deaths because abortion care is denied or delayed or the introduction of extreme constitutional amendments such as North Carolina House Bill 1232, where men might be legally allowed to kill women who have abortions. This bill will hopefully not pass, but the fact that it is even being considered is an example of how deeply far we have fallen.

Psychopatriachy is the open and unapologetic death of compassion; as Elon Musk said: “Empathy is the fundamental weakness of western civilization.” This means a kind of contempt for anything that appears to be emotional, alive, feminine, caring.

Strength in the form of dissociation is revered. When you feel nothing, no guilt, no shame, no horror at your actions, you can better serve your goals and the state. When you are ruled by your blind devotion to the president, the boss, the father, you become capable of doing anything in his name.

Psychopatriachy is renaming the Department of Defense the “Department of War”, well, the “High-T Department of War”, as Hegseth calls it, wanting all military personnel aged 30 and over to “have the right testosterone levels” to operate at their “absolute best” and to optimize “natural capabilities”, “longevity”, and “readiness”. Preparing a psycho army driven by chemicals beyond their control.

Psychopatriarchy is wanting to livestream a firing squad. It’s the endless genocide in Gaza, the outright murdering of babies, toddlers, mothers, fathers, journalists, doctors. It’s the US bombing a girls school in Iran and murdering 120 girl children and 26 teachers, and no one ever taking responsibility for one of the worst war crimes since Vietnam.

It’s illegally kidnapping presidents and randomly murdering people by bombing them in boats in the middle of the sea. It’s masked men dragging away wailing children from their parents.

It’s killing activists in the streets: Renee Good and Alex Pretti. It’s intimidating and threatening deportation to those who disagree with you: Ilhan Omar. It’s creating the conditions for the lynching of Black people across the United States.

It’s tearing down ancient grandmother trees to build walls to keep suffering people out or to landscape a golf course. It’s the coldhearted, discompassionate billionaire class taking everything, erasing everyone.

Psychopatriarchy is the decimation of all forms of accountability. Infinite impunity. No supreme court, no Department of Justice, no leaders, no Congress. Withdrawing or refusing to be part of any international courts or abiding by international law. When there is no accountability, when there is no place to turn for justice, a society loses its moral footing and begins to fall.

Psychopatriachy is not just a political notion. It’s a state of existence, a blight on the condition of humanity locking us into daily terror, cruelty, depression, malaise, a manufactured sense of powerlessness, alienation and a desire to disappear.

It is a kind of low-level anxiety, an ongoing foreshadowing or feeling of imminent destruction coming from multiple directions at once, and rather than reducing these threats (AI, nuclear weapons, climate catastrophes, pandemics), the psychopatriarchs are accelerating all these things. AI is charging forward with no regulation, escalating the nuclear arms race, increasing drilling of oil at breakneck speed.

Psychopatriarchy is jet fuel to all the other -isms: racism, colonialism, imperialism, capitalism.

It is propelled by its own mad trajectory. We can try to block it (courts); we can starve it (strikes); we can remove it (vote and get them out office). We can name and shame it (speaking out, marches and rallies), refuse to normalize it (write about it, make art about it); we can prosecute it.

We can create a parallel world that is so inviting, generous and caring that even those who are still struggling to break out of the cult will eventually be emboldened.

But what we cannot do is go to sleep, become small and still, with the childlike fantasy that they will not find us. What we cannot do is succumb to it or become them – numb, selfish, hollow and cruel.

Our feelings, our pain, our empathy, our rage, our love, our refusal to turn away will be our salvation. Psychosis is the inability to tell what is real from unreal. Our work is to say what we see and trust what we know, to keep speaking truth to power and go to any lengths to stay connected to reality and each other.

V (formerly Eve Ensler) is a playwright and activist and the founder of V-Day, a global movement to end violence against women and girls

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Kylian Mbappé’s China crisis shows how sensitive Mao’s legacy remains
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Rebecca Bailey
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Real Madrid forward was dropped by brands for comments Chinese media generally steered clear of outlining

It’s been a bad start to the week for the France forward Kylian Mbappé. He missed out on joining the elite roster of Ballon d’Or winners, and instead became the latest high-profile addition to a far less illustrious list – that of foreign brands and individuals charged with “hurting the feelings of the Chinese people”.

The saga began when a video of the Real Madrid player making light of a meme involving him and China’s former leader Mao Zedong began spreading.

Within hours Mbappé found himself condemned online, before being unceremoniously dropped by brands, then held responsible for state television suspending the entire top Spanish league from its schedule. On Tuesday Mbappé apologised – “My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China – as did La Liga, which released a statement saying it “deeply regrets the offence that Kylian Mbappé’s recent comments have caused among Chinese fans”.

Foreign brands from Mercedes to Versace and celebrities from John Cena to Katy Perry have previously been sent to the sin bin for crossing China’s political lines on Tibet, Hong Kong and Taiwan.

Mbappé’s case shows how sensitive Mao’s legacy remains in China 50 years after his death – to the extent that most Chinese coverage of the affair does not even mention what the footballer said.

In the video, Mbappé references a meme of himself and “a guy … I think he was a Chinese dictator”, after which a composite image of Mbappé’s face on Mao’s body pops up. (Mbappé has been nicknamed “the dictator” since his time at Paris Saint-Germain, a joke referring to his perceived influence at the club.)

The football app Dongqiudi was among the first to release a statement condemning his “inappropriate remarks”, but said: “Because his comments were offensive to China and the Chinese people, we cannot translate them.”

Chinese media have reported on reactions such as the brand desertions, and the China Football Association’s lodging of a “stern protest” with Real Madrid – who on Wednesday apologised “to the Chinese people for any offence caused” – but have generally steered clear of outlining Mbappé’s precise offence.

The topic was still trending on Chinese social media on Wednesday morning, with one hashtag relating to the superstar’s apology boasting more than 600m views.

Some posts asked variations on a simple question: “What did he actually say?”

“Many netizens without a VPN are still left in the dark about why all the talk about boycotting Mbappé is actually happening,” said Manya Koetse, editor of the Eye on Digital China newsletter, on X.

Still, many expressed anger at what was characterised as disrespect for, as well as a misunderstanding of, China’s history.

“For the majority of the [Chinese] people, Mao was and is still not seen as negatively as it is believed in the west,” said Mobo Gao, professor of Chinese studies at Adelaide University.

Mao was the founding leader of modern China, but his legacy includes radical policies such as the Great Leap Forward, an industrialisation policy blamed for a famine that killed as many as 30 million people by some estimates.

The ruling Communist party (CCP) maintains Mao was a revolutionary hero, though after his death it acknowledged another extreme policy, the violent Cultural Revolution, was a “grave mistake”.

“There has been intense tension between Mao hatred and Mao support among the Chinese themselves,” said Gao. “This tension is even more keenly felt since the economy has slowed.”

Some scholars have pointed to a resurgence of interest in Mao among younger Chinese, with a yearning for a time they regard as more idealistic and egalitarian – something the CCP is keen to keep in check.

Jennifer Pan, professor of communication at Stanford University, said the difficulty of doing independent social science surveys over the past decade meant “our understanding of what Chinese people actually think is weak”.

“Social media doesn’t fill that gap,” she said. “It’s noisy, unrepresentative, and censored. What we see is that companies, platforms, broadcasters and the foreign ministry moved together quickly. Did this follow public anger, or did this produce public anger? Either is possible, and we can’t tell which came firs.”

Whichever way round, the financial cost for Mbappé is the same. His face is a common sight on Chinese buses, in subways and in online ads, and his commercial deals could be worth “as much as $30m (£22.6m) per year”, estimated Mark Dreyer, author of Sporting Superpower, a book about China’s ambitions in the sector.

However, “as soon as someone else has decided you’ve crossed the line, it’s a race to who can cut ties quickest, who can be the most patriotic”, he said. “Then you have to kiss the ring – there really is no other way if you want to stay in the market.”

Mbappé’s and La Liga’s swift apologies suggest they are trying to avoid a fate like the NBA, whose lucrative pre-season matches were shut out of China for six years after the Houston Rockets’ then general manager, Daryl Morey, voiced support for Hong Kong pro-democracy protests in 2019.

La Liga may have better luck, with the state broadcaster CCTV saying it would listen to what Mbappé had to say, and “more importantly” watch what he does.

On Wednesday a foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, said: “We take seriously the apology the individual concerned has made.”

Dreyer said: “It doesn’t sound like it’s an instant: ‘All is forgiven.’ But it sounds like they’re going to be a little bit more, for want of a better word, reasonable.”

https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/oc.title: ‘Deceptively simple’: Gullah Geechee art exhibition illustrates that beauty lies in the details
https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/oc.author: Adria R Walker
https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/oc.text:
Exhibition at the Cameron Art Museum in North Carolina centers the work of artist Jonathan Green, tying together contemporary art and Gullah heritage

In Time to Rejoice, a 2005 oil on canvas painting by artist Jonathan Green, nine women, each dressed in vibrantly colored shirts and skirts, with wide-brimmed hats obscuring their faces, gather in a clearing. They’re facing one woman who dances in the center, her arms outstretched, seemingly in ecstasy, a leg towards the sky. Her hat hovers off her head; only her face is visible, though, with her eyes closed, she doesn’t gaze at the viewer. It is an intimate scene, perhaps of sisters, friends or comrades.

The painting evokes a moment from Toni Morrison’s novel Beloved, in which Baby Suggs offers freedom and peace to formerly enslaved people who are gathered with her in a clearing: “In this here place, we flesh; flesh that weeps, laughs; flesh that dances on bare feet in grass. Love it. Love it hard. Yonder they do not love your flesh. They despise it … And O my people they do not love your hands. Those they only use, tie, bind, chop off and leave empty. Love your hands! Love them. Raise them up and kiss them … and all your inside parts that they’d just as soon slop for hogs, you got to love them. The dark, dark liver – love it, love it and the beat and beating heart, love that too.”

Time to Rejoice is curator Ben Billingsley’s favorite in the Cameron Art Museum’s new exhibition, Rooted in Memory: The Gullah Geechee Vision of Jonathan Green, on view now through 24 January in Wilmington, North Carolina.

“You can see that they’re wearing blue chains, very contemporary kinds of clothing,” Billingsley said. “So suddenly this is not the 18th century, this is not the 19th century, this is here and now. It really ties together the contemporary culture to this longstanding tradition that has been there since these people arrived on these shores.”

Green was born in Gardens Corner, South Carolina, and trained at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. His Gullah Geechee heritage greatly informs his work.

An anonymous family of donor members of the museum has collected Green’s work for three generations. The family temporarily loaned some of their personal collection to the museum, allowing them to “not only honor [Green’s] work, but also show the behind the scenes of how a collection develops and how generational collecting can develop over time”, Billingsley said.

As the museum was creating the exhibition, Billingsley realized that it made sense to include art and objects that highlight the broader Gullah Geechee culture. The resulting exhibition, which ties together contemporary art and history, also includes traditional Gullah Geechee creations, such as sweet grass baskets, quilts and Gullah dolls. The museum also received works on loan from the South Carolina State Museum, the Gibbes Museum and the Charleston Museum for the exhibition.

In some ways, the art is “deceptively simple”, Billingsley said. It’s easy to look at Green’s work, to process the full image. But the more viewers sit with the work and take it in, the more detail they discover.

“There are hundreds of brushstrokes per square inch, and the deeper you get into looking at them, the more you start to uncover what I think he’s really saying about his own experience and the experience of the people that he paints,” he said.

Rooted in Memory includes some of Green’s paintings of women, which Billingsley said, “create an interesting tension”.

“Most of the time, the women’s faces are somewhat obscured – either they have their back to the viewer or maybe they’re looking down, they may have a hat brim covering the face,” he said. “It makes me want to know what they’re doing, what they are thinking. It also allows them to somewhat be almost like universal avatars. You can imagine people you know in your life in that scenario because of the degree of anonymity in the face, especially if you’re in the rural south-east of the country. It very much feels like familiar territory.”

Included in the exhibition are four watercolors by Green that diverge from his traditional style and stand out in contrast to his other work. The watercolors are costume designs that Green was commissioned to paint for the Sapelo festival for a production of Porgy and Bess.

“His inspiration for these was to imagine what if the fashion, the fabric traditions, the printing traditions, weaving traditions from west Africa had come into our culture, not through forced labor and forced arrival,” Billingsley said. “But if they had arrived here through willing immigrants who continued to bring their culture into the contemporary mainstream.”

https://www.theguardian.com/film/ng-inte.title: Film buffs love it. Trump and Tom Hanks hosted it. Can TCM survive a Hollywood mega-merger?
https://www.theguardian.com/film/ng-inte.author: Alaina Demopoulos
https://www.theguardian.com/film/ng-inte.text:
Since 1994, Turner Classic Movies has been a haven for old film lovers. Now with Skydance’s David Ellison calling the shots, fans are panicking over its unclear future

I have made many attempts to lessen the existential disaster we call Tuesday – tacos, trivia – but lately only one thing works. Every night just before 8pm, I hide my phone under a pillow in the next room, plate up a carb-heavy dinner, and turn on Turner Classic Movies (TCM) for Sweater Weather, a series of films dedicated to the transitional season.

Every Tuesday in October, Alicia Malone, an affable Australian film historian wearing business casual and a flippy bob, introduces a double feature. These are often midcentury melodramas featuring striking leads, serpentine plots, and the burnt hues of fall rendered in indulgent Technicolor. Like All That Heaven Allows (1955), about a widow who finds herself crushed under the weight of 1950s suburban conformity – and the teeny waistline of her swing skirts – while nursing a crush on her much-younger gardener. Or Leave Her to Heaven (1945), about a beautiful socialite so obsessed with her hapless husband that she will kill anyone who threatens their bond.

In these films, everyone has their original teeth and no one takes Ozempic. It’s my weekly break from doomscrolling, from whatever-maxxing, from the maddening norm of vertical content. I want to live in the world of Sweater Weather cinema all year long.

TCM has aired old movies since 1994, when the cable channel was launched by CNN’s founder, Ted Turner. The businessman was obsessed with movies – his favorite, Gone with the Wind, christened the network’s first broadcast – and had acquired MGM studio’s big film catalog from which to pull titles. At the time, deeper-cut movies rarely played on major networks, and real buffs had to trawl library archives to find what they were looking for.

From the start, TCM projected a reverence for the medium, airing uncut films in a wide range of genres – a 1930s screwball comedy in one slot, an 80s slasher flick in the next. Katharine Hepburn and Spencer Tracy are never interrupted by commercials for car insurance or pharmaceuticals. The network’s present-day hosts – led by Ben Mankiewicz, grandson of Citizen Kane scribe Herman J Mankiewicz – and guest stars serve up insider stories as they present each film. Tom Hanks once spoke on TCM of having to tell Bette Davis, then an intimidating grande dame of the screen, that she had stolen his wife’s seat at an Academy Awards afterparty. When Amy Madigan won an Oscar earlier this year for best supporting actress in Weapons, TCM brought her on to talk about past roles, including one alongside the late Gene Hackman.

Even Donald Trump appeared on TCM, in 2007, where in typical fashion he compared himself to Charles Foster Kane, the wealthy yet pitiable tycoon from Mankiewicz and Orson Welles’s masterpiece, Citizen Kane.

I am not someone who feels sentimental about brands or companies. I like to think I’m smart enough to know they will never love me back. But TCM is different. Karie Bible, an author and tour guide at Hollywood Forever Cemetery, interment site of many icons, feels the same way.

Bible started watching the channel as a college student in the 90s. “It’s kind of emotional to explain, but TCM has been like a close, comforting friend during some very dark hours of my life,” she said. “When I was in the hospital about to have a kidney operation I was watching it.”

Bible remembers lying on a gurney after surgery, watching Alfred Hitchcock’s Rear Window and then the 1960s horror flick What Ever Happened to Baby Jane? “When they came to wheel me out, I told them I wasn’t going until Baby Jane was over,” Bible said. “My dad had to take away the remote so they could take me off the table.”

TCM does not share ratings, but in 2020, 68.2m homes had access to it: retirees, small-town kids and director Martin Scorsese, who reportedly keeps TCM on in his editing suite. I would not say I am dating my boyfriend solely for his TCM subscription, but when he dropped that he had one during our first date, I decided there would be a second. It signals something charmingly analog, an instinct to choose careful curation over autopopulating recommendations on streamers such as Netflix, Amazon Prime and HBO.

Can a network like TCM, which is programmed by people who clearly think a lot about what to put on air, survive in this media ecosystem?

In early October, when Paramount Skydance announced its acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery – and therefore a collection of cable channels including CNN, MTV and TCM – fans panicked. A flowchart allegedly produced by the new mega-media company Skydance listing its new properties made the rounds on a Reddit forum for TCM viewers; TCM’s logo was notably absent. “This is very ominous,” one user wrote. “Doomed,” wrote another. (The image is of unknown origin; Skydance’s website includes TCM on a list of brands.)

It felt like deja vu. In 2023, after the $43bn merger of Warner Bros and Discovery, executives laid off several TCM executives, including longtime head of programming Charles Tabesh, an enthusiastic champion of both obscure and well-known movies. The move disturbed film buffs, who saw it as a death knell for the network. Heavyweight TCM fans including Scorsese and fellow directors Paul Thomas Anderson and Steven Spielberg called Warner Bros Discovery’s head, David Zaslav, who acquiesced by bringing Tabesh back (though not the 70 TCM staffers also cut). There was a sigh of relief among certain circles: art had prevailed.

Now comes Skydance. Staff are reportedly bracing for layoffs across the company, which carries $80bn in debt due to the merger. “One of the easiest ways to remedy some of that debt is to sell some of the linear TV assets,” said Gabriel Miller, co-founder of the Industry, a newsletter about film production. “Obvously [Skydance CEO] David Ellison isn’t going to sell CNN, but something like Comedy Central or BET might be something that potentially ends up getting sold.”

TCM, too? The official line is that the network is staying put for now, IndieWire reported. A representative for TCM declined to comment on the record to the Guardian. A representative for Skydance did not comment on the company’s intentions for TCM.

Because the network does not air commercials, it cannot make money off of ads. It instead relies on carriage and streaming fees (there is an app available for people who already have a TV subscription through traditional cable or a live TV streaming service).

It also hosts live events, including a Los Angeles film festival and “classic film cruise” that set sail earlier this month.

Marsha Gordon is a history professor who penned a biography of Ursula Parrott, the 1920s novelist who is credited for inventing the word “ex-wife”. Gordon spoke at a recent TCM festival, introducing a 35mm print of The Divorcee, an adaptation of Parrott’s work that is older than the Empire State Building. The screening took place at 10am on a Friday morning; Gordon expected maybe 30 people in the audience. Nearly 500 people showed up. “They were reacting exactly as you would imagine people would have reacted in 1930: laughing and holding their breath and boo-ing at the right places,” she said.

Programmers for the festival and the daily TV schedule have a “sense of play”, Gordon said. They want viewers to have a good time. See: Creepy Cinema, an annual celebration of campy Halloween co-hosted by Sex and the City actor Mario Cantone, who often uses his airtime to give impressions of stars such as Joan Crawford or Bette Davis.

In February, social media users (gleefully) accused TCM of sending a message with its decision to air Gaslight before Trump’s State of the Union. The 1944 film, about a husband who slowly convinces his wife that she has gone insane, spawned the eponymous term relating to the type of psychological manipulation Trump and other men have been accused of. “The counter programming at @tcm remains unmatched,” comedian Patton Oswalt posted on Threads. The timing could have been coincidental: that night, TCM scheduled a series of remakes that had been nominated for Academy Awards, a category that Gaslight falls into. (A representative for TCM declined to comment on the theory at the time.)

Coincidences like this might not go over well with David Ellison, son of Larry, the eighth-richest man in the world and a Trump ally who donated $45m to a Pac supporting his candidacy in 2024. The younger Ellison has downplayed his own connection to the Trump administration, saying he doesn’t “want to politicize” Skydance and highlighting its “good relationship[s]” with the Biden administration and Democratic California governor Gavin Newsom.

Then again, Ellison has one thing in common with me: he claims to love film. The industry scion originally founded Skydance to produce his passion projects. “I think he’s someone who actually cares about cinema and is going to try to make [TCM] work,” said Miller of the Industry newsletter.

Chris Yogerst, an author and media historian who wrote a book on the original Warner brothers, is similarly optimistic.
