He could see a near future where TCM pivots to streaming-only – like the highbrow Criterion Collection, which is celebrated for its library but lacks the friendly host setup of TCM. “They could make a hub [on HBO Max] or an app where the brand still serves the same format, but it’s just adapting to the digital era a little bit more effectively,” Yogerst said.

Reports of TCM’s death may be exaggerated – and are also great PR, said Peter Saraf, chair of New York University’s Tisch School of the Arts. “When Zaslav tried to shut down TCM, he actually did it such an amazing promotional favor,” Saraf said. “So many people came out and said, you cannot do this. Just the fear of something going away makes you want to watch it even more. I think it would be very foolish of Ellison to even consider touching it.”

So Sweater Weather cinema continues, at least for the rest of fall. And as always, I will be there. This week, a friend suggested making plans Tuesday night. I countered with happy hour, explaining my prior commitment. She said that’s fine, and that we should meet up close to my apartment – she would like to come over after and watch TCM, too.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Airbnb feels like a soulless rip-off – and its hosts are revolting | Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Excuse me if I feel no sympathy for the property owners who have threatened strike action because guests no longer have to do their chores. Whatever happened to the company’s initial guff about building community?

To Airbnb or not to Airbnb, that is the question. Would you like to help pay someone’s mortgage and clean their house and fork out an extortionate cleaning fee and abide by a 90-page list of house rules? Or would you like to check into a nice hotel where you get fresh towels and a tiny chocolate on your pillow?

Airbnb’s business is booming, so plenty of people are still choosing the first option. Nevertheless, the hospitality giant seems to have realised travellers are sick of being handed ridiculous chore lists, and is reining in some of its more tyrannical hosts. Last week Airbnb posted updated guidelines stating guests can no longer be asked to complete tasks that “require significant effort or time or would typically be performed by a cleaner”.

This entirely reasonable stipulation has gone down exactly how you’d expect from landlords who want to charge hotel-like fees without providing hotel-like services. Some hosts are desperately trying to find loopholes, while others are calling for a strike. “Even if we all unlist our properties for just a day or two, we can send a powerful message,” one budding revolutionary wrote in a Facebook group for Airbnb hosts. “Airbnb built its empire on OUR properties. It’s time we reminded them who actually holds the power.”

I’ve tried to avoid Airbnb ever since a stay where the coffee table was proclaimed off-limits for coffee cups and there was a snake in the basement. So I can’t say I have much sympathy for hosts who are melting down about not being able to force their guests to scrub the floors.

That said, I fully support a general Airbnb strike. Despite all the guff about building community, the platform is as soulless as every other tech company. It has enabled Israeli settlers to make money from illegal settlements built on stolen land, for example. And it has supercharged property speculation. In the name of maximising profits, it has also gone through the same enshittification as other once-shiny startups. What was once a fun and inexpensive way to travel often now feels like a bland rip-off.

So, please, disgruntled hosts, go ahead and remind Airbnb who actually holds the power. And don’t stop with Airbnb. If every one of those small-time property moguls channelled that same energy into protecting democracy rather than their bank balance, the world would be a far better place to live.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: ‘What you live for’: Fleetwood revel in seismic Arsenal shock after Dowman sees red
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Will Unwin at Highbury
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Fleetwood’s manager, Matt Lawlor, hailed the club’s victory as one for all football after his side shocked the Premier League champions, Arsenal, on penalties in the Carabao Cup. The side 18th in League Two held their nerve in the shootout, Conor Haughey hitting the winner to reach the quarter-finals.

The goalkeeper, Jay Lynch, was Fleetwood’s other hero, saving from Bruno Guimarães to set up the chance for victory. Aaron Loupalo‑Bi and Viktor Gyökeres ensured it finished 1-1 in normal time, but Arsenal ended up a man light after Max Dowman was shown a red card for reacting to a challenge.

Asked if Fleetwood’s win was the story of the season, Lawlor said: “Yeah, I hope so. Football’s getting a little bit more, I don’t know, clinical and sanitised. And that to me there was that feeling that we all get as football fans. That was what you kind of live for, isn’t it? To be a part of it is special. To be giving that to football fans, and especially Fleetwood fans, is unbelievably special. And yeah, something that I’m really proud of.”

Lawlor was clearly emotional at full-time as many of the 4,000 home supporters streamed on to the pitch to celebrate beating a team 84 places above them. “I was trying to not cry and I didn’t. I’ve managed to hold it,” he said. “My family, my little boy here, we’re all local. I was turning around and people were screaming at me in the crowd and people that I knew and grew up with, that I went to school with or they’ve got a loose connection, and people that jumped out on to the pitch.

“That’s really special and really emotional. To do something that special early in my career as well, it’s an emotional night. It is emotional. Emotional for the players, emotional for me.”

This was Dowman’s second red card of the month, having been sent off for England Under-19s, providing a steep learning curve for the talented teenager. Mikel Arteta was clearly unimpressed:“When we prepare the context of the match, we were very clear on the things you expect, the things that emotionally we have to dominate.

“It was very clear,” added Arteta, who appeared to aim criticism at Dowman as he walked past him after being sent off.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘Elonville’: Mississippi residents say Musk’s xAI is buying up homes if they don’t sue over noise
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Oliver Milman with data visuals by Daniel Wolfe
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Several homes have been purchased near datacenters and one resident said realtor outlined target to buy more than 400

People in a Mississippi neighborhood, many of whom dislike a nearby power plant central to Elon Musk’s artificial intelligence ambitions, have received a stark offer – to sell their houses to his company and make way.

Real estate agents have been going door to door in Southaven, Mississippi, on behalf of xAI, Musk’s AI company that was folded into the SpaceX entity in February, touting a deal to purchase houses as long as the owners agree to not join a lawsuit against the company over the power plant’s noise.

This plan could potentially swallow up almost the entire neighborhood of Colonial Hills, on the western flank of Southaven. A realtor told one resident there is a target to purchase 418 homes, with 18 homeowners already agreeing to sell, according to a recording of a conversation heard by the Guardian. xAI did not respond to questions over these numbers and its plans for the neighborhood and has previously said it intends to be be a good neighbor; it denies all claims in the noise lawsuit.

The homes, the realtor and the local mayor say, will house xAI staff as the company continues its explosive expansion in the area, with three of its datacenters springing up in Southaven and adjoining Memphis, Tennessee, in just the past two years. This frantic pace, and the all-hours noise from gas turbines installed without permits to power the datacenters, has dismayed some locals.

“It sounds like an airplane engine but it’s continuous, it’s incredibly loud,” said Elizabeth Rose, a piano teacher, of the xAI site which sits about two miles from her home. “I’ve been woken up at 2am by it, I’ve been woken up at 3am by it. I sometimes have to just get away from it because it makes me so angry.”

Rose said she was shocked when the power plant, a former Duke Energy site housing 69 temporary gas turbines to feed the new datacenters, began its low-level growl in August last year. “All of a sudden there was a plant there,” she said. “And now I get the feeling they are trying to expand the buyout to the entire neighborhood. It will become Elon Musk’s little playground, basically. Elonville.”

The market value offers for these homes, in an area where the average house price is about $180,000, is a comparatively small outlay in creating the world’s largest cluster of AI supercomputers as envisioned by Musk, a technologist who is the world’s richest person and a major Republican donor.

Since July 2024, xAI has constructed three vast datacenters – called Colossus I, Colossus II and Macrohardrr – in the Memphis and Southaven conurbation, which sprawls across Tennessee’s border with Mississippi. Musk is currently spending up to four nights a week in an Airstream trailer in the Memphis area as he personally oversees the build-out of the datacenters to further develop the Grok AI chatbot.

“We’re seeing the fastest growth I’ve ever seen in my life for Grok bot,” Musk said during a SpaceX earnings call this month. “I’ve never seen anything grow this fast.”

Musk has spent around half a billion dollars helping elect Republicans in the last two election cycles and his zeal for datacenters is shared by Donald Trump, who has said anyone who opposes such development will become “backwards and poor”.

As is common in the broader grassroots backlash against datacenters, however, some residents in Southaven say they have been trampled upon in this gold rush. Three locals, anguished by the din of expansion, filed a lawsuit in June complaining of “near-constant noise, vibrations and other nuisance-level harms” from the nearby xAI power plant.

Jason Haley, one of the three plaintiffs, said he never considered himself an activist or political in any way but has been driven to distraction by the noise of the gas turbines that sit about half a mile from his home, which he has owned for the past 20 years.

“There’s a high-pitched hum and then another sound like an airplane over your house,” he said. “It’s been so torturous I can’t sleep, I just leave the house or turn on some music until I fall asleep completely exhausted. It drives you insane. You also lose hope because you’re being ignored or dismissed. There’s no escape.”

Exasperated by fruitless exchanges with Southaven’s mayor and enraged by Tate Reeves, the Republican, pro-AI Mississippi governor, claiming that a curb on datacenters are “surrendering the future of technology to China”, Haley lodged the lawsuit and started posting videos on social media of himself monitoring the rumbling noise levels.

“I thought I’d make some noise of my own because of this bullshit,” said Haley. “I didn’t know anything about Elon, still don’t know the man. But our governor saying I don’t love America because I don’t like being tortured by noise? That is just asinine and ignorant. We’ve got to hold people accountable when they are harming other people, I don’t care who you voted for, who you pray for or who your favorite team is.”

The allegations of heedless noise are denied by xAI, which has previously said that “we care deeply about being good neighbors” and has varied its power output and built sound-dampening walls. In a letter handed to nearby residents in Colonial Hills, MZX, the xAI subsidiary that operates the site, states that it “requires property for its business purposes” and is prepared to buy nearby houses with a contractual condition – that they do not join Haley’s class action lawsuit.

This offer is starting to see results. Since 9 October, five neighborhood homes have been bought by MZX, according to DeSoto county records. Gavin Foust, who lives near Haley and said his elderly neighbors have just agreed to sell, predicts more will follow.

“They are ideal neighbors and planned to live their rest of their lives in that house but they want to get out of Dodge now because they don’t want to be bothered by these turbines,” said Foust, who added he won’t accept the offer himself due to its requirement not to sue.

“My hearing was damaged when I was in the army but I can still hear this thing, it’s like a jet engine. Why would you put it in a city? Why push people out? It’s reckless and shameful.”

Foust, a paramedic, grew up in the unassuming western reaches of Southaven, a district filled with affordable, 1960s homes and quiet, close-knit communities. This serenity has been upended by the noise from the xAI power plant, he said, as well as its air pollution.

Dozens of temporary, truck-sized gas turbines have been running at the xAI premises without permits required by federal law, the US Environmental Protection Agency has determined. The EPA has also said the permit requirements are a matter for the state to enforce.

While no on-site air pollution monitoring has been done, the Southern Environmental Law Center estimated the toxic emissions from these turbines, which are typically highly polluting, have caused $44m in annual health costs.

In April, environmental groups and the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) sued in federal court to stop use of the turbines, only for the US Department of Justice to unsuccessfully try to block the lawsuit by arguing xAI technology has been used to wage war on Iran and is therefore required for national security reasons.

“It’s been pretty shady from the get-go,” said Foust. “A lot of people in this neighborhood suffer from conditions exacerbated by all the nitrogen oxide, formaldehyde and other garbage put out by these turbines. For kids with asthma or elderly people with COPD [chronic obstructive pulmonary disease] it’s a mess all round. It’s pretty frustrating.”

In July, xAI agreed with state regulators to transform the power plant into a newer, permanent gas-fired facility by next summer, which should lessen the noise coming from the temporary turbines. Given the company’s repeated use of gas turbines without a federal permit and separate fines it may face for storm water violations, though, opponents remain wary.

“I’ve had hopes all along that haven’t come through,” said Haley. “The same company said it wasn’t polluting the air. I’m still hopeful but I’m not confident.”

The opposition to the datacenter influx hasn’t been universal, Haley acknowledged. Some locals aren’t too bothered by the noise while others actively champion the influx of cash into one of the poorest states in the union. Local businesses have experienced a surge in new activity, with the mayor hailing the datacenters for helping deliver new jobs and opportunity to the area.

“This development will produce unprecedented tax revenue for DeSoto county taxpayers that will enhance the quality of life for all,” said Darren Musselwhite, Southaven’s mayor, who oversaw a land swap deal with xAI that resulted in a new police and firefighter training center for the city.

“The buyout is not intended to be a company city at this point,” Musselwhite said of the property purchases. “This has never been mentioned to me. The buyout has multiple purposes which are to provide homes for some employees and a goodwill gesture from a good corporate citizen for those who perceive the industrial development near them as a negative.”

Musselwhite said dealing with the noise is a “top priority” for him but that city monitors have not detected a breach of a local noise ordinance limit of 70 decibels. Critics point to evidence that lower levels of noise, of 50 decibels or more like that recorded near the power plant, may be linked to adverse health impacts if persistent.

For those who can’t stand this noise, there is little to celebrate. Haley said the controversy has drawn the community together and made him question how AI is being “pushed down everyone’s throat”. He added: “Put it this way, I’m now registered to vote.” Rose, the piano teacher, said her roommate would accept three or four times the value of their home but she would still be opposed to such a sale.

“I wouldn’t take the offer if it was up to me, just to make things difficult for Elon,” she said. “I hate AI, I never understood why it was invented. I refuse to use it because I know touching it will cause that plant to crank up.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Flávio Bolsonaro on flight to Miami after fleeing Brazil amid election defeat
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Tiago Rogero in Brasília
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Far-right senator and family expected to land in US after crossing into Argentina and then flying out of Ecuador

A jet carrying the far-right Brazilian senator Flávio Bolsonaro has left Guayaquil in Ecuador and is on its way to Miami, Florida, where it is expected to arrive mid-morning on Wednesday.

After losing Sunday night’s election to the incumbent president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Bolsonaro disappeared for more than 24 hours, until Argentina’s migration authorities said he had entered the country by land on Tuesday night.

There, he boarded a Gulfstream IV registered as LV-JQW. The aircraft had been parked at Puerto Iguazú airport since the early hours of the previous morning, when the first reports emerged in Argentinian media that he intended to flee on it.

Bolsonaro, the son of the jailed former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro, boarded the jet with his wife and two daughters at about 11.30pm, bound for Guayaquil, reportedly to avoid Brazilian airspace. They made a brief stop in Ecuador, and have continued to the Miami-Opa Locka executive airport. The senator is expected to hold a press conference in the US at some point on Wednesday.

A senior US state department official told media outlets that visas would be granted to Bolsonaro and his family, and on Tuesday night the US president said he would approve their move to the country.

“They’re fine people. The election was very strange, and I thought it was terrible,” Donald Trump said, as he returned from a campaign event in Texas. “I didn’t take sides, you know. I know them both. I know Lula. I know Flavio a little bit. I know the father very well.”

Lula called Bolsonaro’s flight “shameful”. “This is what the Bolsonaro family are like. Brazil is their second homeland. Their first homeland is licking the boots of the US, as they’ve become accustomed to doing,” he said at an event celebrating his 81st birthday in Brasília.

Some in the Brazilian government suspected Bolsonaro allies had spent Tuesday privately telling the press he was already on his way to the US to distract from his real plan through Argentina. The federal police are facing criticism for failing to prevent him leaving the country.

There is a gap between the last time he was seen by allies at about 6pm on Monday and the moment he entered Argentina late on Tuesday. It remains unclear how or when he travelled to the border, or where he was during that time.

Footage from a television channel there shows two vans crossing the border checkpoint and then being escorted by airport security officers to the airport.

Shortly after the election result, police asked the supreme court to order Bolsonaro’s passport to be retained over concerns he could flee, citing an interview given last Friday by his brother, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro.

Speaking on a podcast in the US, where he is in self-imposed exile and lobbying the Trump administration against Lula, Eduardo said if his brother were to lose the election, he should not concede and should go to the US.

O Globo newspaper reported that the escape had been planned for weeks as a contingency in case he lost, and that Eduardo had been its main organiser, holding talks with US officials about receiving the senator.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.title: Judge rules Trump-appointed US prosecutor in Los Angeles is not serving legally – US politics live
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.author: Chris Hippensteel (now) and Tom Ambrose (earlier)
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.text:
Department of Justice says it intends to appeal as administration tries to keep president’s ally Bill Essayli in office

A federal judge has ruled that Republican Bill Essayli is not legally serving as the top US prosecutor in Los Angeles.

Essayli was disqualified from overseeing two criminal prosecutions. The order, however, will not immediately go into effect, and the Department of Justice (DoJ) has said it intends to appeal.

The ruling was part of a long-running legal battle challenging the Trump administration’s maneuvers to keep Essayli in office despite not being confirmed by the US Senate.

Essayli, a former Republican state lawmaker and ally of Donald Trump, became an interim US attorney in April 2025, but he was not formally nominated by the president, which allowed him to lead the office without going through the standard confirmation process.

After Essayli’s “interim” appointment ended last July, the Trump administration gave him an “acting” title, then kept him on as a “first assistant” after a judge ruled he was unlawfully serving as US attorney.

But in August, a federal appellate court ruled against a Nevada justice department leader in a similar case, and the judge overseeing Essayli’s case cited that higher court’s ruling on Tuesday, issuing another order saying he was still acting unlawfully.

Michael Seabright, the federal judge, said Essayli was illegally serving, even with a “special attorney” and “first assistant” designation by the Trump administration, and the judge said he could no longer participate in or supervise two ongoing prosecutions where the attorneys had challenged his position.

“We respectfully disagree with the court’s order,” Essayli said in a statement on Tuesday. “The President and the Attorney General have every right to select supervisors within the Justice Department.”

Faced with widespread voter discontent over the spike in oil prices since he attacked Iran, Donald Trump staged his rally in Corpus Christi, Texas on Tuesday alongside a vast oil tanker, the Angerona, which, the president said, had just arrived from Venezuela bearing a personal gift for him: a million barrels of oil.

A senior State Department official told the Associated Press that the US will “will issue visas to Flávio Bolsonaro and his family and allow them entry into the United States”.

In his remarks to supporters in Lubbock, Texas, Trump attacked James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate, for having shown compassion for transgender children who demonstrated for their rights at the Texas state capitol in 2023.

Trump lied that “our gasoline prices are lower than when Barack Hussein Obama – our oil prices, gasoline, lower than they were with Obama”.

The US Federal Reserve is expected to leave interest rates unchanged on Wednesday during its last rate-setting meeting before the midterm elections, keeping rates at one of the highest pre-election levels seen in over 20 years.

Last month, Fed officials raised rates for the first time since 2023, citing rising inflation. Inflation has hovered for years above the Fed’s target rate of 2%, and for most of this year, the annualized inflation rate has remained above 3%.

The move infuriated Donald Trump, who said that “interest rates in the United States should be 1% or less”.

Though inflation rose higher in September, going from 3.4% in August to 3.7%, a pause would signal the central bank is taking a wait-and-see approach ahead of the midterms next week.

Interest rates determine the cost of interest for loans, including for credit cards, mortgage and some savings accounts. During times of high inflation, raising rates can slow price increases.

Multiple Fed leaders have suggested in recent weeks that the central bank has room for a pause, even if most Fed economists are predicting one more rate hike before the end of the year.

“The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time,” Fed governor Christopher Waller said earlier this month.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/live.title: Russell Brand says he couldn’t find anyone to give evidence on his behalf in rape and sexual assault trial – latest updates
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/live.author: Taz Ali
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/live.text:
Brand, 51, has been charged with three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of attempted indecent assault

Earlier, Brand told the court that he had struggled to find anyone to give evidence on his behalf, saying the consequences of the September 2023 investigation by the Sunday Times, Times, and Channel 4 Dispatches were “devastating”.

His barrister, Ian White, asked: “Were you able to persuade a single person with relevant evidence to give to come to give evidence on your behalf?”

Brand later told the court he did not consider the Dispatches investigation a documentary, saying: “I call it a TV show.”

Brand told the court he invited the woman to his flat where they had consensual sex.

He said he generally used condoms “in first sexual encounters, particularly and especially if the partner wants that.”

Winter asked Brand whether they moved on to anal sex, Brand told the court that they did and that the woman said it was her first time.

Winter asked Brand whether the woman expressed any reluctance, to which Brand replied “coyness, one might say”.

Brand replied that he did, telling the court he said “something along the lines of ‘you’ll love it’”.

Brand told the court that the woman consented to continuing sex without a condom.

Winter has now turned to count 6, in which a woman alleged Brand anally raped her in 2009 after watching his comedy gig at Hammersmith Apollo.

Brand told the court that he had a “striking” and “memorable” sexual encounter with the woman in a dressing room before the alleged incident. He had saved her number on his phone with the initials “AP”, which he told the court meant “anal play”.

Brand told jurors he was “excited and enthusiastic” about meeting her again.

Winter moved on to count 5, in which a woman alleged Brand sexually assaulted her when she was in her 20s and working at a radio station in 2004 or 2005.

Winter asked Brand whether there was any question he grabbed the woman’s breast shortly after meeting her, Brand said: “Absolutely not.”

“That’s not the way I would have behaved – it’s obviously criminal but it’s obviously vulgar,” Brand told jurors.

Winter then went on to ask Brand about the third and fourth charge of sexual assault and rape, in which a woman alleged Brand grabbed her breasts before pulling her into a toilet at a bar in Soho and orally raped her in 2004.

Brand said he invited her to go into the lavatory to “fool around”. When asked by Winter whether she was happy to do so, he said “yes”.

Winter asked Brand about the second count of attempted indecent assault, in which it is alleged he tried to drag a female MTV worker into a toilet in 2001.

Winter asked whether Brand “intended any non-consensual assault, sexual or otherwise” on the woman.

Winter asked Brand if he got consent from the first alleged complainant when he had sex with her. Brand told the court: “Consent is fundamental, essential, necessary and, indeed, in many ways more important than sex itself.”

He said there was “no question in my mind” that he got consent from the woman “because of the talking and the intimacy”.

Winter is asking Brand about the first alleged complainant, a woman who alleged she was raped by the comedian after meeting him on the fringes of the Labour party conference in Bournemouth in 1999.

Brand told the court she had invited him to her hotel room, and that he “thought at the bare minimum it’s better than sleeping in shared accommodation” with his team, and that he “hoped and thought that there was a possibility of sex”.

Brand told the court that around the time of the Channel 4 Dispatches documentary, which reported the allegations as part of an investigation with the Times and the Sunday Times, his baby son had to have open heart surgery at the Great Ormond Street hospital in London.

He told jurors that the hospital refused to let him stay with his son “due to the materials published”.

Brand’s barrister, Ian Winter, began by going through the indictment and asking him if he committed the offences, to which he replied “no” to each.

Shortly after the prosecution concluded its case this morning, Brand took to the stand to give evidence as the defence begins.

The defence is to begin presenting its case in Russell Brand’s trial at Southwark crown court, where he faces allegations of rape and sexual assault against six women.

The prosecution’s case has drawn to a close after nearly two weeks of evidence, with the jury to hear from the defence today.

In yesterday’s hearing, the jury was told by the judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, that the indecent assault charge against Brand has been amended to attempted indecent assault. It relates to an allegation that Brand grabbed a female MTV worker by the arm and tried to drag her into a toilet. Bennathan told jurors he had reached the conclusion that there was insufficient evidence to support the charge of indecent assault.

The court also heard Brand was interviewed by police on four occasions – in November and December 2023, January 2024 and July 2025. Brand’s pre-prepared statement to police in November 2023 was read out in court by the prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones.

In it, he said: “As I have repeatedly stated publicly and written about extensively, I led a very promiscuous life in the past, which I have spent years openly denouncing.

Brand, 51, has been charged with three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of attempted indecent assault, in allegations dating between 1999 and 2009. He has pleaded not guilty to all the charges.

We will be bringing you live updates throughout the day as the trial continues.

https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.title: ‘I knead the audience, like a baker!’ House music legend Peven Everett on life after cancer and vanquishing the ‘Disco Sucks’ movement
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.author: Kate Hutchinson
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.text:
A new documentary follows the Chicagoan from child trumpet prodigy to Gabriel-singing icon and DIY maverick. ‘Not everybody wants to see musical genius’, he says

At We Out Here festival in Dorset in August, thousands of people could be heard singing a trumpet melody as if it was a giant brass-band karaoke session. On stage was Peven Everett, performing a rendition of Gabriel, one of the most celebrated anthems in dance-music history. Co-created with producer Roy Davis Jr, the best-known version, which blew up in UK clubs in the mid-90s, is a spiritual garage-house track about the “archangel of love” that can bring both punters and DJs to tears.

But Everett is much more than one song. Damon Albarn of Gorillaz tells me that “Peven has a once-in-a-generation voice … he’s a great inspiration to us all.” We Out Here founder, Gilles Peterson says that the Chicagoan is, alongside Detroit’s Moodymann and Amp Fiddler, “the closest thing dance music has to a Prince-type figure”. A prolific multi-instrumentalist and one-man cottage industry, Everett’s catalogue spans more than 500 tracks, across house, neo-soul, hip-hop, samba and more.

As with Prince, Everett’s audience can expect something different with each performance; they’re often improvised and don’t have strict setlists. “I’m kneading the audience into position, like a baker,” says the 51-year-old. He claims the Prince-fluence goes both ways after the latter attended one of his shows in the mid-to-late 2000s. “He started going more into dance music at that exact time,” says Everett. “He knew what I was doing: he’d seen it for himself.”

When we speak, Everett is preparing to join Gorillaz for the Chicago stop of their world tour. It’ll be the first time he’s been on stage with them since 2022, having contributed to their 2017 album Humanz. “It’s going to be one of the hardest things I’ve ever had to do,” he says. “I used to have some control over how much I gave emotionally, but tomorrow, I don’t think I’ll have that.” Two years ago, Everett was diagnosed with stage four lung cancer, just as his career was gathering pace. “A part of me feels like I let the people down by getting sick,” he says. “I missed a step.”

He’s now completed treatment and his life and artistry is the subject of a new documentary by Denholm Hewlett (son of Jamie, the visual artist behind Gorillaz). “People always refer to him as a house music artist,” says Hewlett. “But he was a trumpet prodigy by the age of 12 and was raised by jazz royalty.” Before dance music, Everett gave up a scholarship at Boston’s Berklee College of Music to go on the road with his mentor, Betty Carter, and the Marsalis brothers, Wynton and Branford. When he was 21, a 1995 New York Times article asked whether Everett was the next Miles Davis.

But Everett returned to Chicago to look after his ailing mother, where he teamed up with the producer Roy Davis Jr. Out of those mid-90s sessions came 1999 deep house staple Watch Them Come, as well as Gabriel. The original version of Gabriel has more of a typical four-to-the-floor beat but it was its Live Garage Mix that resonated in the UK as DJs found that its swung drums matched the pace of the nascent UK garage scene.

It was rereleased in 1997, reaching No 22 in the charts. At the time, US dance music was often associated with a big “diva” vocal; in the documentary, producer Marc Cary claims that Everett “brought a richness to house music” that previously didn’t exist.

Peterson says the song has become a dance-music standard, while Everett recalls dancing at Chicago’s Red Dog club in the early 2000s, when he claims that Thomas Bangalter of Daft Punk and vocalist Benjamin Diamond approached him. Two years earlier, they had a huge hit with Music Sounds Better With You under the name Stardust. “That was funny. They were like, ‘Yo, we made Stardust because of Gabriel, we used that as a template.’ I guess it’s kind of a compliment. At least they had the grace to tell me.”

Though some early Gabriel promos did not mention his name, and some have known the song as a Roy Davis Jr track, Everett says he was not simply a hired hand (he also played that unmistakable trumpet part). “When I go into any studio,” says Everett, “I make the vocals: I arrange them, I sing them. I make the horn and keyboard parts: I arrange them, I play them.” In the past, Everett has raised the subject of his contributions to the track on social media; today he can only say “the situation itself is still pending”.

Despite releasing other contemporary house classics such as 2007’s Stuck – and soundtracking the Hermès catwalk at Paris fashion week last January – Everett is far from a household name. In an interview in the documentary, Moodymann says Everett is “everyone’s favourite artist, you just don’t know it yet”; elsewhere in the film, he is compared to Stevie Wonder and James Brown.

Yet Everett runs a DIY enterprise, and has self-released more than 50 albums on his Studio Confession Entertainment label. “He’d make an album in one week and then burn it on to CDs and sell them at record stores in Chicago,” says Hewlett. “People haven’t been able to keep up.”

“For the majority of my career, I’ve been blacklisted,” Everett claims obliquely, citing his home town music industry in particular. Why? “For being a musical genius,” he replies. “Not everybody wants to see that.”

Everett sees himself as following on from where musical greats such as Marvin Gaye and Barry White left off in the late 1970s, as disco’s name was being sullied by the racist, homophobic “Disco Sucks” movement. “That didn’t sit right with me, it was hateful,” Everett says. “It tarnished great music. So I said, guess what? I’m gonna make the records that I know should have happened right after.”

The day after our interview, a video circulates of Everett and Albarn at Gorillaz’s Chicago show, as an emotional Everett prepares to sing the late Bobby Womack’s part on the Gorillaz tune Stylo. Artists as varied as Shirley Manson of Garbage, Kelela and Honey Dijon commented on the video with words of support. Everett says that his time was always supposed to be now. “I’m glad that I did it this way,” he says. “I maintain control of my catalogue, I still have the enjoyment of making music, and I got through a huge disease. I feel blessed.”

“He’s going to have his moment,” adds Hewlett. “It feels like he’s just getting started.”

https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.title: ‘I am mother, leader, warrior of the Amazon’: Nemonte Nenquimo on why the west needs to be rescued
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.author: Oliver Balch
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.text:
The Waorani leader says millennia of living in harmony with their surroundings give Indigenous groups unique insights into the consumerist west

Every Waorani child knows the story of the boa’s mouth. How the snake inches forward, watching, its movements almost imperceptible, before it strikes, swallowing its victim whole.

Nemonte Nenquimo knows the boa’s bite. Beguiled as a young girl by the blue eyes and bright dresses of an American missionary child in her Amazon village in Ecuador, she consented to be baptised and left home to study at a church school.

“My grandfather used to tell me that the global system of money and material things is like the boa. It attracts people, it bewitches,” the 41-year-old Indigenous activist says. “It’s a fact, I’ve lived it.”

The Nenquimo of today has travelled far from her teenage self. Feted by Time magazine as one of the world’s 100 most influential people, this vocal activist for Indigenous rights proudly identifies as a “mother, leader, and warrior of the Amazon”.

Dressed in ceremonial dress, her eyes masked behind an achiote-seed red dye and with a sacred palm-fibre band around her head, she was in Europe in September to collect the €1m Gulbenkian prize for humanity.

The prize recognises her leadership of the Ceibo Alliance, a coalition of four forest peoples spanning Ecuador, Peru and Colombia that she helped co-found back in 2014 and that fights to defend Amazonian lands and cultures.

Born into a Waorani community in the southern Ecuadorian Amazon, Nenquimo first grabbed international headlines when she issued an open letter to global leaders in which, among other stinging truths, she denounced the “white man that knows too little for the power that he wields”.

The viral letter was prompted by the Covid-19 pandemic, which claimed the lives of thousands of forest peoples across the Amazon, including that of the prominent Kayapó chief Paulinho Paiakan.

“The outside world comes with beautiful words, ‘We save, we bring a project of salvation’, [but] you’re not saving; you’re really killing my people, my ancestors, my territory,” she says.

Through the Ceibo Alliance, Nenquimo has done much to resist the outside world’s encroachment. The “pillaging” of the Amazon rainforest, a magnet for loggers, oil companies, cattle ranchers and goldminers over recent decades. Years ago, she spearheaded a successful legal case against the Ecuadorian government’s decision to license a 202,000-hectare (500,000-acre) plot of Waorani historic lands for oil exploration.

Other tactics deployed by the alliance include an “Indigenous guard” system, where volunteer patrols use drones, camera traps and other monitoring equipment to track illegal incursions into their land.

But opposition is fierce. Last year, following a nationwide protest organised by Ecuador’s main Indigenous group (Conaie), the Ceibo Alliance had its bank accounts frozen without warning.

Violence from drug gangs and illegal miners is also spilling over into Indigenous territories, Nenquimo warns. In neighbouring Colombia, for example – which includes territories of two of the Alliance’s people groups, the A’i Cofán and Siona – 39 land activists were murdered last year, almost one-third of all such killings globally.

Her fight extends beyond land protection. The incursion of cowori (the Waorani word for “white man”) is also undermining the rich linguistic, cultural and spiritual traditions of the forest peoples, she argues.

“Through their ‘salvation’, they make us disconnect from our own connection with the plants, with the spirit of the jaguar, with healing,” she says. “The Waorani people have even begun to stop taking ayahuasca, which is a sacred medicine for all Amazonian peoples.”

Yet, Nenquimo vehemently rejects any narrative of victimhood. She says that it’s the west that really needs rescuing. Moreover, the rainforest defender believes people groups like hers have answers to hand.

First, the west has an imperative to reconnect with Mother Earth. The forest, as Nenquimo is fond of saying, is her community’s “market, pharmacy, hardware store and place of worship”. To destroy it, therefore, is to jeopardise their survival.

“We are not destroyers. We do not pollute the river. Gold is what we have to leave. Petroleum is the blood of our ancestors,” she says. “The water you drink, the air you breathe – as Indigenous peoples, we are protecting it.”

Connecting with nature extends to connecting with those who inhabit and guard it, she adds. Millennia of living in harmony with their surroundings give Indigenous groups unique insights that the consumerist west would gain by rediscovering them. Hence her antipathy to international charities and other well-meaning groups that impose sustainability solutions born of their own market mentality, such as carbon credit schemes and “sustainable” commercial agriculture.

In her recent memoir, We Will Not Be Saved, Nenquimo goes further, arguing that “connectedness involves responsibilities”; not least for those in industrial economies to beware the boa and question their pursuit of relentless economic growth.

Learning to overcome the barriers that divide us is also critical, she maintains. As a union of distinct peoples with a history of inter-tribal conflict, the Ceibo Alliance demonstrates in microcosm what is possible when old enmities are left behind.

That journey begins with empathy, she says. In her memoir, she recalls realising that for the judges in her landmark court case to “truly see” her, she must also see them: “Not as enemies … not as caricatures of conquest but rather as people.”

Last, and arguably hardest, is finding the humility to genuinely listen and the strength to truly love. This Waorani leader has every reason to hate the cowori: under their hand, disease, pollution, deforestation and, in her own lived experience, sexual abuse have been inflicted upon her people.

If the world’s “developed” countries are to be saved – from the desire to take, to own, to control – then acknowledging that the planet’s last remaining “primitive” peoples might have something valuable to impart merits consideration, she suggests.

“If you don’t have a mind or heart to love, then what’s the point? It’s just being angry, wanting to devour, wanting to accumulate,” she says. “When we die, we will go with a light, peaceful spirit. We won’t have to suffer in our spirit.”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Will it be AI or the climate crisis that ends humanity? We can make it neither | Adam McKay and Philip Eubanks
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Adam McKay and Philip Eubanks
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Both of these threats have the same roots: private entities seeking to cash in. We have the power to stand against them

A summer of extreme heat, entire villages obliterated in Nepal, a super El Niño breaking records, Exxon publicly saying we may reach 3C by 2050 – could it possibly be any worse?

As climate activists and funders, we’ve spent years warning about a self-evident, imminent, avoidable climate calamity. Whether by making award-winning films (Don’t Look Up and Just Look Up) to warn the public, or by funding protest groups across the planet that bravely stand up for a livable future, we’ve been sounding the alarm to wake the public up.

Lately, as climate disasters and AI expansion wreak havoc on communities globally, warnings are arriving from everywhere all at once.

Daniel Kokotajlo, a former AI forecaster for OpenAI, recently testified before the Senate that today’s AI models are now trained to pursue goals no human gave them, and then they hide the fact that they’ve done it. Kokotajlo put the odds of AI companies automating their own work by the end of 2028 at about 50%, and, if that happens, the AI safety community warns the technology could improve faster than humans can monitor it, and eventually become too difficult to shut down.

These speculative warnings have earned alarm from mainstream media, politicians and civil society alike. Some critics suggest the warnings are marketing ploys by the AI industry to set up an arms race, using the false specter of AI apocalypse to capture government funding. Others think it might be an attempt to avoid accountability: by treating the machines as gods, we might conveniently forget their maker.

Either way, the debate keeps missing the damage AI is doing right now, polluting communities around the world, or the damage of new AI partnerships with the oil and gas industry. And we don’t just mean emissions from datacenter infrastructure alone. The harms run much deeper.

A recent study in Nature revealed an alliance between oil majors and the tech industry to use AI for new exploration and extraction – in effect adding up to 1.8 gigatonnes of carbon dioxide (the equivalent of Russia’s annual emissions) to the atmosphere.

Meanwhile, AI is flooding our information ecosystems with disinformation that erodes public trust, or it “hallucinates” nuclear threats, almost sparking war between the US and China.

It feels as if we’re in a race over which apocalyptic ending comes first. How about none of them?

At the heart of this sits the same fundamental question: who decides our future? Right now, whether the threat is AI or climate, or a mix of both, the answer is the same: a handful of private corporations, billionaires and their political enablers, making choices that will enrich them but devastate billions of people.

A datacenter that drains water from a drought-stricken town, burns gas for power, and runs AI that helps oil companies find more oil is both a climate fight and an AI fight.

Communities are resisting, and winning. Data Center Watch counted at least 120 US datacenter projects worth nearly $200bn blocked or delayed in the first half of 2026, with opposition in 49 states. Heatmap News found at least 20 canceled outright in the first three months of the year alone, a record.

These are the early stages of what we believe is poised to become a global movement against corporate and billionaire capture of our water, the land that grows our food, and the air we breathe.

At Climate Emergency Fund, we’ve put half our funding toward grassroots groups at the forefront of this fight, and we hope to scale that up before the year is out. We’re asking other funders to join us in this work, which at its core is meant to build thriving communities, not AI datacenters.

This fight can continue to grow into a cohesive, sustained, strategic movement. It is one of our last best chances to tackle not only climate change, but also a corporate billionaire class that has decided it has the right to control and steal the future for the rest of us.

The goal is a future in which the possibility of the end of the world no longer needs a daily check-in. Our existential threats are the result of human activity – systems built by people, on purpose, for money. Things built that way can be unbuilt, and we can choose to build another, better, world.

“Solving” these crises doesn’t require settling whether the machines or the seas get us first. It only requires deciding we don’t want to learn the answer. We have everything we need, except time.

But with the time we have, we can take drastic action now. And instead of pouring billions into datacenters and tech IPOs, we must fund those fighting for a thriving future.

Adam McKay is the Academy Award-winning director of The Big Short, Vice and Don’t Look Up; the founder of Yellow Dot Studios; and a board director for Climate Emergency Fund

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Coalition talks loom in Israel as Netanyahu and Eisenkot blocs set to fall short of majority
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Julian Borger in Jerusalem
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Projections show votes for Palestinian parties surged in a tight contest that saw the highest turnout in decades

Analysis: Rise of Palestinian parties in Knesset will redraw Israel’s political landscape

Israel’s future hung in the balance on Wednesday morning as it became clear that Benjamin Netanyahu had lost his governing majority, and his political fate now depends on whether opposition Jewish parties are prepared to forge a common front with Palestinian parties, whose support surged in Tuesday’s elections.

The leader of the Jewish opposition bloc, the retired general Gadi Eisenkot, appeared to rule out such a broad coalition in a premature declaration of victory overnight for what he called a “Zionist majority”.

As the vote count proceeded on Wednesday, initial exit poll projections that Eisenkot’s bloc would have a narrow lead over Netanyahu’s coalition looked increasingly in doubt as the prime minister’s bloc edged ahead, with the votes of deployed soldiers and other absentee ballots yet to be counted.

With 70% of votes counted, both Jewish blocs looked certain to fall short of the 61 Knesset seats needed for a majority government, leaving Eisenkot and his allies facing a clear choice: either make a pact with Arab Israeli parties heading for a record result of 16-19 seats, or hand Netanyahu a political lifeline in the form of new elections or a unity government.

Donald Trump took credit for Netanyahu’s better than expected performance so far, claiming his overt backing in the run-up to the vote had made the difference. “When the endorsement went out, it helped him a lot,” Trump said, adding that the result appeared to be heading for a stalemate or a Netanyahu win.

Yair Golan, the leader of the centre-left Democrats, a junior partner in Eisenkot’s Change bloc, urged Eisenkot to negotiate with the two Palestinian parties, the Joint List and Ra’am (the United Arab List).

“We have no future here if we don’t stop being afraid. And if we don’t put an end to racism. We can no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist distinction between Jewish and Arab votes,” Golan said in a post on X.

“Anyone who tries to erase the votes of Arab citizens is surrendering to Netanyahu and giving up on Israel,” he added, pointing out that Netanyahu relied on ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties that were non-Zionist and opposed conscription for their constituents.

Noa Landau, a commenter writing in Haaretz, argued that by making Zionism the test for forming a coalition, excluding potential partners, while the prime minister had not, Eisenkot had fallen “into the trap Netanyahu laid for him over the course of the election campaign”.

The Joint List leader, Yousef Jabareen, said its strong performance meant it “can’t be ignored under any political scenario”. He said Netanyahu’s government, especially its extremist national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, “has made life bitter for every Arab citizen”.

“We will be ready to pave the way to oust the government of Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir and Smotrich – and send them home,” Jabareen said. Another Joint List official described the choice facing the Jewish opposition as “supremacy or building democracy”.

Counting all the votes could take another few days, with absentee ballots the last to be tallied. Most of those are from deployed soldiers. The army vote usually swings right, but that broad picture may be complicated by the fact that a lot of older, more moderate reservists are now on active duty.

Once all the votes are accounted for, it will be up to Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, to give one of the party leaders six weeks to form a government. If the first choice fails, the opportunity passes to his rival. In the weeks of political wrangling likely to ensue, both Netanyahu and Eisenkot are expected to lure defectors from each other’s camps.

Netanyahu would remain in office in a caretaker capacity until a new majority is formed. He might expect to benefit if the deadlock leads to another round of elections. Tens of thousands of diaspora Israelis who returned to vote on Tuesday, and were mostly opposed to the governing coalition, might not return for another vote, for example.

Tuesday’s election came as Israel is fighting accusations of genocide in Gaza and ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in the West Bank. Netanyahu is separately wanted by the international criminal court for alleged war crimes.

The election was widely seen as a referendum on the 77-year-old leader, and the vote drew 77.7% turnout, the highest since 1999, with marked increases in the number of serving military members voting.

Political deadlock has led to repeated votes in the past. Between 2019 and 2022, Israel held five elections.

Netanyahu is Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, governing for 19 of the past 30 years, and its most tenacious political survivor. Entangled in a long-running corruption trial, Netanyahu and his far-right coalition had stoked xenophobic fears and suggested Israel would be vulnerable to a nuclear attack without him.

The campaign, febrile even by Israeli standards, included Netanyahu posting a picture of a nuclear explosion devastating Tel Aviv on the eve of the polls opening.

Since the deadly attack launched by Hamas on Israel’s southern communities on 7 October 2023, Israel has devastated Gaza and killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, fought Hezbollah in Lebanon, occupied new territory in Syria and launched a war with the US against Iran.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Dream say WNBA finals concerns went unheeded as teams prepare for 12.30pm Thursday start
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Guardian sport
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
The Atlanta Dream say their concerns about finding a suitable home venue for the WNBA finals went unheeded as they prepare to play the Golden State Valkyries in a crucial Game 6 on Thursday.

The Dream’s normal home, Gateway Center Arena, has a capacity of about 3,500 people. To accommodate the increased interest in the team during the finals, the Dream have played their two home games so far at the Atlanta Hawks’ State Farm Arena, which can seat more than 17,000 fans.

However, the Hawks play the Cleveland Cavaliers on Thursday night, meaning the Dream and Valkyries will play Game 6 at 12.30pm EDT on the same day. That means Valkyries fans in their home state of California will watch the game at 9.30am local time. Golden State lead the best-of-seven series 3-2.

In an open letter to their fans on Tuesday, the Dream said they had raised concerns about a possible scheduling clash months ago, but the calls went unheeded.

“This incredible run by our players has … made something else abundantly clear: the Atlanta Dream has earned the right to be taken seriously,” the Dream wrote in the letter. “Two months ago, when the WNBA finalized playoff dates and times, we raised concerns that the W Finals schedule conflicted with NBA games at State Farm Arena. As we moved through the playoffs, we reiterated those concerns. Our concerns did not receive the attention, nor the urgency that they deserved.”

The letter did not elaborate on the exact concerns the team raised, or who they raised them with at the WNBA.

According to ESPN, WNBA teams were told the dates for this season’s playoffs in December 2025.

The WNBA, NBA, Dream, Golden State and the finals’ broadcasting partners had discussions over the weekend about the best solution to the venue problem. In Tuesday’s letter, the Dream said playing Game 6 during the afternoon was the best option available.

“As much as we have great affection and nostalgia for Gateway Center Arena, we believed that our fans and the city wanted the opportunity to be a part of this historic series, and to see it played on a world-class stage,” the letter said. “That meant State Farm Arena.”

The Valkyries’ Kiah Stokes and Veronica Burton have urged fans to call in sick so they can see their team potentially clinch the title in only their second season in the WNBA. Meanwhile, the Dream’s Allisha Gray said her main focus was the game itself, not the start time.

“It’s the finals,” Gray said. “We just got to do what we’ve got to do. We are locked in on winning Game 6 whether it’s 8am, 10pm, midnight. We got a championship to win.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: RFK Jr assailed over ‘wildly racist tirade’ about Arabs at Michigan campaign stop
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Richard Luscombe
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
US health secretary falsely claims at Mike Rogers rally that Arabs have never won major prizes in science or literature

Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary, faced backlash on Wednesday for a “wildly racist tirade” during a campaign stop in Michigan in which he falsely asserted that Arabs never won major awards in science or literature.

Kennedy was speaking at the Monday night event in Grand Rapids in support of Mike Rogers, the Republican US Senate candidate who is trailing his Democratic midterms opponent Abdul El-Sayed, a Muslim, in polling.

“There’s 500 million Arabs in the world, and yet they don’t produce science, they don’t win the ⁠Nobel prize, they don’t win the Fields prize, they don’t win the Wolf prize, they don’t produce literature,” Kennedy said.

A factcheck published on Tuesday by the Associated Press showed that Arabs have won, or been short-listed, for all those awards in recent years.

The ⁠Council on American-Islamic Relations called Kennedy’s Islamophobic remarks “a ⁠textbook display of ​unvarnished racism and bigotry”, and the US healthcare advocacy organization Protect Our Care condemned his “wildly racist tirade”.

Hillary Scholten, a Democratic congresswoman representing west Michigan, who declined to endorse El-Sayed this summer, said Kennedy’s comments were “disgraceful and have no place in public service”.

In a statement posted to her Facebook page late Tuesday, Scholten said: “As secretary of health and human services, he has a responsibility to serve all Americans, not use his position to demean entire communities with bigoted and demonstrably false claims.

“Arab Americans are our neighbors, colleagues, health care professionals, scientists, educators, and public servants. Their contributions to science, literature, medicine, and countless other fields are undeniable.

“The last I checked, Secretary Kennedy has neither a medical degree nor a Nobel peace prize, and his rhetoric has undermined public confidence in health science. Maybe he should sit this one out.”

Kennedy’s comments came as part of an attack on the Muslim Brotherhood, a global Islamic group with branches that have been designated terrorist organizations by the US government.

The rise of the group had “created stagnant societies”, Kennedy said, ending what he called “a golden age [in which] Islamic lands were the center, the foundation for art and literature and science and engineering, and they were highly tolerant and pluralistic and cosmopolitan”.

Other Trump administration officials have tried to paint El-Sayed as a supporter of Islamic radicalism, including the president himself, who at a rally in Port Huron, Michigan, on Sunday called the Democrat “a jihadist” who was “on the side of the terrorists”.

JD Vance, the vice-president, escalated the inflammatory attacks at an event in Howell, Michigan, on Tuesday, during which he sought to connect El-Sayed’s politics to violent leftwing protests in Paris that saw thousands arrested.

“I guarantee you, if those rioters were burning down New York, or Detroit, the Hasan Pikers and El-Sayeds would be right there leading them and cheering them on,” Vance said, referring to Piker, an outspoken socialist commentator and influencer.

Rogers has also spoken out against El-Sayed’s alleged links to the Muslim Brotherhood, despite questions over his own relationship with the group. In 2012, as chair of the House intelligence committee, he said the US should have talks with the movement after Mohamed Morsi, who was backed by the Muslim Brotherhood, won the Egyptian election.

El-Sayed has repeatedly denied any ties to the group, and disavowed it in a town hall event in Michigan last week that went viral for a confrontation over the issue with a heckler who turned out to be a former aide to Josh Hawley, the Republican US senator for Missouri.

Chris Murphy, the US senator for Connecticut who joined other senior Democratic politicians canvassing for El-Sayed in Michigan last week, also condemned Kennedy’s comments.

“I really think ​everyone needs to pay ‌attention to this coordinated campaign ​to delegitimize Muslim Americans, ​not just as citizens but as humans,” he said, reported by Reuters.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.title: The pro-Trump prosecutor trying to stop California ballots from being counted
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.author: Sam Levin in Los Angeles
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.text:
Bill Essayli has launched a crusade against ‘voter fraud’, in his latest push to pursue Maga-aligned cases

Since he was sworn in last year, Bill Essayli, the top US prosecutor in southern California, has devoted his office to Donald Trump’s agenda – bringing splashy cases against sanctuary policies, protesters and the rights of young trans athletes.

But Essayli’s latest crusade has significantly raised the stakes of his partisan remaking of one of the country’s largest US attorney’s offices: he is fighting to block thousands of votes from being counted in the upcoming midterms.

In the weeks leading up to the high-stakes election, Essayli has sued California to try to force the state to set aside ballots from 20,000 voters whom the Department of Justice (DoJ) contends “are likely noncitizens”, demanding the state verify their eligibility before counting their votes. State election officials say the DoJ’s data is unreliable and its demands logistically impossible. They also argue that the federal government is risking disenfranchising US citizens and undermining the integrity of the results.

Essayli, 40, hasn’t stopped there. Last week, his office charged 13 green card holders accused of unlawfully registering to vote – one 72-year-old defendant was dramatically arrested in front of news cameras and paraded in a DoJ promotional video. Essayli has also threatened to prosecute election officials, saying anyone who “knowingly processes” a ballot by a noncitizen would be “opening themselves to legal jeopardy”. An appeals court on Monday issued an initial ruling against the DoJ’s bid to set aside votes.

The moves have stunned democracy and constitutional law experts, who say that voting by noncitizens is extremely rare and that it was extraordinary for the DoJ to pursue these types of cases so aggressively.

“This is all in service of an intentional effort to chill the vote in California,” said Sergio Perez, a former DoJ lawyer and civil rights advocate. “It’s improper politicization of the office. And it’s unheard of for a US attorney to engage in this kind of activity on the eve of an election.”

Defense lawyers and former prosecutors say the efforts are less surprising when seen as part of a pattern: Essayli is relentlessly pursuing Maga-aligned cases. The strategy has drawn the ire of another pillar of the justice system: judges have excoriated his office for acting in “bad faith”, violating civilians’ rights and relying on vindictive tactics.

Several high-profile prosecutions have fallen apart amid legal scrutiny. Still, the impact on southern California residents has been profound: the Guardian found defendants who were jailed for months before cases collapsed and one wrongfully arrested due to apparent mistaken identity.

“He’s targeting people who want to exercise free speech, he’s targeting the most vulnerable, he’s targeting the least dangerous individuals,” said Ian Wallach, a Los Angeles-based defense lawyer. “These are politically motivated cases where they’re charging people and building their cases later. It’s shameful and shocking.”

Experts agree Essayli has shattered the norms of his office. And in one pivotal case this week, a federal judge ruled Essayli was acting “unlawfully”, with a decision that calls into question his future at the justice department.

Essayli started his career at the DoJ as an assistant prosecutor in the US attorney’s office for the central district of California, which includes LA, serving from 2014 to 2018. He developed a reputation as a “hard-charging” prosecutor with a strong pro-law enforcement, “back the blue” mentality, according to a former DoJ attorney, who requested anonymity to speak candidly about a former colleague. Essayli was known in the office for having political stances that diverged from the rest of the office, his former colleague said, including proudly backing Trump during the 2016 Republican primaries when Trump’s candidacy was still considered fringe.

In 2022, Essayli was elected to the state assembly as a Republican in a district east of LA. During his time in the assembly, he made headlines railing against “woke” California policies and sparring with Democratic colleagues – once banging his desk on the assembly floor and shouting: “You’re a fucking liar!” when his mic was cut. He fought to ban trans girls from girls’ sports teams, in one 2024 school board meeting singling out a specific trans youth athlete, misgendering her and calling her participation on a track team “unacceptable”.

Essayli didn’t name the student, but Abigail Jones, then 16, knew he was talking about her as the only out female trans athlete in her class. Now 18, she recalled watching in anguish as he used her to advance his career: “To have powerful figures in government targeting me was just mind-blowing. He’s a state representative who is supposed to be serving thousands of people … He was inciting hatred.”

In April 2025, after Trump took office for a second term, the administration brought Essayli, with his elevated political profile, back to the DoJ, now with significantly more power. He was not formally nominated by Trump as the top prosecutor in the LA district, but appointed interim US attorney, allowing him to lead the office without Senate confirmation.

As he was sworn in on 2 April in a private ceremony, Essayli pledged to work “tirelessly” to implement the “priorities of the president”.

As top prosecutor for a district home to 20 million people, Essayli oversees roughly 500 staffers, and he quickly began devoting resources to prosecuting Trump’s critics.

After Trump launched a fierce crackdown on immigrants in the Los Angeles region in spring 2025 and residents took to the streets en masse, Essayli aggressively targeted Angelenos accused of interfering with immigration officers. “If you impede our agents or strike them, you will end up in handcuffs,” he posted on his X account in June, accompanied by the mugshot of one person he had charged.

The cases, often stemming from minor, chaotic clashes between militarized officers and angry or frightened residents, were atypical for the DoJ, and reports in the LA Times and Bloomberg suggested Essayli in some cases overruled prosecutors who advised against charges due to insufficient evidence.

In one instance, the sources told both publications, Essayli was overheard shouting at a subordinate to ignore the DoJ “justice manual”, which says prosecutors generally should only bring charges they can win.

Since spring 2025, Essayli’s office has prosecuted 113 people for alleged crimes against immigration officers, mostly charges of impeding, conspiring against or assaulting agents, according to data the DoJ shared with the Guardian. As of mid-September, 33 of them had charges dismissed, and nine people were acquitted by juries. Only four people were found guilty at trial, only two of which were felonies. Thirteen pleaded guilty to felonies, and the remainder were resolved as misdemeanor pleas, with a handful of trials still pending.

These are “unprecedented” results for federal prosecutors, who normally have a conviction rate well above 90%, said Laurie Levenson, a Loyola law professor and former DoJ attorney.

Some protester cases quickly collapsed because prosecutors had relied on uncorroborated officer statements or because video footage contradicted the chargers. For others, the cases dragged on.

One Angeleno profoundly affected by Essayli’s mission was Jonathon Redondo-Rosales, a 37-year-old jailed for six months on charges that he assaulted a federal officer – with a cloth hat.

Video from an August 2025 anti-ICE protest at a federal building showed Redondo-Rosales dancing in front of a government vehicle that slowly made contact with him, then briefly rolling on the hood of the car, at which point an officer lunged at him. Redondo-Rosales appeared to stumble backwards and swat back at the officer with his sun hat in his hand. Multiple officers took Redondo-Rosales to the ground, pepper-sprayed him and left his face bloodied. An officer said Redondo-Rosales had hit him with a fist, according to court filings from the defense. But the DoJ’s case faltered when footage contradicted the officer’s claim that he was punched, and records revealed the officer in a separate case had failed to disclose his own criminal conviction for harassment.

Just before the start of the trial in February, prosecutors moved to dismiss the case “without prejudice”, which would have left the door open to refile charges. The federal judge overseeing the case said that move by the government was in “bad faith” and dismissed the charges “with prejudice” – case closed.

Recounting his six months in jail denied bail in a recent interview, Redondo-Rosales said: “Not knowing when you’re going to get out, that stressed me the most. People inside said: ‘Plead guilty and you’ll go home,’ but I wasn’t going to do that, because I wasn’t guilty. I didn’t assault him.” He said he was grateful the dismissal allowed him to keep protesting: “They’re just trying to shut us up … but I wanted to be able to continue documenting all of this. People need to see what’s going on.”

Essayli’s office charged Sandra Samame, 25, with “stalking” and “conspiracy” to dox an ICE agent, after she and others followed an officer driving away from the federal building in August 2025. The group thought the agent was going to a raid, she recalled in an interview, but ended up inadvertently following him to his home. Unlike Redondo-Rosales, Samame went to trial – and won. Two co-defendants were convicted, but she was found not guilty of both charges after her attorney argued she had simply exercised her free speech. She was freed after spending about three months in jail, during which time she lost her job as a vet tech and failed her classes.

“The administration is trying to make ICE agents out as heroes, so they need villains, which is why they try to villainize us activists and undocumented people,” Samame told the Guardian. Her message to Essayli, she said, is: “The truth prevails always and people are not scared to stand up for their community, no matter to what extent the government is willing to go, to put us away, to criminalize us.”

Essayli’s office declined repeated interview requests and did not respond to inquiries about the cases.

Essayli has brought other splashy “tough on crime” cases that turned out to be shockingly thin – and in one case appeared to be based on false identification.

In two unconventional operations, federal officers swarmed MacArthur Park in May and Skid Row in October, for “takedowns” targeting “drug markets” and “high-crime areas of Los Angeles”. Typically, street-level drug crimes would be handled by local law enforcement, but Essayli, targeting an area known for its unhoused population, said the government was “reclaiming MacArthur Park from criminals and drug addicts”.

He charged 25 defendants with drug crimes and, in a press release, suggested the DoJ was going after big-time dealers and gang leaders. But for some defendants, their charges told a different story.

Anthony Solis, a defense lawyer, represented one man in the MacArthur Park case accused of selling 0.4 grams of meth for $20 to an informant. In his 25-year career, Solis said, he had never seen a quantity that small in federal court – even 10 times that amount would not normally warrant federal charges: “It’s not a big conspiracy. It’s not large quantities. It’s teeny-tiny amounts of drugs.” His client could face years in prison.

Wallach, the defense lawyer, represents another defendant who sold 0.15 grams of fentanyl to an informant. His client has no criminal convictions and a medical assistant degree, but had been struggling with addiction, the lawyer said in a court filing. If the defendant’s case were brought in state court, he would likely be placed in a diversion program, where he could get treatment and have the charges dismissed; now that he has a felony conviction, that will severely diminish his job prospects.

“It’s not the ‘worst of the worst’, it’s the ‘neediest of the needy’. What public benefit does this provide?” Wallach said.

In the Skid Row cases earlier this month, Essayli announced 23 arrests, saying he was working to “dismantle the networks flooding Skid Row with deadly drugs”. But when defense lawyer Robert Bernstein arrived at court to represent one of the arrested men, he noticed the DoJ’s complaint included a photo that was clearly not his client appearing before him – the man in the photo was also Black, but had different features. Bernstein said he pleaded for his client to be released, but prosecutors demanded he remain jailed.

Bernstein soon learned his client was actually at a probation office at the time prosecutors said he was on camera selling fentanyl. Prosecutors dismissed the case – after the man had spent two nights in jail.

Bernstein said it appeared the mistake originated with investigating officers, but argued the charges should never have been brought: “They are pursuing these improperly investigated cases with no review by the federal prosecutors – in this case, seeking a criminal complaint and arrest warrant for the wrong person, then arguing he be detained without bail. It’s ridiculous.”

Some of Essayli’s failed prosecutions have flown under the radar, but others have been high profile. In June, Essayli’s office suffered a bruising mistrial in an arson case against a man accused of igniting the 2025 Palisades fire after defense attorneys poked holes in prosecutors’ theories. In September, his prosecutors were dealt a not guilty verdict in a murder-for-hire trial against Lil Durk, after the Chicago rapper’s lawyers attacked the credibility of witnesses.

And last month, a judge dismissed Essayli’s lawsuit seeking to force California to ban trans girls from women’s sports. That case targeted Abigail Jones, whom Essayli had attacked at the school board years prior. Jones, identified as “Student 2” and “male” in Essayli’s complaint, said she felt some relief at the dismissal: “This was not a case the DoJ could win.” But she still worries Essayli will find other ways to target her and other trans girls.

Meanwhile, Essayli’s office has undergone dramatic change. Already by July 2025, reports indicated the office had lost roughly one-third of his legal staff, some senior prosecutors resigning after Essayli reportedly intervened to negotiate a cushier deal for a former sheriff who had already been convicted of excessive force. Essayli also faced heat for dismissing corporate fraud charges against a restaurateur who was a Trump donor.

“Many people left because they felt the Department of Justice had really lost the mission of justice,” said Julius Nam, a former California central district prosecutor, who was working in a different DoJ division when Essayli started. “The internal policies were not being followed – they were being bent to serve the political statements that the higher-ups were trying to make.”

Essayli’s campaign against “voter fraud” is his latest departure from DoJ traditions. But his ability to continue leading the charge is now being called into question.

For months, defense attorneys have sought to have Essayli disqualified from his position because of his lack of Senate confirmation, as required by law for US attorneys.

Since Essayli’s “interim” appointment officially ended last July, the Trump administration has maneuvered to keep him in charge, giving him an “acting” title and keeping him on as “first assistant” after a judge ruled he was unlawfully serving as “US attorney”. But Essayli’s position keeps facing challenges in court and similar schemes by Trump’s DoJ have failed. Alina Habba, Trump’s former personal lawyer, was disqualified from the top prosecutor job in New Jersey in December. A federal appellate court ruled against a Nevada DoJ leader in a similar case in August.

On Tuesday, the same judge who ruled against Essayli last year again decided he was “unlawfully serving as a ‘de facto’ United States attorney”. The judge disqualified Essayli from overseeing two cases where lawyers had challenged his position. The order does not go into immediate effect, and the DoJ intends to appeal.

Essayli’s office said in a statement that the matter would ultimately be decided by the US supreme court.

When reporters followed Essayli out of a recent court hearing in the disqualification case, he smirked and delivered a statement he seemed to have rehearsed: “The president runs the executive branch, and nothing here is going to change that.”

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/no-hel.title: ‘You have to believe’: Qwan’tez Stiggers, the New York Jets player who went from delivery driver to the NFL
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/no-hel.author: Gavin Willacy
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/no-hel.text:
When Stiggers’ father died, he dropped out of college to help his mother and 12 siblings. He thought his football dream had ended but made it in the end

Qwan’tez Stiggers had only been in college for a few days when his world fell apart. Seven months after the car crash that put him in a coma, Stiggers’ father died.
