“It of course didn’t come from out of the blue: we’ve been well aware of problems,” Cassingham wrote. “It was a cascade of problems piling up on one another, from the business model to mistakes by management to the mentioned crisis in fuel cost and availability, and more.”

Pamela Reckamp, a 59-year-old resident of the ship, told NBC News that company officials on the ship had held a meeting last month where they asked cabin owners to help them raise $1m so the ship could depart Ha Long Bay, Vietnam.

“She said: ‘If we don’t get this money, we have about four days of the ship running,’” Reckamp said. “‘Then the lights will go off and the AC will go off.’”

Carol Larson, 69, lived on the ship for 18 months along with her sister, Crystal Lavering, 72, she told the Associated Press. Larson, who is from California, expressed hopes that the journey could still be salvaged because she said the decision to live at sea had improved her health.

Larson told the outlet that she bought her cabin for $120,000, paid in installments, with additional monthly maintenance fees under a program that offered her the option of living onboard the ship for up to 15 years.

Larson blamed Donald Trump for the problems facing the ship and the suspended journey, as the war on Iran caused fuel costs to rise significantly. Despite the issues, however, Larson said she did not regret her investment.

“Because it was a startup company, I believe that it was a risk,” she said. “From the very first day, I said to myself that if it lasts a year, I can walk away and feel like I got my money’s worth … I still feel that way. I feel blessed to have been part of the experiment of residential cruising.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘A revolution in slow motion’: is Arizona’s wealthiest district finally done with Trump?
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Mary Jo Pitzl in Scottsdale, Arizona
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Circumstances are ripe for change in this onetime Republican stronghold given the current dissatisfaction with Trump agenda, experts say

Donald Trump has repeatedly asked voters to pretend that he is on the ballot in November’s crucial midterm elections. And in the comfortable confines of Arizona’s most affluent and fiercely contested congressional district, Trump is definitely on voters’ minds.

But whether that helps or hurts the warring congressional candidates in this sun-drenched swath of suburbia, where Teslas and walled-in luxury homes dominate, depends on who you ask.

“Any politician on the face of the Earth who’s a Republican is not getting my vote,” Tom Wolfe, a lifelong Republican, said while sitting down to a lunch of a burger and fries. Trump’s endorsement was a “death knell”, the 82-year-old said. He plans to vote for Democrats in next week’s elections.

For David McGahan, a retired accountant reveling in his retirement life in Rio Verde, a desert enclave outside Scottsdale, the economy and the country are working well under Trump.

“I like the course the country is on,” McGahan said while pumping gas at a local Costco. “Mostly,” he conceded, when a reporter noted the $101 charge for his fill-up.

Cushioned between blue cities and red counties, America’s suburbs have emerged nationally as political battlegrounds. That is especially true of Arizona’s first congressional district, which includes north Scottsdale and Paradise Valley.

Here, among the high-end golf courses and desert estates with breathtaking mountain views, the competition between Democrat Amish Shah – an emergency room doctor who narrowly lost the seat in 2024 – and Republican Jay Feely – a former National Football League kicker backed by Trump – could help determine control of the House in November.

Since Trump’s election a decade ago, Republicans’ hold on the district has slipped, though the party still maintains a voter registration advantage. The seat is open, after the Republican congressman David Schweikert opted to not seek a ninth term.

“These are your McCain-type voters,” said Matt Grodsky, a Democratic political strategist referring to the late Arizona senator and 2008 Republican presidential nominee, John McCain. They’re business owners, hold college degrees and relatively tuned in to politics.

Given the current dissatisfaction with the Trump agenda and no incumbent with built-in name ID, Grodsky said circumstances were ripe for a change in this onetime Republican stronghold.

With a median income of $102,000, 33% of residents holding a bachelor’s degree and 22% with an advanced degree, voters in the district lean conservative, but don’t fit comfortably in Trump’s Make America Great Again (Maga) movement , said Mike Noble, founder of Noble Predictive Insights, a non-partisan pollster based in Arizona.

Voters here helped deliver a slew of recent Democratic victories, including a succession of Democrats to the state’s two Senate seats, a slight tilt to Joe Biden in 2020, and a slate of top statewide officials in 2022 when voters rejected Maga-aligned candidates. But Schweikert managed to hold on, albeit narrowly.

More cracks appeared in 2024, when the ambassador to the UN, Nikki Haley, won nearly 25% of the district’s vote in the state’s presidential primary – even though Trump had already clinched the Republican nomination.

Months later, while Trump easily won a second term from Arizona voters, the victory margin in the district was 3% compared with 5.5% statewide.

“We’re watching a bit of a political revolution play out in slow motion,” said Stan Barnes, a political consultant and former Republican state senator.

The shift comes from voters like Greg Edmunds who was a Republican for most of his life, backing candidates such as McCain and George W Bush. Trump’s ascension in the party changed all that; he is now a registered independent.

In the battle for Congress, Edmunds said Feely’s well-publicized embrace of Trump – amplified by the pro-Shah campaign – makes the choice an easy one. He will vote for Shah to help block Trump’s agenda.

“We just can’t have a rubber-stamp Congress,” the Scottsdale resident said. “I can’t vote for someone like that.”

In September, as Trump’s approval ratings slipped nationwide, the influential Cook Political Report changed its rating of the Feely-Shah race from “toss-up” to “leans Democrat”.

Feely supporters say the district is still conservative at heart, and voters ultimately are motivated by a desire to keep taxes low and make prices more affordable. That makes Feely a good fit for the district, said Adam Kwasman, a Republican and member of the Scottsdale city council. An early backer of Feely, Kwasman likened his demeanor to that of the former Arizona governor Doug Ducey: pro-business, genial and decidedly not a flamethrower.

“The Shah campaign is grasping at straws if they think the Republican nominee for Congress is a problem,” Kwasman said, pointing to the district’s preference for conservatives and downplaying the constant reminders of Trump’s backing of Feely.

Feely, who Trump not only endorsed but also encouraged to drop his campaign in a neighboring district to run in congressional district one, has leaned hard on his football ties, hosting regular “huddles” with his team and peppering roadsides with campaign signs with a football motif.

His opponent, Shah, has football ties of his own. He was on the sidelines as a team doctor for the New York Jets during Feely’s stint there as a kicker. The two never met, but the coincidence has made for a fun bit of common ground in a race where the two candidates disagree sharply on key issues from healthcare and datacenters to tariffs and congressional accountability.

Feely’s campaign, with hefty support from Turning Point Action, has sought to portray Shah as a socialist, posting signs that link the Democrat to Senator Bernie Sanders.

Shah, who won the party’s nomination again this year after a nasty primary battle against a rival backed by the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, firmly rejects the socialist label. Meanwhile, his campaign has touted an endorsement from the former state house speaker Rusty Bowers, a Republican who resisted pressure from Trump to overturn the results of the 2020 election in Arizona.

Independents will be key to who prevails in the 3 November election. After Republicans, independents are the second biggest voting bloc in the district, as well as the state. Democrats are in third place.

For Cindy Cummens, her choice is clear: Shah. She likes that, during his time as a state lawmaker, Shah worked with Republicans, often to the dismay of his Democratic colleagues.

“I’m tired of one side voting only one way, whether it’s Democrats or Republicans,” she said, adding that bipartisan cooperation could resolve issues such as high prices, from gas to groceries.

No Labels, a small startup party that is trying to claim the independent lane, endorsed Shah for his willingness to work across the political aisle, said Paul Johnson, the No Labels chairman.

To qualify, Shah had to sign a pledge to uphold the US constitution, effectively vowing to abide by the rule of law. No Labels invited Feely to sign the pledge, but did not receive a response.

Since the July primary, Feely has backed away from his earlier enthusiasm to highlight the president’s support. His campaign signs and website no longer tout the endorsement and he did not attend Trump’s mid-October visit to Arizona. However, he was the only Arizona official or candidate to speak at the Republican party’s midterm convention in Texas last month, an event many Republicans in competitive races skipped.

Earlier this month, Feely said he was grateful to have the backing of former senator Kyrsten Sinema, an Arizona Democrat-turned-independent. Though she has not publicly endorsed his campaign, Feely pointed to her support as a sign that he can appeal to voters of all stripes.

Barnes, the political consultant, called the Republican’s de-emphasis of Trump a savvy move that follows a time-honored tradition of shifting to the middle after winning the party’s base in the primary.

“He can’t win solely by being the Trump candidate,” Barnes said, noting that Shah, too, had struck a more centrist tone.

Shah had previously supported a universal, single-payer healthcare system, but now instead says he wants to add a public option to the mix of other insurance plans to ensure all Americans are covered.

Although not an issue the candidates have spent time openly debating, abortion – a major topic in the 2024 race – could be decisive in this tight race. Two years ago, district voters strongly supported a statewide ballot measure that ensured abortion rights in Arizona, with 64.8% in favor.

Reproductive Freedom for All has targeted the district, pumping a six-figure investment into messaging that highlights Feely’s anti-abortion stance and promoting Shah’s “very solid” support for reproductive rights.

In 2024, Shah helped collect voter signatures to put abortion rights on the ballot. Feely voted against the initiative, and says abortion policy should be a matter of local, not federal, control.

“The bottom line is what the federal government does on abortion can wipe out the gains we made by amending our state constitution to lock in a fundamental right to abortion,” said Athena Salman, director of Arizona campaigns for Reproductive Rights.

Protecting reproductive rights resonates with Donna and Henry Male, both of whom are voting for Shah.

“Women’s rights are absolutely top of my list,” Donna Hale said. She worries about the future facing her 28-year-old daughter, especially with two years left in Trump’s term.

Henry Male dropped his lifelong Republican registration after Trump’s first term, but was frustrated with the party’s opposition to abortion long before then.

Male said he didn’t know much about Shah, but considered the Democrat his only option this year: “There’s not a chance in hell I’ll support Jay Feely.”

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: Russell Brand tells trial he had sex obsession but consent is ‘non-negotiable’
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Press Association
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Former comedian, in court on rape and sexual assault charges, denies setting goal to sleep with 5,000 women

Russell Brand has told a court he had an obsession with sex as a younger man but denied setting himself a “goal” to sleep with 5,000 women.

The former comedian, 51, said as he gave evidence in his rape trial that he had never forced himself on a woman, telling jurors consent was “non-negotiable” and “more important than sex itself”.

Brand said he blamed the media for his downfall after being the focus of reporting on sexual misconduct claims, and told Southwark crown court he had been unable to find any friends or former colleagues willing to give evidence in his defence as the trial approached.

He has been accused by six women of sexual assaults between 1999 and 2009, including rape in a hotel room and sexual assaults in a bar, at a radio station and at Channel 4. The court heard he stored the number of a fan who has accused him of rape with the letter “T” next to her name, meaning “tart”.

Under intense questioning from the prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones KC, Brand denied pretending to be gay in his pursuit of women.

The comedian’s former friend Mark Pinheiro had told the trial Brand had boasted on a car journey to the Labour party conference in Bournemouth about his techniques for “pulling” women and allegedly revealed an ambition to sleep with 5,000 women.

He replied: “I don’t agree, I don’t recall the conversation you are referring to.”

But Brand admitted he was “obsessed” with sex in his younger years. Karmy-Jones asked him: “Do you accept that you were desperate for it and sometimes couldn’t function without it?”

The prosecutor said Brand had not answered police questions when first challenged over the claims and accused him of “forging” his case around the evidence of his alleged victims, a suggestion he rejected.

At times, Brand went completely silent when Karmy-Jones posed a question, leading her to ask whether he found the questions “difficult to answer”.

Turning to Pinheiro’s claims about their car journey conversation, and the suggestion he wanted to sleep with 5,000 women, he said: “While I don’t remember, it’s entirely possible it’s the kind of badinage I would have engaged in when I was 24.”

He added that it would have been a “joke” if he had told Pinheiro he would not leave a situation with a woman without a conquest. “That sounds specifically like a riff on a Woody Allen joke when he said the only advice my dad ever gave me on his deathbed was ‘always try and f*** the waitress’.”

On the Bournemouth trip, Brand is accused of raping a woman he met on the last night of a week of performances of the Soapbox Cabaret, an event staged on the fringes of the 1999 Labour party conference. Brand told the court he had been “pretty excited” to go to the conference, at a time before he was famous, but conceded he was “more interested in having sex than the show”.

It was suggested Brand had pretended to be gay in order to convince the woman he is accused of raping to let him join her in her hotel room.

Karmy-Jones then produced a page from Brand’s book My Booky Wook, which featured a picture of him aged seven with the caption: “This is the exact moment when I decided to act gay to attract girls. It took 15 years to produce results.”

“Is that what you did Mr Brand? Pretend to be gay to attract women?” asked the prosecutor.

“No,” Brand replied. He then added: “It’s a joke. ‘Look at me, I’m a little boy in my garden and 15 years later … I was meeting women.’ It was a joke.”

Among the allegations Brand faces is that he raped a fan after meeting her at one of his Hammersmith Apollo standup performances in 2009. He told the court he stored her name next to the letter T, which he said stood for “tart”.

The woman alleges Brand forced himself on her during an encounter at his north London townhouse, a few days after she had willingly engaged in a threesome with the star backstage at the Apollo.

Asked what he meant by the word “tart”, he replied: “That was what I used to denote casual hookups.” He also put two asterisks next to the woman’s name, which he told the jury meant: “Never, ever forget this individual, this is a memorable encounter.”

Brand is accused of anally raping the woman when she came to his home. He said in evidence he was “excited and enthusiastic” before their meeting, and he believed she was consenting because of how she had behaved during the backstage threesome.

He suggested the woman had not said “no” or told him to stop during sex, and described her attitude as “coquettishness, coyness”. He said the encounter was consensual.

He said he could not remember exchanging texts with the woman months later during a chance encounter at the Edinburgh festival, but accepted it was possible he had messaged to say he wanted to “push you further”. He said he may have been intimating they could “have sex more, maybe have another threesome”, and conceded he may have said “sorry” when she told him he had treated her “like an animal”.

But he told the court the apology would have been because she “expressed sadly, unhappiness, regret”.

At the start of his evidence, Brand repeatedly and tersely said the word “no” when the individual claims were put to him and he was asked if he had raped and sexually assaulted the women.

Brand is accused of three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one charge of attempted indecent assault. He denies all the charges.

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.title: Iranian film-maker Jafar Panahi given new prison sentence and has assets seized
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.author: Deepa Parent
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.text:
Charges against him are unclear after return to Iran despite being sentenced last year for ‘propaganda activities’

An Iranian court has handed the award-winning film director Jafar Panahi a new prison sentence of five years and one month and ordered the seizure of all his assets.

The 66-year-old, who won the Palme d’Or at Cannes last year for It Was Just an Accident, was sentenced in absentia, his lawyer, Mostafa Nili, told the Iranian news outlet Emtedad. The court also imposed a two-year travel ban and barred him from using social media for two years, Nili said.

The charges against Panahi remain unclear. He returned to Iran in March from an overseas trip to promote It Was Just an Accident, despite having been sentenced in absentia last year to a year in prison ‌for “propaganda activities against the system”.

A friend of the film-maker, an activist based in Europe, told the Associated Press that he had spoken with Panahi on Monday evening after the sentencing and the film-maker had not been detained.

Nili said Panahi currently faced three open legal cases, and had not been notified of the hearing date for the latest one. He only learned of the proceedings after his client’s bank accounts were frozen last week.

Moein Khazaeli, a human rights lawyer at Dadban, a legal counselling centre for Iranian activists, said the sentencing, and the confiscation of Panahi’s assets, could violate Iran’s constitution, unless the authorities establish a clear legal basis linking the property to an alleged offence.

Speaking to the Guardian while in the US earlier this year, Panahi warned that the current “cycle of violence” in Iran could continue.

“What I have been depicting in this film is when the cycle of violence continues, then it becomes very difficult to stop it,” Panahi said. “Unfortunately, because of the savagery that is being carried out by the state, the fear is that this cycle of violence will continue.”

The latest sentence has raised concerns among fellow artists over the risks facing those who continue to work independently in Iran.

The Iranian actor Setareh Maleki, who was forced into exile after starring in Mohammad Rasoulof’s Oscar-nominated film The Seed of the Sacred Fig, told the Guardian: “One of the greatest fears of a dictatorship is losing control over the stories people tell. When those stories cross borders and reach the world, they become impossible to silence. Jafar Panahi has told his stories too, and his sentence proves once again just how deeply the Islamic Republic fears even the act of storytelling.”

Inside Iran, a film-maker currently shooting a film in secret expressed support for Panahi. “We all support him, who brings us great pride. He hasn’t remained silent and instead voices demands of the Iranian people,” said the film-maker, who did not want to give her name.

She said she believed Panahi’s latest sentence was linked to his calls for unity during the January protests and his support for diverse voices inside Iran, including supporters of Reza Pahlavi, the exiled son of Iran’s former shah.

The Iranian-British actor Nazanin Boniadi also condemned the ruling, saying: “Jafar Panahi has spent decades turning censorship into cinematic resistance, bearing witness to the suffering and resilience of the Iranian people. His latest draconian prison sentence is yet another attempt to silence a courageous artist whose work exposes the realities of repression in Iran.”

In a recent report, the US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran warned that Iranian authorities are intensifying their crackdown on artists, writers, poets, musicians and other cultural figures, “pulling peaceful voices into the same coercive security and judicial apparatus used to suppress dissent across Iran”.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Three plead guilty in $9m romance fraud scam targeting elderly Americans
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Maya Yang
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Twin brothers, 22, from Ghana and a 53-year-old American woman targeted older adults in 25 US states, officials say

Three people have pleaded guilty in a $9m romance fraud scam that targeted elderly Americans.

On Monday, the US attorney’s office in the northern district of Ohio announced that twin brothers from Ghana and an American woman pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud.

Identified as Jamal Abubakari, Kamal Abubakari, both 22, and Amanda Joy Opoku-Boachie, 53, of Kula, Hawaii, the trio targeted more than 130 victims in 25 states, as well as in Germany and Austria.

The Abubakaris and Opoku-Boachie targeted older Americans on dating websites and social media platforms from July 2024 to April 2026, conspiring with others to “fake personas to establish close, personal relationships with the victims which were often romantic in nature”, according to the justice department.

The trio at times used “artificial intelligence-driven video platforms to engage victims under fictitious female personas”, the justice department said.

The victims, after being misled by false stories, would then wire money to bank accounts controlled by the conspiracy members, with portions of the funds also being distributed to co-conspirators in Ghana and elsewhere.

As part of their scheme, the trio said they allegedly needed the money for medical emergencies, investment opportunities or travel fees to visit the victims, according to court documents reviewed by outlets.

“Victims report that they are left with absolutely nothing to sustain their lives going forward after a lifetime of work and saving. In addition, individual victims are ashamed and deprived of the trust they once had in their fellow human beings,” prosecutors said in the documents.

As part of their plea agreement, the Abubakaris and Opoku-Boachie agreed to forfeit jewellry which investigators seized at the time of their arrests, including luxury timepieces, as well as high-end watches, rings, chains, medallions and earrings.

They face a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison, with sentencing for the brothers scheduled for 9 February 2027 and 10 February 2027 for Opoku-Boachie.

Other co-conspirators are awaiting extradition from Ghana where seized assets estimated to be worth more than $3m include a Lamborghini, a Tesla Cybertruck, a Mercedes-Benz and a BMW, the justice department said.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: The bottomless depths of Donald Trump’s midterm rally bigotry
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: David Smith in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Both Obama and Trump are on the campaign trail, but only one of them appears to be descending into madness

This was originally published in This Week in Trumpland. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday.

Barack Obama versus Donald Trump. It is the presidential election that never happened but has come to define an era of US politics.

Obama is back on the campaign trail for the midterms, still electrifying crowds, earning shouts of “We love you!” and skewering his successor. “What’s up with the gold?” he asked a crowd in Detroit. “I mean, he’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.” This has, predictably, set off a mini culture war involving questions of elitism and the tastefulness of chain restaurants.

Trump’s election to the White House 10 years ago next month owed much to a racist backlash against America’s first Black president as white Christians shifted from majority to minority. He had pushed conspiracy theories about Obama’s birthplace and promised to build a border wall to keep out criminals and rapists.

Indeed, election campaigns are a furnace in which pretence burns away and essential character is exposed. They certainly bring out the worst in Trump. This year’s midterms effort, in which he is averaging about a rally a day and fighting bad polls like a cornered animal, is a case in point.

Has any president’s closing message ever been so Islamophobic, misogynistic and racist, not to mention downright deranged and bizarre? It is like watching a man vomit up bigotry that has been poisoning his soul for decades. Just when you think Trump has hit rock bottom, he produces a jackhammer and starts tunnelling to a new nadir of nastiness.

He still relishes calling Obama by his full name, Barack Hussein Obama, with an emphases on Hussein. Now he has Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who would become the first Muslim senator if elected, in his sights.

In Port Huron, Michigan, on Sunday, he called El-Sayed a “jihadist” who is “on the side of the terrorists” and would “have to go through a metal detector before he’s allowed to go into the Senate”. Trump repeatedly invoked the 11 September 2001 terrorist attacks, drawing a comparison between stopping El-Sayed from entering the Senate chamber and the passengers who fought back against the hijackers onboard United flight 93.

There is no evidence for any of this. But Trump is on an Islamophobic tear. He has repeatedly attacked Ilhan Omar, the Somali-born congresswoman of Minnesota, while his justice department banged on her door at 6am to investigate alleged fraud in her family’s immigration paperwork. Omar has said she is “confident in the fact that I didn’t do anything wrong”.

One of Trump’s standard punchlines now is the racist and false assertion that 98% of people from Somalia in the US don’t work for a living. “They don’t really have to work because they steal so much,” he told one rally. “They all have a Mercedes-Benz.”

He told his overwhelmingly white fanbase: “Can you believe, low IQ, and they live better than you do? I don’t know what’s going on. Maybe they’re not as low as we think.”

Another highly peculiar theme of Trump’s rally blitz has been his obsession with the male physique. He said of the Ohio senator Jon Husted: “I looked at his ass, and then I looked at his legs. I said, ‘His ass, shit, it’s like, it’s like a pile of muscle.’” He also claimed to have “fallen in love” with Tim Scott, the South Carolina senator.

The objectification is not limited to men. Back in Michigan, Trump turned his attention to the posterior of the rapper Nicki Minaj. “I looked at one hell of a beautiful ass before: Nicki Minaj,” he said. “That’s hard to miss. Stand up! That’s hard to miss.”

How is all of this resonating with Trump’s supporters? I called Sharon Anderson, who has been to 81 Trump rallies and was entirely untroubled by his comment. She said: “If a woman puts her ass out there for attention and somebody pays attention to it – Trump didn’t try to rape her – what’s the big deal?”

Anderson, 70, who is from Etowah, Tennessee, and went to her first Trump rally in 2015, dismisses the notion that he is getting worse. “I’ve been doing this for 11 years. He’s not changed a bit in my opinion. Now, a lot of what he says is reported and a lot of what he says isn’t reported.”

Does she have any concerns about the president’s mental health? “Absolutely not! Do you know anyone that could do what he does? He speaks an hour and a half to an hour and 45 minutes every rally. It’s almost supernatural in my opinion,” she said.

Yet Trump, who is 80, has started making strange guttural sounds, somewhere between a burp and a hiccup, in the middle of a sentence. And on Sunday he unleashed a 1,300-word rant on social media about his relationship with the comedian Bill Maher, branding him a “COMPLETE AND TOTAL LOSER” and telling him: “Bill: Don’t call anymore. It’s useless.”

Judging by the midterm polls that favour Democrats, Obama might have the upper hand in this latest struggle between the two men. As power slips inexorably from Trump’s grasp, as it must for all lame duck presidents, how much more desperate and extreme can he become? What new degradations await?

His rantings and ravings are a grim omen as he enters the Apocalypse Now phase of his presidency. Like Col Kurtz, he is a god to a fanatical but shrinking band of followers. Like Col Kurtz, he may be on a final descent into madness. Two more years? The horror, the horror.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘Like Saddam opened a Cheesecake Factory’: was Obama’s joke about Trump’s interior design ‘elitist’?
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Matthew Cantor in Los Angeles
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Obama has been accused of ‘snobbery’ over his Trump diss, as people rush to defend the restaurant chain’s ‘affordable opulence’

Around lunchtime on Tuesday, a Rolls-Royce stopped at the intersection of Beverly Drive and Dayton Way in Beverly Hills, California. Local people in athleisure walked past Balenciaga, Dior and Prada boutiques, as visitors on Hollywood bus tours ogled nearby Rodeo Drive, where Burberry and Louis Vuitton shops meet at a celebrated street corner.

Up the street, across from the upmarket Erewhon grocery store – home to $21 smoothies – a few diners sat outside an American landmark: the Cheesecake Factory.

The beloved restaurant chain began here in Beverly Hills in 1978; now it has hundreds of locations across the US and Canada. And this week, it’s become the US’s latest surreal culture-war touchstone.

It started when Barack Obama, campaigning for Democrats in Ohio, made a joke that hit Donald Trump right in the real estate. Referring to his successor’s remodeling obsession, the former president said: “He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory. Just gold everywhere.”

The joke was about maximalism: Saddam had 100 palaces and loved gold plating, and the Cheesecake Factory, while affordable for many, offers swanky surroundings that a curmudgeon might describe as over the top. While the Beverly Hills restaurant has a fairly staid interior, a nearby location at Los Angeles’s Grove mall has a grand staircase, floral paintings on the ceilings and an ornate balcony.

Obama’s comments got a laugh at the rally – which surely contained many Cheesecake Factory customers – and went viral. It’s likely the former president knew he would touch a nerve, given Trump’s twin fixations on remodeling and on Obama himself.

Asked by a reporter whether he had a response to Obama, “who made fun of the Cheesecake Factory, comparing it to the White House”, Trump spent nearly two full minutes explaining that the work had been done by the “finest artisans”, that Obama “doesn’t notice dirt and filth” – a racist trope – and that Trump himself only spends “five minutes a day, 10 minutes a day” addressing the problem. (Later that day, he spent another 10 minutes talking about it.)

But the framing of the question – posed by a reporter for LindellTV, founded by the Trump-supporting My Pillow founder Mike Lindell – pointed to what has become a rightwing talking point: the out-of-touch Obama, these critics claim, was mocking restaurant for regular people. The Cheesecake Factory isn’t cheap – a burger will run you about $20 – but it’s positioned as a treat that won’t break the bank.

The conservative political strategist Corinne Clark Barron tweeted: “KEEP THE CHEESECAKE FACTORY OUT OF YOUR ELITIST MOUTH.” On CNN, the New York Post columnist Lydia Moynihan said the remarks showed “how elitist he and the party that he continues to lead has become”. On Fox News, a chyron announced: “Obama criticized for Cheesecake Factory ‘snobbery’”.

This seems to deliberately misconstrue the joke’s primary target, which was the president, not the restaurant. It also conveniently forgets the first half, about Saddam Hussein, who was not known for minimalist taste. Nevertheless, the pitchforks were out, and the Trump administration deployed a true man of the people – the treasury secretary and hedge fund founder Scott Bessent – to dine there.

In fact, he “always” does, as he was at great pains to point out. “I had a great meal, always have a great meal,” he told a Fox Business reporter. He ordered “what I always have: the French Dip Cheeseburger”. Bessent, whose net worth is roughly $600m, said he would “tell the Martha’s Vineyard set to give it a try”.

The median home price in Beverly Hills, home to the first Cheesecake Factory, is $4m; the restaurant itself is far more affordable than the 90210 zip code might suggest. But as Bessent himself proved, the restaurant’s clientele includes plenty of elites: Jennifer Lawrence, Miley Cyrus and Drake are all reportedly fans. It’s a stretch to suggest Obama was punching down here.

That said, given the fierce devotion the restaurant inspires, Obama was perhaps taking a risk even mentioning it – especially at a time when the cost of living is on the ballot. “I think it’s a little bit sad that the pettiness of politics would create that soundbite, knowing all our challenges going on in the country today,” Rick McCormack, who helped create the restaurant’s decor, told CNN’s David Mack. Odes to the restaurant and its “affordable opulence”, as Mack puts it, abound.

In the Atlantic, Elaine Godfrey praises its “sumptuousness: the orange, inviting glow from the knobbly chandeliers; the floral frescoes and painted columns; the generous fountain pops and the dense wedges of cake”. A Redditor puts it more simply: “I can eat the whole plate of food like a savage and waddle to my car afterward with a piece of cheesecake to go.” The food is indeed good, and plentiful: the chain is known for its enormous and diverse menu, with items ranging from fried mac and cheese to avocado egg rolls to vegan cobb salad. There’s also, of course, lots of cheesecake, including but not limited to the mind-boggling Oreo Dream Extreme. On Tuesday, the chain reported third-quarter revenue of $1.03bn, up from $907.2m a year before. It’s routinely named among Fortune’s 100 best companies to work for.

In short, everyone loves the Cheesecake Factory, from Birmingham, Alabama, to Des Moines, Iowa, to Beverly Hills, where the autumn sun shone this week over warm baskets of complimentary bread. Surely it can take a joke.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: New study estimates 75% of deceased ex-NFL players had brain disease CTE
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Marina Dunbar
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Research looked at prevalence of chronic traumatic encephalopathy in 2,362 players who died in 2008-2023

A new study published on Wednesday estimates that about 75% of former NFL players who died over a 15-year period had evidence of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE).

The research, published in Jama Network Open and conducted by a Boston-based team, examined the estimated prevalence of the degenerative brain disease among NFL players who died from 2008 through 2023. Researchers found that the estimated rate of CTE among these players was substantially higher than the rates observed in brain samples collected from the general population.

The analysis included records from 2,362 deceased former NFL players who spent an average of five years in the league. Of the nearly 400 players whose brains were donated for examination, 93.5% showed evidence of CTE.

Researchers said the findings represented the first attempt to estimate how widespread CTE was among all former NFL players who died during the 2008-2023 period, rather than limiting the analysis to individuals whose brains were donated for research.

Physical changes associated with the condition include brain atrophy, which involves the loss of brain tissue, and accumulations of tau protein, a characteristic also associated with Alzheimer’s disease.

The difference compared with the broader population was substantial. According to the study’s authors, less than 1% of brain samples from community-based brain banks contain evidence of CTE.

However, the presence of CTE-related changes in the brain does not necessarily mean a person will develop dementia or experience declining cognitive abilities. Some individuals with the condition may never develop noticeable symptoms.

Researchers estimated that approximately 27% of the former NFL players included in the analysis had dementia.

CTE can also damage areas of the brain responsible for emotional control and behavior. Potential symptoms include depression, memory problems, severe mood changes and other behavioral difficulties.

“We recognize these findings may cause concern for the community of living players and their families,” Yorghos Tripodis, the study’s senior author, said in a statement released by Mass General Brigham. “We want them to know that we and others are standing by to provide support, and that we have hope for those living with CTE.

“Discoveries from the brain bank have already brought us significantly closer to a diagnosis during life, at which point our most important goal will be to develop effective treatments for CTE,” Tripodis added.

The findings follow another study released in August, which determined that at least one in four of former NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 had CTE.

Following the publication of the earlier study, the NFL addressed its efforts to improve player safety in a statement: “The NFL continuously strives to make the game of football safer, including by implementing ⁠strategies to reduce concussions and head impacts.”

A number of high-profile NFL players who took their own lives – including Junior Seau, Dave Duerson and Aaron Hernandez – were found to have had CTE when their brains were analyzed after their deaths.

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: Bone of contention: why dog trainers are at war
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Guardian Staff
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
It’s the canine equivalent of gentle v tough parenting – and there is no sign of a ceasefire. So what is the correct way to get man’s best friend to behave?

What are they fighting about? There are two camps: “positive” trainers, and “balanced” trainers. The former rely on rewards, the latter on a range of disciplinary stimuli, which might extend to prong collars that dig into a dog’s neck when it pulls.

What do the balanced ones say about the positive ones? “It’s all treats, treats, treats, so help me God,” the dog trainer Brian Lee told the Wall Street Journal. “It’s no different than giving your kid a BMW on his 16th birthday.”

And how do positive trainers address these allegations? “I kind of laugh at this whole idea that using treats in training is somehow going to spoil dogs,” says another dog trainer Victoria Stilwell.

I don’t see this getting resolved any time soon. Rewarding dogs with too many treats is “the biggest problem with dog training at the moment,” says the animal behaviourist Dr Ian Dunbar, despite standing in the positive camp.

If I’m honest this war of words doesn’t sound that heated. But it’s getting worse thanks to social media.

To be fair, everything is getting worse thanks to social media. Positive trainers call balanced trainers cruel; balanced trainers call positive trainers “treat-slinging wieners”.

Is this the dog version of the “gentle parenting” v Fafo parenting debate from earlier this year? It’s similar, but I don’t think anybody was recommending prong collars in that instance.

Is treat-slinging v discipline the only issue? There’s also a parallel war about the virtues of online training versus in-person training.

Which is best? Some say in-person is the only way. “You can’t resolve temperament issues over the phone,” Dunbar told the Times recently. “It’s insane.”

I see Dunbar has more than one dog in this fight. But Siobhan Dunn, who runs online courses, disagrees. “We’re working with owners all over the UK, many of whom would never have been able to reach us in person,” she says.

I’m confused – who’s right? It may help you to know that in-person training can cost £150 an hour.

Any signs of a ceasefire in the training wars? Lee has already called for calm on Instagram. “The criticising culture has been exhausted,” he wrote. “It’s time to put down the ‘dog training approach’ pitchforks.”

Did people respond positively to his message of calm? Not so far. “There is literally NOTHING in your bio that tells me you actually have an education in canine behaviour,” wrote another trainer.

Do say: “Dog rewards don’t have to be food-based – what about a trip to the theatre?”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: I’ve been watching the 7 Up TV series. And one change in the way we behave really struck me | Adrian Chiles
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Adrian Chiles
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Before mobile phones, being filmed was very rare – and if you were, you acted naturally. Today, our relationship to the camera is very, very different

Not for the first time, I got something wrong. As someone who made a living being on camera, I developed theories about what it takes to be yourself on screen. My main thought was that everyone in the world would soon be able to do it, because they’d be getting so much practice.

Once upon a time, hardly anybody was filmed or videoed. When the head of my middle school announced in assembly one morning that there would be television cameras in the dinner hall at lunchtime, every child woke up. For once the headteacher had our full and undivided attention. Consternation was in the air. This would have been about 1979. Regional television news probably needed pictures to cover a story about school dinners or something. Nobody, but nobody, in the school that day missed that evening’s edition of Midlands Today. It was a big deal. I saw the back of my head, and was agog.

In the home, being filmed was just as rare. Before smartphones, before camcorders, moving pictures of domestic life were few and far between. Growing up in the last decades of the last century I was aware of the existence of cine cameras but knew of no one who owned such an exotic, perhaps even vaguely sinister piece of kit.

By the time I first appeared on television in the mid-90s, the dam was starting to burst. Not only did I stand as proof that any Tom, Dick or Harry could have a go at TV presenting, but camcorders were proliferating. Babies bawling, toddlers toddling, kiddies doing “shows”, teenagers sulking, grandads snoozing – all were preserved for posterity, or at least until the tapes were lost for ever in some dark corner. Now there can’t be a human being in the UK of whom there isn’t some video footage on a smartphone, in the cloud, or wherever these things exist.

The ubiquity of video cameras surely means we’re more natural in front of them. But looking natural is different to being natural. It might even be the opposite.

This dawned on me when talking to the remarkable Tony Walker, who 63 years ago was one of the seven-year-olds featured on the longitudinal documentary series which started with Seven Up! and has now concluded with 70 Up. From the back of Tony’s black cab I listened as he told me how this little East End rascal had barely seen a TV, let alone a TV camera, before the day Michael Apted’s crew came bowling into his life. I went back and binge-watched the series from the beginning – 7, 14, 21 Up and so on – and, while this group obviously gained experience of television every seven years, from the outset it’s striking how naturally everyone speaks. This is not despite, but because of, their lack of practice. They’re blisteringly honest and are being – dread phrase – their authentic selves. They’ve yet to learn how to be anything else.

The same thought is provoked by Chris Terrill’s seminal BBC series, Soho Stories, now repeated 30 years after it first went out. Chris, embedded in the Soho area of central London for a year, mines a rich seam of characters: Gwen the student/burlesque dancer, Mark the tailor, Danny the wannabe actor and so on. Even as recently as 1996 it’s noticeable that they don’t have enough of a grasp of the grammar of television to be able to do anything other than reveal an unvarnished, unmediated version of themselves. The lack of guile is at the heart of their honesty.

Fast forward to 2026 and it’s guile galore. Influencers, vloggers, clever dicks, dicks, whoever – all are talking to camera with disarming competence, entirely at home with the form and quite coruscatingly natural. Yet natural is the last thing they are. To see what natural really looks like, examine people’s expressions on very old black and white photographs, back before they’d worked out what faces to pull. Compare and contrast with today, in which everyone’s acquired the knack of presenting a carefully, if unconsciously, curated version of themselves. The level of naturalness is a lot of things, but the one thing it isn’t is natural. If you want natural, go back to the days before folks had worked out how to pretend to be natural.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Putin hails Elon Musk’s ‘genius’ amid plans for Russian version of Starlink
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Russia plans to build own version of US billionaire’s satellite communications to help attack Ukraine

Vladimir Putin praised Elon Musk’s genius and said he was in touch with Starlink’s controlling shareholder as Russia develops its own satellite communications for its military to use against Ukraine.

The Russian president, speaking at a summit with African leaders in Moscow, was comparing the Earth-orbiting network built by Musk’s SpaceX with Russia’s gradual efforts to build its own Rassvet constellation.

“Elon Musk is a genius, a true genius,” the Russian leader said, according to the Tass news agency. “How many of these [satellites] does he have in orbit? More than 5,000, and we’re only taking the first steps.”

The true number of active SpaceX satellites is estimated at about 10,000, which provide the high-speed internet service that has been the subject of a diplomatic row between Musk, the US and Ukraine earlier this month.

A military version of Starlink, called Starshield, was suddenly restricted one night in the middle of October, preventing Ukraine from conducting medium drone attacks and hampering some of its anti-drone air defences.

Initially, Musk, an ally of the US president, Donald Trump, denied that he had ordered a throttling of the internet connection, before saying at the end of last week that he had closed a loophole in which the civilian Starlink had been used by the military.

Putin appeared to be trying to flatter Musk, whose control of the communications technology has raised questions about the US billionaire’s leverage over the White House and the impact he is able to have on Ukraine’s war effort.

“We are in close contact with our American partners – including Mr Musk – because it is very important, in orbit, not to get in each other’s way and ​to maintain a certain level of discipline and order,” Putin said.

Starlink does not work in Russia and its use by Russia inside Ukraine was restricted earlier this year. Meanwhile, Moscow has begun to develop an alternative system, though, with an estimated 26 working satellites, its capacity is limited.

Last week, after about 10 days of restriction, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, announced that “Starlink and Starshield operations have been restored” and that the speeds were “now where they need to be”.

Few believe the issue is permanently settled, with relations between Zelenskyy and Trump fraught in the run-up to the US midterm elections next Tuesday. Trump has also reached out to Putin, agreeing to buy diesel from Moscow early in October in an effort to reduce the oil price before Americans go to the polls.

Zelenskyy said on Wednesday that he hoped proposed trilateral peace talks, involving Ukraine, Russia and the US, would take place between 6 and 10 November in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the UAE, shortly after the midterms.

“We are waiting for the American side. I think that they’ll be ready with all the answers after the elections,” the Ukrainian leader said at a press conference in The Hague with the Dutch prime minister, Rob Jetten.

Earlier, Zelenskyy said he had spoken to Andy Burnham, the UK prime minister, as it emerged that Britain would provide £10bn in extra financing for Ukraine over the next three years – and an immediate £500m for air defence systems.

The additional aid was, Zelenskyy said, “a truly strong and very timely step” that came “as Russia needs to see and feel that Ukraine will not be left alone” as the war heads towards what is expected to be its most difficult winter yet.

John Healey, the UK chancellor, announced the extra funding as part of the government’s annual budget. “The prime minister and I called President Zelenskyy to tell him about our commitments in the budget today. He told us: ‘You’ve made my day’.”

The Dutch government also said it would provide €500m in military support for the winter, and a further €1.2bn in non-military aid, partly to help fund urgent repairs to Ukraine’s utilities and manufacturing.

Kyiv has been relentlessly attacked by Moscow this autumn as Russian forces fail to make progress on the frontlines in the east of Ukraine.

Russia had launched more than 100 ballistic missiles against Kyiv and the surrounding region since the middle of October, Zelenskyy said overnight, hitting power plants and other key targets in an effort to cause a humanitarian crisis in the capital.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: FDA scientists opposed Trump administration’s move to ease peptide access
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Effort to loosen rules on unproven peptide drugs, favored by RFK Jr, faced fierce pushback from agency scientists

A plan to give people in the United States easier access to unproven peptide drugs favored by the US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, was opposed by most Food and Drug Administration scientific staff members, who had limited input in drafting the policy, according to six people familiar with its development.

The document posted online on Wednesday by Kennedy’s Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) covers a handful of injectable peptides promoted within the wellness industry for building muscle, healing injuries and boosting energy.

The effort on peptides, driven almost entirely by HHS, faced overwhelming pushback among FDA drug staffers who warned it could undermine the agency’s longstanding mission of keeping unproven health products off the US market, according to the people familiar with its development.

The people spoke to the Associated Press on the condition of anonymity to discuss confidential government deliberations. An HHS spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The policy directs the FDA not to take action against specialty pharmacies that sell a half-dozen wellness peptides, including BPC-157, TB-500 and KPV. Under FDA rules, those chemicals would otherwise be considered illegal drugs because they have not gone through the agency’s rigorous review process for safety and effectiveness.

Some peptides occur naturally in the human body, where they trigger hormones needed for growth, metabolism and healing. Drug companies have brought several to market as medications, including mainstay treatments for diabetes and weight loss. But the chemicals subject to the new policy haven’t been approved as safe and effective by the FDA.

Kennedy has called himself a “big fan” of peptides and recently described using BPC-157 to treat a muscle injury.

The new document represents a step back from HHS’s original plans, according to two of the people who discussed its development.

HHS officials initially wanted the FDA to draft an official regulation that would add BPC-157 and other peptides to a list of drug substances deemed safe for use by compounding pharmacies, specialty businesses that make customized medications.

FDA officials warned that the agency’s scientific staffers had major safety concerns and would not support a regulation deeming them safe. HHS officials moved to a different approach that directs the FDA not to enforce its rules against pharmacies that compound the substances.

FDA staffers ultimately provided technical assistance in drafting the HHS plan, including guardrails intended to improve safety, such as requiring pharmacies to use peptide ingredients from FDA-registered factories.

Kennedy has said that US compounding pharmacies must be allowed to sell peptides because Americans are turning to “gray market” products imported from China and other countries.

Decisions about regulating peptides and compounding pharmacies have almost always come from the FDA, which has an office dedicated to protecting US consumers from unsafe or poor-quality compounded drugs.

The issue of compounding safety became a greater focus for the FDA after a deadly outbreak of fungal meningitis in 2012 was linked to contaminated injections from a Massachusetts compounding pharmacy. Once a niche business, compounding has grown into a multibillion-dollar industry, providing customized medications to doctors, clinics and hospitals.

It’s extremely rare for HHS to take the lead in drafting policies over the compounding industry, former FDA officials said. However, federal law technically gives HHS authority over essentially all drug regulations, which are then delegated to the FDA.

Many in the US who are using peptides today do not deal with a doctor or a pharmacy to get the injections, but often order vials online sold by chemical manufacturers based in China. Peptide sellers often try to skirt US regulations by labeling their products as “for research use only” because the FDA does not regulate research chemicals.

In 2023, the FDA added more than a dozen peptides, including BPC-157 and TB-500, to its list of substances that should not be compounded due to risks of allergic reactions, kidney damage and tumor growth.

At a meeting in July, FDA staffers reiterated that more than half a dozen peptides brought forward for reconsideration remained unproven in terms of safety and effectiveness.

The new policy from HHS avoids a direct confrontation with FDA staffers because it only directs the FDA not to enforce certain rules.

HHS ultimately included several safety measures suggested by FDA staffers, according to two of the people. Besides sourcing ingredients from FDA-registered facilities, compounders will be directed to collect information on side effects for safety analysis and verify the chemical identity of peptides.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Guardian view on Israel’s elections: Netanyahu lost his mandate. If opponents unite, he’ll lose power too | Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
His chief rival should reject the prime minister’s anti-democratic vision and work with Palestinian Israeli parties

Benjamin Netanyahu has lost his mandate but not, so far, power. While final votes are still being tallied, most voters picked his opponents on Tuesday. His bloc’s share of seats remains the largest, but appears to have slumped by around 10, leaving it below the 61 needed for a majority in the Knesset. Palestinian Israeli parties surged, and are projected to almost double the 10 seats they held. The result is that Mr Netanyahu’s main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, a former head of the military, now faces a choice: fall into line with Mr Netanyahu’s racist fearmongering or work with Arab-led parties.

The prime minister who oversaw shocking security failures ahead of the Hamas atrocities of 7 October 2023 still pitches himself as “Mr Security”. On trial for corruption, he has persistently attacked democratic institutions, especially the judiciary. He embraced and then indulged the ultra-right as they cheered on brutal settler violence in the occupied West Bank. (Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich lost ground in these polls, but perhaps due to their vision’s permeation of mainstream politics more than a revolt against it.) Mr Netanyahu’s war on Iran has destabilised the region. The tens of thousands of Palestinians killed by his government’s genocidal war on Gaza have barely featured in the election campaign, but its cost for Israeli hostages and international support for Israel have been noted by voters.

Mr Netanyahu relied on fear, campaigning with the slogan “the right or Palestine” and accusing Palestinian citizens of Israel, around a fifth of its population, of trying to “steal the election”. They have often boycotted their democratic right, in a system stacked against them, with politics moving rightwards. Mr Eisenkot’s bloc gives them little reason for optimism; Tuesday’s turnout testifies to their desperation to see an end to the most extreme government in Israel’s history. Millions of Palestinians living under illegal Israeli occupation got no vote at all.

Mr Netanyahu, the consummate survivor, may pin his hopes on another election. For now, as incumbent, he holds extra cards. The greatest danger is that he pushes Donald Trump into a renewed offensive on Iran after the midterms, seeing perma-war as political salvation.

Mr Eisenkot, one of many burned by their dealings with the prime minister, is unlikely to risk a “unity government”. His bloc could remove Mr Netanyahu “if it is brave enough”, observed Ahmad Tibi of the Joint List ticket of Palestinian parties. In campaigning, most opposition Israeli politicians ruled out a coalition with the Joint List or Ra’am (the United Arab List) – except on terms that they will not accept. But the Palestinian parties have made clear that they are open to cooperation and there is precedent. Mr Netanyahu himself reportedly made overtures to Ra’am in 2021; instead it joined the coalition that unseated him.

“We can no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist distinction between Jewish and Arab votes,” wrote Yair Golan, head of the centre-left Democrats – noting that Mr Netanyahu talks of a Zionist majority but relies on the support of non-Zionist Haredi parties. Mr Eisenkot may fear that supporters will not tolerate a deal but they will not thank him for failing to boot out Mr Netanyahu when given the chance. That would also allow the prime minister to turn this result into an ideological victory. Israel defines itself as Jewish and democratic. Mr Eisenkot and his partners should accept every vote and citizen as equal.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: ‘It all happened in a split-second’: survivors recount details of deadly train crash in Spain
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Sam Jones in Urda
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Passengers describe carriages full of seriously injured people after crash that has claimed at least 68 lives

Josimar Medina woke a little before 9am on Wednesday to find himself airborne and hurtling through his carriage on the fast train from Madrid to Seville.

“I remember flying through the air and looking for my girlfriend, who was also shooting through the air,” said Medina, a 37-year-old tourist from the northern Peruvian city of Chiclayo.

Once he landed, he looked around and realised just how lucky he and his girlfriend, Vitoria Maia, had been.

“I saw people with cuts, people covered in blood, people missing limbs, and I saw one person who had nothing left below the chest,” said Medina. “I saw people with their heads crushed and people with mutilated arms.”

The Peruvian stood recounting the details of Wednesday’s deadly rail crash, in which at least 68 people were killed and dozens more were injured, wearing a light brown T-shirt stained with the blood of a young American man he had helped move to safety.

Medina and Maia had been in the seventh carriage of the state-operated Renfe train that smashed into the back of a train run by the private Iryo company on the same line from the capital to the south of Spain. Had they been any further forward, they could well have been among the accident’s fatalities.

As it was, the couple climbed out of the train and helped the injured while they waited for medics and Guardia Civil officers to arrive at the scene of the crash, which took place amid vineyards and olive groves near the small town of Urda in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha, near the city of Toledo.

Within hours of the crash, Urda had been transformed into a frantic emergency response centre, with a local sports centre pressed into service as a triage post for the walking wounded. Cars, vans and trucks from the emergency services in Castilla-La Mancha and neighbouring Madrid crowded the streets.

Fredrich and Arabella Barilea, a couple from the Philippines who now live in Dubai, were on the Iryo train, and Fredrich was sent flying by the impact.

“One guy was shouting: ‘Get out! Get out! Another train could hit!” said Fredrich. “We saw all the people were also getting off. Many of them had head injuries and were covered in blood. We just got as far away from the train as we could.”

Eventually, buses arrived to ferry the lightly injured survivors to Urda – although the Barileas said they were too shocked and confused to know where exactly they had been brought.

“It all happened in a split second,” said Arabella. “The table we were sitting at just disappeared in the crash. I feel like we’re on our second life. You never know what could happen. We’re very grateful.”

Around the couple, people queued patiently on the street as they waited to board coaches. Wearing torn and bloodstained clothes and, in some cases, bandages on their heads, they stared, mute and uncomprehending. Spain may have been in mourning, as the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said during his visit to Urda, but many of those fortunate enough to survive Spain’s second major rail crash in less than a year were still too deep in shock to begin grieving.

Ata Yelkaya, a young tourist from Turkey, usually takes the bus when he travels around Spain. On Wednesday, however, he had decided to try the Iryo. Sleepy and assuming his train had come to a halt at a station, he had switched off his tablet and pulled up his hood in preparation for a nap. At 8.53am, he felt what he would later learn was the impact of the Renfe train smashing into the carriages behind him.

“I woke up with a bump and hit my head on the seat in front of me,” he said, “I looked across at an elderly couple near me and saw that the woman had a cut in her eyebrow. That’s when I knew something serious had happened.”

When he looked out of the window, he saw the carriages behind his – carriage No 5 – had come off the track and that many people had been killed or injured.

“Everyone was in shock but I tried to help other people get off the train,” he said. “I’m from Turkey and I lived through the 2023 earthquake there, so I stayed calm and tried to think about what to do and how to get out. It was only when I got out and saw some of the dead people that it hit me. I think everyone was in shock; too shocked even to panic or to scream.”

Wednesday’s disaster stirs memories of the Adamuz rail crash in January, in which 46 people died. Once again, a small town has found itself at the centre of a national disaster and, once again, local people have rallied to help, bringing food and water to a hall that had been set up as a centre for those searching for their relatives.

But, as also happened at Adamuz, the solidarity and kindness on display is likely to turn to anger over the coming hours as people seek answers as to how one of Europe’s most modern and extensive high-speed rail networks could experience two deadly collisions that have between them claimed at least 114 lives in the space of just 10 months. With a snap general election just a month away, many voters could use their votes to register their fury over another rail disaster. The “inexplicable circumstances” that led to the crash – as Spain’s transport minister has called them – will need to be explained as swiftly and thoroughly as possible.

For all the rush to action and unity on display, there was also a sickening sense of deja vu. One woman from Urda, who had spent the morning driving people to town from the crash site, had few words to describe what she had seen and heard.

“Mejor no verlo,” she said – “it’s better not to see something like this”. Again.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Education secretary Linda McMahon plans to spend nearly $43,000 on office furniture
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ariana Baio
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Trump ally, who is seeking to shutter the department, had said office relocation would save taxpayers $4.8m annually

The Trump administration has insisted its controversial education cuts are saving “millions of dollars” after it was reported that Linda McMahon, secretary of education, is planning to spend roughly $43,000 on new furniture for her office.

McMahon’s office told Congress that the secretary’s current furniture was worn out and “cannot be configurationally or aesthetically integrated into the agency’s new office space”, according to non-public records seen by the New York Times.

In March, McMahon – who is seeking to permanently shutter the Department of Education – announced the department would relocate from its headquarters in the Lyndon B Johnson building to a smaller building in downtown Washington DC, which housed the US Agency for International Development (USAID) before the Trump administration closed it down.

McMahon claimed the relocation would save taxpayers $4.8m annually. Now, the education secretary’s office needs new furniture for the office, including a new desk, conference table, chairs and other items, an unnamed senior official told the New York Times.

Savannah Newhouse, the education department’s press secretary, claimed in a statement the administration was “saving taxpayers millions of dollars” through its education cuts, adding: “Believe it or not, just like in the private sector, new federal offices need places to sit, write, and meet.”

Though McMahon is reportedly planning to furnish her new office at the department, her overall goal is to diminish staffing and remove responsibilities that her department oversees, in effect shutting it down.

Shortly after returning to office in 2025, Donald Trump signed an executive order directing McMahon, a former executive at World Wrestling Entertainment turned cabinet member, to close the Department of Education.

The Department of Education was established by Congress and can only be dissolved at the direction of Congress, but the Republican-controlled chambers have not moved to do so. But the administration has taken steps to reduce the department’s power. So far, the administration has nearly halved the department’s staffing through workforce reductions and moved department-specific responsibilities to other agencies through “interagency agreements”.

Among those, special education services have been moved to the Department of Health and Human Services and civil rights enforcement efforts have been moved to the justice department.

Trump and McMahon have insisted that effectively shuttering the Department of Education will give states more authority over education, despite states already controlling most of their education policies, and eliminate unnecessary bureaucratic processes.

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.title: ‘We sold out tickets within 13 minutes’: new novel from romantasy author Sarah J Maas sparks fan mania
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.author: Emma Loffhagen
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.text:
Move over Oasis – 6,000 people tried to buy 220 tickets to a masquerade ball to celebrate the release of A Court of Splintered Harmony, while specialist bookshops catering for the genre report huge sales

When The Spicy Librarian, a romance bookshop in Leamington Spa, announced a masquerade ball to celebrate the new Sarah J Maas novel, 6,000 people tried to buy 220 tickets. “We sold out within 13 minutes,” says the shop’s co-founder Ali Maynard James. “As soon as tickets went on sale, our website crashed”.

The shop was one of many across the UK marking the release of A Court of Splintered Harmony, the first instalment of Maas’s A Court of Thorns and Roses series in more than five years. On Monday night, bookshops threw parties and opened past midnight – and The Spicy Librarian hired a stately home to mark the occasion.

The book, the sixth in the series known to fans as Acotar, went on sale at 12.01am on Tuesday. Few releases carry as much commercial weight – the first book, a dark retelling of Beauty and the Beast, was published in 2015, with later books following the adventures of Feyre across the faerie lands of Prythian. By 2021 the series had sold 13m copies, and across her three interlinked fantasy series, Maas has now sold more than 75 m books in 40 languages.

The Spicy Librarian, which bills itself as Europe’s largest independent romance bookshop, held its ball at Ragley Hall in Warwickshire, where riders dressed as “fae warriors” carried torches on horseback. Tickets were £149 – the shop ran the event again the following night, which also sold out, and ordered about 750 copies to cover both balls and its pre-orders.

“We gave everyone the books at midnight, and people started reading them immediately,” says Maynard James. “Some people stayed up and devoured the whole thing in a few hours.”

Maas is the biggest name in romantasy, a genre combining fantasy and romance which has grown from an online niche into one of publishing’s most lucrative categories. Last year, Onyx Storm by Rebecca Yarros – another romantasy star – had the biggest first week for a hardback novel in the UK since Harper Lee’s Go Set a Watchman in 2015. In 2024, booming sales of romance and fantasy helped push UK fiction revenue above £1bn for the first time. The genre’s readers are largely young women, and much of its growth has played out on TikTok.

“It’s been such a long wait for this book, people are just itching to get their hands on it,” says Starlin Marot, owner of Bad Girl Books in Oxford, the UK’s first romantasy-only bookshop. “For so many of us, the series has been like a gateway drug into the genre, or into reading itself.”

In Oxford, Marot had only planned to open Bad Girl Books for half an hour after midnight, for a couple of readers who had asked on Instagram. Instead, a queue formed outside. “It was just crazy, like a flurry of people came in,” she says. “I was honestly not expecting that many people just for half an hour. But it shows how popular these books are!”

Her midnight release doubled as a pyjama party. “It was cute and cosy vibes,” Marot says. “We had Acotar-themed cakes and drinks.”

In London, romance bookshop Main Character Books decided against a midnight opening, serving breakfast to readers collecting pre-orders instead and holding an evening party for 45 people. “We decorated the entire store,” says owner Cassie Simmons. “In early October we had more pre-orders than we expected … we doubled our order at the publisher.” After Tuesday’s sales, the shop ordered again. “We’re going through stock even faster than we expected.”

The latest book is the first part of a four-part story. A Court of Forgotten Melody, out on 12 January, contains the next two parts, and the last is still being written.

“I think it’s definitely the five-year wait and the hype that’s been going up online,” says Simmons.

Maynard James, who says Acotar got her reading for pleasure again after becoming a mother, believes its heroines are a big part of the draw for its largely female fanbase. “They aren’t women that are damsels in distress that need rescuing or saving,” she says. “They almost prioritise themselves before they prioritise love. We want the women to be the centre of their own story.”

For the specialist shops, the boom is showing up in the till. “Sales are so much higher than I even anticipated for the year already,” says Marot. “It’s so exciting.”

While a Hulu adaptation of Acotar was announced in 2021, Maas has now bought back rights. “I want to see everything adapted the way I envision it, and the way I know fans want it”, she said in March.
